```markdown
- the only place we need to update an issue file when the issue is partially complete is the "current behavior" section. We don't need to add append-logs to the end, it's better to update the main body to align with the current design, and the current behavior with the current status.
```

### feedback_cross_language_pitfalls.md

```markdown
---
name: Cross-language design pitfalls
description: Three approaches the user rejected when designing SoraMech's cross-language wire format
type: feedback
originSessionId: e9ed70c7-2b63-425c-987c-6431040bedfb
---
When designing anything that touches the cross-language data path, avoid these three shapes — the user pushed back on each and the rejections are load-bearing for the architecture.

**1. Don't propose runtime "handles" that route operations back to the originating spec.**

**Why:** Real library functions in the wild (qsort, libcurl, anything from libc) expect actual native values — a real `int (*)(int,int)` function pointer, a real `char *` — not a SoraMech-issued id string. They can't be modified to participate in our runtime's routing scheme. The wire must carry data the destination spec can fully reconstruct into a native value, not opaque tokens.

**How to apply:** When a value seems hard to serialize (function pointers, coroutines, opaque pointers), decompose to data primitives (address + signature, bytecode + upvalues, ptr + length). If the destination needs a callable, the destination spec synthesizes one at reconstruction time (libffi trampoline for C, `ffi.cast` for LuaJIT). The "phone home" callback that the trampoline performs internally is fine — it's an artifact of the destination spec's reconstruction, not exposed in the wire format. What's forbidden is a wire primitive that says "operations on this value cross back to the source."

**2. Don't propose pair-wise language conversion paths (lua→c, c→lua, etc.).**

**Why:** N languages means N² conversion paths, which means adding a new language breaks the existing ones. The wire must use a language-agnostic intermediate (JSON) and every spec must implement only the two pair-symmetric callbacks (`to_json`, `from_json`). New language = implement those two functions, nothing else touches.

**How to apply:** Never write code that names two specific languages in a conversion context. Specs only ever see JSON on the wire. If a JSON primitive needs an extension (like `$function_pointer`), it lives in the universal JSON contract, not as a lua-spec-specific or c-spec-specific concept.

**3. Don't propose per-function annotations for type ambiguities (lengths, discriminators, callback signatures).**

**Why:** The user pointed out that "discriminator" is a vocab word the system has no general way to ask about. We can't prompt "which param is the length?" because that pairing convention lives in the function's English documentation, not its types. Asking the user to write annotations means asking them to know specialized vocabulary they didn't sign up for.

**How to apply:** When a function signature has ambiguous types (`char *` with no length, `union` with no tag, `void *` with no signature), expose each parameter as a separate input slot on the box. The user wires the slots according to the function's documentation — `p` from one source, `n` from another. The system never infers pairings; the user expresses them by wiring. If the destination needs a length and no length wire is provided, the wire compile fails with a plain-English fix-it message ("destination needs length, source provides only a pointer — wire a length input here").

**Common thread:** all three rejections are the same principle in different clothes — **SoraMech bends to the language, not the other way around.** Users write idiomatic code in their language. Libraries are used as-is. Specs are self-contained and pair-symmetric. The system stays out of the user's vocabulary.

```

### project_cross_language_wire.md

```markdown
---
name: Cross-language wire format
description: Dual-ring slot per port (native ring + JSON ring + ordering ring). JSON only at language borders. Per-edge classification at graph load; per-cell precision at runtime.
type: project
originSessionId: 5670858b-274f-49c4-89b8-a4b83ce33d7c
---
Design corrected 2026-05-21 — replaces the older "JSON always" framing.

**Each input slot is a dual-ring buffer.** Per port: one `ring_native` (consumer-language native bytes), one `ring_json` (JSON bytes from cross-language producers), and one `ring_order` of `(which_ring, idx)` tuples in arrival order. Allocate `ring_json` and `ring_order` lazily — same-language-only ports pay nothing for them.

**Push selects ring by per-edge bit.** Producer's spec writes native bytes to `ring_native` if `output_edge_native[j]` is true; otherwise calls `native_to_json` and writes to `ring_json`. Either way, pushes a `(which_ring, idx)` tuple to `ring_order`.

**Pop reads ordering ring first.** Dispatch pops `ring_order`, gets `(which_ring, idx)`, then pops the indicated cell. The consumer's spec receives `(input_data[i], input_native[i])` per input port and dispatches per flag — decode native or decode JSON.

**Why dual-ring instead of per-port classification.** Per-port (slot is all-JSON if any fan-in is cross-lang) is the pessimistic approximation — same-language values eat JSON cost on mixed-fan-in ports. Dual-ring is precise per cell: a port fed by one Lua box and one C box keeps the Lua cells native and JSON-encodes only the C-sourced cells.

**Why JSON for the cross-language ring (not pair-wise paths, not type-annotated raw bytes).** JSON's structure is self-describing — every language has a natural mapping for object/array/number/string/bool/null. Adding language K means K's spec implements its own `native_to_json` and `json_to_native`. N spec-pairs, not N² language-pair paths. The native ring's format is each spec's private choice — Lua may pick msgpack or `cjson.encode` or a custom binary form; C uses `memcpy` of the wrapper struct; Bash uses strings.

**Sentinel primitives for non-JSON-mappable values.** `$ref` (pointer + length into the large-value heap), `$function_pointer`, `$lang_opaque` ("these bytes are language-X-internal"). Carried inside the JSON ring as object-shaped sentinels. Cross-language receivers that can't reconstruct fail at wire compile.

**`$function_pointer` reconstruction — wrapper binary + persistent subprocess (issue 318, amended 2026-05-22).** Earlier design had the consumer's spec FFI-cast the raw process-local address. Rejected: FFI is language-pair-specific, biases SoraMech toward the Lua↔C corner, breaks the N-not-N² rule. Replacement: at map-compile time the compiler asks the *producing* spec to compile the referenced function + its enumerable dependencies into a standalone wrapper binary on disk that speaks a small line protocol on stdio. The consumer spec spawns one persistent subprocess per `$function_pointer` it receives and talks to it over the same socket-like channel used for any out-of-process spec. Every language pays the same price; new languages only implement "compile a function to a wrapper binary" — no pair-wise FFI knowledge required.

**Spec `invoke` signature change.** Collapses `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` into one `invoke` with per-input/per-output flags: `int invoke(handle, ..., const int *input_native, int n_inputs, int output_native, void *out_buf, ...)`. The spec dispatches per input internally. This is the contract change that unblocks 306/307's typed marshalling.

**Two compile-time layers stack:**
- **Per-edge classification (issue 312, this design)** — graph loader computes `input_edge_native[]` and `output_edge_native[]` on each box; dispatch routes pushes accordingly. This issue is the wire-format design.
- **Same-language source merge (issue 313, research / blocked)** — concatenate every same-language box's source into one translation unit per language. Boxes still run as separate thread-pool tasks; what 313 thins is the spec invocation overhead inside the merged region (direct call into the worker's `lua_State` instead of dlsym + marshal + bridge). The dual-ring slot machinery does NOT collapse — tasks still need slots to wait for sibling inputs. 313 makes the ring cells cheaper to read/write; it doesn't remove them.

**Three rejected design shapes** (kept here so they don't get reinvented):
1. **Handles back-routing to the owning spec** — library functions in the wild can't be modified to use SoraMech-shaped handles. Rejected.
2. **Pair-wise language paths** — every new language would have to grow N-1 translation paths against existing languages. Rejected. The dual-ring's "two rings per slot" is the dimension-cap that prevents this.
3. **Per-function discriminator / length annotations on the wire** — the system has no universal vocabulary to ask "is param 2 the length?" Rejected; the user expresses these by wiring two separate input slots.

**How to apply:** When discussing wire format, slot store shape, dispatch routing, or spec callbacks: think dual-ring (native, JSON, ordering) per slot, per-edge classification at push time, per-cell tag at pop time, JSON-only-at-borders, language-private native bytes everywhere else.

```

### project_custom_translation_specs.md

```markdown
---
name: Custom translation specs per port
description: Users can override the default native/JSON wire path on any input port for any reason — a knob in the wire format vocabulary (issue 246)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**Per-port custom translation specs** let the user intervene at a specific input port and replace the default dual-ring decode path with user-written code. The override applies to that one port; the rest of the graph uses the default native-or-JSON path from issue 312.

**Motivating cases (any reason qualifies, not just cross-language):**
- Cross-language ambiguity the default specs can't infer: a C++ class with methods landing at a C box (drop methods? expose as fn pointers? restructure?), a `void *` carrying a libcurl handle, a union whose discriminator is on a separate wire.
- Same-language reshape: massaging a value into a different shape on its way in (rename fields, drop a layer, project a subset) without adding a transform box on the canvas.
- Validation / coercion: clamp a number, enforce a schema, fail loudly on unexpected shapes.

**How it composes with the dual-ring design:**
- The custom spec runs at *pop* time on the consumer side, after the ordering ring has been consulted and the cell has been read from the appropriate ring. The user's code receives the decoded value (native or JSON-decoded) and produces whatever the consumer's `invoke` will see.
- A port with a custom translation gets its own wire color in the editor (issue 245) — visible signal that this port doesn't use the default path.

**Why:** The default native/JSON contract covers the cases JSON's structure handles cleanly. Everything outside that needs a user escape hatch — *and* the same hatch is useful for purely-local "I want this input shaped differently" cases. One mechanism, many uses.

**How to apply:** When the design needs an override knob on the cross-language path, propose "custom translation spec on the destination port" rather than inventing per-function annotations, type discriminator metadata, or producer-side conversion hints (all three were rejected — see feedback_cross_language_pitfalls). The port is the unit of override; the spec is user code; the rest stays default.

```

### project_editor_visual_language.md

```markdown
---
name: Editor visual language for wires
description: Wire color in the canvas editor encodes language pairing across the edge, not just routing kind — a UI invariant future work should respect (issue 245)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**Wires are colored by language pairing across the edge**, with a separate color for wires whose destination port carries a user-written custom translation (issue 246). Pre-245 wires were colored purely by routing kind (default slate-blue, comparator branches orange/blue/green).

**The pairing-based palette:**
- **Same-language hop** — the wire carries native bytes; default neutral color.
- **Cross-language hop (forest green, ~`#228b22`)** — different producer/consumer languages; runtime translates via JSON at the wire. The color is a standing reminder that encode + decode is happening on that hop.
- **Custom-translation hop** — a third distinct color signaling the destination port has a user-written translation spec overriding the default path.
- Branch-routing colors (orange/blue/green from comparator boxes) compose on top — routing kind and language pairing are orthogonal axes the editor must show simultaneously.

**Why:** The runtime treats same-lang and cross-lang hops very differently (dual-ring slot design, issue 312), but pre-245 the editor gave the box author no visual signal that the JSON translation step existed. It was invisible until someone read the dispatch code. Translation cost should be legible from the canvas.

**How to apply:** Any future editor work that touches wire rendering must preserve "color encodes language pairing." Don't propose recoloring schemes that overload the cross-language signal onto another concept. New routing concepts get new axes (line style, glyphs, animation) rather than stealing color. When discussing wire visuals, name both axes — routing kind AND language pairing — even if only one is changing.

```

### project_encapsulated_map.md

```markdown
---
name: Encapsulated map as box
description: A sub-map opens as a single box on a parent canvas. Data boxes marked externally-supplied become input ports; write boxes marked externally-consumed become output ports. The documented exception to single-output-per-box (issue 248, amended 2026-05-23)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**A map directory has two ways to be opened:** as the top-level graph (existing map-select UI), or as an **encapsulated box** on the currently-edited parent map (issue 248). Opening through the file browser while a parent map is open instantiates the sub-map as a single box on the parent's canvas.

**The encapsulation contract — symmetric input and output toggles:**
- **Inputs:** any `data` box inside the sub-map can be toggled "externally-supplied" in its inspector. Each such box becomes a typed input port on the encapsulated box.
- **Outputs:** any `write` box inside the sub-map can be toggled "externally-consumed" in its inspector. Each such box surfaces as a **distinct output port** on the encapsulated box. A write box with the toggle on can still write to its `path` if one is set — the file destination and the parent-wire destination are independent.

**Encapsulated maps are the documented exception to issue 218's "single output per box" rule.** They have *N* output ports — one per externally-consumed write box, where *N* may be zero (pure side-effect map), one, or many. Every other box kind still has exactly one output.

**Rejected earlier design (2026-05-21):** packing all write-box outputs into a single byte-blob with a leading null-terminated size index, single wire out. Rejected 2026-05-23 because it would have repurposed file-writing machinery to emit strings into wires — substituting one mechanism for another. The symmetric toggle design preserves the `write` box's "terminate a value" semantics and treats the destination kind as a mode toggle.

**Why:** Encapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph. The parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals — it sees declared input ports, declared output ports, and known semantics. Sub-maps can be edited independently, reused across parents, and packaged once for distribution. This is the closest SoraMech gets to "user-defined functions" while staying graph-native.

**How to apply:** When discussing map composition, reuse, or "how do users build libraries of behavior" — encapsulation is the answer. Don't propose alternative function-abstraction mechanisms (named subgraphs as text references, macro-style inlining, blob-packed outputs) without explicitly weighing them against the symmetric-toggle shape. Both toggles (`externally-supplied` on data boxes, `externally-consumed` on write boxes) are the user-facing port-declaration mechanism — don't invent a separate "ports manifest" file.

```

### project_soramech.md

```markdown
---
name: SoraMech project context
description: Core architecture decisions, file layout, and execution model for SoraMech, across phase 2 (current) and phase 3 (designed)
type: project
originSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a
---
SoraMech is a visual FSM/dataflow editor and execution engine at /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/.

**Why:** Primary use case is LLM orchestration on the SoraMind Alpine cluster. Strings flow between boxes like variables. History is explicit, loaded from disk only when a box needs it.

**Three independent programs sharing a map directory:**
- `src/006-server-main.lua` — thin HTTP file CRUD proxy. No runner management.
- Runner — phase 2: `src/007-runner-main.lua` (synchronous Lua). Phase 3: `soramech-pool` (C binary, designed in issues 301–311, not yet built).
- `assets/index.html` — vanilla JS canvas editor. Editor only — no run button. Compile button (issue 222) is a phase 2 placeholder; it triggers the phase 3 build pipeline (issue 219).

**Key architecture decisions (current truth):**
- Each box is its own JSON file in `boxes/<id>.json`. Connections written to BOTH endpoint files; loader validates both ends agree — hard error if not.
- **Single output wire per box** (issue 218 complete). No `outputs` array. The function returns one value; routing is by `from_branch` on the connection.
- **Comparator-based branching** (issue 210) — replaces the earlier `branch` box kind with named ports. A box may carry a `comparand`; the dispatch layer fires `lt`/`eq`/`gt` connections. No spec is invoked for comparators.
- **Iterator boxes** (issue 221) — pure routing primitives, no `ref`/`fn`. Dispatch layer cycles through `iterator_outputs` based on a per-task counter.
- **Phase 2 drivers** are shell scripts under `drivers/` (one process per call, stdout as channel). **Phase 3 language specs** are `.so` libraries under `langs/<name>/spec.so` loaded via `dlopen` (issue 303). Lua and C are in-process; Bash is out-of-process via Unix domain socket.
- Data files: per-map JSON in `data/`. Section-level `constant` flag. Accessed via `libs/soramech-data.lua`.
- State/ephemeral: `tmp/` is a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Phase 2 writes `last-run.json` (single doc). Phase 3 writes `last-run.jsonl` (JSON Lines, issue 311) — decoupled from the editor, consumed by LLMs / CLI viewers / test harness.
- **Phase 3 runtime model**: C pool runner owns a 3d-rts task pool; per-task slots in process heap (issue 302) with refcounting and a separate large-value heap; dispatch layer (304) is the worker action; graph loader is C (305), no embedded Lua at the runner level. Phase 2's synchronous executor retires when phase 3 lands.

**How to apply:** When working on any component, respect the three-way separation. Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server. Map directory format is the only shared contract. The phase 2 driver model and the phase 3 spec model coexist conceptually (phase 2 is current, phase 3 is fully designed) but the runtime mechanism differs entirely; box JSON and the editor are unchanged across the cutover.

```

### project_threading.md

```markdown
---
name: threading_model
description: SoraMech's threading model — phase 2 synchronous, phase 3 SoraMech-owned C thread pool with per-port slots and language specs
type: project
originSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a
---
**Phase 2 (current)**: synchronous executor in `src/004-executor.lua`. Single-threaded, sequential box execution. One driver shell-out per box call. The phase 2 path goes away when phase 3 lands — no fallback, no coroutine intermediate.

**Phase 3 (designed, not yet built)**: C pool runner with a SoraMech-owned thread pool. The 3d-rts pool at `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` is the **design reference**, not vendored — SoraMech owns its pool implementation so the spawn primitive, worker context, init barrier, and iterator-pinning extensions are all under our control. The architecture is fully specified across issues 301–313.

Key phase 3 concepts:
- **Per-input-port slots** (not per-task), allocated at graph load and durable for the run. Each slot is a ring buffer (`n_cells` cells of `cell_capacity` bytes). 1-cell slots use peek-not-drain (literals, single-push wires); N-cell slots use pop-and-drain (queued / multi-push wires). No per-slot refcounting — slot lifetime is the whole run.
- **Tasks are ephemeral**: spawned dynamically by the dispatch layer when a box's input set is ready. Tasks carry just `box_id` and a counter snapshot. Box state (counter, input slots, language handle) is durable.
- **Language specs** under `langs/<name>/spec.so`, loaded via `dlopen` at startup. Uniform `lang_spec_t`. No language is privileged.
- **Same-language fast path** (issue 312): wire format defaults to JSON, but two adjacent same-language boxes use the language's native serialization (Lua `lua_dump`, C struct memcpy). Compile-time wire classification picks the path.
- **In-process specs** (Lua, C) via `lua_pcall` / `dlsym`. **Out-of-process specs** (Bash) via Unix domain sockets to a persistent per-worker subprocess.
- **Dispatch layer** (304) is the worker-side action: pop inputs → branch on box mode → invoke spec → push to downstream input slots → end. No blocking, no wait lists; tasks spawn on input arrival and run to completion.
- **Iterator and comparator routing** in the dispatch layer. Comparator runs the function and routes by output value. Iterator skips the function and routes by per-box counter (atomic spawn-time increment). Iterator tasks parallelize across workers; ordering preserved via per-push counter tags on consumer slots.
- **No-null rule** (issue 230): every input port must be wired, given a literal, or marked optional. Compile fails on missing inputs.
- **Init barrier**: pool startup waits until every worker has run every spec's `init(worker_idx)` before submitting tasks. Avoids tasks landing on uninitialized handles.
- **Hard-crash error policy**: nonzero return from any spec aborts the program.
- **Blocking semantics**: long-running operations tie up a worker. Pool size is the budget. Cooperative split (kickoff + check-done iterator) avoids holding a worker. See `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.

**Effil is explicitly NOT used.** Coroutines are not used. The C pool is the chosen mechanism. 3d-rts is referenced as design inspiration, not vendored.

**How to apply:** When discussing threading, parallelism, or cross-language IPC: phase 2 is synchronous shell-out drivers; phase 3 is the SoraMech-owned C pool runner with `lang_spec_t`, per-port slot stores, and dispatch-layer routing. Never suggest effil. 3d-rts is a reference, not a dependency. Issues 301–313 carry the design.

```

Strings flow between boxes like variables. History is explicit, loaded from disk only when a box needs it.\n\n**Three independent programs sharing a map directory:**\n- `src/006-server-main.lua` — thin HTTP file CRUD proxy. No runner management.\n- Runner — phase 2: `src/007-runner-main.lua` (synchronous Lua). Phase 3: `soramech-pool` (C binary, designed in issues 301–311, not yet built).\n- `assets/index.html` — vanilla JS canvas editor. Editor only — no run button. Compile button (issue 222) is a phase 2 placeholder; it triggers the phase 3 build pipeline (issue 219).\n\n**Key architecture decisions (current truth):**\n- Each box is its own JSON file in `boxes/<id>.json`. Connections written to BOTH endpoint files; loader validates both ends agree — hard error if not.\n- **Single output wire per box** (issue 218 complete). No `outputs` array. The function returns one value; routing is by `from_branch` on the connection.\n- **Comparator-based branching** (issue 210) — replaces the earlier `branch` box kind with named ports. A box may carry a `comparand`; the dispatch layer fires `lt`/`eq`/`gt` connections. No spec is invoked for comparators.\n- **Iterator boxes** (issue 221) — pure routing primitives, no `ref`/`fn`. Dispatch layer cycles through `iterator_outputs` based on a per-task counter.\n- **Phase 2 drivers** are shell scripts under `drivers/` (one process per call, stdout as channel). **Phase 3 language specs** are `.so` libraries under `langs/<name>/spec.so` loaded via `dlopen` (issue 303). Lua and C are in-process; Bash is out-of-process via Unix domain socket.\n- Data files: per-map JSON in `data/`. Section-level `constant` flag. Accessed via `libs/soramech-data.lua`.\n- State/ephemeral: `tmp/` is a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Phase 2 writes `last-run.json` (single doc). Phase 3 writes `last-run.jsonl` (JSON Lines, issue 311) — decoupled from the editor, consumed by LLMs / CLI viewers / test harness.\n- **Phase 3 runtime model**: C pool runner owns a 3d-rts task pool; per-task slots in process heap (issue 302) with refcounting and a separate large-value heap; dispatch layer (304) is the worker action; graph loader is C (305), no embedded Lua at the runner level. Phase 2's synchronous executor retires when phase 3 lands.\n\n**How to apply:** When working on any component, respect the three-way separation. Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server. Map directory format is the only shared contract. The phase 2 driver model and the phase 3 spec model coexist conceptually (phase 2 is current, phase 3 is fully designed) but the runtime mechanism differs entirely; box JSON and the editor are unchanged across the cutover.\n",

Single-threaded, sequential box execution. One driver shell-out per box call. The phase 2 path goes away when phase 3 lands — no fallback, no coroutine intermediate.\n\n**Phase 3 (designed, not yet built)**: C pool runner with a SoraMech-owned thread pool. The 3d-rts pool at `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` is the **design reference**, not vendored — SoraMech owns its pool implementation so the spawn primitive, worker context, init barrier, and iterator-pinning extensions are all under our control. The architecture is fully specified across issues 301–313.\n\nKey phase 3 concepts:\n- **Per-input-port slots** (not per-task), allocated at graph load and durable for the run. Each slot is a ring buffer (`n_cells` cells of `cell_capacity` bytes). 1-cell slots use peek-not-drain (literals, single-push wires); N-cell slots use pop-and-drain (queued / multi-push wires). No per-slot refcounting — slot lifetime is the whole run.\n- **Tasks are ephemeral**: spawned dynamically by the dispatch layer when a box's input set is ready. Tasks carry just `box_id` and a counter snapshot. Box state (counter, input slots, language handle) is durable.\n- **Language specs** under `langs/<name>/spec.so`, loaded via `dlopen` at startup. Uniform `lang_spec_t`. No language is privileged.\n- **Same-language fast path** (issue 312): wire format defaults to JSON, but two adjacent same-language boxes use the language's native serialization (Lua `lua_dump`, C struct memcpy). Compile-time wire classification picks the path.\n- **In-process specs** (Lua, C) via `lua_pcall` / `dlsym`. **Out-of-process specs** (Bash) via Unix domain sockets to a persistent per-worker subprocess.\n- **Dispatch layer** (304) is the worker-side action: pop inputs → branch on box mode → invoke spec → push to downstream input slots → end. No blocking, no wait lists; tasks spawn on input arrival and run to completion.\n- **Iterator and comparator routing** in the dispatch layer. Comparator runs the function and routes by output value. Iterator skips the function and routes by per-box counter (atomic spawn-time increment). Iterator tasks parallelize across workers; ordering preserved via per-push counter tags on consumer slots.\n- **No-null rule** (issue 230): every input port must be wired, given a literal, or marked optional. Compile fails on missing inputs.\n- **Init barrier**: pool startup waits until every worker has run every spec's `init(worker_idx)` before submitting tasks. Avoids tasks landing on uninitialized handles.\n- **Hard-crash error policy**: nonzero return from any spec aborts the program.\n- **Blocking semantics**: long-running operations tie up a worker. Pool size is the budget. Cooperative split (kickoff + check-done iterator) avoids holding a worker. See `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.\n\n**Effil is explicitly NOT used.** Coroutines are not used. The C pool is the chosen mechanism. 3d-rts is referenced as design inspiration, not vendored.\n\n**How to apply:** When discussing threading, parallelism, or cross-language IPC: phase 2 is synchronous shell-out drivers; phase 3 is the SoraMech-owned C pool runner with `lang_spec_t`, per-port slot stores, and dispatch-layer routing. Never suggest effil. 3d-rts is a reference, not a dependency. Issues 301–313 carry the design.\n",

Phase 2 uses shell-script drivers; phase 3 will use `.so` language specs via `dlopen` with Unix-domain-socket out-of-process specs for bash. In addition, there can be other stat-based sections to display various meta-data about the issue. There may also be a related documents or tools section. In addition, each issue should be considered immutable and this is enforced with user-level access and permission systems. It is necessary to preserve consent of access to imagination. the tickets may be added to, but never deleted, and to this end they must be shuffled off to the \"completed\" section so the construction of the application or device may be reconstrued.       "content":"# SoraMech — Architecture\n\n## Three programs, one data format\n\nSoraMech is three independent programs that share a common on-disk\nformat: the map directory. None of the three knows about the others\nat runtime.\n\n```\n  Browser (assets/index.html)\n       |  HTTP (file CRUD)\n       v\n  src/006-server-main.lua       [map directory]\n                                maps/<name>/\n                                  meta.json\n                                  boxes/\n                                  data/\n                                  src/\n                                  compiled/   (after compile button)\n                                  tmp/ -> /tmp/<name>/\n       ^\n       | reads & writes\n  Runner (one of):\n    src/007-runner-main.lua     ← phase 2, synchronous Lua interpreter\n    soramech-pool (binary)      ← phase 3, C thread pool runner\n```\n\n### src/006-server-main.lua (the editor's HTTP backend)\n\nThin file CRUD proxy. Receives JSON requests from the browser and\ntranslates them into reads and writes on the map directory. No logic\nbeyond path validation and basic consistency checks (e.g. reject a\ndelete if the box is still referenced by another box's connection\nlist).\n\nStarted with: `luajit src/006-server-main.lua [port]` (default 7700).\nThe `run` script at the project root starts the server and opens the\neditor.\n\nThe editor is editor-only — no run button, no run results display.\nThe runner is invoked separately, by command line. `last-run.jsonl`\n(issue 311) is the runner's output, consumed by external tooling, not\nby the editor.\n\n### Phase 2 runner — `src/007-runner-main.lua`\n\nSynchronous Lua interpreter. Loads a map directory, validates the\ngraph, walks boxes in dependency order, invokes language drivers per\nbox (`drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/c.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`). Each box\ninvocation is wrapped in a `task_fn(inputs) -> outputs` boundary that\nmatches the phase 3 thread pool's action signature.\n\nThis is the development target while the editor is being built out.\n\n### Phase 3 runner — `soramech-pool` (planned, issues 301–311)\n\nC binary that owns a SoraMech-built thread pool (3d-rts is the\ndesign reference, not vendored). Each box invocation is a pool\ntask; worker threads run them concurrently. Language code is\ncalled through **language specs** (issue 303), shared libraries\n(`langs/<name>/spec.so`) loaded via `dlopen` at startup. Lua and C\nspecs are in-process; the Bash spec talks to a persistent\nsubprocess over a Unix domain socket. Wire values live in\n**per-input-port slots** in process heap memory (issue 302) — ring\nbuffers durable for the run, plus a large-value heap for\nvariable-size payloads.\n\nPhase 3 replaces the phase 2 runner wholesale. The synchronous path\ndoes not survive into phase 3; the editor and the map directory\nformat are unchanged across the cutover.\n\n### assets/index.html (the editor)\n\nStatic HTML + vanilla JS. Infinite-scroll canvas. Box diagram editor.\nTalks to `src/006-server-main.lua` for all file operations. No run\nbutton, no compile button (yet — issue 222 adds a placeholder\n\"Compile\" button as part of phase 2). The runner is invoked\nseparately.\n\n## Map directory format\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/\n  meta.json          — { name, description, entry_box_id, src_dirs?, lang? }\n  boxes/\n    <id>.json        — one file per box (see Box file format below)\n  data/\n    <name>.json      — Lua table as JSON; sections have \"constant\": bool\n  src/\n    *.lua, *.c, *.sh — box function source files\n  compiled/          — produced by the compile button (issue 222)\n    pool-runner      — the compiled C entry point for this map\n    src/             — copy of every source file the map uses\n    bin/             — compiled .so files (C boxes via the C language spec)\n    manifest.json    — every box, its language, its compiled artifact path\n  tmp/               — symlink to /tmp/<name>/\n    last-run.json    — phase 2 run snapshot (single document)\n    last-run.jsonl   — phase 3 run log (JSON Lines, issue 311)\n    logs/            — additional run logs\n```\n\nNote: the phase 2 `drivers.json` file is gone. Language selection in\nphase 2 is by file extension via the `drivers/` directory; in phase 3\nthe spec registry resolves languages by `box.lang` against\n`langs/<name>/spec.so` — no map-local config file needed.\n\n## Box file format\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"trim\",\n  \"label\": \"Trim whitespace\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"lua\",\n  \"ref\": \"src/strings.lua\",\n  \"fn\": \"trim\",\n  \"inputs\": [\n    { \"name\": \"text\", \"type\": \"string\" }\n  ],\n  \"output_capacity\": 4096,\n  \"connections\": [\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"trim\",\n      \"from_branch\": null,\n      \"to_box\": \"next-box-id\",\n      \"to_input\": \"text\"\n    }\n  ],\n  \"ui\": { \"x\": 120, \"y\": 340 }\n}\n```\n\nEvery box has exactly **one output wire**. There is no `outputs`\narray. Whatever the function returns travels down the single output\nwire as one value (issue 218). Multiple values that need to travel\ntogether are encoded as JSON or a struct and decoded downstream.\n\n`output_capacity` declares the maximum number of bytes the slot\nallocator (issue 302) reserves for the output. `0` (or omitted) means\nvariable-size — the slot stores a handle into the large-value heap.\n\n### Comparator boxes\nA box may carry a `comparand` field (a literal number as a string).\nWhen set, the dispatch layer compares the input value to the\ncomparand and fires only the connection whose `from_branch` matches\n`\"lt\"` / `\"eq\"` / `\"gt\"`. Comparators have no `ref` / `fn` — the\nrouting logic lives in the dispatch layer (issue 304). The output\nslot carries the input value through unchanged.\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"classify\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"comparand\": \"0\",\n  \"inputs\": [{ \"name\": \"value\", \"type\": \"number\" }],\n  \"connections\": [\n    { \"from_box\": \"classify\", \"from_branch\": \"lt\", \"to_box\": \"negative\", \"to_input\": \"n\" },\n    { \"from_box\": \"classify\", \"from_branch\": \"eq\", \"to_box\": \"zero\",     \"to_input\": \"n\" },\n    { \"from_box\": \"classify\", \"from_branch\": \"gt\", \"to_box\": \"positive\", \"to_input\": \"n\" }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\nThe earlier `branch` box kind with named ports is removed (see issue\n210). Comparator + `from_branch` is the only branching mechanism.\n\n### Iterator boxes\nA box may carry an `iterator_outputs` field — an ordered array of\noutput slot names. The dispatch layer routes the input value to the\nslot named `iterator_outputs[counter]`, advances the counter (mod\nlength), and re-spawns itself to consume the next queued input. No\nfunction is invoked — iterators are pure routing primitives. Issue\n221 covers the model; 213 covers the queued-input semantics.\n\n### Connections\nConnections are written to BOTH endpoint box files. The runner\nvalidates at load time that both ends agree. Disagreement is a hard\nerror.\n\n```json\n{ \"from_box\": \"...\", \"from_branch\": null|\"lt\"|\"eq\"|\"gt\"|\"<iter-slot>\",\n  \"to_box\": \"...\",   \"to_input\": \"...\" }\n```\n\n`from_branch` is `null` for plain call boxes (single output wire).\n\n## Language spec system (phase 3)\n\nEach language is a **spec** — a `.so` library at\n`langs/<name>/spec.so` that exports a `lang_spec_t` symbol with\n`init` / `teardown` / `compile` / `invoke` callbacks. The pool runner\nloads every `langs/*/spec.so` at startup via `dlopen`. The spec\ncontract (issue 303) is uniform across languages; no language is\nprivileged.\n\nReference specs ship with SoraMech:\n- `langs/lua/spec.so` — in-process via `lua_State`, no compile step (issue 306)\n- `langs/c/spec.so`   — in-process via `dlopen`, with a compile step that generates a wrapper (issue 307)\n- `langs/bash/spec.so`— out-of-process via Unix domain socket to a persistent subprocess (issue 308)\n\nA user adds a new language (Python, Rust, anything) by writing a new\nspec under `langs/<name>/`. SoraMech itself does not transpile or\nconvert source between languages.\n\nThe phase 2 `drivers/*.sh` scripts retire when phase 3 lands. They\nimplement the same idea (one process per call, stdout as channel)\nthat the spec system replaces with persistent runtimes and\nlength-prefix-framed sockets / direct function pointers.\n\n## Execution model — phase 2 (synchronous)\n\nThe runner walks the graph depth-first from the entry box. Each box\ncall:\n\n1. Collect inputs: read wired output values from predecessor boxes.\n2. Invoke driver: shell out to the appropriate driver script.\n3. Collect output: decode single JSON value from driver stdout.\n4. Store output: held in runner memory, keyed by box id.\n5. Fire connections: enqueue boxes whose input dependencies are now\n   met.\n\nEach step is wrapped in a `task_fn` boundary so the runner can be\nswapped for the phase 3 pool runner without changing the box\nexecution model. Phase 2 is single-threaded.\n\n## Execution model — phase 3 (thread pool)\n\nThe C pool runner owns a SoraMech-built thread pool with N worker\nthreads (3d-rts is the design reference, not vendored). Each box\ninvocation is a task. The dispatch layer (issue 304) is the\nworker-side action: read inputs from slots → branch on box mode\n→ invoke the language spec (or route directly, for comparators /\niterators) → push output to downstream input slots.\n\nSlots are **per-input-port** ring buffers (issue 302), allocated\nat graph load and durable for the run. 1-cell slots use peek\n(literals, single-push wires); N-cell slots use pop (multi-push\nwires, queues from iterators). Iterator counter is per-box state,\nincremented atomically at task spawn time so iterator tasks can\nparallelize across workers; pushes carry counter tags so consumer\nslots preserve invocation order. Run termination is governed by\nthe pool's active-task counter — when it hits zero with no\npending spawns, the run is over.\n\nThe pool runner has no embedded Lua. It is C from `main` down to the\nlanguage spec boundary; only inside a Lua spec's `invoke` does Lua\ncode run, and only inside that worker's `lua_State`. The graph\nloader is also pure C (issue 305) — phase 2's\n`src/003-loader.lua` retires.\n\nSee `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` for the full IPC and threading\ndiscussion, including the blocking-semantics constraint on long-\nrunning operations.\n\n## Data files\n\nPersistent data lives in `data/<name>.json`. Format:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"constant\": false,\n  \"fields\": {\n    \"history\": [],\n    \"config\": { \"constant\": true, \"value\": { \"model\": \"soramind-default\" } }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nTop-level `constant: true` makes the whole file read-only.\nIndividual fields can be flagged constant within an otherwise\nmutable file. Accessed via `libs/soramech-data.lua`.\n\nEphemeral state (scratch tables, run logs, the `last-run.jsonl`\noutput) goes to `tmp/`, a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Survives\nthe run but not a reboot — intentionally.\n",

Multiple values that need to travel\n136\ttogether are encoded as JSON or a struct and decoded downstream.\n137\t\n138\t`output_capacity` declares the maximum number of bytes the slot\n139\tallocator (issue 302) reserves for the output. `0` (or omitted) means\n140\tvariable-size — the slot stores a handle into the large-value heap.\n141\t\n142\t### Comparator boxes\n143\tA box may carry a `comparand` field (a literal number as a string).\n144\tWhen set, the dispatch layer compares the input value to the\n145\tcomparand and fires only the connection whose `from_branch` matches\n146\t`\"lt\"` / `\"eq\"` / `\"gt\"`. Comparators have no `ref` / `fn` — the\n147\trouting logic lives in the dispatch layer (issue 304). The output\n148\tslot carries the input value through unchanged.\n149\t\n150\t```json\n151\t{\n152\t  \"id\": \"classify\",\n153\t  \"kind\": \"call\",\n154\t  \"comparand\": \"0\",\n155\t  \"inputs\": [{ \"name\": \"value\", \"type\": \"number\" }],\n156\t  \"connections\": [\n157\t    { \"from_box\": \"classify\", \"from_branch\": \"lt\", \"to_box\": \"negative\", \"to_input\": \"n\" },\n158\t    { \"from_box\": \"classify\", \"from_branch\": \"eq\", \"to_box\": \"zero\",     \"to_input\": \"n\" },\n159\t    { \"from_box\": \"classify\", \"from_branch\": \"gt\", \"to_box\": \"positive\", \"to_input\": \"n\" }\n160\t  ]\n161\t}\n162\t```\n163\t\n164\tThe earlier `branch` box kind with named ports is removed (see issue\n165\t210). Comparator + `from_branch` is the only branching mechanism.\n166\t\n167\t### Iterator boxes\n168\tA box may carry an `iterator_outputs` field — an ordered array of\n169\toutput slot names. The dispatch layer routes the input value to the\n170\tslot named `iterator_outputs[counter]`, advances the counter (mod\n171\tlength), and re-spawns itself to consume the next queued input. No\n172\tfunction is invoked — iterators are pure routing primitives. Issue\n173\t221 covers the model; 213 covers the queued-input semantics.\n174\t\n175\t### Connections\n176\tConnections are written to BOTH endpoint box files. The runner\n177\tvalidates at load time that both ends agree. Disagreement is a hard\n178\terror.\n179\t\n180\t```json\n181\t{ \"from_box\": \"...\", \"from_branch\": null|\"lt\"|\"eq\"|\"gt\"|\"<iter-slot>\",\n182\t  \"to_box\": \"...\",   \"to_input\": \"...\" }\n183\t```\n184\t\n185\t`from_branch` is `null` for plain call boxes (single output wire).\n186\t\n187\t## Language spec system (phase 3)\n188\t\n189\tEach language is a **spec** — a `.so` library at\n190\t`langs/<name>/spec.so` that exports a `lang_spec_t` symbol with\n191\t`init` / `teardown` / `compile` / `invoke` callbacks. The pool runner\n192\tloads every `langs/*/spec.so` at startup via `dlopen`. The spec\n193\tcontract (issue 303) is uniform across languages; no language is\n194\tprivileged.\n195\t\n196\tReference specs ship with SoraMech:\n197\t- `langs/lua/spec.so` — in-process via `lua_State`, no compile step (issue 306)\n198\t- `langs/c/spec.so`   — in-process via `dlopen`, with a compile step that generates a wrapper (issue 307)\n199\t- `langs/bash/spec.so`— out-of-process via Unix domain socket to a persistent subprocess (issue 308)\n200\t\n201\tA user adds a new language (Python, Rust, anything) by writing a new\n202\tspec under `langs/<name>/`. SoraMech itself does not transpile or\n203\tconvert source between languages.\n204\t\n205\tThe phase 2 `drivers/*.sh` scripts retire when phase 3 lands. They\n206\timplement the same idea (one process per call, stdout as channel)\n207\tthat the spec system replaces with persistent runtimes and\n208\tlength-prefix-framed sockets / direct function pointers.\n209\t\n210\t## Execution model — phase 2 (synchronous)\n211\t\n212\tThe runner walks the graph depth-first from the entry box. Each box\n213\tcall:\n214\t\n215\t1. Collect inputs: read wired output values from predecessor boxes.\n216\t2. Invoke driver: shell out to the appropriate driver script.\n217\t3. Collect output: decode single JSON value from driver stdout.\n218\t4. Store output: held in runner memory, keyed by box id.\n219\t5. Fire connections: enqueue boxes whose input dependencies are now\n220\t   met.\n221\t\n222\tEach step is wrapped in a `task_fn` boundary so the runner can be\n223\tswapped for the phase 3 pool runner without changing the box\n224\texecution model. Phase 2 is single-threaded.\n225\t\n226\t## Execution model — phase 3 (thread pool)\n227\t\n228\tThe C pool runner owns a SoraMech-built thread pool with N worker\n229\tthreads (3d-rts is the design reference, not vendored). Each box\n230\tinvocation is a task. The dispatch layer (issue 304) is the\n231\tworker-side action: read inputs from slots → branch on box mode\n232\t→ invoke the language spec (or route directly, for comparators /\n233\titerators) → push output to downstream input slots.\n234\t\n235\tSlots are **per-input-port** ring buffers (issue 302), allocated\n236\tat graph load and durable for the run. 1-cell slots use peek\n237\t(literals, single-push wires); N-cell slots use pop (multi-push\n238\twires, queues from iterators). Iterator counter is per-box state,\n239\tincremented atomically at task spawn time so iterator tasks can\n240\tparallelize across workers; pushes carry counter tags so consumer\n241\tslots preserve invocation order. Run termination is governed by\n242\tthe pool's active-task counter — when it hits zero with no\n243\tpending spawns, the run is over.\n244\t\n245\tThe pool runner has no embedded Lua. It is C from `main` down to the\n246\tlanguage spec boundary; only inside a Lua spec's `invoke` does Lua\n247\tcode run, and only inside that worker's `lua_State`. The graph\n248\tloader is also pure C (issue 305) — phase 2's\n249\t`src/003-loader.lua` retires.\n250\t\n251\tSee `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` for the full IPC and threading\n252\tdiscussion, including the blocking-semantics constraint on long-\n253\trunning operations.\n254\t\n255\t## Data files\n256\t\n257\tPersistent data lives in `data/<name>.json`. Format:\n258\t\n259\t```json\n260\t{\n261\t  \"constant\": false,\n262\t  \"fields\": {\n263\t    \"history\": [],\n264\t    \"config\": { \"constant\": true, \"value\": { \"model\": \"soramind-default\" } }\n265\t  }\n266\t}\n267\t```\n268\t\n269\tTop-level `constant: true` makes the whole file read-only.\n270\tIndividual fields can be flagged constant within an otherwise\n271\tmutable file. Accessed via `libs/soramech-data.lua`.\n272\t\n273\tEphemeral state (scratch tables, run logs, the `last-run.jsonl`\n274\toutput) goes to `tmp/`, a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Survives\n275\tthe run but not a reboot — intentionally.\n276\t"
```json
      }],
```

```json
{
  "userType":"external",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-12T21:06:49.104Z",
  "entrypoint":"cli",
  "gitBranch":"master",
  "sourceToolAssistantUUID":"47449432-78f9-48ac-aaf5-6c25d133e978",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "sessionId":"585b6e65-7287-44e7-b133-8bdf3479a266",
  "parentUuid":"47449432-78f9-48ac-aaf5-6c25d133e978",
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",

  "toolUseResult":{
    "type":"text",
    "file":{
      "content":"# 233 — Unified `routing` schema for branching boxes\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Concept\n\nA \"branching box\" is a regular call box whose output, after the\nfunction runs, is sent to **one of several** downstream\ndestinations rather than to all of them. Same function, same\ninputs, same output value — only the routing decision differs.\nCurrently we have two flavors:\n\n- **Comparator**: routes the function's output by comparing it\n  to a stored threshold. Three fixed branches (`lt` / `eq` /\n  `gt`).\n- **Iterator**: routes the function's output to one of N branches\n  in round-robin fashion, advancing a counter on every call.\n\nThe two are the same shape (function runs → output gets routed)\nwith different rules for picking the branch. The current schema\nhas them as separate top-level fields (`comparand` and\n`iterator_outputs`), which makes them look like unrelated\nfeatures. They aren't.\n\n(For \"send the same value to multiple destinations,\" the user\njust pulls multiple wires out of a single output port — fan-out\nalready works on plain call boxes. No routing decision needed.)\n\n### Branch-level fan-out\n\nFan-out applies on a per-branch basis even for branched boxes. If\nthe comparator's `lt` port has three wires going to three\ndifferent consumers, then each time the routing decision picks\n`lt`, all three wires receive the value (a copy is pushed into\neach consumer's input slot). On a subsequent invocation that\npicks `eq`, only the wires hanging off the `eq` port fire.\n\nEach branch port acts like its own little plain-call output port\nwhen it fires. The routing decision picks **which branch** fires;\nthe branch's own fan-out picks **which consumers** receive the\nvalue when it does.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEvery call box carries a `routing` field. No implicit defaulting:\nplain boxes have `routing: { \"kind\": \"plain\" }`, the same way\nbranched boxes carry their own kind. Explicit and consistent —\nno \"what if I forget the routing field\" surprises at validation\ntime.\n\n```json\n{ \"id\": \"plain-call\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"ref\": \"...\", \"fn\": \"...\",\n  \"inputs\": [...],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" } }\n\n{ \"id\": \"score-router\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"ref\": \"src/score.lua\", \"fn\": \"score\",\n  \"inputs\": [...],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"comparator\", \"comparand\": 4 } }\n\n{ \"id\": \"round-robin\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"ref\": \"src/dispatch_msg.lua\", \"fn\": \"dispatch_msg\",\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"iterator\", \"n_outputs\": 3 } }\n```\n\nRouting kinds defined in this design: `plain`, `comparator`,\n`iterator`, `randomizer`, `weighted`, `distributor`. Of those,\n**this issue ships `plain`, `comparator`, and `iterator` only**\n— that's the surface area already in production, just unified\nunder one schema. The other three (`randomizer`, `weighted`,\n`distributor`) are designed below for context but split into\ntheir own follow-on issue files when this one is implemented, so\neach ships independently.\n\nThe `routing.kind` field picks which dispatch-layer rule decides\nthe branch. Schema validates the kind value and the kind-specific\nparameters together.\n\n**The function always runs**, regardless of routing kind. The\nfunction produces the value; routing decides where the value\ngoes.\n\n### kind=\"plain\"\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n```\n\nOne output port. The function's output value fans to every wire\nattached to that port unconditionally. No routing decision; the\ndispatch layer skips the branch picker and pushes to all wires.\n\nThis is the default for new boxes; the editor sets it\nautomatically when a box is created.\n\n### kind=\"comparator\"\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"comparator\", \"comparand\": \"<number>\" }\n```\n\nThree output ports: `lt`, `eq`, `gt` (fixed names; ports aren't\nrenameable per the editor's port-immutability rule). The\nfunction's output value is compared to `comparand`; the matching\nbranch fires.\n\n#### Multi-band comparator (planned brainstorm)\n\nThe current 3-branch lt/eq/gt design is a special case of \"value\nfalls into a numeric range, fire the corresponding branch.\" A\ngeneralization:\n\n```json\n\"routing\": {\n  \"kind\": \"comparator\",\n  \"thresholds\": [3, 7, 11, 17]\n}\n```\n\nFive output ports get named by the threshold positions —\n`below_3`, `between_3_7`, `between_7_11`, `between_11_17`,\n`above_17`. With `thresholds: [4]` this becomes the current\n3-branch lt/eq/gt (with `eq` being \"exactly 4\"), so the legacy\nshape is one configuration of the new one.\n\n**Equality bands via doubled thresholds.** Encode the current\n`eq` semantics by repeating a threshold value: `thresholds: [3, 3]`\nmeans \"less than 3, exactly 3, greater than 3\" — three bands, the\nmiddle one being a zero-width point that fires only on exact\nequality. With `thresholds: [3, 3, 7, 7]` you get five bands:\n`< 3`, `== 3`, `3 < x < 7`, `== 7`, `> 7`. The editor sees a\nlist of thresholds; the runtime sees doubled values as\n\"point bands.\"\n\nThis means the legacy 3-branch lt/eq/gt is exactly\n`thresholds: [c, c]` — the eq case is just a zero-width band at\nthe comparand. Behind the scenes the editor can present the\nsingle-comparand UI but store `[c, c]` so the dispatch layer has\none consistent representation.\n\nDefer the schema specifics — the single-comparand case ships\nfirst; multi-band is a follow-on once we have a use case that\nactually needs more than three.\n\n### kind=\"iterator\"\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"iterator\", \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n```\n\n`n_outputs` output ports, named conventionally (`out_0`, `out_1`,\n…). Every invocation reads the box's `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot\nvia `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs)`; that index picks\nthe branch.\n\nThe function still runs and produces the routed value. Iterator\ndefaults the function to a passthrough identity if the user\nhasn't picked a `ref` / `fn` — but the user is free to attach\nany function whose output should be round-robin-distributed.\n\n### kind=\"randomizer\"\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"randomizer\", \"n_outputs\": 4 }\n```\n\nPicks a branch uniformly at random per invocation.\nImplementation: hash the counter-slot value into the branch\nindex, so the distribution is deterministic-given-seed but\nspread across branches.\n\n```c\nuint32_t i = slot_read_inc(counter_slot, UINT32_MAX);\nuint32_t branch = hash(i) % n_outputs;\n```\n\n`hash` is a cheap mixing function (xorshift, FNV); not\ncryptographic. The point is breaking up the monotonic counter so\nconsecutive calls don't go to consecutive branches.\n\n### kind=\"weighted\"\n\n```json\n\"routing\": {\n  \"kind\":    \"weighted\",\n  \"weights\": [0.8, 0.2]\n}\n```\n\nProbability-based distribution. With `[0.8, 0.2]` and two output\nports, 80% of invocations fire branch 0, 20% fire branch 1.\n\nImplementation: at compile time, weights are normalized into a\ncumulative table on a `0..PRECISION-1` integer scale (e.g.\n`PRECISION = 1000`). Per call:\n\n```c\nuint32_t r = slot_read_inc(counter_slot, PRECISION);\n// pre-computed cumulative: [0..799] → branch 0, [800..999] → branch 1\nuint32_t branch = lookup_band(r, cumulative_table);\n```\n\nSame counter-slot machinery as iterator and randomizer; the\ndifference is the mapping from counter to branch.\n\n**Inspector UI for weighted routing**: a horizontal slider with\nN knobs dividing it into N+1 segments — except really N segments\nsince each knob is the boundary between adjacent segments. A\nwider segment means a larger fraction of invocations flow down\nthat path. Below the slider, one line per output port:\n\n```\nout_0    [▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓░░░░░░░░░░░░]    80%\nout_1    [░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░▓▓▓▓]    20%\n```\n\nEach line shows the output port name on the left, a visual band\nin the middle indicating its slice of the distribution, and the\npercentage on the right. Adjusting the slider knobs updates the\npercentages live; the percentages are also editable directly\n(typing `30` into the right column shifts the relevant knob).\n\n### kind=\"distributor\" (load-aware)\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"distributor\", \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n```\n\nSends the value to the **least-busy** downstream consumer:\ninspects the fill levels of the input slots wired to each branch\nand picks the branch whose downstream slot has the fewest queued\nvalues.\n\nImplementation: dispatch action peeks the `tail - head` count on\neach downstream input slot and picks the minimum. Tied branches\nfall back to atomic-counter round-robin so ties don't always go\nto the same branch.\n\nThis is the only routing kind that's not purely\nself-contained — it reads downstream slot state — but it doesn't\nadd any new dispatch-layer concept beyond querying slot fill\n(which the slot store already knows).\n\n### Future kinds\n\nThe pattern is: any new routing kind plugs in at one place\n(`routing.kind` value + dispatch-layer branch picker). All\nexisting kinds and any future ones live entirely in the dispatch\nlayer + slot store + editor — never in language specs, never in\nuser-written functions.\n\n## Iterator + function: ships as \"function always runs\"\n\nIterator boxes always run their function. The dispatch action\nbecomes uniform across routing kinds:\n\n```\n1. Read inputs (pop / peek per port mode).\n2. Invoke spec (always — function runs regardless of routing kind).\n3. Pick branch via routing.kind:\n     comparator   → compare(output, comparand)\n     iterator     → slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs)\n     randomizer   → hash(slot_read_inc(counter_slot, MAX)) % n_outputs\n     weighted     → cumulative lookup\n     distributor  → argmin(downstream fill)\n     (no routing) → fan to all outgoing wires\n4. Push function output to outputs[picked branch] (or all wires if\n   no routing).\n```\n\nA single dispatch path for all branching boxes; the routing rule\nplugs into step 3.\n\n## Schema migration\n\nFew enough existing maps that we can hand-migrate them. The\nloader does **not** carry a legacy-shape adapter; once this\nships, all map files are expected to use the `routing` field. If\na map with the old shape is opened, the schema validator rejects\nit and the user (or a one-off migration script) updates it.\n\nIf we end up wanting a one-off script, it walks `maps/<name>/boxes/*.json`\nand rewrites:\n- `comparand: X` → `routing: { kind: \"comparator\", comparand: X }`\n- `iterator_outputs: [...]` → `routing: { kind: \"iterator\", n_outputs: len(...) }`\n- everything else → no change\n\nBut for the current map count, manual edits are faster than\nwriting the script.\n\n## Inspector UI\n\nA `routing` selector in the inspector replaces the separate\n`compare` toggle and `iterator` toggle. The dropdown's options\nexpand as new routing kinds ship:\n\n```\nmode:    [plain ▾ | comparator | iterator]\n```\n\nPer-kind controls below the dropdown — for the kinds shipped in\nthis issue:\n- **plain**: nothing extra.\n- **comparator**: numeric `comparand` input. (Multi-band UI is\n  the brainstorm above, lands in its own issue.)\n- **iterator**: `n_outputs` integer input.\n\nOutput ports re-render to match the routing kind: 1 dot for\nplain, 3 fixed dots (lt/eq/gt) for comparator, N dots for\niterator. Port names follow the routing kind's convention; not\nuser-renameable (issue 224's read-only-port-name rule).\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\nThis issue ships `plain`, `comparator`, and `iterator` only —\nthe existing surface area unified under one schema. The other\nkinds get follow-on issue files (one per kind: randomizer,\nweighted, distributor, multi-band-comparator) opened when this\nissue is implemented.\n\n1. `src/001-schema.lua`: accept `routing` field with `kind` ∈\n   `{plain, comparator, iterator}`; reject legacy `comparand` /\n   `iterator_outputs`.         "content":"1\t# 233 — Unified `routing` schema for branching boxes\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Concept\n7\t\n8\tA \"branching box\" is a regular call box whose output, after the\n9\tfunction runs, is sent to **one of several** downstream\n10\tdestinations rather than to all of them. Same function, same\n11\tinputs, same output value — only the routing decision differs.\n12\tCurrently we have two flavors:\n13\t\n14\t- **Comparator**: routes the function's output by comparing it\n15\t  to a stored threshold. Three fixed branches (`lt` / `eq` /\n16\t  `gt`).\n17\t- **Iterator**: routes the function's output to one of N branches\n18\t  in round-robin fashion, advancing a counter on every call.\n19\t\n20\tThe two are the same shape (function runs → output gets routed)\n21\twith different rules for picking the branch. The current schema\n22\thas them as separate top-level fields (`comparand` and\n23\t`iterator_outputs`), which makes them look like unrelated\n24\tfeatures. They aren't.\n25\t\n26\t(For \"send the same value to multiple destinations,\" the user\n27\tjust pulls multiple wires out of a single output port — fan-out\n28\talready works on plain call boxes. No routing decision needed.)\n29\t\n30\t### Branch-level fan-out\n31\t\n32\tFan-out applies on a per-branch basis even for branched boxes. If\n33\tthe comparator's `lt` port has three wires going to three\n34\tdifferent consumers, then each time the routing decision picks\n35\t`lt`, all three wires receive the value (a copy is pushed into\n36\teach consumer's input slot). On a subsequent invocation that\n37\tpicks `eq`, only the wires hanging off the `eq` port fire.\n38\t\n39\tEach branch port acts like its own little plain-call output port\n40\twhen it fires. The routing decision picks **which branch** fires;\n41\tthe branch's own fan-out picks **which consumers** receive the\n42\tvalue when it does.\n43\t\n44\t## Intended behavior\n45\t\n46\tEvery call box carries a `routing` field. No implicit defaulting:\n47\tplain boxes have `routing: { \"kind\": \"plain\" }`, the same way\n48\tbranched boxes carry their own kind. Explicit and consistent —\n49\tno \"what if I forget the routing field\" surprises at validation\n50\ttime.\n51\t\n52\t```json\n53\t{ \"id\": \"plain-call\",\n54\t  \"kind\": \"call\",\n55\t  \"ref\": \"...\", \"fn\": \"...\",\n56\t  \"inputs\": [...],\n57\t  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" } }\n58\t\n59\t{ \"id\": \"score-router\",\n60\t  \"kind\": \"call\",\n61\t  \"ref\": \"src/score.lua\", \"fn\": \"score\",\n62\t  \"inputs\": [...],\n63\t  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"comparator\", \"comparand\": 4 } }\n64\t\n65\t{ \"id\": \"round-robin\",\n66\t  \"kind\": \"call\",\n67\t  \"ref\": \"src/dispatch_msg.lua\", \"fn\": \"dispatch_msg\",\n68\t  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"iterator\", \"n_outputs\": 3 } }\n69\t```\n70\t\n71\tRouting kinds defined in this design: `plain`, `comparator`,\n72\t`iterator`, `randomizer`, `weighted`, `distributor`. Of those,\n73\t**this issue ships `plain`, `comparator`, and `iterator` only**\n74\t— that's the surface area already in production, just unified\n75\tunder one schema. The other three (`randomizer`, `weighted`,\n76\t`distributor`) are designed below for context but split into\n77\ttheir own follow-on issue files when this one is implemented, so\n78\teach ships independently.\n79\t\n80\tThe `routing.kind` field picks which dispatch-layer rule decides\n81\tthe branch. Schema validates the kind value and the kind-specific\n82\tparameters together.\n83\t\n84\t**The function always runs**, regardless of routing kind. The\n85\tfunction produces the value; routing decides where the value\n86\tgoes.\n87\t\n88\t### kind=\"plain\"\n89\t\n90\t```json\n91\t\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n92\t```\n93\t\n94\tOne output port. The function's output value fans to every wire\n95\tattached to that port unconditionally. No routing decision; the\n96\tdispatch layer skips the branch picker and pushes to all wires.\n97\t\n98\tThis is the default for new boxes; the editor sets it\n99\tautomatically when a box is created.\n100\t\n101\t### kind=\"comparator\"\n102\t\n103\t```json\n104\t\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"comparator\", \"comparand\": \"<number>\" }\n105\t```\n106\t\n107\tThree output ports: `lt`, `eq`, `gt` (fixed names; ports aren't\n108\trenameable per the editor's port-immutability rule). The\n109\tfunction's output value is compared to `comparand`; the matching\n110\tbranch fires.\n111\t\n112\t#### Multi-band comparator (planned brainstorm)\n113\t\n114\tThe current 3-branch lt/eq/gt design is a special case of \"value\n115\tfalls into a numeric range, fire the corresponding branch.\" A\n116\tgeneralization:\n117\t\n118\t```json\n119\t\"routing\": {\n120\t  \"kind\": \"comparator\",\n121\t  \"thresholds\": [3, 7, 11, 17]\n122\t}\n123\t```\n124\t\n125\tFive output ports get named by the threshold positions —\n126\t`below_3`, `between_3_7`, `between_7_11`, `between_11_17`,\n127\t`above_17`. With `thresholds: [4]` this becomes the current\n128\t3-branch lt/eq/gt (with `eq` being \"exactly 4\"), so the legacy\n129\tshape is one configuration of the new one.\n130\t\n131\t**Equality bands via doubled thresholds.** Encode the current\n132\t`eq` semantics by repeating a threshold value: `thresholds: [3, 3]`\n133\tmeans \"less than 3, exactly 3, greater than 3\" — three bands, the\n134\tmiddle one being a zero-width point that fires only on exact\n135\tequality. With `thresholds: [3, 3, 7, 7]` you get five bands:\n136\t`< 3`, `== 3`, `3 < x < 7`, `== 7`, `> 7`. The editor sees a\n137\tlist of thresholds; the runtime sees doubled values as\n138\t\"point bands.\"\n139\t\n140\tThis means the legacy 3-branch lt/eq/gt is exactly\n141\t`thresholds: [c, c]` — the eq case is just a zero-width band at\n142\tthe comparand. Behind the scenes the editor can present the\n143\tsingle-comparand UI but store `[c, c]` so the dispatch layer has\n144\tone consistent representation.\n145\t\n146\tDefer the schema specifics — the single-comparand case ships\n147\tfirst; multi-band is a follow-on once we have a use case that\n148\tactually needs more than three.\n149\t\n150\t### kind=\"iterator\"\n151\t\n152\t```json\n153\t\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"iterator\", \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n154\t```\n155\t\n156\t`n_outputs` output ports, named conventionally (`out_0`, `out_1`,\n157\t…). Every invocation reads the box's `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot\n158\tvia `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs)`; that index picks\n159\tthe branch.\n160\t\n161\tThe function still runs and produces the routed value. Iterator\n162\tdefaults the function to a passthrough identity if the user\n163\thasn't picked a `ref` / `fn` — but the user is free to attach\n164\tany function whose output should be round-robin-distributed.\n165\t\n166\t### kind=\"randomizer\"\n167\t\n168\t```json\n169\t\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"randomizer\", \"n_outputs\": 4 }\n170\t```\n171\t\n172\tPicks a branch uniformly at random per invocation.\n173\tImplementation: hash the counter-slot value into the branch\n174\tindex, so the distribution is deterministic-given-seed but\n175\tspread across branches.\n176\t\n177\t```c\n178\tuint32_t i = slot_read_inc(counter_slot, UINT32_MAX);\n179\tuint32_t branch = hash(i) % n_outputs;\n180\t```\n181\t\n182\t`hash` is a cheap mixing function (xorshift, FNV); not\n183\tcryptographic. The point is breaking up the monotonic counter so\n184\tconsecutive calls don't go to consecutive branches.\n185\t\n186\t### kind=\"weighted\"\n187\t\n188\t```json\n189\t\"routing\": {\n190\t  \"kind\":    \"weighted\",\n191\t  \"weights\": [0.8, 0.2]\n192\t}\n193\t```\n194\t\n195\tProbability-based distribution. With `[0.8, 0.2]` and two output\n196\tports, 80% of invocations fire branch 0, 20% fire branch 1.\n197\t\n198\tImplementation: at compile time, weights are normalized into a\n199\tcumulative table on a `0..PRECISION-1` integer scale (e.g.\n200\t`PRECISION = 1000`). Per call:\n201\t\n202\t```c\n203\tuint32_t r = slot_read_inc(counter_slot, PRECISION);\n204\t// pre-computed cumulative: [0..799] → branch 0, [800..999] → branch 1\n205\tuint32_t branch = lookup_band(r, cumulative_table);\n206\t```\n207\t\n208\tSame counter-slot machinery as iterator and randomizer; the\n209\tdifference is the mapping from counter to branch.\n210\t\n211\t**Inspector UI for weighted routing**: a horizontal slider with\n212\tN knobs dividing it into N+1 segments — except really N segments\n213\tsince each knob is the boundary between adjacent segments. A\n214\twider segment means a larger fraction of invocations flow down\n215\tthat path. Below the slider, one line per output port:\n216\t\n217\t```\n218\tout_0    [▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓░░░░░░░░░░░░]    80%\n219\tout_1    [░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░▓▓▓▓]    20%\n220\t```\n221\t\n222\tEach line shows the output port name on the left, a visual band\n223\tin the middle indicating its slice of the distribution, and the\n224\tpercentage on the right. Adjusting the slider knobs updates the\n225\tpercentages live; the percentages are also editable directly\n226\t(typing `30` into the right column shifts the relevant knob).\n227\t\n228\t### kind=\"distributor\" (load-aware)\n229\t\n230\t```json\n231\t\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"distributor\", \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n232\t```\n233\t\n234\tSends the value to the **least-busy** downstream consumer:\n235\tinspects the fill levels of the input slots wired to each branch\n236\tand picks the branch whose downstream slot has the fewest queued\n237\tvalues.\n238\t\n239\tImplementation: dispatch action peeks the `tail - head` count on\n240\teach downstream input slot and picks the minimum. Tied branches\n241\tfall back to atomic-counter round-robin so ties don't always go\n242\tto the same branch.\n243\t\n244\tThis is the only routing kind that's not purely\n245\tself-contained — it reads downstream slot state — but it doesn't\n246\tadd any new dispatch-layer concept beyond querying slot fill\n247\t(which the slot store already knows).\n248\t\n249\t### Future kinds\n250\t\n251\tThe pattern is: any new routing kind plugs in at one place\n252\t(`routing.kind` value + dispatch-layer branch picker). The dispatch action\n260\tbecomes uniform across routing kinds:\n261\t\n262\t```\n263\t1. Read inputs (pop / peek per port mode).\n264\t2. Invoke spec (always — function runs regardless of routing kind).\n265\t3. Pick branch via routing.kind:\n266\t     comparator   → compare(output, comparand)\n267\t     iterator     → slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs)\n268\t     randomizer   → hash(slot_read_inc(counter_slot, MAX)) % n_outputs\n269\t     weighted     → cumulative lookup\n270\t     distributor  → argmin(downstream fill)\n271\t     (no routing) → fan to all outgoing wires\n272\t4. Push function output to outputs[picked branch] (or all wires if\n273\t   no routing).\n274\t```\n275\t\n276\tA single dispatch path for all branching boxes; the routing rule\n277\tplugs into step 3.\n278\t\n279\t## Schema migration\n280\t\n281\tFew enough existing maps that we can hand-migrate them. {
```
```json
  "userType":"external",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-12T21:06:50.130Z",
  "entrypoint":"cli",

  "toolUseResult":{
    "type":"text",
    "file":{
      "content":"# 230 — Required inputs, the optional flag, and no-null-from-missing\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA box's input port can be left without a wire and without a literal\nvalue. The phase 2 executor runs the box anyway; the function on\nthe other end gets `nil` (Lua), unset (Bash), or whatever default\nthe language hands a missing positional arg. Errors only surface if\nthe function happens to reference the missing arg in a way the\nlanguage can't tolerate (e.g. `string.upper(nil)` in Lua).\n\nThis is a class of silent-error bug. The user had a wiring intent,\nforgot to plug something in, and the runtime quietly papered over\nthe mistake.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEvery input port is in one of three states by **compile time**:\n\n1. A wire is connected to it.\n2. A literal value is set on it.\n3. It carries `optional: true` on the port record.\n\n**Compile fails** when any port is in none of those states. The\nerror is precise: which box, which port. The Compile button (issue\n222) is the natural enforcement point, with the same check\nduplicating in the phase 3 graph loader (issue 305).\n\n### \"Optional\" is not \"null\"\n\n`optional: true` says \"this argument doesn't have to be passed.\" It\ndoes not mean \"pass null.\" At the spec boundary, an optional\nunwired un-littered port produces a shorter arg list — the language\nsees fewer arguments, not a null argument. Each language handles\nthat natively:\n\n- **Lua**: omitted args are `nil`. That's a language convention,\n  not a wire-level value. Inside the Lua function, `arg or default`\n  works.\n- **Bash**: a positional arg that wasn't passed is unset.\n  `${arg:-default}` provides a default.\n- **C**: the spec's compile callback (issue 307) generates a wrapper\n  that reads `n_inputs` and only forwards the args that are present.\n\n### Null as an explicit value (allowed)\n\nIf the user needs to pass null because some downstream library\nexpects it, they can — by typing the literal `null` into the value\nfield. That's a string on the wire encoded as JSON null. Each spec\nmaps it to its language's native null on the way in:\n\n| JSON value  | Lua    | Bash       | C       |\n|-------------|--------|------------|---------|\n| `null`      | nil    | empty `\"\"` | `NULL`  |\n| `42`        | 42     | `\"42\"`     | 42      |\n| `\"foo\"`     | `foo`  | `foo`      | `\"foo\"` |\n| `true`      | true   | `\"true\"`   | `1`     |\n\nThe crucial distinction: **explicit null arrives through the\nfunction call as a real argument**; **optional-and-absent does not\narrive at all**. Bash empty-string-vs-unset disappears in the\noptional path because the arg position simply isn't passed.\n\n### Schema\n\nAdd `optional` as an optional boolean on input port records:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"name\": \"config_path\",\n  \"type\": \"string\",\n  \"optional\": true\n}\n```\n\nAbsence means `false`.
```
