      "content":"# 302 — Per-task slot store with wire-held references\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nWire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values\nhave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\naccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n\n## Concept\n\n### Slots belong to input ports, not tasks\n\nEach box has **one slot per input port**, allocated when the graph\nloads and persisting for the life of the run. A wire is a routing\ndeclaration: \"the producer's output port pushes a copy of its value\ninto this consumer's named input slot.\" The producer never owns a\nslot — its output is a routing event, not a stored value.\n\nWhen a producer fires, the dispatch layer copies the value into\nevery downstream input slot wired to that output. Fan-out is N\npushes (one per consumer); fan-in is N producers all pushing into\nthe same consumer's slot. Both behaviors fall out of the same\npush-into-input-slot mechanic.\n\nSlots live in process heap memory, accessible to every worker\nthread. Cross-process visibility is not required: language specs\n(issue 303) only ever receive byte pointers — never raw slot\naddresses — so out-of-process specs (Bash) work via sockets, not\nshared memory.\n\n### Tasks are ephemeral; box state is durable\n\nA **task** is one invocation: pop one value from each of the box's\ninput slots, run the box's logic, push the output to every\ndownstream input slot. Tasks have no persistent identity — they're\njust stack frames on workers. Tasks are spawned dynamically by the\ndispatch layer when a box's input set is ready (every input slot\nholds at least one value).\n\nThe **box** is the durable thing: it owns its input port slots, any\ncounter state (for iterators), its language spec handle, and so\non. The box exists from graph load until run end. Tasks come and\ngo.\n\nThis is uniform across iterator and non-iterator boxes. Both run N\ntimes where N depends on how many invocations their inputs supply\n(possibly 1, possibly thousands). The difference is just what the\ntask does:\n- **Plain call task**: invoke spec on the popped values, push the\n  return to outputs.\n- **Iterator task**: read box's counter, route the popped value to\n  output port `iterator_outputs[counter]`, increment counter mod N.\n  No spec invocation.\n- **Comparator task**: invoke spec on the popped values, compare\n  the return against `comparand`, route to the matching `lt` /\n  `eq` / `gt` branch.\n\n### All slots are ring buffers; read mode varies\n\nThere is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells,\neach of `cell_capacity` bytes. The number of cells (`n_cells`) and\nthe read mode are both compile-time properties of the input port:\n\n- **1-cell + peek mode**: the value the producer wrote stays in the\n  cell. Tasks read via `slot_peek` — read without draining — and\n  every subsequent task on this consumer reads the same value\n  unless the producer overwrites it. Used for **single-push wires**\n  (a literal, or a wire from a producer box whose invocation count\n  is exactly 1). Multiple consumer tasks read the value as many\n  times as needed; the cell is never empty.\n- **N-cell + pop mode**: a queue. Producers push; consumers\n  `slot_pop` — drain one cell per task. Used for **multi-push wires**:\n  any wire whose producer has more than one task invocation\n  during the run. The producer's pushes accumulate, the consumer\n  drains in pop order.\n\nCompile-time analysis classifies each wire. A producer is\n\"runs-once\" if no transitive ancestor is an iterator; otherwise\nit's \"runs-N-times.\" Wires from runs-once producers get 1-cell\npeek slots; wires from runs-N-times producers get N-cell pop slots.\n\n`n_cells` for pop slots is sized for worst-case backlog (or a\ndefault like 64 with growth on demand). Lists grow if the producer\noutruns the consumer past the pre-allocation.\n\nFan-in: multiple producers pushing into the same N-cell pop slot\nland in arrival order. The consumer pops FIFO unless the cell\ncarries an ordering tag (see \"Cell tagging\" below).\n\n### Atomic-counter slot mode\n\nA slot allocated with `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` carries a single\n4-byte unsigned integer cell, read via a special op:\n\n```c\nuint32_t slot_read_inc(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod);\n// Returns the current value mod `mod`, then atomically increments\n// the underlying counter. Concurrent readers each get a distinct\n// value. Counter wraps at 2^32; mod handles N-branch routing.\n```\n\nUsed for iterator counters (issue 304): the iterator box has an\nauto-allocated `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot at load time; the\ndispatch action calls `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_branches)`\nto pick its output branch. Multiple iterator tasks can read\nconcurrently from the same counter slot in parallel — each gets a\nunique routing index — without any per-box mutable state and\nwithout the serial dependency of a self-push counter.\n\nThe slot's \"cell\" is just an `atomic_uint32_t`. No push is ever\nperformed; reads do the work. From the dispatch action's\nperspective it's just another slot; from the slot store's\nperspective the read op is special-cased.\n\n### Cell tagging (for parallel-iterator ordering)\n\nA cell can optionally carry a 4-byte ordering tag alongside its\nsize and data:\n\n```\nCell layout (N-cell pop slot)\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     filled_size\n4       4     tag      (0 if untagged; iterator counter snapshot otherwise)\n8       …     data\n```\n\nSlots created for wires from parallel iterators (issue 304) are\ntagged. Pop on a tagged slot returns the cell with the lowest tag,\nnot the head cell — preserving iterator-counter order across pushes\nthat arrived out of order from parallel iterator workers.\n\nUntagged slots default tag to 0 and pop FIFO at no extra cost. The\ntag-aware pop is a per-slot mode flag set at allocation time.\n\n### Asynchrony\nThe store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\nfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\nis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n\n## Slot layout\n\nEach slot is a header followed by `n_cells` cells, each `cell_capacity`\nbytes. The header tracks ring-buffer state and lifetime:\n\n```\nSlot header\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     cell_capacity   (bytes per cell, set at allocation)\n4       4     n_cells         (ring size, set at allocation)\n8       4     head            (read index, mod n_cells)\n12      4     tail            (write index, mod n_cells; cells_filled = tail - head)\n16      1     touched         (per-slot lock: 0=free, 1=another thread mutating)\n17      3     _pad\n20      …     cells           (n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes))\n```\n\nEach cell stores a 4-byte filled-size followed by `cell_capacity`\nbytes of value data. Cells have wildly different capacities across\nslots — capacity is per-slot, not global. The C convention of passing\nsizes alongside arrays applies: the task that allocates a slot knows\nhow big it needs the cells.\n\n`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any header mutation\n(push, pop, refcount changes). A reader that finds `touched == 1`\nspins until it clears. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock —\nif contention proves to matter, replace with a proper mutex without\nchanging the API.\n\nWrites to a cell complete with a memory barrier before `tail` is\nadvanced, so a reader that observes `head < tail` is guaranteed to\nsee the complete value at the head cell.\n\n## Lifetime\n\nSlots are owned by the box that holds the input port. They live\nfrom graph load until run end. There is no per-slot reference\ncounting and no end-of-stream propagation — the slot is freed\nwhen the run ends, alongside its owning box.\n\nRun termination is governed entirely by the pool's active-task\ncounter (issue 301): when no task is running and no further spawns\nare pending, the run is over. There's nothing the slot store needs\nto track to make this work.\n\n### No wait lists\n\nTasks never park on slots. Tasks are spawned by the dispatch\nlayer's spawn-on-input-arrival rule and run to completion; they\nnever block. A slot that has no value yet simply means the\nspawn rule hasn't fired for that consumer yet. No wait list,\nno per-slot wake-up traversal — just a check after each push.\n\n## Backing store\n\nSlots are allocated from process heap memory. The slot store owns a\nper-run allocator (described under \"Allocation strategy\" below) that\nhands out memory chunks to slots. Plain `malloc`-class memory is\nsufficient — every worker thread in the process can read and write\nit, and no spec ever needs to access it from a child process.\n\nSynchronization within a slot uses the per-slot `touched` flag for\nheader mutations. There is no allocator-wide mutex on the\nread/write path; only the per-size-class free lists in the\nallocator have their own locks.\n\n## Slot creation\n\nSlot creation happens at **graph load**, not per task. The graph\nloader walks every box, allocates one ring buffer per input port,\nand parks the slot on the box's per-port slot table. The dispatch\nlayer never allocates new slots at runtime in the steady state —\nall slots that will ever exist are created up front.\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);\n```\n\n`cell_capacity` and `n_cells` come from compile-time analysis of\nthe graph. Boxes downstream of iterators get larger `n_cells` to\nabsorb the iterator's worst-case backlog.\n\nIf a slot's pre-allocated `n_cells` proves too small at runtime\n(producer outpaces consumer beyond the pre-allocation), the slot's\nring grows — see \"Allocation strategy\" below.\n\n## C API surface\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc       (slot_store_t *s, int cell_capacity, int n_cells, int flags);\nvoid      slot_push        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size, uint32_t tag);\nint       slot_peek        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // 1-cell: read without draining\nint       slot_pop         (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // N-cell: drain head (or lowest-tag)\nuint32_t  slot_read_inc    (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod);            // SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER only\nint       slot_has_value   (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);                          // for spawn-rule check\n```\n\nFlags include:\n- `SLOT_TAGGED`: cells carry ordering tags; `slot_pop` returns the\n  lowest-tag cell.\n- `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER`: slot holds a single atomic uint32; reads\n  via `slot_read_inc` only. `slot_push` / `slot_peek` / `slot_pop`\n  are not valid on atomic-counter slots.\n\nPush always takes a `tag` argument; untagged slots ignore it (or\ntreat 0 as \"no order\").\n\n1-cell peek slot use: producer `push` once at startup (literal) or\nwhen its single invocation completes (single-push wire). All\nconsumer tasks `peek` to read the value as many times as their box\nruns. The cell is never empty after the initial push.\n\nN-cell pop slot use: producers `push` repeatedly. Consumer tasks\n`pop` one cell each. For tagged slots, `pop` returns the\nlowest-tag cell; for untagged, FIFO. Pop on an empty slot is a\nbug — the spawn rule guarantees the slot is non-empty before a\ntask spawns.\n\nThere is no `slot_ref` / `slot_unref` — slot lifetime is the run.\n\n## Submission timing\n\nTasks are spawned dynamically in response to slot pushes. Each box\nhas small per-box state used by the dispatch layer:\n\n```\nbox_runtime_state {\n    slot_id_t  *input_slots;     // one per input port (set at load)\n    int        *port_modes;      // PEEK or POP, per input port\n    int         n_inputs;\n    slot_id_t   counter_slot;    // iterator only: SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER slot;\n                                 // 0 / unused otherwise\n};\n```\n\nThe spawning rule:\n- When a producer pushes to one of a box's input slots, the\n  dispatch layer checks **does every input slot have a value\n  available?** \"Available\" means:\n  - For peek-mode (1-cell) slots: cell has been written at least\n    once. Once a peek slot is filled, it stays available — every\n    subsequent spawn-check on this box passes the peek-port check.\n  - For pop-mode (N-cell) slots: queue is non-empty.\n- If yes, spawn a `dispatch_task_t` and submit to the pool. The\n  task pops (or peeks) one value from each input slot when it\n  runs.\n- Each push that completes the input set triggers exactly one\n  spawn. Multiple pushes accumulate in pop slots; each pop\n  consumes one, and if more remain, the next push (or check)\n  re-fires the spawn rule.\n\nThis makes the pool's queue the rate buffer: pushes accumulate\nin pop slots (possibly multiple per slot), and one task per\naccumulated value gets spawned.\n\nTasks never block on slots. They're spawned after inputs are\nready, run to completion, and disappear. Blocking-and-waking\nmachinery is unnecessary — the spawn-on-arrival rule is the\nsynchronization primitive.\n\nThe pool's queue is the only queue. There is no separate \"blocked\ntasks\" structure.\n\n## Allocation strategy: size-class free lists with coalescing fallback\n\nThe slot store uses a segregated free-list allocator. The map is\nanalyzed at compile time to enumerate every distinct slot size the\ngraph will need (each call box declares its output slot size; each\nqueued-input ring declares its total size from cell capacity × queue\ndepth). The allocator builds one free list per distinct size class.\n\nVariable-size and unknown-size payloads (a long LLM response, an\narray whose length is not known until runtime) are handled by a\nseparate **large-value heap** described below — not by allocating\nhuge slots up front.\n\n### The lists\nEach size class is an array (or linked list) of free slots of exactly\nthat size. At startup, each list is pre-populated with enough slots\nto cover the static box count for that size. Lists grow during the\nrun if demand exceeds the pre-allocation.\n\nEach list has its own mutex — allocation and deallocation in different\nsize classes never contend with each other.\n\n### Allocation\nGiven a request for size N bytes:\n1. Find the smallest size class with `class_size ≥ N`.\n2. If that class has a free slot, pop it. Done.\n3. Otherwise, try the next larger size class. Repeat.\n4. If a larger class hits, the slot is oversized for the request.\n   Try to slice the unused tail into a residual slot. If the residual\n   is at least as large as the smallest size class, push it onto that\n   class's list. Otherwise skip the slice — oversize the allocation\n   and live with the waste until the slot is freed.\n5. If no size class has a free slot, attempt to coalesce: walk the\n   address-ordered chunk list looking for adjacent free chunks that\n   together meet the requested size. If found, merge them and return\n   the combined chunk.\n6. If coalescing fails, grow the region (see \"Growth\" below) and\n   append the new slots to the appropriate lists. Then try again.\n7. After steps 5 or 6 complete, queue a deferred cleanup task on the\n   pool. Cleanup runs on a worker thread later and walks the\n   chunk list to opportunistically coalesce contiguous free chunks\n   into the largest possible chunks. Cleanup is best-effort — it\n   does not block any other thread. If memory fragments faster than\n   cleanup can keep up, the next allocation grows the heap; that's\n   fine.\n\n### Deallocation\nWhen refcount drops to zero, the slot is pushed onto its size class's\nfree list. The deallocator also performs a cheap eager-coalesce step:\ncheck the slot's two physical neighbors; if either is free, merge\nthem and push the combined chunk onto the appropriate size class.\nThis is O(1) given the doubly-linked chunk list (see below) and keeps\nsmall-scale fragmentation in check without needing the deferred\ncleanup task to run.\n\n### Physical-order chunk list (for coalescing)\nCoalescing needs to know which chunks are physically adjacent in\nmemory. The size-class free lists don't carry that information.\n\nTwo viable representations:\n\n- **Doubly-linked list** of all chunks (free and allocated) in\n  address order. Splits and merges are O(1) given the chunk pointer.\n  Neighbor lookup is O(1). Pointer chasing is the cost.\n- **Two parallel arrays** (`start[i]`, `end[i]`) sorted by start\n  address. Lookup by binary search is O(log N), but inserts and\n  deletes are O(N) without an additional index. Cache-friendly to\n  scan.\n\nThe linked list is simpler and has the right asymptotic behavior for\nsplits/merges, which dominate. Start there. If profiling later shows\nlist traversal is hot, switch to the array form with an auxiliary\nindex — the API doesn't change.\n\n### Large-value heap (variable-size payloads)\n\nFor values whose size is not known at compile time — long LLM\nresponses, dynamically-sized arrays, anything where the upper bound\nis not a useful number to allocate — the slot does not hold the value\ndirectly. Instead, the slot holds a small fixed-size handle:\n\n```\n{ uint32_t size; uint32_t lvh_offset; }\n```\n\n`lvh_offset` points into a separate **large-value heap**, a\nplain `malloc`-backed region used only for variable-size payloads.\nWhen a box produces a 4 MB LLM response, the dispatch layer:\n1. Allocates 4 MB in the large-value heap.\n2. Writes the bytes there.\n3. Stores the handle (size = 4 MB, offset = …) in the slot.\n\nThe consumer reads the handle from the slot, follows the offset,\ncopies the bytes (or works with them in place). When the slot's\nrefcount hits zero, the slot's deallocator also frees the\nlarge-value-heap region.\n\nThe slot allocator is unchanged — it always sees fixed-size slots.\nThe two-tier approach keeps the hot path simple while still\nsupporting unbounded outputs.\n\nA box opts into large-value output by declaring its output as\n\"variable-size\" in the graph. Compile-time-known outputs use the\nfixed-size path with no indirection.\n\n### Growth\nWhen all size-class lists are exhausted and coalescing cannot satisfy\na request, the allocator grows by calling `malloc` for a new region,\ndividing it into slots, and appending them to the relevant size-class\nlists. Plain heap memory is fine — no spec needs cross-process access\nto slot memory.\n\n### Why this design\n- Compile-time enumeration makes every common allocation a single\n  pop from a list. No size-comparison loops, no walks of free space.\n- Slicing residuals cannot fragment beyond the granularity of the\n  smallest declared size class, since smaller residuals are simply\n  not split.\n- Coalescing is the safety valve for unusual allocation patterns,\n  and it costs nothing on the common path.\n- Growth is rare — if pre-allocation matches static demand, it never\n  fires.\n\n## No type tags\n\nSlots store opaque bytes. The producer wrote N bytes; the consumer\nreads N bytes. What those bytes mean is the language spec's business\non each side, and the wire's metadata in the graph (issue 219's\ncompiler can check producer-output type vs consumer-input type at\nbuild time). The slot store does not interpret values — it does not\nneed to know if they are strings, numbers, JSON, images, or anything\nelse. Removed the type-tag field from the header for that reason.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.\n2. Unit test single-value slots: thread A writes, thread B reads,\n   refcount decrements, slot freed when last ref dropped.\n3. Unit test ring-buffer slots: multiple producers push, single consumer\n   drains in order, no values lost or duplicated.\n4. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: shared memory created at\n   startup, store handle passed to the dispatch layer.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point, owns the shared memory region\n- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task dispatch reads/writes slots\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued input model that\n  ring-buffer slots implement\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2\n",

        "content":"1\t# 302 — Per-task slot store with wire-held references\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\tWire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values\n8\thave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\n9\taccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n10\t\n11\t## Concept\n12\t\n13\t### Slots belong to input ports, not tasks\n14\t\n15\tEach box has **one slot per input port**, allocated when the graph\n16\tloads and persisting for the life of the run. A wire is a routing\n17\tdeclaration: \"the producer's output port pushes a copy of its value\n18\tinto this consumer's named input slot.\" The producer never owns a\n19\tslot — its output is a routing event, not a stored value.\n20\t\n21\tWhen a producer fires, the dispatch layer copies the value into\n22\tevery downstream input slot wired to that output. Fan-out is N\n23\tpushes (one per consumer); fan-in is N producers all pushing into\n24\tthe same consumer's slot. Both behaviors fall out of the same\n25\tpush-into-input-slot mechanic.\n26\t\n27\tSlots live in process heap memory, accessible to every worker\n28\tthread. Cross-process visibility is not required: language specs\n29\t(issue 303) only ever receive byte pointers — never raw slot\n30\taddresses — so out-of-process specs (Bash) work via sockets, not\n31\tshared memory.\n32\t\n33\t### Tasks are ephemeral; box state is durable\n34\t\n35\tA **task** is one invocation: pop one value from each of the box's\n36\tinput slots, run the box's logic, push the output to every\n37\tdownstream input slot. Tasks have no persistent identity — they're\n38\tjust stack frames on workers. Tasks are spawned dynamically by the\n39\tdispatch layer when a box's input set is ready (every input slot\n40\tholds at least one value).\n41\t\n42\tThe **box** is the durable thing: it owns its input port slots, any\n43\tcounter state (for iterators), its language spec handle, and so\n44\ton. The box exists from graph load until run end. Tasks come and\n45\tgo.\n46\t\n47\tThis is uniform across iterator and non-iterator boxes. Both run N\n48\ttimes where N depends on how many invocations their inputs supply\n49\t(possibly 1, possibly thousands). The difference is just what the\n50\ttask does:\n51\t- **Plain call task**: invoke spec on the popped values, push the\n52\t  return to outputs.\n53\t- **Iterator task**: read box's counter, route the popped value to\n54\t  output port `iterator_outputs[counter]`, increment counter mod N.\n55\t  No spec invocation.\n56\t- **Comparator task**: invoke spec on the popped values, compare\n57\t  the return against `comparand`, route to the matching `lt` /\n58\t  `eq` / `gt` branch.\n59\t\n60\t### All slots are ring buffers; read mode varies\n61\t\n62\tThere is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells,\n63\teach of `cell_capacity` bytes. The number of cells (`n_cells`) and\n64\tthe read mode are both compile-time properties of the input port:\n65\t\n66\t- **1-cell + peek mode**: the value the producer wrote stays in the\n67\t  cell. Tasks read via `slot_peek` — read without draining — and\n68\t  every subsequent task on this consumer reads the same value\n69\t  unless the producer overwrites it. Used for **single-push wires**\n70\t  (a literal, or a wire from a producer box whose invocation count\n71\t  is exactly 1). Multiple consumer tasks read the value as many\n72\t  times as needed; the cell is never empty.\n73\t- **N-cell + pop mode**: a queue. Producers push; consumers\n74\t  `slot_pop` — drain one cell per task. Used for **multi-push wires**:\n75\t  any wire whose producer has more than one task invocation\n76\t  during the run. The producer's pushes accumulate, the consumer\n77\t  drains in pop order.\n78\t\n79\tCompile-time analysis classifies each wire. A producer is\n80\t\"runs-once\" if no transitive ancestor is an iterator; otherwise\n81\tit's \"runs-N-times.\" Wires from runs-once producers get 1-cell\n82\tpeek slots; wires from runs-N-times producers get N-cell pop slots.\n83\t\n84\t`n_cells` for pop slots is sized for worst-case backlog (or a\n85\tdefault like 64 with growth on demand). Lists grow if the producer\n86\toutruns the consumer past the pre-allocation.\n87\t\n88\tFan-in: multiple producers pushing into the same N-cell pop slot\n89\tland in arrival order. The consumer pops FIFO unless the cell\n90\tcarries an ordering tag (see \"Cell tagging\" below).\n91\t\n92\t### Atomic-counter slot mode\n93\t\n94\tA slot allocated with `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` carries a single\n95\t4-byte unsigned integer cell, read via a special op:\n96\t\n97\t```c\n98\tuint32_t slot_read_inc(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod);\n99\t// Returns the current value mod `mod`, then atomically increments\n100\t// the underlying counter. Concurrent readers each get a distinct\n101\t// value. Counter wraps at 2^32; mod handles N-branch routing.\n102\t```\n103\t\n104\tUsed for iterator counters (issue 304): the iterator box has an\n105\tauto-allocated `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot at load time; the\n106\tdispatch action calls `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_branches)`\n107\tto pick its output branch. Multiple iterator tasks can read\n108\tconcurrently from the same counter slot in parallel — each gets a\n109\tunique routing index — without any per-box mutable state and\n110\twithout the serial dependency of a self-push counter.\n111\t\n112\tThe slot's \"cell\" is just an `atomic_uint32_t`. No push is ever\n113\tperformed; reads do the work. From the dispatch action's\n114\tperspective it's just another slot; from the slot store's\n115\tperspective the read op is special-cased.\n116\t\n117\t### Cell tagging (for parallel-iterator ordering)\n118\t\n119\tA cell can optionally carry a 4-byte ordering tag alongside its\n120\tsize and data:\n121\t\n122\t```\n123\tCell layout (N-cell pop slot)\n124\tOffset  Size  Field\n125\t------  ----  -----\n126\t0       4     filled_size\n127\t4       4     tag      (0 if untagged; iterator counter snapshot otherwise)\n128\t8       …     data\n129\t```\n130\t\n131\tSlots created for wires from parallel iterators (issue 304) are\n132\ttagged. Pop on a tagged slot returns the cell with the lowest tag,\n133\tnot the head cell — preserving iterator-counter order across pushes\n134\tthat arrived out of order from parallel iterator workers.\n135\t\n136\tUntagged slots default tag to 0 and pop FIFO at no extra cost. The\n137\ttag-aware pop is a per-slot mode flag set at allocation time.\n138\t\n139\t### Asynchrony\n140\tThe store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\n141\tfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\n142\tis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n143\t\n144\t## Slot layout\n145\t\n146\tEach slot is a header followed by `n_cells` cells, each `cell_capacity`\n147\tbytes. The header tracks ring-buffer state and lifetime:\n148\t\n149\t```\n150\tSlot header\n151\tOffset  Size  Field\n152\t------  ----  -----\n153\t0       4     cell_capacity   (bytes per cell, set at allocation)\n154\t4       4     n_cells         (ring size, set at allocation)\n155\t8       4     head            (read index, mod n_cells)\n156\t12      4     tail            (write index, mod n_cells; cells_filled = tail - head)\n157\t16      1     touched         (per-slot lock: 0=free, 1=another thread mutating)\n158\t17      3     _pad\n159\t20      …     cells           (n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes))\n160\t```\n161\t\n162\tEach cell stores a 4-byte filled-size followed by `cell_capacity`\n163\tbytes of value data. Cells have wildly different capacities across\n164\tslots — capacity is per-slot, not global. The C convention of passing\n165\tsizes alongside arrays applies: the task that allocates a slot knows\n166\thow big it needs the cells.\n167\t\n168\t`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any header mutation\n169\t(push, pop, refcount changes). A reader that finds `touched == 1`\n170\tspins until it clears. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock —\n171\tif contention proves to matter, replace with a proper mutex without\n172\tchanging the API.\n173\t\n174\tWrites to a cell complete with a memory barrier before `tail` is\n175\tadvanced, so a reader that observes `head < tail` is guaranteed to\n176\tsee the complete value at the head cell.\n177\t\n178\t## Lifetime\n179\t\n180\tSlots are owned by the box that holds the input port. They live\n181\tfrom graph load until run end. There is no per-slot reference\n182\tcounting and no end-of-stream propagation — the slot is freed\n183\twhen the run ends, alongside its owning box.\n184\t\n185\tRun termination is governed entirely by the pool's active-task\n186\tcounter (issue 301): when no task is running and no further spawns\n187\tare pending, the run is over. There's nothing the slot store needs\n188\tto track to make this work.\n189\t\n190\t### No wait lists\n191\t\n192\tTasks never park on slots. Tasks are spawned by the dispatch\n193\tlayer's spawn-on-input-arrival rule and run to completion; they\n194\tnever block. A slot that has no value yet simply means the\n195\tspawn rule hasn't fired for that consumer yet. No wait list,\n196\tno per-slot wake-up traversal — just a check after each push.\n197\t\n198\t## Backing store\n199\t\n200\tSlots are allocated from process heap memory. The slot store owns a\n201\tper-run allocator (described under \"Allocation strategy\" below) that\n202\thands out memory chunks to slots. Plain `malloc`-class memory is\n203\tsufficient — every worker thread in the process can read and write\n204\tit, and no spec ever needs to access it from a child process.\n205\t\n206\tSynchronization within a slot uses the per-slot `touched` flag for\n207\theader mutations. There is no allocator-wide mutex on the\n208\tread/write path; only the per-size-class free lists in the\n209\tallocator have their own locks.\n210\t\n211\t## Slot creation\n212\t\n213\tSlot creation happens at **graph load**, not per task. The graph\n214\tloader walks every box, allocates one ring buffer per input port,\n215\tand parks the slot on the box's per-port slot table. Boxes downstream of iterators get larger `n_cells` to\n225\tabsorb the iterator's worst-case backlog.\n226\t\n227\tIf a slot's pre-allocated `n_cells` proves too small at runtime\n228\t(producer outpaces consumer beyond the pre-allocation), the slot's\n229\tring grows — see \"Allocation strategy\" below.\n230\t\n231\t## C API surface\n232\t\n233\t```c\n234\tslot_id_t slot_alloc       (slot_store_t *s, int cell_capacity, int n_cells, int flags);\n235\tvoid      slot_push        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size, uint32_t tag);\n236\tint       slot_peek        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // 1-cell: read without draining\n237\tint       slot_pop         (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // N-cell: drain head (or lowest-tag)\n238\tuint32_t  slot_read_inc    (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod);            // SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER only\n239\tint       slot_has_value   (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);                          // for spawn-rule check\n240\t```\n241\t\n242\tFlags include:\n243\t- `SLOT_TAGGED`: cells carry ordering tags; `slot_pop` returns the\n244\t  lowest-tag cell.\n245\t- `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER`: slot holds a single atomic uint32; reads\n246\t  via `slot_read_inc` only. `slot_push` / `slot_peek` / `slot_pop`\n247\t  are not valid on atomic-counter slots.\n248\t\n249\tPush always takes a `tag` argument; untagged slots ignore it (or\n250\ttreat 0 as \"no order\").\n251\t\n252\t1-cell peek slot use: producer `push` once at startup (literal) or\n253\twhen its single invocation completes (single-push wire). Multiple pushes accumulate in pop slots; each pop\n293\t  consumes one, and if more remain, the next push (or check)\n294\t  re-fires the spawn rule.\n295\t\n296\tThis makes the pool's queue the rate buffer: pushes accumulate\n297\tin pop slots (possibly multiple per slot), and one task per\n298\taccumulated value gets spawned.\n299\t\n300\tTasks never block on slots. They're spawned after inputs are\n301\tready, run to completion, and disappear. Blocking-and-waking\n302\tmachinery is unnecessary — the spawn-on-arrival rule is the\n303\tsynchronization primitive.\n304\t\n305\tThe pool's queue is the only queue. There is no separate \"blocked\n306\ttasks\" structure.\n307\t\n308\t## Allocation strategy: size-class free lists with coalescing fallback\n309\t\n310\tThe slot store uses a segregated free-list allocator. The map is\n311\tanalyzed at compile time to enumerate every distinct slot size the\n312\tgraph will need (each call box declares its output slot size; each\n313\tqueued-input ring declares its total size from cell capacity × queue\n314\tdepth). The allocator builds one free list per distinct size class.\n315\t\n316\tVariable-size and unknown-size payloads (a long LLM response, an\n317\tarray whose length is not known until runtime) are handled by a\n318\tseparate **large-value heap** described below — not by allocating\n319\thuge slots up front.\n320\t\n321\t### The lists\n322\tEach size class is an array (or linked list) of free slots of exactly\n323\tthat size. At startup, each list is pre-populated with enough slots\n324\tto cover the static box count for that size. Lists grow during the\n325\trun if demand exceeds the pre-allocation.\n326\t\n327\tEach list has its own mutex — allocation and deallocation in different\n328\tsize classes never contend with each other.\n329\t\n330\t### Allocation\n331\tGiven a request for size N bytes:\n332\t1. Find the smallest size class with `class_size ≥ N`.\n333\t2. If that class has a free slot, pop it. Done.\n334\t3. Otherwise, try the next larger size class. Repeat.\n335\t4. If a larger class hits, the slot is oversized for the request.\n336\t   Try to slice the unused tail into a residual slot. If the residual\n337\t   is at least as large as the smallest size class, push it onto that\n338\t   class's list. Otherwise skip the slice — oversize the allocation\n339\t   and live with the waste until the slot is freed.\n340\t5. If no size class has a free slot, attempt to coalesce: walk the\n341\t   address-ordered chunk list looking for adjacent free chunks that\n342\t   together meet the requested size. If found, merge them and return\n343\t   the combined chunk.\n344\t6. If coalescing fails, grow the region (see \"Growth\" below) and\n345\t   append the new slots to the appropriate lists. Then try again.\n346\t7. After steps 5 or 6 complete, queue a deferred cleanup task on the\n347\t   pool. Cleanup runs on a worker thread later and walks the\n348\t   chunk list to opportunistically coalesce contiguous free chunks\n349\t   into the largest possible chunks. Cleanup is best-effort — it\n350\t   does not block any other thread. If memory fragments faster than\n351\t   cleanup can keep up, the next allocation grows the heap; that's\n352\t   fine.\n353\t\n354\t### Deallocation\n355\tWhen refcount drops to zero, the slot is pushed onto its size class's\n356\tfree list. The deallocator also performs a cheap eager-coalesce step:\n357\tcheck the slot's two physical neighbors; if either is free, merge\n358\tthem and push the combined chunk onto the appropriate size class.\n359\tThis is O(1) given the doubly-linked chunk list (see below) and keeps\n360\tsmall-scale fragmentation in check without needing the deferred\n361\tcleanup task to run.\n362\t\n363\t### Physical-order chunk list (for coalescing)\n364\tCoalescing needs to know which chunks are physically adjacent in\n365\tmemory. The size-class free lists don't carry that information.\n366\t\n367\tTwo viable representations:\n368\t\n369\t- **Doubly-linked list** of all chunks (free and allocated) in\n370\t  address order. Splits and merges are O(1) given the chunk pointer.\n371\t  Neighbor lookup is O(1). Pointer chasing is the cost.\n372\t- **Two parallel arrays** (`start[i]`, `end[i]`) sorted by start\n373\t  address. Lookup by binary search is O(log N), but inserts and\n374\t  deletes are O(N) without an additional index. Cache-friendly to\n375\t  scan.\n376\t\n377\tThe linked list is simpler and has the right asymptotic behavior for\n378\tsplits/merges, which dominate. Start there. If profiling later shows\n379\tlist traversal is hot, switch to the array form with an auxiliary\n380\tindex — the API doesn't change.\n381\t\n382\t### Large-value heap (variable-size payloads)\n383\t\n384\tFor values whose size is not known at compile time — long LLM\n385\tresponses, dynamically-sized arrays, anything where the upper bound\n386\tis not a useful number to allocate — the slot does not hold the value\n387\tdirectly. Instead, the slot holds a small fixed-size handle:\n388\t\n389\t```\n390\t{ uint32_t size; uint32_t lvh_offset; }\n391\t```\n392\t\n393\t`lvh_offset` points into a separate **large-value heap**, a\n394\tplain `malloc`-backed region used only for variable-size payloads.\n395\tWhen a box produces a 4 MB LLM response, the dispatch layer:\n396\t1. Allocates 4 MB in the large-value heap.\n397\t2. Writes the bytes there.\n398\t3. Stores the handle (size = 4 MB, offset = …) in the slot.\n399\t\n400\tThe consumer reads the handle from the slot, follows the offset,\n401\tcopies the bytes (or works with them in place). When the slot's\n402\trefcount hits zero, the slot's deallocator also frees the\n403\tlarge-value-heap region.\n404\t\n405\tThe slot allocator is unchanged — it always sees fixed-size slots.\n406\tThe two-tier approach keeps the hot path simple while still\n407\tsupporting unbounded outputs.\n408\t\n409\tA box opts into large-value output by declaring its output as\n410\t\"variable-size\" in the graph. Compile-time-known outputs use the\n411\tfixed-size path with no indirection.\n412\t\n413\t### Growth\n414\tWhen all size-class lists are exhausted and coalescing cannot satisfy\n415\ta request, the allocator grows by calling `malloc` for a new region,\n416\tdividing it into slots, and appending them to the relevant size-class\n417\tlists. Plain heap memory is fine — no spec needs cross-process access\n418\tto slot memory.\n419\t\n420\t### Why this design\n421\t- Compile-time enumeration makes every common allocation a single\n422\t  pop from a list. No size-comparison loops, no walks of free space.\n423\t- Slicing residuals cannot fragment beyond the granularity of the\n424\t  smallest declared size class, since smaller residuals are simply\n425\t  not split.\n426\t- Coalescing is the safety valve for unusual allocation patterns,\n427\t  and it costs nothing on the common path.\n428\t- Growth is rare — if pre-allocation matches static demand, it never\n429\t  fires.\n430\t\n431\t## No type tags\n432\t\n433\tSlots store opaque bytes. The producer wrote N bytes; the consumer\n434\treads N bytes. What those bytes mean is the language spec's business\n435\ton each side, and the wire's metadata in the graph (issue 219's\n436\tcompiler can check producer-output type vs consumer-input type at\n437\tbuild time). The slot store does not interpret values — it does not\n438\tneed to know if they are strings, numbers, JSON, images, or anything\n439\telse. Removed the type-tag field from the header for that reason.\n440\t\n441\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n442\t1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.\n443\t2. Unit test single-value slots: thread A writes, thread B reads,\n444\t   refcount decrements, slot freed when last ref dropped.\n445\t3. Unit test ring-buffer slots: multiple producers push, single consumer\n446\t   drains in order, no values lost or duplicated.\n447\t4. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: shared memory created at\n448\t   startup, store handle passed to the dispatch layer.\n449\t\n450\t## Relevant files\n451\t- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point, owns the shared memory region\n452\t- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)\n453\t- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n454\t- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task dispatch reads/writes slots\n455\t- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued input model that\n456\t  ring-buffer slots implement\n457\t- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2\n458\t"

      "content":"# 304 — Task dispatch layer (C, replaces synchronous executor)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe synchronous executor at `src/004-executor.lua` walks the graph in\ndependency order, calling each box's driver, capturing stdout, decoding\nJSON, and propagating values to downstream boxes. Single-threaded,\nblocking, runs in Lua coroutines.\n\n## Concept\n\nThe task dispatch layer is the C component that runs inside each pool\nworker. The pool calls a single C action — `dispatch_action` — per\ntask. That action is the one place in the runtime that:\n\n- Reads from and writes to slots\n- Calls `lang_spec->invoke`\n- Picks the output branch per `routing.kind` (issue 233)\n- Pushes the function's output to the picked branch's downstream\n  input slots, triggering downstream task spawns\n\nThere is no Lua-level executor in the phase 3 path. `004-executor.lua`\nis replaced wholesale.\n\n## Task struct\n\nA task is one ephemeral invocation of a box. Its struct carries\njust the box ID:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    int  box_id;          // index into the graph's box array\n} dispatch_task_t;\n```\n\nThere is no per-task counter. Iterator counter state lives in a\n`SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot owned by the box (see issue 302); the\naction reads and atomically increments it via `slot_read_inc`\nwhen it needs the routing index.\n\nThere is no `input_slots` or `output_slot` array on the task —\nthe box's input slots are durable per-box state (see issue 302).\nThe action looks them up through `box_runtime_state[box_id]`.\n\nOutput is a routing event, not a stored value. When the action\nfinishes, it pushes copies of the return value into the input\nslots of every downstream box wired to this output (or only the\nmatching branch for comparators and iterators).\n\nTasks are spawned by the dispatch layer's \"spawn on input ready\"\nrule (issue 302). Each spawn allocates a fresh `dispatch_task_t`\non the pool's task allocator, pre-populated with the box ID. The\naction's first read of the input slots is what drains them — pop\nor peek one cell per input port, per the port's mode.\n\n## The dispatch action\n\n```c\naction_result_t dispatch_action(task_ctx_t *ctx, void *arg);\n```\n\nPhases, in order:\n\n### 1. Read inputs into byte buffers\n\nTasks are spawned only when every input port has a value\navailable (issue 302's spawn-on-input-ready rule), so the action\ndoes not need to check or block — input availability is the spawn\nprecondition.\n\nFor each input port:\n- **Peek-mode (1-cell) port**: `slot_peek` into a heap buffer.\n  The cell is not drained; subsequent tasks on this box read the\n  same value.\n- **Pop-mode (N-cell) port**: `slot_pop` into a heap buffer. One\n  cell drains; values queued behind it remain. For tagged slots,\n  pop returns the lowest-tag cell; for untagged, FIFO.\n\nVariable-size payloads work via the large-value heap (issue 302):\nthe cell holds a `{size, offset}` handle that points into the\nheap; the spec follows the handle if it needs the bytes.\n\nBuffers are freed when the action ends.\n\n### 3. Dispatch is uniform across routing kinds\n\nEvery call box runs its function (phase 4) and pushes the\nfunction's output (phase 5). The only thing that varies is which\ndownstream branch receives the push (phase 5b — the branch-pick).\n\nBoxes carry an optional `routing` field (issue 233):\n- No `routing`: plain call. Function runs; output fans to all\n  outgoing wires unconditionally.\n- `routing.kind: \"comparator\"`: function runs; output is\n  compared to `comparand`; only the matching `lt` / `eq` / `gt`\n  branch fires.\n- `routing.kind: \"iterator\"`: function runs; output is routed to\n  `outputs[slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs)]`.\n- `routing.kind: \"randomizer\" / \"weighted\" / \"distributor\"`:\n  function runs; output is routed by the kind-specific rule.\n\nThe function always runs. There is no \"iterator skips invoke\"\ncase — the iterator differs from a plain call only in how the\nfunction's output is routed, not in whether the function runs.\nIterators that want passthrough behavior use an identity function\n(or the editor defaults to one when no `ref`/`fn` is set).\n\n### 4. Invoke (every call box)\nLook up the box's language spec by its `lang` field. Find the\nworker's language handle in `current_worker->handles[lang_idx]`.\nCall `lang->invoke` with:\n- `handle` — the per-worker language runtime state\n- `file_path`, `fn_name` — the box's function source\n- `input_data[]`, `input_sizes[]` — pointers and sizes for each\n  input buffer\n- `out_buf`, `out_buf_capacity`, `*out_size` — the output buffer the\n  spec writes into\n\nThe spec is the bridge between the language's native call convention\nand bytes. Inside `invoke` it:\n1. Loads the function (cached: e.g. `luaL_loadfile` once per file,\n   `dlsym` once per function).\n2. Pushes the input bytes into the language's native types (Lua\n   strings on the Lua stack, C pointers in registers, etc.).\n3. Calls the function and receives the return value in the language's\n   native form.\n4. Serializes the return value back into bytes in `out_buf` and\n   sets `*out_size`.\n5. Returns 0 for success, nonzero for any failure.\n\nNonzero return aborts the program (issue 303).\n\nThe output buffer for `invoke` is heap-allocated to the box's\ndeclared maximum output size. If the box's output is variable-size\n(uses the large-value heap, issue 302), the spec writes into that\nheap and stores the handle in `out_buf`.\n\n### 5. Write output (push to downstream input slots)\n\nThe action picks the branch (or branches) and pushes the\nfunction's output. Branch picking dispatches on `routing.kind`:\n\n- **No routing field** (plain call): push to every outgoing\n  connection.\n- **comparator**: compare output to `comparand`, push to the\n  matching `lt` / `eq` / `gt` connection only.\n- **iterator**: `idx = slot_read_inc(box->counter_slot,\n  n_outputs)`; push to the connection at branch `out_idx`.\n- **randomizer / weighted / distributor**: kind-specific rule,\n  same shape (compute `idx`, push to that one connection). See\n  issue 233 for the rules.\n\nFor routing kinds that derive an order tag (iterator,\nrandomizer, weighted), the push carries `tag = idx` so consumers\ndownstream of parallel iterators preserve order.\n\nAfter each push, the spawn-on-input-ready check (issue 302) fires\non the receiving box. If that push completes its input set, a\nfresh task spawns for the consumer.\n\n### 6. (No phase 6)\n\nSlots are durable for the run; tasks don't unref. Run termination\nis governed by the pool's active-task counter (issue 301). The\ndispatch action goes from phase 5 directly to phase 7.\n\n### 7. Post-action: nothing for the action itself\n\nRouting already happened in phase 5. Counter advancement, where\napplicable, happened inside `slot_read_inc` during phase 5 (the\nread-and-increment is the same op). No box-level mutable state\nneeds touching here.\n\n### 8. Return ACT_DONE\nThe action completes. The pool decrements the active-task counter\n(issue 301). If the counter reaches zero and the runner is waiting,\nthe run ends.\n\n## Initial submission\n\nAt startup, the pool runner walks the graph and pushes the\nliteral-input values (from `value` fields on input ports) directly\ninto the corresponding input slots. Boxes whose input set becomes\nfully populated by literals — entry-point boxes — immediately\nsatisfy the spawn-on-input-ready condition, and their first task\ngets queued. From there, every subsequent task spawn follows from\nthe regular phase-5 push → spawn-check chain.\n\nIterator counter state starts at 0; literal-only entry iterators\nspawn their first task at startup and increment from there.\n\n## Iterator counter and parallel iteration\n\nThe iterator's counter lives in a `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot\nallocated for the box at graph load time (issue 302). The\ndispatch action reads and increments it atomically, mid-action:\n\n```c\nuint32_t branch_idx = slot_read_inc(box->counter_slot, n_iter_outputs);\nslot_push(downstream[branch_idx].input_slot, output_buf, output_size,\n          /* tag = */ branch_idx);\n```\n\n`slot_read_inc` returns the current counter value `mod\nn_iter_outputs` and atomically advances the underlying counter.\nConcurrent iterator tasks on different workers each call\n`slot_read_inc` independently and each get a unique value —\n**iterator tasks parallelize across workers**, picking distinct\nbranches without coordination.\n\nNo box-side mutable state, no per-task counter snapshot. The\ncounter is just data in a slot the dispatch layer reads.\n\n## Cross-iterator pairing under parallel iteration\n\nWith parallel iterator tasks, push ordering at the consumer is\nnon-deterministic — task 6 of iterator A may push to consumer C\nbefore task 5 if 6 happened to land on a faster worker. FIFO pop\nat C would consume them out of iteration order.\n\nThe fix is **counter-tagged pushes**. Each iterator push (in phase\n5) carries the counter value the action read for this invocation:\n\n```c\nslot_push(downstream.input_slot, output_buf, output_size,\n          /* tag = */ branch_idx_or_counter_snapshot);\n```\n\nConsumer slots downstream of iterators are allocated with the\n`SLOT_TAGGED` flag (issue 302). `slot_pop` on a tagged slot\nreturns the cell with the lowest tag — preserving iterator-counter\norder regardless of push race.\n\nCompile-time analysis decides which slots are tagged: any slot\nwhose feeding wire originates (transitively, through a fan-out\nchain) at an iterator branch gets tagged. Slots not downstream of\niterators are untagged and pop FIFO at no extra cost.\n\nPlain-call and comparator pushes carry tag = 0 (or the snapshot of\ntheir own iterator-ancestor's counter, if applicable, propagated\nthrough their phase-5 pushes). Tags compose naturally through\nmulti-hop chains.\n\n### Cross-iterator pairing of multiple iterator inputs\n\nWhen non-iterator consumer C has two input ports wired from two\ndifferent iterators A and B, each input port has its own tagged\nqueue. Both queues pop in tag order independently:\n- C's task K pops the K-th tag from A's queue (which equals A's\n  K-th invocation's value).\n- The same K-th tag from B's queue.\n\nPairing by tag = `(A_K, B_K)` for every K, deterministic\nregardless of which iterator's tasks run faster.\n\n## Routing kinds (issue 233)\n\nEvery call box runs its function. Routing kinds differ only in\nhow the function's output is dispatched to downstream\nconnections:\n\n| `routing.kind`   | Output ports        | Branch picker                                                |\n|------------------|---------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|\n| (absent / plain) | single port         | fan to all outgoing connections                              |\n| `comparator`     | `lt` / `eq` / `gt`  | compare(output, comparand) → lt/eq/gt                        |\n| `iterator`       | `out_0` … `out_N-1` | `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, N)`                             |\n| `randomizer`     | `out_0` … `out_N-1` | `hash(slot_read_inc(counter_slot, MAX)) % N`                 |\n| `weighted`       | `out_0` … `out_N-1` | cumulative-band lookup against a counter scaled to PRECISION |\n| `distributor`    | `out_0` … `out_N-1` | argmin over downstream slot fill levels                      |\n\nPlain call (no `routing` field) skips the branch picker entirely\n— phase 5 fans the output to all wires. The function still runs\nthe same as for any branched call. Issue 233 carries the schema\nand the per-kind UI.\n\n## Open questions\n\n(none currently — earlier questions resolved as follows:)\n\n- Output buffer sizing: heap-allocated to the box's declared output\n  size at runtime. No fixed cap. Variable-size outputs go through the\n  large-value heap (issue 302).\n- Queued-input slot lifetime: producers hold refs while alive,\n  consumer holds a ref while consuming, slot freed when all drop.\n  References are the producer-liveness tracking mechanism.\n- Comparator output encoding: dispatch layer handles comparison\n  semantics directly. No spec involvement, no encoded \"branch tag\" in\n  the slot — the branch is a routing-time value computed by the\n  dispatch layer from the input.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Define `dispatch_task_t` and the `dispatch_action` skeleton.\n2. Implement phase 1 (input check + ACT_BLOCK on slot wait list).\n3. Implement phase 2 (input read into heap-allocated buffers).\n4. Implement phase 4 (invoke for plain call boxes).\n5. Implement phase 5 (output write via slot_push).\n6. Implement phase 6 (unref consumed single-value inputs).\n7. Smoke test: `hello` map (one plain call box, no routing) end-to-end\n   through the pool. Assert the output slot contains the expected\n   value.\n8. Implement plain-call fan-out firing (phase 7, plain case).\n9. Implement comparator routing (phase 3 + phase 7 comparator case).\n   Test `branch-test` map.\n10. Implement iterator routing and self-respawn (phase 3 + phase 7\n    iterator case). Test an iterator map.\n11. Wire up entry-box initial submission in the pool runner.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — synchronous executor that this layer replaces\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool that runs this action\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot API used here\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — `invoke` interface called here\n- `issues/221-iterator-box.md` — iterator routing and self-rescheduling\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator routing\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued-input slot semantics\n",

Iterator counter state lives in a\n39\t`SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot owned by the box (see issue 302); the\n40\taction reads and atomically increments it via `slot_read_inc`\n41\twhen it needs the routing index.\n42\t\n43\tThere is no `input_slots` or `output_slot` array on the task —\n44\tthe box's input slots are durable per-box state (see issue 302).\n45\tThe action looks them up through `box_runtime_state[box_id]`.\n46\t\n47\tOutput is a routing event, not a stored value. When the action\n48\tfinishes, it pushes copies of the return value into the input\n49\tslots of every downstream box wired to this output (or only the\n50\tmatching branch for comparators and iterators).\n51\t\n52\tTasks are spawned by the dispatch layer's \"spawn on input ready\"\n53\trule (issue 302). Each spawn allocates a fresh `dispatch_task_t`\n54\ton the pool's task allocator, pre-populated with the box ID. The\n55\taction's first read of the input slots is what drains them — pop\n56\tor peek one cell per input port, per the port's mode.\n57\t\n58\t## The dispatch action\n59\t\n60\t```c\n61\taction_result_t dispatch_action(task_ctx_t *ctx, void *arg);\n62\t```\n63\t\n64\tPhases, in order:\n65\t\n66\t### 1. Read inputs into byte buffers\n67\t\n68\tTasks are spawned only when every input port has a value\n69\tavailable (issue 302's spawn-on-input-ready rule), so the action\n70\tdoes not need to check or block — input availability is the spawn\n71\tprecondition.\n72\t\n73\tFor each input port:\n74\t- **Peek-mode (1-cell) port**: `slot_peek` into a heap buffer.\n75\t  The cell is not drained; subsequent tasks on this box read the\n76\t  same value.\n77\t- **Pop-mode (N-cell) port**: `slot_pop` into a heap buffer. One\n78\t  cell drains; values queued behind it remain. For tagged slots,\n79\t  pop returns the lowest-tag cell; for untagged, FIFO.\n80\t\n81\tVariable-size payloads work via the large-value heap (issue 302):\n82\tthe cell holds a `{size, offset}` handle that points into the\n83\theap; the spec follows the handle if it needs the bytes.\n84\t\n85\tBuffers are freed when the action ends.\n86\t\n87\t### 3. Dispatch is uniform across routing kinds\n88\t\n89\tEvery call box runs its function (phase 4) and pushes the\n90\tfunction's output (phase 5). The only thing that varies is which\n91\tdownstream branch receives the push (phase 5b — the branch-pick).\n92\t\n93\tBoxes carry an optional `routing` field (issue 233):\n94\t- No `routing`: plain call. Function runs; output fans to all\n95\t  outgoing wires unconditionally.\n96\t- `routing.kind: \"comparator\"`: function runs; output is\n97\t  compared to `comparand`; only the matching `lt` / `eq` / `gt`\n98\t  branch fires.\n99\t- `routing.kind: \"iterator\"`: function runs; output is routed to\n100\t  `outputs[slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs)]`.\n101\t- `routing.kind: \"randomizer\" / \"weighted\" / \"distributor\"`:\n102\t  function runs; output is routed by the kind-specific rule.\n103\t\n104\tThe function always runs. There is no \"iterator skips invoke\"\n105\tcase — the iterator differs from a plain call only in how the\n106\tfunction's output is routed, not in whether the function runs.\n107\tIterators that want passthrough behavior use an identity function\n108\t(or the editor defaults to one when no `ref`/`fn` is set).\n109\t\n110\t### 4. Invoke (every call box)\n111\tLook up the box's language spec by its `lang` field. Find the\n112\tworker's language handle in `current_worker->handles[lang_idx]`.\n113\tCall `lang->invoke` with:\n114\t- `handle` — the per-worker language runtime state\n115\t- `file_path`, `fn_name` — the box's function source\n116\t- `input_data[]`, `input_sizes[]` — pointers and sizes for each\n117\t  input buffer\n118\t- `out_buf`, `out_buf_capacity`, `*out_size` — the output buffer the\n119\t  spec writes into\n120\t\n121\tThe spec is the bridge between the language's native call convention\n122\tand bytes. Inside `invoke` it:\n123\t1. Loads the function (cached: e.g. `luaL_loadfile` once per file,\n124\t   `dlsym` once per function).\n125\t2. Pushes the input bytes into the language's native types (Lua\n126\t   strings on the Lua stack, C pointers in registers, etc.).\n127\t3. Calls the function and receives the return value in the language's\n128\t   native form.\n129\t4. Serializes the return value back into bytes in `out_buf` and\n130\t   sets `*out_size`.\n131\t5. Returns 0 for success, nonzero for any failure.\n132\t\n133\tNonzero return aborts the program (issue 303).\n134\t\n135\tThe output buffer for `invoke` is heap-allocated to the box's\n136\tdeclared maximum output size. If the box's output is variable-size\n137\t(uses the large-value heap, issue 302), the spec writes into that\n138\theap and stores the handle in `out_buf`.\n139\t\n140\t### 5. Write output (push to downstream input slots)\n141\t\n142\tThe action picks the branch (or branches) and pushes the\n143\tfunction's output. Branch picking dispatches on `routing.kind`:\n144\t\n145\t- **No routing field** (plain call): push to every outgoing\n146\t  connection.\n147\t- **comparator**: compare output to `comparand`, push to the\n148\t  matching `lt` / `eq` / `gt` connection only.\n149\t- **iterator**: `idx = slot_read_inc(box->counter_slot,\n150\t  n_outputs)`; push to the connection at branch `out_idx`.\n151\t- **randomizer / weighted / distributor**: kind-specific rule,\n152\t  same shape (compute `idx`, push to that one connection). See\n153\t  issue 233 for the rules.\n154\t\n155\tFor routing kinds that derive an order tag (iterator,\n156\trandomizer, weighted), the push carries `tag = idx` so consumers\n157\tdownstream of parallel iterators preserve order.\n158\t\n159\tAfter each push, the spawn-on-input-ready check (issue 302) fires\n160\ton the receiving box. Run termination\n166\tis governed by the pool's active-task counter (issue 301). The\n167\tdispatch action goes from phase 5 directly to phase 7.\n168\t\n169\t### 7. Post-action: nothing for the action itself\n170\t\n171\tRouting already happened in phase 5. Counter advancement, where\n172\tapplicable, happened inside `slot_read_inc` during phase 5 (the\n173\tread-and-increment is the same op). No box-level mutable state\n174\tneeds touching here.\n175\t\n176\t### 8. Return ACT_DONE\n177\tThe action completes. The pool decrements the active-task counter\n178\t(issue 301). Boxes whose input set becomes\n186\tfully populated by literals — entry-point boxes — immediately\n187\tsatisfy the spawn-on-input-ready condition, and their first task\n188\tgets queued. The\n198\tdispatch action reads and increments it atomically, mid-action:\n199\t\n200\t```c\n201\tuint32_t branch_idx = slot_read_inc(box->counter_slot, n_iter_outputs);\n202\tslot_push(downstream[branch_idx].input_slot, output_buf, output_size,\n203\t          /* tag = */ branch_idx);\n204\t```\n205\t\n206\t`slot_read_inc` returns the current counter value `mod\n207\tn_iter_outputs` and atomically advances the underlying counter.\n208\tConcurrent iterator tasks on different workers each call\n209\t`slot_read_inc` independently and each get a unique value —\n210\t**iterator tasks parallelize across workers**, picking distinct\n211\tbranches without coordination.\n212\t\n213\tNo box-side mutable state, no per-task counter snapshot. The\n214\tcounter is just data in a slot the dispatch layer reads.\n215\t\n216\t## Cross-iterator pairing under parallel iteration\n217\t\n218\tWith parallel iterator tasks, push ordering at the consumer is\n219\tnon-deterministic — task 6 of iterator A may push to consumer C\n220\tbefore task 5 if 6 happened to land on a faster worker. Each iterator push (in phase\n224\t5) carries the counter value the action read for this invocation:\n225\t\n226\t```c\n227\tslot_push(downstream.input_slot, output_buf, output_size,\n228\t          /* tag = */ branch_idx_or_counter_snapshot);\n229\t```\n230\t\n231\tConsumer slots downstream of iterators are allocated with the\n232\t`SLOT_TAGGED` flag (issue 302). `slot_pop` on a tagged slot\n233\treturns the cell with the lowest tag — preserving iterator-counter\n234\torder regardless of push race.\n235\t\n236\tCompile-time analysis decides which slots are tagged: any slot\n237\twhose feeding wire originates (transitively, through a fan-out\n238\tchain) at an iterator branch gets tagged. Slots not downstream of\n239\titerators are untagged and pop FIFO at no extra cost.\n240\t\n241\tPlain-call and comparator pushes carry tag = 0 (or the snapshot of\n242\ttheir own iterator-ancestor's counter, if applicable, propagated\n243\tthrough their phase-5 pushes). Tags compose naturally through\n244\tmulti-hop chains.\n245\t\n246\t### Cross-iterator pairing of multiple iterator inputs\n247\t\n248\tWhen non-iterator consumer C has two input ports wired from two\n249\tdifferent iterators A and B, each input port has its own tagged\n250\tqueue. Routing kinds differ only in\n261\thow the function's output is dispatched to downstream\n262\tconnections:\n263\t\n264\t| `routing.kind`   | Output ports        | Branch picker                                                |\n265\t|------------------|---------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|\n266\t| (absent / plain) | single port         | fan to all outgoing connections                              |\n267\t| `comparator`     | `lt` / `eq` / `gt`  | compare(output, comparand) → lt/eq/gt                        |\n268\t| `iterator`       | `out_0` … `out_N-1` | `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, N)`                             |\n269\t| `randomizer`     | `out_0` … `out_N-1` | `hash(slot_read_inc(counter_slot, MAX)) % N`                 |\n270\t| `weighted`       | `out_0` … `out_N-1` | cumulative-band lookup against a counter scaled to PRECISION |\n271\t| `distributor`    | `out_0` … `out_N-1` | argmin over downstream slot fill levels                      |\n272\t\n273\tPlain call (no `routing` field) skips the branch picker entirely\n274\t— phase 5 fans the output to all wires. The function still runs\n275\tthe same as for any branched call.       "content":"# 301 — Thread pool lifecycle and per-worker initialization\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe executor (`src/004-executor.lua`) runs boxes synchronously in a\nsingle Lua coroutine. There is no thread pool, no pthreads, and no\nper-thread language runtime state.\n\n## Phase model\n\nPhase 2 is the synchronous interpreter path. It is the development\ntarget while editor work is in progress.\n\nPhase 3 is the thread pool path. It is the only execution path going\nforward. The synchronous interpreter does not stay around as an\nalternative entry point — once phase 3 lands, the pool runner\nreplaces it. There is no \"fallback to synchronous\" mode.\n\n### Phase 2 → 3 refactor surface\n\nThe following components are replaced (not extended) in phase 3:\n\n| Phase 2 file                  | Phase 3 replacement                  |\n|-------------------------------|--------------------------------------|\n| `src/003-loader.lua`          | C loader inside `src/008-pool-runner.c` |\n| `src/004-executor.lua`        | C task dispatch layer (issue 304)    |\n| `src/007-runner-main.lua`     | `src/008-pool-runner.c`              |\n| `drivers/*.sh`                | Language runtime spec (issue 303)    |\n\nAll threading-pool-adjacent functionality is C code that lives next to\nthe pool. There is no embedded Lua runtime for graph loading or\ndispatch — Lua appears only as a language runtime that boxes can use,\non equal footing with C, Bash, and any future language.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### Pool source\nThe thread pool is **SoraMech-owned**, written from scratch under\n`libs/task-pool/`. The 3d-rts pool at\n`/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h`\nis the **design reference**, not a dependency. We need full control\nover the spawn primitive, the worker context, the init barrier\n(below), and iterator-pinning extensions — all reasons not to inherit\nan external implementation.\n\nThe pool exposes (at minimum):\n\n```c\npool_t *pool_create(int n_workers);\nvoid    pool_destroy(pool_t *p);\nvoid    pool_spawn(pool_t *p, action_fn_t fn, void *arg);\nvoid    pool_wait_quiescent(pool_t *p);   // blocks until active count hits zero\nvoid    pool_init_barrier(pool_t *p);     // see \"Init barrier\" below\n```\n\n3d-rts's frame-ring + park-on-slot machinery is referenced for\npatterns; we don't reimplement features we don't need.\n\n### Where the pool lives in the process\nThe pool is owned by the map runner's C entry point. One pool per map\nrun. It is created after the graph is loaded and validated, and\ndestroyed after the run completes.\n\nThe C entry point (`src/008-pool-runner.c`):\n\n```c\nint main(int argc, char **argv) {\n    // 1. parse map path from argv\n    // 2. load and validate graph (C loader, no Lua involved)\n    // 3. determine which language runtimes the map uses\n    // 4. allocate per-input-port slots for every box (issue 302)\n    // 5. pool = pool_create(n_workers)\n    // 6. init per-worker language runtime handles for each language present\n    // 7. pool_init_barrier(pool)  ← block until every worker is fully initialized\n    // 8. push every input port's literal value into its slot\n    // 9. spawn tasks for boxes whose input set is now satisfied\n    // 10. pool_wait_quiescent(pool)\n    // 11. write last-run.jsonl\n    // 12. pool_destroy(pool)\n}\n```\n\n### Init barrier\n\nWorkers are not safe to dispatch tasks to until **every worker has\nfully completed init for every language spec the map uses**. If the\nmain thread spawns a task before a worker's `lua_State` is up, the\ntask lands on a null handle.\n\n`pool_init_barrier` is the join point:\n\n1. Each worker's startup runs all `lang->init(worker_idx)` calls in\n   a defined order, populating its `worker_ctx_t.handles[]`.\n2. After completing its inits, each worker increments a shared\n   atomic `workers_ready` counter and blocks on a condition\n   variable.\n3. The main thread waits until `workers_ready == n_workers`.\n4. Main thread broadcasts the condition variable; all workers\n   release simultaneously and begin pulling tasks.\n\nThis is a one-shot barrier — it runs once at pool startup. After\nquiescence it doesn't re-engage; teardown takes a different path.\n\nThe barrier also protects against partial init failures: if any\nworker's `init` returns an error, the barrier never completes and\nthe main thread can detect it via a timeout or per-worker status\nflag.\n\n### Graph loading: ported to C\nThe graph loader is ported from `src/003-loader.lua` to C and lives\ninside (or alongside) `008-pool-runner.c`. The pool runner has no\nembedded Lua state for loader purposes. JSON parsing uses a small\nvendored C JSON library (cJSON or similar; decision deferred to\nimplementation).\n\nLua appears in the runner only when a box's language is Lua — and even\nthen, only inside that worker's language runtime handle. The pool\nrunner itself does not link to liblua at the top level.\n\n### Per-worker language runtimes\nNo language is treated as the \"native\" or preferred language at the\nthread level. Every box — regardless of language — goes through the\nsame task dispatch path. The per-box cost is determined by that box's\ninvocation wrapper, not by any map-level language setting.\n\nEach worker thread holds a set of language runtime handles, one per\nlanguage it may be asked to run. These are initialized once at pool\nstartup, before any tasks are submitted, and torn down at shutdown:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void   *handles[N_LANGS];   // opaque per-language runtime state\n    int     thread_idx;\n} worker_ctx_t;\n```\n\nOnly the language handles actually needed by the map are initialized.\nIf the map contains no Bash boxes, no Bash handle is started for any\nworker. The graph loader determines which languages are present and\npasses that set to the pool runner at startup.\n\nThe per-language initialization protocol is defined by the language\nruntime spec (issue 303). The pool runner calls each spec's `init`\nfunction at startup and its `teardown` function at shutdown.\n\n### Worker context access\nWorker context is stored in thread-local storage (`__thread\nworker_ctx_t *current_worker`), set by each worker immediately after\nthe thread is started. This avoids per-task `pthread_self()` lookups.\n\n### Pool size\nNumber of worker threads defaults to the number of logical CPUs\n(`sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`), capped at a compile-time maximum\n(`MAX_WORKERS`, initially 16). Can be overridden by an environment\nvariable `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n\n### Slots are owned by input ports (issue 302)\nEach box has one ring-buffer slot per input port, allocated at\ngraph load time and durable for the run. The pool runner walks\nevery box during the load step and populates a per-box slot table.\nSlots are not allocated per-task; tasks pop and push but never\nallocate. See issue 302 for the slot lifecycle and lifetime model.\n\n### Quiescence\nThe runner tracks an active-task counter, incremented on `pool_spawn`\nand decremented when a task reaches `ACT_DONE`. The main thread waits\non a condition variable that signals when the counter reaches zero.\n\nThis naturally handles iterators that re-queue themselves: each\nre-queue increments the counter, each completion decrements. When the\ncounter reaches zero, the run is over.\n\nDeadlock is not a concern at runtime. The graph validator (running at\nload) rejects non-iterator cycles and inputs without producers. Errors\ninside a task crash the program (issue 303), so there is no\nhalf-completed-producer case to worry about.
