      "content":"# 303 — Language runtime spec: pluggable per-language invocation\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nEach language has an ad-hoc driver script (`drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`,\n`drivers/c.sh`). The driver is invoked per box call: spawn a process, run\nthe function, read stdout, exit. Adding a new language means writing a new\ndriver script and modifying the executor to know about it.\n\nThere is no shared interface, no persistent runtime, and no way for a user\nto add a language without touching SoraMech internals.\n\n## Concept\n\nThe language runtime spec is the user-extensible interface that defines how\na language's functions are invoked from inside the thread pool. Every\nlanguage goes through this interface — there is no special path for any\nlanguage. Lua is a spec. C is a spec. Bash is a spec. A user adding Python\nwrites another spec.\n\nThe pool runner does not know how to \"run a Lua function.\" It knows how to\ncall `lang->invoke(...)`. The Lua spec is the thing that knows how to run a\nLua function.\n\nThe user provides the bridging code. SoraMech does not transpile, rewrite,\nor convert box source between languages. If the user wants Rust, the user\nwrites a Rust spec.\n\n## The interface\n\nEach language spec is a C library that exports a single symbol:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;       // \"lua\", \"bash\", \"c\", \"python\", ...\n    const char *file_ext;   // \".lua\", \".sh\", \".c\", \".py\" — for box file resolution\n\n    // Once-per-worker. Returns an opaque handle stored in worker_ctx.\n    // Called at pool startup, before any tasks run.\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n\n    // Once-per-worker. Called at pool shutdown.\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n\n    // Optional: called once per box source file at map load.\n    // For languages that compile (C → .so), this is where compilation\n    // happens. For languages that don't (Lua, Bash), this is NULL.\n    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path);\n\n    // The invocation. Inputs are arrays of (bytes, size) pairs,\n    // already read from slots by the dispatch layer. The spec writes\n    // its return value into out_buf and sets *out_size.\n    //\n    // Returns 0 on success, nonzero on error.\n    int   (*invoke)(void *handle,\n                    const char *file_path,\n                    const char *fn_name,\n                    const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes, int n_inputs,\n                    void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n\nextern lang_spec_t soramech_lang_spec;\n```\n\nThe spec library is built as a `.so` and loaded by the pool runner at\nstartup via `dlopen` / `dlsym`. The runner iterates `langs/*/spec.so`,\nloads each, and registers it under its `name`.\n\n## Slot access boundary\n\nSpecs do not see slot IDs. The dispatch layer (issue 304) reads input\nvalues from slots into raw byte buffers, hands them to `invoke`, receives\nthe output bytes, and writes them to the output slot. This decouples\nspecs from slot internals — a spec only deals with values.\n\nIf a future language wants zero-copy access (e.g. memory-mapping a slot\ndirectly into a Python bytearray), the interface can be extended. Do not\nadd it preemptively.\n\n## Per-language layout\n\nSpecs live under `langs/<name>/`:\n\n```\nlangs/lua/\n    spec.c              ← implements lang_spec_t (handles → lua_State)\n    Makefile            ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so             ← built artifact\n\nlangs/bash/\n    spec.c              ← bridges to bash-server.sh via Unix domain socket\n    bash-server.sh      ← persistent subprocess started by spec.init\n    Makefile\n\nlangs/c/\n    spec.c              ← uses dlopen/dlsym; compile = gcc -shared -fPIC\n    Makefile\n\nlangs/python/           ← user-added; not shipped\n    spec.c\n    Makefile\n```\n\nThe pool runner has no compiled-in knowledge of any specific language.\nEven Lua is loaded as a `.so` at startup. This keeps the boundary honest\n— there is no temptation to special-case the \"shipped\" languages.\n\n## Built-in specs (shipped, not privileged)\n\nSoraMech ships specs for:\n- **Lua** — handle is a `lua_State`. `invoke` calls `luaL_loadfile` (cached)\n  + `lua_pcall`. Args pushed as Lua strings; return read as Lua string.\n- **C** — handle is a small `dlopen` handle cache. `compile` runs\n  `gcc -shared -fPIC -o <out_path> <src_path>`. `invoke` does\n  `dlsym` + direct call.\n- **Bash** — handle is a Unix domain socket connected to a persistent\n  bash subprocess (`bash-server.sh`). `invoke` sends a framed request,\n  reads a framed response.\n\nThese are the reference implementations. They demonstrate the spec\ninterface for in-process FFI (Lua, C) and for out-of-process socket\nservers (Bash, and any future language whose runtime cannot be embedded).\n\n## Compilation\n\nThe optional `compile` hook runs at map load (or at editor compile-button\ntime, issue 219). For C, it produces a `.so` next to the source. For\nLua and Bash, no compilation step is needed; `compile` is `NULL`.\n\nCompilation outputs go in the map's `compiled/bin/` directory (issue\n222). The dispatch layer passes the compiled artifact path to `invoke`,\nnot the original source path, when a compiled artifact exists.\n\n## Iterator counter prepending\n\nThe iterator counter (issue 221) is prepended to the input array by the\ndispatch layer, not by the spec. From the spec's perspective, an\niterator box just has one extra input. The spec doesn't know which\ninput is the counter — that's a graph-level concept.\n\n## Errors crash the program\n\nA nonzero return from `invoke` is a fatal error. The dispatch layer\nprints the error context (box id, function name, language) to stderr\nand aborts the process. There is no recovery, no retry, no per-task\n\"failed\" state, no fallback. There are no timeouts on stalled tasks,\nno wait-list garbage collection, no failure propagation through the\ngraph.\n\nThe reasoning: a task that cannot produce a correct return value is a\nbug. Bugs do not belong in production. Building in detection and\nrecovery for bug states adds runtime cost and complexity to handle a\ncase that should not exist. If a bug surfaces in production, the\nprogram crashes loudly; the developer fixes the bug and redeploys.\n\nThe spec is still responsible for catching language-level errors (Lua\n`error()`, C signals it can intercept, Bash nonzero exit) and\ntranslating them into a nonzero return — so that the dispatch layer\nsees a clean signal instead of an undefined post-error state. Once\nreturned, the program ends.\n\n## User-facing documentation\n\nThe interface is published in `langs/lang-spec.h`, which every spec\nimplementation includes. That header is the source of truth for the\ncontract.\n\nUser-facing docs that mention the language spec system:\n- `README.md` — short paragraph in the features list pointing out that\n  any language can be added by writing a spec, with a one-line example\n  of what that means\n- `docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written) — the long-form guide\n  on writing a spec: walk through the Lua spec as a small reference,\n  show what `init` / `invoke` / `teardown` do, point at the C spec for\n  the `compile`-using case and the Bash spec for the\n  socket-server case\n- `docs/000-table-of-contents.md` — index entry for the new doc\n\nWithout these the spec system is invisible — users would never know it\nexists or how to extend it.\n\n## Open questions\n\n(none currently)\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Write `langs/lang-spec.h` — the public interface header.\n2. Write `langs/lua/spec.c` first. Lua is the easiest because it's already\n   our default language and the existing driver gives a reference behavior.\n3. Write `langs/c/spec.c` — adds `compile` callback, exercises the dlopen\n   path.\n4. Write `langs/bash/spec.c` + `langs/bash/bash-server.sh` — exercises\n   the out-of-process socket model. This is the proof that languages\n   without an embeddable runtime fit the same interface.\n5. Pool runner registry: `dlopen` every `langs/*/spec.so` at startup,\n   register by `name`. Box files are routed to specs by `file_ext`.\n6. Smoke test: a map with one Lua box, one C box, one Bash box, all\n   running in the pool, all going through the spec interface. No\n   special-cased code paths.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`, `drivers/c.sh` — current ad-hoc\n  drivers, replaced by `langs/<name>/spec.c`\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool startup invokes\n  spec `init` per worker per language\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — dispatch layer reads slots and\n  passes raw bytes to specs (specs do not touch slots)\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — calls `invoke` per task\n- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` — compile button\n  runs spec `compile` for every box\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — Option 1 (FFI) and Option 3 (Unix\n  socket) describe the two execution models specs implement\n",

        "content":"1\t# 303 — Language runtime spec: pluggable per-language invocation\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\tEach language has an ad-hoc driver script (`drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`,\n8\t`drivers/c.sh`). The driver is invoked per box call: spawn a process, run\n9\tthe function, read stdout, exit. Adding a new language means writing a new\n10\tdriver script and modifying the executor to know about it.\n11\t\n12\tThere is no shared interface, no persistent runtime, and no way for a user\n13\tto add a language without touching SoraMech internals.\n14\t\n15\t## Concept\n16\t\n17\tThe language runtime spec is the user-extensible interface that defines how\n18\ta language's functions are invoked from inside the thread pool. Every\n19\tlanguage goes through this interface — there is no special path for any\n20\tlanguage. Lua is a spec. C is a spec. Bash is a spec. A user adding Python\n21\twrites another spec.\n22\t\n23\tThe pool runner does not know how to \"run a Lua function.\" It knows how to\n24\tcall `lang->invoke(...)`. The Lua spec is the thing that knows how to run a\n25\tLua function.\n26\t\n27\tThe user provides the bridging code. SoraMech does not transpile, rewrite,\n28\tor convert box source between languages. If the user wants Rust, the user\n29\twrites a Rust spec.\n30\t\n31\t## The interface\n32\t\n33\tEach language spec is a C library that exports a single symbol:\n34\t\n35\t```c\n36\ttypedef struct {\n37\t    const char *name;       // \"lua\", \"bash\", \"c\", \"python\", ...\n38\t    const char *file_ext;   // \".lua\", \".sh\", \".c\", \".py\" — for box file resolution\n39\t\n40\t    // Once-per-worker. Returns an opaque handle stored in worker_ctx.\n41\t    // Called at pool startup, before any tasks run.\n42\t    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n43\t\n44\t    // Once-per-worker. Called at pool shutdown.\n45\t    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n46\t\n47\t    // Optional: called once per box source file at map load.\n48\t    // For languages that compile (C → .so), this is where compilation\n49\t    // happens. For languages that don't (Lua, Bash), this is NULL.\n50\t    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path);\n51\t\n52\t    // The invocation. Inputs are arrays of (bytes, size) pairs,\n53\t    // already read from slots by the dispatch layer. The spec writes\n54\t    // its return value into out_buf and sets *out_size.\n55\t    //\n56\t    // Returns 0 on success, nonzero on error.\n57\t    int   (*invoke)(void *handle,\n58\t                    const char *file_path,\n59\t                    const char *fn_name,\n60\t                    const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes, int n_inputs,\n61\t                    void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n62\t} lang_spec_t;\n63\t\n64\textern lang_spec_t soramech_lang_spec;\n65\t```\n66\t\n67\tThe spec library is built as a `.so` and loaded by the pool runner at\n68\tstartup via `dlopen` / `dlsym`. The runner iterates `langs/*/spec.so`,\n69\tloads each, and registers it under its `name`.\n70\t\n71\t## Slot access boundary\n72\t\n73\tSpecs do not see slot IDs. The dispatch layer (issue 304) reads input\n74\tvalues from slots into raw byte buffers, hands them to `invoke`, receives\n75\tthe output bytes, and writes them to the output slot. This decouples\n76\tspecs from slot internals — a spec only deals with values.\n77\t\n78\tIf a future language wants zero-copy access (e.g. memory-mapping a slot\n79\tdirectly into a Python bytearray), the interface can be extended. Do not\n80\tadd it preemptively.\n81\t\n82\t## Per-language layout\n83\t\n84\tSpecs live under `langs/<name>/`:\n85\t\n86\t```\n87\tlangs/lua/\n88\t    spec.c              ← implements lang_spec_t (handles → lua_State)\n89\t    Makefile            ← builds spec.so\n90\t    spec.so             ← built artifact\n91\t\n92\tlangs/bash/\n93\t    spec.c              ← bridges to bash-server.sh via Unix domain socket\n94\t    bash-server.sh      ← persistent subprocess started by spec.init\n95\t    Makefile\n96\t\n97\tlangs/c/\n98\t    spec.c              ← uses dlopen/dlsym; compile = gcc -shared -fPIC\n99\t    Makefile\n100\t\n101\tlangs/python/           ← user-added; not shipped\n102\t    spec.c\n103\t    Makefile\n104\t```\n105\t\n106\tThe pool runner has no compiled-in knowledge of any specific language.\n107\tEven Lua is loaded as a `.so` at startup. This keeps the boundary honest\n108\t— there is no temptation to special-case the \"shipped\" languages.\n109\t\n110\t## Built-in specs (shipped, not privileged)\n111\t\n112\tSoraMech ships specs for:\n113\t- **Lua** — handle is a `lua_State`. `invoke` calls `luaL_loadfile` (cached)\n114\t  + `lua_pcall`. Args pushed as Lua strings; return read as Lua string.\n115\t- **C** — handle is a small `dlopen` handle cache. `compile` runs\n116\t  `gcc -shared -fPIC -o <out_path> <src_path>`. `invoke` does\n117\t  `dlsym` + direct call.\n118\t- **Bash** — handle is a Unix domain socket connected to a persistent\n119\t  bash subprocess (`bash-server.sh`). `invoke` sends a framed request,\n120\t  reads a framed response.\n121\t\n122\tThese are the reference implementations. They demonstrate the spec\n123\tinterface for in-process FFI (Lua, C) and for out-of-process socket\n124\tservers (Bash, and any future language whose runtime cannot be embedded).\n125\t\n126\t## Compilation\n127\t\n128\tThe optional `compile` hook runs at map load (or at editor compile-button\n129\ttime, issue 219). For C, it produces a `.so` next to the source. For\n130\tLua and Bash, no compilation step is needed; `compile` is `NULL`.\n131\t\n132\tCompilation outputs go in the map's `compiled/bin/` directory (issue\n133\t222). The dispatch layer passes the compiled artifact path to `invoke`,\n134\tnot the original source path, when a compiled artifact exists.\n135\t\n136\t## Iterator counter prepending\n137\t\n138\tThe iterator counter (issue 221) is prepended to the input array by the\n139\tdispatch layer, not by the spec. From the spec's perspective, an\n140\titerator box just has one extra input. The spec doesn't know which\n141\tinput is the counter — that's a graph-level concept.\n142\t\n143\t## Errors crash the program\n144\t\n145\tA nonzero return from `invoke` is a fatal error. The dispatch layer\n146\tprints the error context (box id, function name, language) to stderr\n147\tand aborts the process. There is no recovery, no retry, no per-task\n148\t\"failed\" state, no fallback. There are no timeouts on stalled tasks,\n149\tno wait-list garbage collection, no failure propagation through the\n150\tgraph.\n151\t\n152\tThe reasoning: a task that cannot produce a correct return value is a\n153\tbug. Bugs do not belong in production. Building in detection and\n154\trecovery for bug states adds runtime cost and complexity to handle a\n155\tcase that should not exist. If a bug surfaces in production, the\n156\tprogram crashes loudly; the developer fixes the bug and redeploys.\n157\t\n158\tThe spec is still responsible for catching language-level errors (Lua\n159\t`error()`, C signals it can intercept, Bash nonzero exit) and\n160\ttranslating them into a nonzero return — so that the dispatch layer\n161\tsees a clean signal instead of an undefined post-error state. Once\n162\treturned, the program ends.\n163\t\n164\t## User-facing documentation\n165\t\n166\tThe interface is published in `langs/lang-spec.h`, which every spec\n167\timplementation includes. That header is the source of truth for the\n168\tcontract.\n169\t\n170\tUser-facing docs that mention the language spec system:\n171\t- `README.md` — short paragraph in the features list pointing out that\n172\t  any language can be added by writing a spec, with a one-line example\n173\t  of what that means\n174\t- `docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written) — the long-form guide\n175\t  on writing a spec: walk through the Lua spec as a small reference,\n176\t  show what `init` / `invoke` / `teardown` do, point at the C spec for\n177\t  the `compile`-using case and the Bash spec for the\n178\t  socket-server case\n179\t- `docs/000-table-of-contents.md` — index entry for the new doc\n180\t\n181\tWithout these the spec system is invisible — users would never know it\n182\texists or how to extend it.\n183\t\n184\t## Open questions\n185\t\n186\t(none currently)\n187\t\n188\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n189\t\n190\t1. Write `langs/lang-spec.h` — the public interface header.\n191\t2. Write `langs/lua/spec.c` first. Lua is the easiest because it's already\n192\t   our default language and the existing driver gives a reference behavior.\n193\t3. Write `langs/c/spec.c` — adds `compile` callback, exercises the dlopen\n194\t   path.\n195\t4. Write `langs/bash/spec.c` + `langs/bash/bash-server.sh` — exercises\n196\t   the out-of-process socket model. This is the proof that languages\n197\t   without an embeddable runtime fit the same interface.\n198\t5. Pool runner registry: `dlopen` every `langs/*/spec.so` at startup,\n199\t   register by `name`. Box files are routed to specs by `file_ext`.\n200\t6. Smoke test: a map with one Lua box, one C box, one Bash box, all\n201\t   running in the pool, all going through the spec interface. No\n202\t   special-cased code paths.\n203\t\n204\t## Relevant files\n205\t\n206\t- `drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`, `drivers/c.sh` — current ad-hoc\n207\t  drivers, replaced by `langs/<name>/spec.c`\n208\t- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool startup invokes\n209\t  spec `init` per worker per language\n210\t- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — dispatch layer reads slots and\n211\t  passes raw bytes to specs (specs do not touch slots)\n212\t- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — calls `invoke` per task\n213\t- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` — compile button\n214\t  runs spec `compile` for every box\n215\t- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — Option 1 (FFI) and Option 3 (Unix\n216\t  socket) describe the two execution models specs implement\n217\t"

      "content":"# 311 — Integration tests & run output (`last-run.json`)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nPhase 2 writes a `last-run.json` after every map run, recording per-\nbox invocations, inputs, outputs, and any errors. The editor reads\nit to display a run summary. Phase 2 testing is ad-hoc: a few maps\nin `maps/` (`hello`, `branch-test`, `classify-demo`, `driver-test`)\nthat the developer runs by hand to verify the synchronous executor\nstill works.\n\nPhase 3 changes the shape of the problem: many concurrent\ninvocations, possibly thousands per run when iterators are in play,\nwritten from multiple worker threads. The phase 2 \"build a single\ntable at end of run\" approach does not survive that. And the\nexisting maps cover only a small slice of the new surface (no\nqueued inputs, no large iterator counts, no fan-in).\n\nThis issue covers two things that go together: the format and\nwriter for the run output, and the integration test plan that\nexercises the phase 3 runtime end-to-end.\n\n## Part A — Run output\n\n### Decoupling from the editor\n\nThe editor (phase 2) is being scoped down to a pure map editor — it\ndoes not know how to run maps and does not display run results.\n`last-run.json` is therefore not a UI feed. It exists for:\n\n- LLM consumption — agents reading the file to understand what a\n  run did\n- CLI-driven inspection — a future viewer utility (out of scope\n  here) that pretty-prints the file\n- Test harness consumption — the integration tests below diff the\n  written file against expected output\n\nDecoupling means the writer's design is driven by these consumers,\nnot by editor rendering needs.\n\n### File format: JSON Lines\n\nThe phase 2 single-document format does not work when the runner is\nstreaming events from many threads. Use JSON Lines instead — one\nJSON object per line, each line is one event, the file grows\nmonotonically as the run proceeds.\n\nEvent types:\n\n```jsonl\n{\"event\":\"run_start\", \"ts\":1234567890.123, \"map\":\"maps/classify-demo\", \"n_workers\":16}\n{\"event\":\"task_submit\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"box_id\":\"classify\", \"worker_idx\":-1}\n{\"event\":\"task_start\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"worker_idx\":3}\n{\"event\":\"task_end\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"worker_idx\":3, \"duration_us\":127, \"output_size\":12}\n{\"event\":\"slot_alloc\", \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5, \"size\":256, \"n_cells\":1}\n{\"event\":\"slot_free\", \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5}\n{\"event\":\"run_end\", \"ts\":..., \"duration_us\":1850, \"n_tasks\":7}\n```\n\nJSONL is append-only, which makes thread-safe writing tractable: a\nsingle mutex around the write call serializes the lines, and each\nline is self-contained so a partial line on crash is recoverable\n(reader skips the broken trailing line).\n\nThe reader (LLM, viewer, test harness) parses one line at a time;\ntotal file size doesn't have to fit in memory.\n\n### What gets logged\n\nPer-task: submission, start, end, duration, output size. Inputs\nand outputs are NOT logged by default — for iterator boxes\nproducing thousands of invocations, logging every value bloats\nthe file unbounded. There is a verbosity switch:\n\n- `SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1` — log inputs and outputs (truncated past\n  some byte limit, e.g. 4 KB) per task. For debugging.\n- Default: log task lifecycle but not values.\n\nSlot allocator events (alloc, free, coalesce, grow) at a separate\nverbosity level. Off by default; on under `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1`.\nFor diagnosing memory issues.\n\n### Writer mechanism\n\nA single dedicated writer thread inside the runner consumes events\nfrom a multi-producer single-consumer ring buffer. Worker threads\npush event records (small fixed-size structs) into the ring; the\nwriter pulls them, serializes to JSON, and writes lines to the\nfile. This avoids per-event mutex contention — the ring buffer is\nthe only shared state, and a well-written MPSC ring is lock-free\non the producer side.\n\nAlternative considered: each worker writes its own log file, merge\nat end. Simpler concurrency, but readers would have to merge by\ntimestamp — and any cross-event reasoning (was task A still\nrunning when task B ended?) requires the merge anyway.\n\nThe writer thread is started after the pool is created and joined\nbefore `pool_destroy`. It also handles `run_end` as the very last\nevent, including the final summary.\n\n### File location\n\n`<map-dir>/last-run.jsonl` (note: `.jsonl` not `.json` — the\nextension reflects the format change). Overwritten on every run.\n\nA rotated archive (`last-run.jsonl.1`, `.2`, …) is out of scope.\nUsers who want history copy the file before re-running.\n\n## Part B — Integration tests\n\n### Scope\n\nEnd-to-end tests of the pool runner against real map directories.\nEach test is:\n\n1. A map directory under `tests/maps/<name>/`\n2. An expected `last-run.jsonl` (or a comparison spec) under\n   `tests/expected/<name>.jsonl`\n3. A test driver script that runs the map and diffs\n\nThe test driver is `scripts/run-tests.sh`. It iterates\n`tests/maps/`, runs each, diffs against expected (with a normalizer\nthat drops timestamps, durations, worker indices — anything non-\ndeterministic), and reports pass/fail.\n\n### Test maps\n\nCoverage targets:\n\n| Test map                  | What it exercises                                    |\n|---------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|\n| `hello`                   | Single Lua box, one input, one output                |\n| `data-only`               | Data box → call box. No inputs, just stored values   |\n| `fan-out-3`               | One output → three consumer boxes (peek, refcount)   |\n| `fan-in-iterator`         | Three producers → iterator with queued input         |\n| `comparator-routing`      | Comparator with all three branches (lt/eq/gt)        |\n| `iterator-100`            | Iterator with 100 input values, round-robin to 3 paths |\n| `multilang`               | One Lua box, one C box, one Bash box, all wired      |\n| `large-output`            | Box producing a 1 MB string (variable-size heap)     |\n| `cycle-detector-fail`     | Non-iterator cycle — load must abort                 |\n| `missing-input-fail`      | Connection references a nonexistent box — load aborts|\n| `box-error-fail`          | Box function returns nonzero — runner aborts         |\n\nThe `*-fail` tests verify error behavior — the runner is expected\nto exit nonzero with a precise error message. The driver matches\nexit code and stderr against expected.\n\n### Test driver\n\n```bash\n# scripts/run-tests.sh\nfor test_dir in tests/maps/*/; do\n    name=$(basename \"${test_dir}\")\n    expected=\"tests/expected/${name}.jsonl\"\n\n    actual=$( \"${SOURCE_DIR}/soramech-pool\" \"${test_dir}\" )\n    rc=$?\n\n    if [ -f \"${expected}.exit\" ]; then\n        # *-fail tests: assert exit code and stderr substring\n        check_failure \"${name}\" \"${rc}\" \"${test_dir}/last-run.jsonl\"\n    else\n        # success tests: diff normalized last-run.jsonl\n        check_success \"${name}\" \"${test_dir}/last-run.jsonl\" \"${expected}\"\n    fi\ndone\n```\n\n`normalize_jsonl` strips timestamps, durations, worker indices,\nslot ids, and task ids (all non-deterministic) and sorts events by\nevent type. The result should be deterministic across runs.\n\n### Phase 3 demo map\n\nA single map under `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/` that\ndemonstrates everything working together:\n\n- Multiple entry-point data boxes\n- Lua, C, and Bash boxes all wired together\n- An iterator with a queued input\n- A comparator routing into different downstream paths\n- A large-output box (variable-size heap)\n- Non-trivial graph topology (≥ 10 boxes)\n\nRun with `./run.sh` from the demo directory. Prints a short summary\nof what happened (parsing the `last-run.jsonl`) so the demo is\nvisible without a viewer utility.\n\nThis satisfies the standing project rule (CLAUDE.md) that each\nphase produces a runnable demo in `issues/completed/demos/`.\n\n### Test infrastructure constraints\n\n- Tests must not depend on the editor or any HTTP server\n- Tests must not depend on internet access\n- Tests must run in under 60 seconds total on a developer machine\n- Tests must be deterministic when normalized (any\n  non-determinism is normalized out, not papered over with retries)\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Whether to log inputs/outputs by default. Useful for development,\n  noisy for production. Current decision: opt-in via env var,\n  default off.\n- Slot-event logging: also opt-in. Useful for diagnosing memory\n  issues. Off by default.\n- File format: JSON Lines is the choice. An alternative was a\n  protobuf or msgpack binary log, which is faster to write but\n  harder to inspect by hand. JSONL wins on inspectability.\n- Whether to keep timestamps as Unix epoch floats or ISO 8601\n  strings. Epoch floats are smaller and easier to diff. Stick with\n  floats.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n### Run output (Part A)\n1. Define the event struct and JSONL line format. Start with\n   `run_start`, `task_start`, `task_end`, `run_end`.\n2. Implement the MPSC ring buffer for events.\n3. Implement the writer thread: pulls from ring, serializes,\n   appends a line to the output file.\n4. Wire event emission into the pool runner: `run_start` at\n   startup, `task_start` and `task_end` in the dispatch action,\n   `run_end` after quiescence.\n5. Add the verbosity env vars and the optional event types.\n\n### Tests (Part B)\n6. Create `tests/maps/` and `tests/expected/` directory structure.\n7. Write the `hello` test as the first end-to-end smoke check.\n8. Write the test driver `scripts/run-tests.sh` and the JSONL\n   normalizer.\n9. Add tests one at a time as each runtime feature lands. The\n   `*-fail` tests can land before their corresponding successful\n   tests if the failure path is implemented first.\n10. Build the phase 3 demo map under `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/`\n    once the rest of phase 3 is implemented.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `scripts/run-tests.sh` — test driver (to be written)\n- `tests/maps/`, `tests/expected/` — test fixtures (to be created)\n- `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/` — phase 3 demo (to be built)\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — emits run_start / run_end\n- `src/dispatch.c` — emits task_start / task_end\n- `src/slot-store.c` — emits slot_alloc / slot_free (verbose mode)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot events\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task lifecycle events\n- `issues/305-c-graph-loader.md` — load-time errors\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — `make test` invokes this\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — blocking semantics relevant to\n  test design\n",

        "content":"1\t# 311 — Integration tests & run output (`last-run.json`)\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\t\n8\tPhase 2 writes a `last-run.json` after every map run, recording per-\n9\tbox invocations, inputs, outputs, and any errors. The editor reads\n10\tit to display a run summary. Phase 2 testing is ad-hoc: a few maps\n11\tin `maps/` (`hello`, `branch-test`, `classify-demo`, `driver-test`)\n12\tthat the developer runs by hand to verify the synchronous executor\n13\tstill works.\n14\t\n15\tPhase 3 changes the shape of the problem: many concurrent\n16\tinvocations, possibly thousands per run when iterators are in play,\n17\twritten from multiple worker threads. The phase 2 \"build a single\n18\ttable at end of run\" approach does not survive that. And the\n19\texisting maps cover only a small slice of the new surface (no\n20\tqueued inputs, no large iterator counts, no fan-in).\n21\t\n22\tThis issue covers two things that go together: the format and\n23\twriter for the run output, and the integration test plan that\n24\texercises the phase 3 runtime end-to-end.\n25\t\n26\t## Part A — Run output\n27\t\n28\t### Decoupling from the editor\n29\t\n30\tThe editor (phase 2) is being scoped down to a pure map editor — it\n31\tdoes not know how to run maps and does not display run results.\n32\t`last-run.json` is therefore not a UI feed. It exists for:\n33\t\n34\t- LLM consumption — agents reading the file to understand what a\n35\t  run did\n36\t- CLI-driven inspection — a future viewer utility (out of scope\n37\t  here) that pretty-prints the file\n38\t- Test harness consumption — the integration tests below diff the\n39\t  written file against expected output\n40\t\n41\tDecoupling means the writer's design is driven by these consumers,\n42\tnot by editor rendering needs.\n43\t\n44\t### File format: JSON Lines\n45\t\n46\tThe phase 2 single-document format does not work when the runner is\n47\tstreaming events from many threads. Use JSON Lines instead — one\n48\tJSON object per line, each line is one event, the file grows\n49\tmonotonically as the run proceeds.\n50\t\n51\tEvent types:\n52\t\n53\t```jsonl\n54\t{\"event\":\"run_start\", \"ts\":1234567890.123, \"map\":\"maps/classify-demo\", \"n_workers\":16}\n55\t{\"event\":\"task_submit\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"box_id\":\"classify\", \"worker_idx\":-1}\n56\t{\"event\":\"task_start\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"worker_idx\":3}\n57\t{\"event\":\"task_end\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"worker_idx\":3, \"duration_us\":127, \"output_size\":12}\n58\t{\"event\":\"slot_alloc\", \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5, \"size\":256, \"n_cells\":1}\n59\t{\"event\":\"slot_free\", \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5}\n60\t{\"event\":\"run_end\", \"ts\":..., \"duration_us\":1850, \"n_tasks\":7}\n61\t```\n62\t\n63\tJSONL is append-only, which makes thread-safe writing tractable: a\n64\tsingle mutex around the write call serializes the lines, and each\n65\tline is self-contained so a partial line on crash is recoverable\n66\t(reader skips the broken trailing line).\n67\t\n68\tThe reader (LLM, viewer, test harness) parses one line at a time;\n69\ttotal file size doesn't have to fit in memory.\n70\t\n71\t### What gets logged\n72\t\n73\tPer-task: submission, start, end, duration, output size. Inputs\n74\tand outputs are NOT logged by default — for iterator boxes\n75\tproducing thousands of invocations, logging every value bloats\n76\tthe file unbounded. There is a verbosity switch:\n77\t\n78\t- `SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1` — log inputs and outputs (truncated past\n79\t  some byte limit, e.g. 4 KB) per task. For debugging.\n80\t- Default: log task lifecycle but not values.\n81\t\n82\tSlot allocator events (alloc, free, coalesce, grow) at a separate\n83\tverbosity level. Off by default; on under `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1`.\n84\tFor diagnosing memory issues.\n85\t\n86\t### Writer mechanism\n87\t\n88\tA single dedicated writer thread inside the runner consumes events\n89\tfrom a multi-producer single-consumer ring buffer. Worker threads\n90\tpush event records (small fixed-size structs) into the ring; the\n91\twriter pulls them, serializes to JSON, and writes lines to the\n92\tfile. This avoids per-event mutex contention — the ring buffer is\n93\tthe only shared state, and a well-written MPSC ring is lock-free\n94\ton the producer side.\n95\t\n96\tAlternative considered: each worker writes its own log file, merge\n97\tat end. Simpler concurrency, but readers would have to merge by\n98\ttimestamp — and any cross-event reasoning (was task A still\n99\trunning when task B ended?) requires the merge anyway.\n100\t\n101\tThe writer thread is started after the pool is created and joined\n102\tbefore `pool_destroy`. It also handles `run_end` as the very last\n103\tevent, including the final summary.\n104\t\n105\t### File location\n106\t\n107\t`<map-dir>/last-run.jsonl` (note: `.jsonl` not `.json` — the\n108\textension reflects the format change). Overwritten on every run.\n109\t\n110\tA rotated archive (`last-run.jsonl.1`, `.2`, …) is out of scope.\n111\tUsers who want history copy the file before re-running.\n112\t\n113\t## Part B — Integration tests\n114\t\n115\t### Scope\n116\t\n117\tEnd-to-end tests of the pool runner against real map directories.\n118\tEach test is:\n119\t\n120\t1. A map directory under `tests/maps/<name>/`\n121\t2. An expected `last-run.jsonl` (or a comparison spec) under\n122\t   `tests/expected/<name>.jsonl`\n123\t3. A test driver script that runs the map and diffs\n124\t\n125\tThe test driver is `scripts/run-tests.sh`. It iterates\n126\t`tests/maps/`, runs each, diffs against expected (with a normalizer\n127\tthat drops timestamps, durations, worker indices — anything non-\n128\tdeterministic), and reports pass/fail.\n129\t\n130\t### Test maps\n131\t\n132\tCoverage targets:\n133\t\n134\t| Test map                  | What it exercises                                    |\n135\t|---------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|\n136\t| `hello`                   | Single Lua box, one input, one output                |\n137\t| `data-only`               | Data box → call box. No inputs, just stored values   |\n138\t| `fan-out-3`               | One output → three consumer boxes (peek, refcount)   |\n139\t| `fan-in-iterator`         | Three producers → iterator with queued input         |\n140\t| `comparator-routing`      | Comparator with all three branches (lt/eq/gt)        |\n141\t| `iterator-100`            | Iterator with 100 input values, round-robin to 3 paths |\n142\t| `multilang`               | One Lua box, one C box, one Bash box, all wired      |\n143\t| `large-output`            | Box producing a 1 MB string (variable-size heap)     |\n144\t| `cycle-detector-fail`     | Non-iterator cycle — load must abort                 |\n145\t| `missing-input-fail`      | Connection references a nonexistent box — load aborts|\n146\t| `box-error-fail`          | Box function returns nonzero — runner aborts         |\n147\t\n148\tThe `*-fail` tests verify error behavior — the runner is expected\n149\tto exit nonzero with a precise error message. The driver matches\n150\texit code and stderr against expected.\n151\t\n152\t### Test driver\n153\t\n154\t```bash\n155\t# scripts/run-tests.sh\n156\tfor test_dir in tests/maps/*/; do\n157\t    name=$(basename \"${test_dir}\")\n158\t    expected=\"tests/expected/${name}.jsonl\"\n159\t\n160\t    actual=$( \"${SOURCE_DIR}/soramech-pool\" \"${test_dir}\" )\n161\t    rc=$?\n162\t\n163\t    if [ -f \"${expected}.exit\" ]; then\n164\t        # *-fail tests: assert exit code and stderr substring\n165\t        check_failure \"${name}\" \"${rc}\" \"${test_dir}/last-run.jsonl\"\n166\t    else\n167\t        # success tests: diff normalized last-run.jsonl\n168\t        check_success \"${name}\" \"${test_dir}/last-run.jsonl\" \"${expected}\"\n169\t    fi\n170\tdone\n171\t```\n172\t\n173\t`normalize_jsonl` strips timestamps, durations, worker indices,\n174\tslot ids, and task ids (all non-deterministic) and sorts events by\n175\tevent type. The result should be deterministic across runs.\n176\t\n177\t### Phase 3 demo map\n178\t\n179\tA single map under `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/` that\n180\tdemonstrates everything working together:\n181\t\n182\t- Multiple entry-point data boxes\n183\t- Lua, C, and Bash boxes all wired together\n184\t- An iterator with a queued input\n185\t- A comparator routing into different downstream paths\n186\t- A large-output box (variable-size heap)\n187\t- Non-trivial graph topology (≥ 10 boxes)\n188\t\n189\tRun with `./run.sh` from the demo directory. Prints a short summary\n190\tof what happened (parsing the `last-run.jsonl`) so the demo is\n191\tvisible without a viewer utility.\n192\t\n193\tThis satisfies the standing project rule (CLAUDE.md) that each\n194\tphase produces a runnable demo in `issues/completed/demos/`.\n195\t\n196\t### Test infrastructure constraints\n197\t\n198\t- Tests must not depend on the editor or any HTTP server\n199\t- Tests must not depend on internet access\n200\t- Tests must run in under 60 seconds total on a developer machine\n201\t- Tests must be deterministic when normalized (any\n202\t  non-determinism is normalized out, not papered over with retries)\n203\t\n204\t## Open questions\n205\t\n206\t- Whether to log inputs/outputs by default. Useful for development,\n207\t  noisy for production. Current decision: opt-in via env var,\n208\t  default off.\n209\t- Slot-event logging: also opt-in. Useful for diagnosing memory\n210\t  issues. Off by default.\n211\t- File format: JSON Lines is the choice. An alternative was a\n212\t  protobuf or msgpack binary log, which is faster to write but\n213\t  harder to inspect by hand. JSONL wins on inspectability.\n214\t- Whether to keep timestamps as Unix epoch floats or ISO 8601\n215\t  strings. Epoch floats are smaller and easier to diff. Stick with\n216\t  floats.\n217\t\n218\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n219\t\n220\t### Run output (Part A)\n221\t1. Define the event struct and JSONL line format. Start with\n222\t   `run_start`, `task_start`, `task_end`, `run_end`.\n223\t2. Implement the MPSC ring buffer for events.\n224\t3. Implement the writer thread: pulls from ring, serializes,\n225\t   appends a line to the output file.\n226\t4. Wire event emission into the pool runner: `run_start` at\n227\t   startup, `task_start` and `task_end` in the dispatch action,\n228\t   `run_end` after quiescence.\n229\t5. Add the verbosity env vars and the optional event types.\n230\t\n231\t### Tests (Part B)\n232\t6. Create `tests/maps/` and `tests/expected/` directory structure.\n233\t7. Write the `hello` test as the first end-to-end smoke check.\n234\t8. Write the test driver `scripts/run-tests.sh` and the JSONL\n235\t   normalizer.\n236\t9. Add tests one at a time as each runtime feature lands. The\n237\t   `*-fail` tests can land before their corresponding successful\n238\t   tests if the failure path is implemented first.\n239\t10. Build the phase 3 demo map under `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/`\n240\t    once the rest of phase 3 is implemented.\n241\t\n242\t## Relevant files\n243\t\n244\t- `scripts/run-tests.sh` — test driver (to be written)\n245\t- `tests/maps/`, `tests/expected/` — test fixtures (to be created)\n246\t- `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/` — phase 3 demo (to be built)\n247\t- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — emits run_start / run_end\n248\t- `src/dispatch.c` — emits task_start / task_end\n249\t- `src/slot-store.c` — emits slot_alloc / slot_free (verbose mode)\n250\t- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n251\t- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot events\n252\t- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task lifecycle events\n253\t- `issues/305-c-graph-loader.md` — load-time errors\n254\t- `issues/309-build-system.md` — `make test` invokes this\n255\t- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — blocking semantics relevant to\n256\t  test design\n257\t"

      "content":"# 312 — Same-language wire fast path: skip JSON for adjacent same-language boxes\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nThe wire format between boxes is JSON (`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`,\nissue 302's \"no type tags\" — slot store stores opaque bytes; the\nlanguage spec encodes/decodes). Every wire pays the JSON encode +\ndecode cost on every value pass, even when the producer and the\nconsumer are the same language and could use a faster\nlanguage-native serialization.\n\nFor a Lua → Lua wire passing a 10-element table:\n1. Producer's spec: `cjson.encode(table)` → string of N bytes\n2. `slot_push(slot, string, N)`\n3. `slot_peek(slot, buf, N)`\n4. Consumer's spec: `cjson.decode(buf)` → Lua table\n\nSteps 1 and 4 are the cost. They're language-agnostic and unnecessary\nwhen both endpoints share a language.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEach language spec exposes **two invoke paths**:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;\n    const char *file_ext;\n\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n    int   (*compile)(...);\n\n    // Universal path — JSON bytes in, JSON bytes out\n    int   (*invoke_json)  (void *handle, /* common args */);\n\n    // Fast path — language-native bytes in, language-native bytes out\n    int   (*invoke_native)(void *handle, /* common args */);\n\n    // Bridges used when a value crosses a language boundary\n    int   (*native_to_json)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n    int   (*json_to_native)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n```\n\n`invoke_native` is required (every spec implements one). Per-language\n\"native\" format:\n- **Lua**: `lua_dump` for closures, `cjson` or msgpack for tables, raw\n  bytes for strings/numbers. Spec's choice as long as it's\n  symmetric with its own decoder.\n- **C**: raw struct memcpy. The compile-time wrapper (issue 307)\n  knows the types; serialization is `memcpy(slot_buf, &val, sizeof\n  val)`.\n- **Bash**: strings only — Bash has no other native form, so the\n  fast path is identical to the JSON path. A spec that\nonly ever talks to itself can skip `invoke_json` (compile error if\na wire crosses to it from another language).\n\n## Compile-time wire classification\n\nEvery wire gets a `fast_path: true | false` flag set at build time\n(issue 309 build step):\n\n```python\nfor wire in graph.wires:\n    src_lang = box_at(wire.from).lang\n    dst_lang = box_at(wire.to).lang\n    wire.fast_path = (src_lang == dst_lang)\n```\n\nThe flag becomes part of the compiled manifest. If any consumer is in a different language, the\nproducer must write JSON (and same-language consumers convert via\n`json_to_native` to recover native form).\n\nTwo ways to decide:\n1. **Per-output decision** — analyze all consumers of the output\n   slot at compile time. All same lang → native; mixed → JSON.\n2. **Always JSON producer / convert at consumer** — simpler, but\n   pays the encode cost even when no cross-language consumer is\n   present.\n\nOption 1 is the right call. The compile step records the producer's\noutput format on the box record (`output_format: \"native\" | \"json\"`),\nand same-language consumers know to read native bytes directly,\ncross-language consumers call `json_to_native` first.\n\n## Runtime dispatch\n\nThe dispatch action's input-read path branches on the wire flag:\n\n```c\nfor (int i = 0; i < n_inputs; i++) {\n    slot_peek(input_slots[i], buf, buf_capacity);\n    if (input_wires[i].fast_path && producer_format == NATIVE) {\n        // bytes are already this language's native form\n        ...\n    } else if (producer_format == JSON) {\n        // bytes are JSON, decode into native form\n        json_to_native(buf, buf_size, native_buf, native_capacity, &native_size);\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\nThen `invoke_native` is called with native-form bytes regardless of\nhow they were obtained. Same on the output side: if the box's output\nformat is `native`, write native bytes; if `json`, encode then\nwrite.\n\n## Edge cases\n\n- **All-same-language graph**: every wire is fast-path; `invoke_json`\n  never runs. Spec writers can stub it out.\n- **All-different-language graph**: every wire is JSON;\n  `invoke_native` handles bytes that came back from `json_to_native`.\n- **One same-language wire, several cross-language wires from the same\n  producer**: the producer writes JSON. Compile\n  flips the flag; the producer now writes JSON. No runtime\n  surprises, no migration.\n\n## Implementation cost\n\nThe two-invoke spec interface adds maybe 30 lines per language\nspec. The compile-time wire classification is one pass over the\ngraph. The dispatch action's input-read branch is one `if` on the\nwire flag. None of this is hot-path complex; the gain is one less\nJSON encode/decode per same-language hop, which is the whole point.\n\n## Future: whole-program same-language compilation\n\nA bigger optimization beyond this issue: at compile time, merge\nall same-language boxes into one translation unit. Consumer's spec: `cjson.decode(buf)` → Lua table\n20\t\n21\tSteps 1 and 4 are the cost. They're language-agnostic and unnecessary\n22\twhen both endpoints share a language.\n23\t\n24\t## Intended behavior\n25\t\n26\tEach language spec exposes **two invoke paths**:\n27\t\n28\t```c\n29\ttypedef struct {\n30\t    const char *name;\n31\t    const char *file_ext;\n32\t\n33\t    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n34\t    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n35\t    int   (*compile)(...);\n36\t\n37\t    // Universal path — JSON bytes in, JSON bytes out\n38\t    int   (*invoke_json)  (void *handle, /* common args */);\n39\t\n40\t    // Fast path — language-native bytes in, language-native bytes out\n41\t    int   (*invoke_native)(void *handle, /* common args */);\n42\t\n43\t    // Bridges used when a value crosses a language boundary\n44\t    int   (*native_to_json)(const void *src, int src_size,\n45\t                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n46\t    int   (*json_to_native)(const void *src, int src_size,\n47\t                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n48\t} lang_spec_t;\n49\t```\n50\t\n51\t`invoke_native` is required (every spec implements one). Per-language\n52\t\"native\" format:\n53\t- **Lua**: `lua_dump` for closures, `cjson` or msgpack for tables, raw\n54\t  bytes for strings/numbers. Spec's choice as long as it's\n55\t  symmetric with its own decoder.\n56\t- **C**: raw struct memcpy. The compile-time wrapper (issue 307)\n57\t  knows the types; serialization is `memcpy(slot_buf, &val, sizeof\n58\t  val)`.\n59\t- **Bash**: strings only — Bash has no other native form, so the\n60\t  fast path is identical to the JSON path. Implement as a thin\n61\t  alias.\n62\t\n63\t`invoke_json` is the universal interop format. Required for any\n64\tlanguage that participates in cross-language wires. A spec that\n65\tonly ever talks to itself can skip `invoke_json` (compile error if\n66\ta wire crosses to it from another language).\n67\t\n68\t## Compile-time wire classification\n69\t\n70\tEvery wire gets a `fast_path: true | false` flag set at build time\n71\t(issue 309 build step):\n72\t\n73\t```python\n74\tfor wire in graph.wires:\n75\t    src_lang = box_at(wire.from).lang\n76\t    dst_lang = box_at(wire.to).lang\n77\t    wire.fast_path = (src_lang == dst_lang)\n78\t```\n79\t\n80\tThe flag becomes part of the compiled manifest. Runtime never\n81\tre-evaluates language pairing.\n82\t\n83\t## Producer-side decision\n84\t\n85\tA producer's output goes into one slot, but multiple consumers may\n86\tread from it. If they're all the same language, the producer can\n87\twrite native bytes. If any consumer is in a different language, the\n88\tproducer must write JSON (and same-language consumers convert via\n89\t`json_to_native` to recover native form).\n90\t\n91\tTwo ways to decide:\n92\t1. **Per-output decision** — analyze all consumers of the output\n93\t   slot at compile time. All same lang → native; mixed → JSON.\n94\t2. **Always JSON producer / convert at consumer** — simpler, but\n95\t   pays the encode cost even when no cross-language consumer is\n96\t   present.\n97\t\n98\tOption 1 is the right call. The compile step records the producer's\n99\toutput format on the box record (`output_format: \"native\" | \"json\"`),\n100\tand same-language consumers know to read native bytes directly,\n101\tcross-language consumers call `json_to_native` first.\n102\t\n103\t## Runtime dispatch\n104\t\n105\tThe dispatch action's input-read path branches on the wire flag:\n106\t\n107\t```c\n108\tfor (int i = 0; i < n_inputs; i++) {\n109\t    slot_peek(input_slots[i], buf, buf_capacity);\n110\t    if (input_wires[i].fast_path && producer_format == NATIVE) {\n111\t        // bytes are already this language's native form\n112\t        ...\n113\t    } else if (producer_format == JSON) {\n114\t        // bytes are JSON, decode into native form\n115\t        json_to_native(buf, buf_size, native_buf, native_capacity, &native_size);\n116\t        ...\n117\t    }\n118\t}\n119\t```\n120\t\n121\tThen `invoke_native` is called with native-form bytes regardless of\n122\thow they were obtained. Same on the output side: if the box's output\n123\tformat is `native`, write native bytes; if `json`, encode then\n124\twrite.\n125\t\n126\t## Edge cases\n127\t\n128\t- **All-same-language graph**: every wire is fast-path; `invoke_json`\n129\t  never runs. Spec writers can stub it out.\n130\t- **All-different-language graph**: every wire is JSON;\n131\t  `invoke_native` handles bytes that came back from `json_to_native`.\n132\t- **One same-language wire, several cross-language wires from the same\n133\t  producer**: the producer writes JSON. Same-language consumer\n134\t  decodes via `json_to_native` (still cheaper than full encode +\n135\t  decode round-trip — only one direction of conversion is paid,\n136\t  not two).\n137\t- **Type changes mid-development**: a wire that was Lua→Lua becomes\n138\t  Lua→C as the user changes a downstream box's language. Compile\n139\t  flips the flag; the producer now writes JSON. No runtime\n140\t  surprises, no migration.\n141\t\n142\t## Implementation cost\n143\t\n144\tThe two-invoke spec interface adds maybe 30 lines per language\n145\tspec. The compile-time wire classification is one pass over the\n146\tgraph. The dispatch action's input-read branch is one `if` on the\n147\twire flag. None of this is hot-path complex; the gain is one less\n148\tJSON encode/decode per same-language hop, which is the whole point.\n149\t\n150\t## Future: whole-program same-language compilation\n151\t\n152\tA bigger optimization beyond this issue: at compile time, merge\n153\tall same-language boxes into one translation unit. The C spec\n154\tbecomes whole-program; the Lua spec produces one bytecode chunk\n155\tcovering every Lua function. Box-boundary crossings become regular\n156\tfunction calls — no slot store, no dispatch layer, no spec\n157\tinvocation. Only cross-language wires retain the slot machinery.\n158\t\n159\tThis is a phase-3.5+ optimization and a much bigger lift —\n160\trequires the spec's `compile` callback to coordinate across all\n161\tboxes of its language, plus a runtime mode that bypasses the\n162\tdispatch layer for fully-merged regions of the graph. The\n163\twire-level fast path in this issue is the immediate, smaller win.\n164\t\n165\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n166\t\n167\t1. **Spec interface** (issue 303): add `invoke_native`,\n168\t   `invoke_json`, `native_to_json`, `json_to_native` callbacks.\n169\t   Update the contract doc.\n170\t2. **Compile step** (issue 309): walk wires, set `fast_path` flag,\n171\t   set `output_format` per box.\n172\t3. **Dispatch action** (issue 304): branch on `fast_path` /\n173\t   `output_format` when reading inputs and when writing the\n174\t   output.\n175\t4. **Per-language specs** (306, 307, 308): implement both invoke\n176\t   paths. Bash's fast path is a thin alias around the JSON path.\n177\t   C's fast path is `memcpy`. Lua's fast path picks a native\n178\t   encoding (cjson for tables; raw bytes for primitives).\n179\t5. **Tests**: smoke tests confirming a 100k-iteration Lua→Lua\n180\t   pipeline with the fast path runs measurably faster than the\n181\t   same pipeline with the JSON path, and that mixed-language\n182\t   pipelines still work.\n183\t\n184\t## Relevant files\n185\t\n186\t- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — adds the new callbacks\n187\t- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — branch on fast_path\n188\t- `issues/309-build-system.md` — wire-flag enrichment\n189\t- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md`, `307-c-language-spec.md`,\n190\t  `308-bash-language-spec.md` — per-spec native implementations\n191\t- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot still stores opaque\n192\t  bytes; the format negotiation is at the spec layer, not the\n193\t  store\n194\t\n195\t## Implementation note: ask the user about type-annotated cross-language encodings\n196\t\n197\tBefore implementing this issue, the implementer must ask the user\n198\tto decide on **type-annotated wire encodings** for cross-language\n199\thops — primitives go raw bytes (4-byte int as 4 bytes, not as the\n200\tJSON string `\"42\"`), strings go length-prefixed UTF-8, structured\n201\ttypes go JSON.       "content":"# 305 — C graph loader (replaces 003-loader.lua)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe phase 2 loader at `src/003-loader.lua` reads a map directory's\n`boxes/*.json`, `data/*.json`, and metadata, decodes JSON via dkjson,\nruns schema validation, builds the in-memory graph table, and detects\nentry boxes. It is Lua. The synchronous executor consumes its output.\n\nThe phase 3 pool runner (issue 301) cannot embed a Lua state for\nloading — Lua appears in the runner only as a per-box language runtime,\nnever as the runner's own scripting layer. The loader is therefore\nported to C and lives inside (or alongside) `src/008-pool-runner.c`.\n\n## Concept\n\nThe C graph loader is the first phase of the pool runner's startup. It:\n1. Walks the map directory.\n2. Parses every JSON file.\n3. Validates schema and connection topology.\n4. Builds a single `graph_t` struct that the pool runner and dispatch\n   layer consume.\n\nThe loader is a one-shot at startup. It crashes the program on any\nvalidation failure (per the hard-crash policy in issue 303). There is\nno recovery, no skip-bad-boxes mode.\n\n## Inputs\n\nThe map directory layout (unchanged from phase 2):\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/\n    meta.json          ← entry box, src_dirs, run-level metadata\n    boxes/*.json       ← one file per box\n    data/*.json        ← static data values (literal inputs)\n    src/*              ← box function source files (resolved via meta.src_dirs)\n```\n\nThe loader is given the map directory path as a C string.\n\n## Output: `graph_t`\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    int           n_boxes;\n    box_t        *boxes;            // array of box descriptors\n    int           n_connections;\n    connection_t *connections;\n    int           n_size_classes;\n    int          *size_classes;     // distinct slot sizes the graph uses\n    int           n_entry_boxes;\n    int          *entry_box_ids;    // indices into boxes[]\n    int           n_languages;\n    const char  **languages;        // distinct language names used\n} graph_t;\n\ntypedef struct {\n    char         *id;               // user-defined box id (\"classifier\", \"stamp\", …)\n    char         *kind;             // \"call\" | \"data\"\n    char         *lang;             // \"lua\" | \"c\" | \"bash\" | ...; NULL for data and iterator/comparator\n    char         *ref;               // file path; NULL for data/iterator/comparator\n    char         *fn;                // function name; NULL for data/iterator/comparator\n    int           n_inputs;\n    input_decl_t *inputs;\n    int           output_capacity;  // bytes; 0 if variable-size (uses large-value heap)\n    int           is_comparator;\n    int           is_iterator;\n    int           n_iter_outputs;\n    char        **iter_output_names;\n    // …\n} box_t;\n\ntypedef struct {\n    int   from_box_id;\n    char *from_branch;              // NULL for plain call; \"lt\"/\"eq\"/\"gt\" for comparator;\n                                    // iterator output name otherwise\n    int   to_box_id;\n    char *to_input_name;\n    int   to_input_index;\n} connection_t;\n```\n\nStrings are owned by the graph (allocated from a single arena attached\nto the graph; freed when the graph is destroyed at the end of the run).\n\n## Loading phases\n\n### 1. Directory walk\nOpen the map directory, enumerate `boxes/`, `data/`, and the optional\n`meta.json`. Each entry is queued for parsing.\n\n### 2. JSON parse\nUse the vendored JSON parser (issue 301 lists cJSON / jsmn / hand-rolled\nas candidates). Each file becomes a parsed JSON tree. Parse errors are\nfatal — print the file path and the parser's error message, abort.\n\n### 3. Schema validation\nBox kinds and what they mean at runtime:\n\n- **`call`** is a verb — a box that runs a function (or, for iterator\n  and comparator variants, a dispatch-layer routing primitive). Each\n  call box becomes a `dispatch_task_t` in the pool when its inputs\n  are ready.\n- **`data`** is a noun — a literal value embedded in the map. It has\n  no function and produces no task in the pool. Its output slot is\n  allocated and filled at startup by the loader and remains filled\n  for the duration of the run; downstream consumers read it like any\n  other slot.\n\nRequired fields per kind:\n- `id`, `kind` always required.\n- For `kind == \"call\"`: either (a) `lang`, `ref`, `fn` (plain call\n  box), or (b) `iterator_outputs` (iterator box, no `ref`/`fn`), or\n  (c) `comparator` field set (comparator box, no `ref`/`fn`).\n- For `kind == \"data\"`: a `value` field; no `inputs` or `connections`\n  (other than outgoing wires from this box's output slot).\n\nBox ids must be unique across the map. Connection endpoints must\nreference valid box ids and valid input names.\n\nSchema rules mirror `src/001-schema.lua`. The C validator is a port of\nthat file's logic, simplified by the absence of port-named branching\n(removed in issue 108 cleanup).\n\n### 4. Topology validation\n- Every connection's `from_box` and `to_box` exist.\n- Every connection's `to_input_name` matches a declared input on the\n  destination box.\n- No non-iterator cycles. The validator runs DFS; any cycle that does\n  not pass through an iterator box is rejected.\n- Every required input has at least one connection feeding it (or is\n  fed by a `data` box).\n\nValidation failure aborts the program with a precise error message —\nwhich box, which connection, what was wrong.\n\n### 5. Slot size class enumeration\nWalk every box and queued-input declaration to enumerate the distinct\nslot sizes the graph will need. Each unique size becomes a size class\nin the slot allocator (issue 302). Output:\n\n```c\ngraph->size_classes      = { 64, 256, 1024, 65536 };  // example\ngraph->n_size_classes    = 4;\n```\n\nThe slot allocator pre-populates each class's free list with\n`n_workers × (count of boxes whose output is this size)` slots. This\ncovers the worst case — every worker concurrently producing an output\nat this size class — without overshooting. Demand beyond this triggers\ngrowth (issue 302); the per-thread multiplier is the right ceiling for\nthe static count, while leaving headroom for iterators that allocate\nper-invocation slots.\n\n### 6. Entry-box detection\nA box is an entry box if either:\n- It has zero inputs, or\n- All of its inputs are connected only to `data` boxes (literal values\n  with no upstream computation).\n\nEntry boxes are submitted to the pool first; everything else fires from\npost-action routing in the dispatch layer.\n\nA map can have any number of entry boxes. The user lays out the\ninitial program state via `data` boxes and entry-point call boxes; the\nrunner submits all entries at once, and the graph propagates from\nthere. There is no singular `main`.\n\n### 7. Language enumeration\nCollect the distinct `lang` values across all plain call boxes. The\npool runner uses this set to decide which language specs (issue 303)\nto load and which per-worker handles to initialize.\n\nIterator and comparator boxes have no `lang` and contribute nothing\nhere.\n\n### Note on built-in primitives vs shipped libraries\n\nThere are two distinct categories of \"things the user gets out of the\nbox,\" and they live in different places:\n\n- **Dispatch-layer primitives** are graph-topology operations whose\n  semantics are routing, not data transformation. Iterator and\n  comparator are the two so far. They have no `lang` / `ref` / `fn` —\n  the dispatch layer implements their behavior directly. Splitter\n  / fan-out is already free via wire fan-out and does not need its\n  own box kind. Possible future primitives: a \"gate\" (forward only\n  when a control input is truthy), a \"merge\" (forward whichever\n  input arrives first). These are not on the roadmap; flagged here\n  so the door stays open.\n- **Shipped libraries** are data-transformation utilities — JSON\n  parse/serialize, file read/write, string concat/split, regex,\n  shell-out. These are language-specific (string semantics differ\n  between Lua, C, and Bash) and ship as `libs/<name>.<ext>` per\n  language. They are not built into the dispatch layer; they are\n  ordinary call-box source files that users wire into their maps.\n  `libs/ollama.lua` is an existing example.\n\nThe distinction matters: dispatch-layer primitives change the graph\nmodel; shipped libraries don't. A dispatch primitive can do things a\nfunction call cannot (like routing on a counter); a library is just\ncode that happens to be vendored.\n\n## Error policy\n\nAny failure in any phase aborts the program. The loader prints:\n- The map path\n- The phase that failed (parse / schema / topology / etc.)\n- The specific file or box that caused the failure\n- The parser's or validator's diagnostic message\n\nThen `exit(1)`. There is no partial-load mode.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- JSON library choice: cJSON (heaviest, easiest, well-maintained),\n  jsmn (tiny, no allocations, manual tree walking), or hand-rolled\n  (smallest dependency footprint, more code). Decision deferred to\n  implementation time.\n### String storage\n\nA \"string arena\" is a single `malloc`-backed buffer the graph loader\nuses to store every string it owns (box ids, file paths, function\nnames, branch tags) packed end-to-end. Each string is a `char *`\npointing into the arena. Allocating a string is just bumping the\narena's offset; freeing happens once when the arena is destroyed at\nthe end of the run, in a single `free(arena_buffer)`.\n\nThis is faster and simpler than calling `malloc` per string: one\n`free` for thousands of strings, no fragmentation, and lookup is\njust a pointer.\n\nThe arena starts small and grows on demand by `realloc`-ing to a\nlarger size when the current buffer fills up. Because every stored\nstring is referenced by a `char *` into the arena, a `realloc` that\nmoves the buffer would invalidate all the pointers — so the loader\neither uses a series of fixed-size chunks (a chunk list rather than a\nsingle growable buffer) or pre-sizes the arena from the file count\nto avoid mid-load realloc. Chunk-list is the standard answer.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Vendor the chosen JSON parser into `libs/json/`.\n2. Define `graph_t`, `box_t`, `connection_t`, `input_decl_t` in\n   `src/008-pool-runner.c` (or a sibling header).\n3. Implement phase 1 (directory walk) and phase 2 (parse). Implement phase 5 (size class enumeration). Output should match\n   the box outputs declared in `maps/hello` and `maps/classify-demo`.\n7. Implement phases 6 (entry boxes) and 7 (languages). Verify against\n   known maps.\n8. Wire the loader into `src/008-pool-runner.c`'s `main` so the pool\n   runner starts by loading and validating before doing anything\n   else.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — phase 2 loader, ported by this issue\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — phase 2 schema validator, also ported\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool runner that owns and uses the loader\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle that\n  consumes the graph\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot allocator that consumes\n  the size class list\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec registry that consumes\n  the language list\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that consumes\n  the box and connection arrays\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — the compiler is the other consumer of\n  the same validation logic; the C loader and the compiler should\n  share validation code if possible\n",

The synchronous executor consumes its output.\n11\t\n12\tThe phase 3 pool runner (issue 301) cannot embed a Lua state for\n13\tloading — Lua appears in the runner only as a per-box language runtime,\n14\tnever as the runner's own scripting layer. The loader is therefore\n15\tported to C and lives inside (or alongside) `src/008-pool-runner.c`.\n16\t\n17\t## Concept\n18\t\n19\tThe C graph loader is the first phase of the pool runner's startup. It:\n20\t1. Walks the map directory.\n21\t2. Parses every JSON file.\n22\t3. Validates schema and connection topology.\n23\t4. Builds a single `graph_t` struct that the pool runner and dispatch\n24\t   layer consume.\n25\t\n26\tThe loader is a one-shot at startup. It crashes the program on any\n27\tvalidation failure (per the hard-crash policy in issue 303). There is\n28\tno recovery, no skip-bad-boxes mode.\n29\t\n30\t## Inputs\n31\t\n32\tThe map directory layout (unchanged from phase 2):\n33\t\n34\t```\n35\tmaps/<name>/\n36\t    meta.json          ← entry box, src_dirs, run-level metadata\n37\t    boxes/*.json       ← one file per box\n38\t    data/*.json        ← static data values (literal inputs)\n39\t    src/*              ← box function source files (resolved via meta.src_dirs)\n40\t```\n41\t\n42\tThe loader is given the map directory path as a C string.\n43\t\n44\t## Output: `graph_t`\n45\t\n46\t```c\n47\ttypedef struct {\n48\t    int           n_boxes;\n49\t    box_t        *boxes;            // array of box descriptors\n50\t    int           n_connections;\n51\t    connection_t *connections;\n52\t    int           n_size_classes;\n53\t    int          *size_classes;     // distinct slot sizes the graph uses\n54\t    int           n_entry_boxes;\n55\t    int          *entry_box_ids;    // indices into boxes[]\n56\t    int           n_languages;\n57\t    const char  **languages;        // distinct language names used\n58\t} graph_t;\n59\t\n60\ttypedef struct {\n61\t    char         *id;               // user-defined box id (\"classifier\", \"stamp\", …)\n62\t    char         *kind;             // \"call\" | \"data\"\n63\t    char         *lang;             // \"lua\" | \"c\" | \"bash\" | ...; NULL for data and iterator/comparator\n64\t    char         *ref;               // file path; NULL for data/iterator/comparator\n65\t    char         *fn;                // function name; NULL for data/iterator/comparator\n66\t    int           n_inputs;\n67\t    input_decl_t *inputs;\n68\t    int           output_capacity;  // bytes; 0 if variable-size (uses large-value heap)\n69\t    int           is_comparator;\n70\t    int           is_iterator;\n71\t    int           n_iter_outputs;\n72\t    char        **iter_output_names;\n73\t    // …\n74\t} box_t;\n75\t\n76\ttypedef struct {\n77\t    int   from_box_id;\n78\t    char *from_branch;              // NULL for plain call; \"lt\"/\"eq\"/\"gt\" for comparator;\n79\t                                    // iterator output name otherwise\n80\t    int   to_box_id;\n81\t    char *to_input_name;\n82\t    int   to_input_index;\n83\t} connection_t;\n84\t```\n85\t\n86\tStrings are owned by the graph (allocated from a single arena attached\n87\tto the graph; freed when the graph is destroyed at the end of the run).\n88\t\n89\t## Loading phases\n90\t\n91\t### 1. Directory walk\n92\tOpen the map directory, enumerate `boxes/`, `data/`, and the optional\n93\t`meta.json`. Each entry is queued for parsing.\n94\t\n95\t### 2. JSON parse\n96\tUse the vendored JSON parser (issue 301 lists cJSON / jsmn / hand-rolled\n97\tas candidates). Each file becomes a parsed JSON tree. Parse errors are\n98\tfatal — print the file path and the parser's error message, abort.\n99\t\n100\t### 3. Schema validation\n101\tBox kinds and what they mean at runtime:\n102\t\n103\t- **`call`** is a verb — a box that runs a function (or, for iterator\n104\t  and comparator variants, a dispatch-layer routing primitive). Each\n105\t  call box becomes a `dispatch_task_t` in the pool when its inputs\n106\t  are ready.\n107\t- **`data`** is a noun — a literal value embedded in the map. It has\n108\t  no function and produces no task in the pool. Its output slot is\n109\t  allocated and filled at startup by the loader and remains filled\n110\t  for the duration of the run; downstream consumers read it like any\n111\t  other slot.\n112\t\n113\tRequired fields per kind:\n114\t- `id`, `kind` always required.\n115\t- For `kind == \"call\"`: either (a) `lang`, `ref`, `fn` (plain call\n116\t  box), or (b) `iterator_outputs` (iterator box, no `ref`/`fn`), or\n117\t  (c) `comparator` field set (comparator box, no `ref`/`fn`).\n118\t- For `kind == \"data\"`: a `value` field; no `inputs` or `connections`\n119\t  (other than outgoing wires from this box's output slot).\n120\t\n121\tBox ids must be unique across the map. Connection endpoints must\n122\treference valid box ids and valid input names.\n123\t\n124\tSchema rules mirror `src/001-schema.lua`. The C validator is a port of\n125\tthat file's logic, simplified by the absence of port-named branching\n126\t(removed in issue 108 cleanup).\n127\t\n128\t### 4. Topology validation\n129\t- Every connection's `from_box` and `to_box` exist.\n130\t- Every connection's `to_input_name` matches a declared input on the\n131\t  destination box.\n132\t- No non-iterator cycles. The validator runs DFS; any cycle that does\n133\t  not pass through an iterator box is rejected.\n134\t- Every required input has at least one connection feeding it (or is\n135\t  fed by a `data` box).\n136\t\n137\tValidation failure aborts the program with a precise error message —\n138\twhich box, which connection, what was wrong.\n139\t\n140\t### 5. Slot size class enumeration\n141\tWalk every box and queued-input declaration to enumerate the distinct\n142\tslot sizes the graph will need. Each unique size becomes a size class\n143\tin the slot allocator (issue 302). Output:\n144\t\n145\t```c\n146\tgraph->size_classes      = { 64, 256, 1024, 65536 };  // example\n147\tgraph->n_size_classes    = 4;\n148\t```\n149\t\n150\tThe slot allocator pre-populates each class's free list with\n151\t`n_workers × (count of boxes whose output is this size)` slots. This\n152\tcovers the worst case — every worker concurrently producing an output\n153\tat this size class — without overshooting. Demand beyond this triggers\n154\tgrowth (issue 302); the per-thread multiplier is the right ceiling for\n155\tthe static count, while leaving headroom for iterators that allocate\n156\tper-invocation slots.\n157\t\n158\t### 6. Entry-box detection\n159\tA box is an entry box if either:\n160\t- It has zero inputs, or\n161\t- All of its inputs are connected only to `data` boxes (literal values\n162\t  with no upstream computation).\n163\t\n164\tEntry boxes are submitted to the pool first; everything else fires from\n165\tpost-action routing in the dispatch layer.\n166\t\n167\tA map can have any number of entry boxes. The user lays out the\n168\tinitial program state via `data` boxes and entry-point call boxes; the\n169\trunner submits all entries at once, and the graph propagates from\n170\tthere. There is no singular `main`.\n171\t\n172\t### 7. Language enumeration\n173\tCollect the distinct `lang` values across all plain call boxes. The\n174\tpool runner uses this set to decide which language specs (issue 303)\n175\tto load and which per-worker handles to initialize.\n176\t\n177\tIterator and comparator boxes have no `lang` and contribute nothing\n178\there.\n179\t\n180\t### Note on built-in primitives vs shipped libraries\n181\t\n182\tThere are two distinct categories of \"things the user gets out of the\n183\tbox,\" and they live in different places:\n184\t\n185\t- **Dispatch-layer primitives** are graph-topology operations whose\n186\t  semantics are routing, not data transformation. Iterator and\n187\t  comparator are the two so far. They have no `lang` / `ref` / `fn` —\n188\t  the dispatch layer implements their behavior directly. Splitter\n189\t  / fan-out is already free via wire fan-out and does not need its\n190\t  own box kind. Possible future primitives: a \"gate\" (forward only\n191\t  when a control input is truthy), a \"merge\" (forward whichever\n192\t  input arrives first). These are not on the roadmap; flagged here\n193\t  so the door stays open.\n194\t- **Shipped libraries** are data-transformation utilities — JSON\n195\t  parse/serialize, file read/write, string concat/split, regex,\n196\t  shell-out. These are language-specific (string semantics differ\n197\t  between Lua, C, and Bash) and ship as `libs/<name>.<ext>` per\n198\t  language. They are not built into the dispatch layer; they are\n199\t  ordinary call-box source files that users wire into their maps.\n200\t  `libs/ollama.lua` is an existing example.\n201\t\n202\tThe distinction matters: dispatch-layer primitives change the graph\n203\tmodel; shipped libraries don't. A dispatch primitive can do things a\n204\tfunction call cannot (like routing on a counter); a library is just\n205\tcode that happens to be vendored.\n206\t\n207\t## Error policy\n208\t\n209\tAny failure in any phase aborts the program. The loader prints:\n210\t- The map path\n211\t- The phase that failed (parse / schema / topology / etc.)\n212\t- The specific file or box that caused the failure\n213\t- The parser's or validator's diagnostic message\n214\t\n215\tThen `exit(1)`. There is no partial-load mode.\n216\t\n217\t## Open questions\n218\t\n219\t- JSON library choice: cJSON (heaviest, easiest, well-maintained),\n220\t  jsmn (tiny, no allocations, manual tree walking), or hand-rolled\n221\t  (smallest dependency footprint, more code). Decision deferred to\n222\t  implementation time.\n223\t### String storage\n224\t\n225\tA \"string arena\" is a single `malloc`-backed buffer the graph loader\n226\tuses to store every string it owns (box ids, file paths, function\n227\tnames, branch tags) packed end-to-end. Each string is a `char *`\n228\tpointing into the arena. Allocating a string is just bumping the\n229\tarena's offset; freeing happens once when the arena is destroyed at\n230\tthe end of the run, in a single `free(arena_buffer)`.\n231\t\n232\tThis is faster and simpler than calling `malloc` per string: one\n233\t`free` for thousands of strings, no fragmentation, and lookup is\n234\tjust a pointer.\n235\t\n236\tThe arena starts small and grows on demand by `realloc`-ing to a\n237\tlarger size when the current buffer fills up. Because every stored\n238\tstring is referenced by a `char *` into the arena, a `realloc` that\n239\tmoves the buffer would invalidate all the pointers — so the loader\n240\teither uses a series of fixed-size chunks (a chunk list rather than a\n241\tsingle growable buffer) or pre-sizes the arena from the file count\n242\tto avoid mid-load realloc. Chunk-list is the standard answer.\n243\t\n244\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n245\t\n246\t1. Vendor the chosen JSON parser into `libs/json/`.\n247\t2. Define `graph_t`, `box_t`, `connection_t`, `input_decl_t` in\n248\t   `src/008-pool-runner.c` (or a sibling header).\n249\t3. Implement phase 1 (directory walk) and phase 2 (parse). Smoke test:\n250\t   load `maps/hello`, print the parsed tree.\n251\t4. Implement phase 3 (schema validation) one rule at a time. Each\n252\t   rule has a unit test against a malformed map fixture.\n253\t5. Implement phase 4 (topology validation), including the cycle\n254\t   detector. Test against `maps/branch-test` (valid) and a fixture\n255\t   with a non-iterator cycle (invalid).\n256\t6. Implement phase 5 (size class enumeration). Output should match\n257\t   the box outputs declared in `maps/hello` and `maps/classify-demo`.\n258\t7. Implement phases 6 (entry boxes) and 7 (languages). Verify against\n259\t   known maps.\n260\t8. Wire the loader into `src/008-pool-runner.c`'s `main` so the pool\n261\t   runner starts by loading and validating before doing anything\n262\t   else.\n263\t\n264\t## Relevant files\n265\t\n266\t- `src/003-loader.lua` — phase 2 loader, ported by this issue\n267\t- `src/001-schema.lua` — phase 2 schema validator, also ported\n268\t- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool runner that owns and uses the loader\n269\t- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle that\n270\t  consumes the graph\n271\t- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot allocator that consumes\n272\t  the size class list\n273\t- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec registry that consumes\n274\t  the language list\n275\t- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that consumes\n276\t  the box and connection arrays\n277\t- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — the compiler is the other consumer of\n278\t  the same validation logic; the C loader and the compiler should\n279\t  share validation code if possible\n280\t"
      }],
