          "content":"<!doctype html>\n<html lang=\"en\">\n<head>\n  <meta charset=\"utf-8\">\n  <meta name=\"viewport\" content=\"width=device-width, initial-scale=1\">\n  <title>§ 04 · IPC & Threading — SoraMech</title>\n  <link rel=\"stylesheet\" href=\"assets/style.css\">\n  <script defer src=\"assets/nav.js\"></script>\n  <script defer src=\"assets/demos.js\"></script>\n</head>\n<body data-page=\"004-ipc-and-threading.html\">\n  <div class=\"shell\">\n    <aside class=\"sidebar\"></aside>\n    <main>\n      <div class=\"content\">\n        <div class=\"page-head\">\n          <div class=\"doc-num\">§ 04 · IPC & Threading Model</div>\n          <h1>How <em>values</em> cross between languages, and how the runner becomes a pool.</h1>\n          <p class=\"lede\">Phase 2 spawns a process per call and pipes stdout. Phase 3 owns a C thread pool, persists per-worker language runtimes, and routes values through addressable slots. Two ends of the rewrite arc, plus the IPC options that informed the choice.</p>\n        </div>\n\n        <h2 id=\"problem\">The problem</h2>\n        <p>The current executor runs boxes sequentially. Each box invocation shells out to a driver script, which starts a new process, runs the function, and exits. The return value passes through stdout. This works but has two structural problems:</p>\n        <ol>\n          <li><strong>Process-per-call cost.</strong> Spawning a process takes roughly 1–10 ms depending on the runtime. For a map with ten boxes, that's dominated by spawn overhead, not by the actual work.</li>\n          <li><strong>stdout is the wrong channel.</strong> A box function that prints debug output corrupts the wire value. Values are transient — they vanish once the pipe is drained. The channel has no addressing, no framing, and no backpressure.</li>\n        </ol>\n        <p>The goal is a design where cross-language calls are fast, values are addressable, and the execution model is ready to parallelize without redesign.</p>\n\n        <h2 id=\"roadmap\">The threading roadmap</h2>\n        <p>Three stages, each building on the last:</p>\n        <ul>\n          <li><strong>Stage 1 — Synchronous (current).</strong> A single-threaded ready-queue walks the graph in dependency order. <code>run_task(box, inputs)</code> in <code>src/004-executor.lua</code> is the task boundary. It blocks until the driver responds.</li>\n          <li><strong>Stage 2 — Coroutine-based non-blocking <span class=\"pill planned\">skipped</span>.</strong> Originally planned as a coroutine scheduler with LuaSocket non-blocking I/O. Skipped — the path goes straight from stage 1 to stage 3.</li>\n          <li><strong>Stage 3 — SoraMech-owned thread pool.</strong> A pool implementation written for SoraMech, with the 3d-rts pool design as a reference. The <code>task_fn</code> boundary swaps in the thread pool. Worker threads pull tasks from the pool; OS-level scheduling replaces any single-threaded ordering. Cross-language calls block a worker thread while other threads continue. True parallelism across cores.</li>\n        </ul>\n        <div class=\"callout copper\">\n          <strong>Note. </strong>Effil-jit is not used. Coroutines are not used. The path goes straight from synchronous (phase 2) to the C pool (phase 3) — no intermediate coroutine stage.\n        </div>\n\n        <h2 id=\"stage-3\">Stage 3 detail — pthreads task model</h2>\n        <p>Each box execution in the thread pool is a <strong>task struct</strong> containing:</p>\n        <ul>\n          <li><strong>Function pointer</strong> — the language-specific invocation wrapper (a C function, since pthreads requires a C entry point)</li>\n          <li><strong>Shared memory pointer</strong> — the region holding the input arguments and return value for this invocation</li>\n          <li><strong>Dependency list</strong> — pointers to the tasks this task is waiting on</li>\n          <li><strong>Waiting list</strong> — pointers to tasks that are waiting on this task</li>\n          <li><strong>Counter</strong> (iterator boxes only) — current iteration index, updated in-place when the iterator re-queues itself</li>\n        </ul>\n        <p>Task structs are allocated once at run start, one per box (not one per invocation). They live for the entire run.</p>\n\n        <h3 id=\"blocking-states\">Blocking and unblocking — pointer-only transitions</h3>\n        <p>When a task cannot run (upstream output not yet available), it is placed in its upstream task's waiting list. This is a pointer move — no allocation, no struct copy. The task struct stays exactly where it is.</p>\n        <p>When an upstream task completes and writes its return value to shared memory, it walks its waiting list and re-adds each entry to the main task queue. Again, a pointer move only. The unblocked task's struct is unchanged; only its position in the queue changes.</p>\n        <p>This means &ldquo;blocked&rdquo;, &ldquo;queued&rdquo;, and &ldquo;running&rdquo; are states defined by which list a task's pointer currently lives in — not by any field in the struct.</p>\n\n        <h3 id=\"per-thread-runtimes\">Per-thread language runtimes</h3>\n        <p>Each worker thread initializes its own language runtimes at startup:</p>\n        <ul>\n          <li><strong>Lua:</strong> one <code>lua_State</code> per thread. Lua states are not thread-safe, but one per thread requires no locking. The task wrapper calls the box function via <code>lua_pcall</code>.</li>\n          <li><strong>C:</strong> the compiled box function is called directly through the function pointer. No interpreter, no overhead beyond the call itself.</li>\n          <li><strong>Bash/other:</strong> a persistent subprocess per thread (Unix domain socket server model — see Option 3 below). The task wrapper sends a request and blocks the thread waiting for the response.</li>\n        </ul>\n\n        <h3 id=\"iterator-requeue\">Iterator self-re-queue</h3>\n        <p>An iterator task does not terminate after one invocation. When it completes:</p>\n        <ol>\n          <li>It increments its <code>counter</code> field in-place (or wraps to 0).</li>\n          <li>It checks its input queue for the next pending value.</li>\n          <li>If a value is waiting: it updates its input pointer and re-adds itself to the main task queue. No allocation — the same task struct re-enters the queue with updated state.</li>\n          <li>If no value is waiting: it adds itself to the upstream task's waiting list, to be re-added when the next input arrives.</li>\n        </ol>\n        <p>Input values are processed one-at-a-time in arrival order. Ten queued inputs means the iterator task visits the queue ten times, advancing the counter and firing a different output path each time.</p>\n\n        <h2 id=\"blocking\">Blocking semantics for long-running operations</h2>\n        <p>The pool's parallelism comes from running N worker threads concurrently on N cores. Each worker is sitting inside a single dispatch task at any given moment. If a box function does something that takes a long time — <code>sleep</code>, blocking I/O, a synchronous network request, waiting on a long-running subprocess — <strong>the worker thread is occupied for the full duration</strong>. It cannot pick up other tasks while it waits.</p>\n\n        <div data-demo=\"threadPool\"></div>\n\n        <p>Concretely:</p>\n        <ul>\n          <li>16-worker pool, 1 box sleeping 10 seconds → the other 15 workers continue normally.</li>\n          <li>16-worker pool, 16 boxes all sleeping → all workers parked, no other task runs until a sleep finishes.</li>\n          <li>The pool size is also the budget for &ldquo;blocking activities&rdquo;. Heavy use of <code>sleep</code>-style boxes means raising <code>SORAMECH_WORKERS</code>.</li>\n        </ul>\n\n        <p><strong>Why the runtime does not have a scheduler:</strong> SoraMech is deliberately not in the business of &ldquo;park this task and wake it at time T.&rdquo; There is no delayed-spawn primitive, no timer thread, no polling loop. Adding one would mean a second concurrency model alongside the pool, with its own synchronization story. Instead, we lean on the pool's existing mechanism: a task either runs (occupying a worker) or is blocked on a slot waiting for a value (parked, no worker held). Long sleeps are an &ldquo;occupying a worker&rdquo; case.</p>\n\n        <div class=\"callout\">\n          <strong>Cooperative pattern. </strong>For users who need many concurrent waits without burning workers, split the operation into &ldquo;kick off the thing&rdquo; (returns immediately) and &ldquo;check whether the thing is done&rdquo; (returns immediately, returns a status), and wire them through an iterator with a queued input. The iterator polls. Each box completes quickly, freeing its worker.\n        </div>\n\n        <h2 id=\"ipc\">The three IPC options</h2>\n\n        <div data-demo=\"ipcOptions\"></div>\n\n        <h3 id=\"ffi\">Option 1 — LuaJIT FFI (Lua ↔ C, in-process)</h3>\n        <p>The Foreign Function Interface lets Lua call C functions that live in a shared library (<code>.so</code>) directly, in the same process, with no subprocess and no channel. You provide a C declaration (<code>ffi.cdef[[ int add(int a, int b); ]]</code>), load the compiled library (<code>ffi.load(\"./mybox.so\")</code>), and call <code>lib.add(3, 4)</code> — the CPU jumps into native code and returns. Overhead is nanoseconds.</p>\n        <p>Since the executor already does mtime-based dynamic compilation (see <code>drivers/c.sh</code>), compiling to a <code>.so</code> instead of a binary is just a flag change (<code>-shared -fPIC</code>). The box function signature changes from <code>main(argc, argv)</code> to a named function with typed arguments — which is strictly cleaner.</p>\n        <p><strong>Limitation:</strong> FFI only works for languages that compile to a C-compatible ABI. Bash cannot. Python can (via <code>ctypes</code> on the other side), but it's awkward. FFI is the right answer for Lua ↔ C only.</p>\n        <p><strong>Cross-platform:</strong> LuaJIT FFI works on Linux, macOS, and Windows. <code>.so</code> becomes <code>.dylib</code> on macOS and <code>.dll</code> on Windows.</p>\n\n        <h3 id=\"shm\">Option 2 — Shared memory (shm_open + mmap)</h3>\n        <p><code>shm_open(\"/soramech-wire-0\", ...)</code> creates a named memory segment managed by the kernel — not a file on disk, but a named object in RAM. <code>mmap()</code> maps it into the calling process's address space. Any other process that opens the same name gets access to the <em>same physical memory</em>. A write in one process is immediately visible in another — no copy, no syscall per access after setup.</p>\n        <p>For SoraMech, each wire between two boxes would correspond to a named shared memory slot. The compiler generates the slot names and the read/write calls. Any language that can call POSIX can participate:</p>\n        <ul>\n          <li>Lua: via LuaJIT FFI calling <code>shm_open</code> + <code>mmap</code> from libc</li>\n          <li>C: natively</li>\n          <li>Bash: via <code>/dev/shm/&lt;name&gt;</code> — on Linux, the tmpfs backing shared memory is exposed as a filesystem path, so bash can <code>cat /dev/shm/soramech-wire-0</code></li>\n        </ul>\n        <p><strong>Performance:</strong> After the initial <code>mmap()</code> setup, reads and writes are pointer dereferences — no syscalls, no copies.</p>\n        <p><strong>Complication:</strong> Shared memory is untyped raw bytes. You need a size header, a type tag, and a synchronization mechanism. None of these are hard but the compiler must generate all of it correctly for every wire.</p>\n        <p><strong>Cross-platform:</strong> Linux full; macOS partial (<code>shm_open</code> works, <code>/dev/shm/</code> doesn't); Windows different API.</p>\n\n        <h3 id=\"usock\">Option 3 — Unix domain socket servers <span class=\"amber\">(chosen)</span></h3>\n        <p>A Unix domain socket is a socket addressed by a filesystem path instead of an IP address and port. <code>/tmp/soramech-bash.sock</code> is a special file; any process on the same machine connects to it with the standard socket API. The kernel routes data directly between processes in memory — no network stack, no loopback, no protocol headers. Performance is bounded by memory bandwidth.</p>\n        <p>Each language runtime runs as a persistent socket server. One server instance per language per worker thread:</p>\n<pre data-lang=\"paths\">/tmp/soramech-bash-0.sock   ← worker thread 0's bash runtime\n/tmp/soramech-bash-1.sock   ← worker thread 1's bash runtime\n/tmp/soramech-c-0.sock      ← worker thread 0's C runtime</pre>\n        <p><strong>Wire protocol:</strong> Length-prefix framing. The sender writes a 4-byte big-endian integer (the message length in bytes), then that many bytes of content. The receiver reads 4 bytes, then reads exactly that many bytes. This handles values containing newlines or null bytes without ambiguity.</p>\n        <p><strong>Cost of idle servers:</strong> An idle server process is blocked on <code>accept()</code> — zero CPU, approximately 3–5 MB RSS for a bash process. For 10 languages × 4 threads = 40 processes ≈ 150–200 MB. Acceptable.</p>\n        <p><strong>Integration with the SoraMech thread pool:</strong></p>\n        <p>Each worker thread owns its set of language server sockets. When <code>run_task</code> calls a cross-language box, it sends to the socket and blocks on the read — the thread blocks, not the whole program. Other workers continue processing other boxes on other cores. The server processes run concurrently on whatever cores the OS schedules them to. This gives real parallelism: a bash box and a C box assigned to different workers can run simultaneously.</p>\n        <p><strong>Cross-platform:</strong> Linux full; macOS full; Windows 10 1803+ (2018) supported.</p>\n\n        <h2 id=\"summary\">Summary comparison</h2>\n        <table>\n          <thead><tr><th>Property</th><th>FFI (.so)</th><th>Shared memory</th><th>Unix domain socket</th></tr></thead>\n          <tbody>\n            <tr><td>Speed (per call)</td>      <td>nanoseconds</td>    <td>nanoseconds*</td>      <td>microseconds</td></tr>\n            <tr><td>Languages supported</td>   <td>C-ABI only</td>     <td>any (with caveats)</td><td>any</td></tr>\n            <tr><td>Parallel connections</td>  <td>N/A (in-process)</td><td>yes (with sync)</td>  <td>yes (natural)</td></tr>\n            <tr><td>Linux</td>                 <td>yes</td>            <td>yes</td>               <td>yes</td></tr>\n            <tr><td>macOS</td>                 <td>yes</td>            <td>partial†</td>          <td>yes</td></tr>\n            <tr><td>Windows</td>               <td>yes (.dll)</td>     <td>no (different API)</td><td>yes (Win10+)</td></tr>\n            <tr><td>Complexity</td>            <td>low</td>            <td>medium</td>            <td>low-medium</td></tr>\n          </tbody>\n        </table>\n        <p class=\"tiny dim\">*After initial mmap setup. †shm_open works; /dev/shm filesystem path does not.</p>\n\n        <p>The compiler (issue 219, folded into issue 309) uses FFI for Lua ↔ C wires where the C source is compiled to a <code>.so</code>, and Unix domain sockets for all other cross-language wires. Same-language Lua wires are direct function calls — no IPC at all.</p>\n\n        <h2 id=\"related\">Relevant files</h2>\n        <ul>\n          <li><code>src/004-executor.lua</code> — <code>run_task</code> boundary, ready-queue</li>\n          <li><code>src/007-runner-main.lua</code> — entry point for the interpreter path</li>\n          <li>issue <code>219</code> — compiler that generates the IPC calls (folded into 309)</li>\n          <li>issue <code>104</code> — task boundary design</li>\n          <li>issue <code>213</code> — queue-per-port, thread pool notes</li>\n          <li><a href=\"002-roadmap.html\">§ 02 · Roadmap</a> — phase plan for threading stages</li>\n        </ul>\n\n        <div class=\"page-nav\">\n          <a href=\"003-driver-system.html\"><span class=\"dir\">◂ back</span><span class=\"title\">Driver System</span></a>\n          <a href=\"005-language-specs.html\" class=\"next\"><span class=\"dir\">next ▸</span><span class=\"title\">Language Specs</span></a>\n        </div>\n      </div>\n    </main>\n  </div>\n</body>\n</html>\n",

        }

The channel has no addressing, no framing, and no backpressure.</li>\n        </ol>\n        <p>The goal is a design where cross-language calls are fast, values are addressable, and the execution model is ready to parallelize without redesign.</p>\n\n        <h2 id=\"roadmap\">The threading roadmap</h2>\n        <p>Three stages, each building on the last:</p>\n        <ul>\n          <li><strong>Stage 1 — Synchronous (current).</strong> A single-threaded ready-queue walks the graph in dependency order. <code>run_task(box, inputs)</code> in <code>src/004-executor.lua</code> is the task boundary. It blocks until the driver responds.</li>\n          <li><strong>Stage 2 — Coroutine-based non-blocking <span class=\"pill planned\">skipped</span>.</strong> Originally planned as a coroutine scheduler with LuaSocket non-blocking I/O. Skipped — the path goes straight from stage 1 to stage 3.</li>\n          <li><strong>Stage 3 — SoraMech-owned thread pool.</strong> A pool implementation written for SoraMech, with the 3d-rts pool design as a reference. The <code>task_fn</code> boundary swaps in the thread pool. Worker threads pull tasks from the pool; OS-level scheduling replaces any single-threaded ordering. Cross-language calls block a worker thread while other threads continue. True parallelism across cores.</li>\n        </ul>\n        <div class=\"callout copper\">\n          <strong>Note. </strong>Effil-jit is not used. Coroutines are not used. The path goes straight from synchronous (phase 2) to the C pool (phase 3) — no intermediate coroutine stage.\n        </div>\n\n        <h2 id=\"stage-3\">Stage 3 detail — pthreads task model</h2>\n        <p>Each box execution in the thread pool is a <strong>task struct</strong> containing:</p>\n        <ul>\n          <li><strong>Function pointer</strong> — the language-specific invocation wrapper (a C function, since pthreads requires a C entry point)</li>\n          <li><strong>Shared memory pointer</strong> — the region holding the input arguments and return value for this invocation</li>\n          <li><strong>Dependency list</strong> — pointers to the tasks this task is waiting on</li>\n          <li><strong>Waiting list</strong> — pointers to tasks that are waiting on this task</li>\n          <li><strong>Counter</strong> (iterator boxes only) — current iteration index, updated in-place when the iterator re-queues itself</li>\n        </ul>\n        <p>Task structs are allocated once at run start, one per box (not one per invocation). They live for the entire run.</p>\n\n        <h3 id=\"blocking-states\">Blocking and unblocking — pointer-only transitions</h3>\n        <p>When a task cannot run (upstream output not yet available), it is placed in its upstream task's waiting list. This is a pointer move — no allocation, no struct copy. The task struct stays exactly where it is.</p>\n        <p>When an upstream task completes and writes its return value to shared memory, it walks its waiting list and re-adds each entry to the main task queue. Again, a pointer move only. The unblocked task's struct is unchanged; only its position in the queue changes.</p>\n        <p>This means &ldquo;blocked&rdquo;, &ldquo;queued&rdquo;, and &ldquo;running&rdquo; are states defined by which list a task's pointer currently lives in — not by any field in the struct.</p>\n\n        <h3 id=\"per-thread-runtimes\">Per-thread language runtimes</h3>\n        <p>Each worker thread initializes its own language runtimes at startup:</p>\n        <ul>\n          <li><strong>Lua:</strong> one <code>lua_State</code> per thread. Lua states are not thread-safe, but one per thread requires no locking. The task wrapper calls the box function via <code>lua_pcall</code>.</li>\n          <li><strong>C:</strong> the compiled box function is called directly through the function pointer. No interpreter, no overhead beyond the call itself.</li>\n          <li><strong>Bash/other:</strong> a persistent subprocess per thread (Unix domain socket server model — see Option 3 below). The task wrapper sends a request and blocks the thread waiting for the response.</li>\n        </ul>\n\n        <h3 id=\"iterator-requeue\">Iterator self-re-queue</h3>\n        <p>An iterator task does not terminate after one invocation. When it completes:</p>\n        <ol>\n          <li>It increments its <code>counter</code> field in-place (or wraps to 0).</li>\n          <li>It checks its input queue for the next pending value.</li>\n          <li>If a value is waiting: it updates its input pointer and re-adds itself to the main task queue. No allocation — the same task struct re-enters the queue with updated state.</li>\n          <li>If no value is waiting: it adds itself to the upstream task's waiting list, to be re-added when the next input arrives.</li>\n        </ol>\n        <p>Input values are processed one-at-a-time in arrival order. Ten queued inputs means the iterator task visits the queue ten times, advancing the counter and firing a different output path each time.</p>\n\n        <h2 id=\"blocking\">Blocking semantics for long-running operations</h2>\n        <p>The pool's parallelism comes from running N worker threads concurrently on N cores. Each worker is sitting inside a single dispatch task at any given moment. If a box function does something that takes a long time — <code>sleep</code>, blocking I/O, a synchronous network request, waiting on a long-running subprocess — <strong>the worker thread is occupied for the full duration</strong>. It cannot pick up other tasks while it waits.</p>\n\n        <div data-demo=\"threadPool\"></div>\n\n        <p>Concretely:</p>\n        <ul>\n          <li>16-worker pool, 1 box sleeping 10 seconds → the other 15 workers continue normally.</li>\n          <li>16-worker pool, 16 boxes all sleeping → all workers parked, no other task runs until a sleep finishes.</li>\n          <li>The pool size is also the budget for &ldquo;blocking activities&rdquo;. Heavy use of <code>sleep</code>-style boxes means raising <code>SORAMECH_WORKERS</code>.</li>\n        </ul>\n\n        <p><strong>Why the runtime does not have a scheduler:</strong> SoraMech is deliberately not in the business of &ldquo;park this task and wake it at time T.&rdquo; There is no delayed-spawn primitive, no timer thread, no polling loop. Adding one would mean a second concurrency model alongside the pool, with its own synchronization story. Instead, we lean on the pool's existing mechanism: a task either runs (occupying a worker) or is blocked on a slot waiting for a value (parked, no worker held). Long sleeps are an &ldquo;occupying a worker&rdquo; case.</p>\n\n        <div class=\"callout\">\n          <strong>Cooperative pattern. </strong>For users who need many concurrent waits without burning workers, split the operation into &ldquo;kick off the thing&rdquo; (returns immediately) and &ldquo;check whether the thing is done&rdquo; (returns immediately, returns a status), and wire them through an iterator with a queued input. The iterator polls. Each box completes quickly, freeing its worker.\n        </div>\n\n        <h2 id=\"ipc\">The three IPC options</h2>\n\n        <div data-demo=\"ipcOptions\"></div>\n\n        <h3 id=\"ffi\">Option 1 — LuaJIT FFI (Lua ↔ C, in-process)</h3>\n        <p>The Foreign Function Interface lets Lua call C functions that live in a shared library (<code>.so</code>) directly, in the same process, with no subprocess and no channel. You provide a C declaration (<code>ffi.cdef[[ int add(int a, int b); ]]</code>), load the compiled library (<code>ffi.load(\"./mybox.so\")</code>), and call <code>lib.add(3, 4)</code> — the CPU jumps into native code and returns. Overhead is nanoseconds.</p>\n        <p>Since the executor already does mtime-based dynamic compilation (see <code>drivers/c.sh</code>), compiling to a <code>.so</code> instead of a binary is just a flag change (<code>-shared -fPIC</code>). The box function signature changes from <code>main(argc, argv)</code> to a named function with typed arguments — which is strictly cleaner.</p>\n        <p><strong>Limitation:</strong> FFI only works for languages that compile to a C-compatible ABI. Bash cannot. Python can (via <code>ctypes</code> on the other side), but it's awkward. FFI is the right answer for Lua ↔ C only.</p>\n        <p><strong>Cross-platform:</strong> LuaJIT FFI works on Linux, macOS, and Windows. <code>.so</code> becomes <code>.dylib</code> on macOS and <code>.dll</code> on Windows.</p>\n\n        <h3 id=\"shm\">Option 2 — Shared memory (shm_open + mmap)</h3>\n        <p><code>shm_open(\"/soramech-wire-0\", ...)</code> creates a named memory segment managed by the kernel — not a file on disk, but a named object in RAM. <code>mmap()</code> maps it into the calling process's address space. Any other process that opens the same name gets access to the <em>same physical memory</em>. A write in one process is immediately visible in another — no copy, no syscall per access after setup.</p>\n        <p>For SoraMech, each wire between two boxes would correspond to a named shared memory slot. The compiler generates the slot names and the read/write calls. Any language that can call POSIX can participate:</p>\n        <ul>\n          <li>Lua: via LuaJIT FFI calling <code>shm_open</code> + <code>mmap</code> from libc</li>\n          <li>C: natively</li>\n          <li>Bash: via <code>/dev/shm/&lt;name&gt;</code> — on Linux, the tmpfs backing shared memory is exposed as a filesystem path, so bash can <code>cat /dev/shm/soramech-wire-0</code></li>\n        </ul>\n        <p><strong>Performance:</strong> After the initial <code>mmap()</code> setup, reads and writes are pointer dereferences — no syscalls, no copies.</p>\n        <p><strong>Complication:</strong> Shared memory is untyped raw bytes. You need a size header, a type tag, and a synchronization mechanism. None of these are hard but the compiler must generate all of it correctly for every wire.</p>\n        <p><strong>Cross-platform:</strong> Linux full; macOS partial (<code>shm_open</code> works, <code>/dev/shm/</code> doesn't); Windows different API.</p>\n\n        <h3 id=\"usock\">Option 3 — Unix domain socket servers <span class=\"amber\">(chosen)</span></h3>\n        <p>A Unix domain socket is a socket addressed by a filesystem path instead of an IP address and port. <code>/tmp/soramech-bash.sock</code> is a special file; any process on the same machine connects to it with the standard socket API. The kernel routes data directly between processes in memory — no network stack, no loopback, no protocol headers. Performance is bounded by memory bandwidth.</p>\n        <p>Each language runtime runs as a persistent socket server. One server instance per language per worker thread:</p>\n<pre data-lang=\"paths\">/tmp/soramech-bash-0.sock   ← worker thread 0's bash runtime\n/tmp/soramech-bash-1.sock   ← worker thread 1's bash runtime\n/tmp/soramech-c-0.sock      ← worker thread 0's C runtime</pre>\n        <p><strong>Wire protocol:</strong> Length-prefix framing. The sender writes a 4-byte big-endian integer (the message length in bytes), then that many bytes of content. The receiver reads 4 bytes, then reads exactly that many bytes. This handles values containing newlines or null bytes without ambiguity.</p>\n        <p><strong>Cost of idle servers:</strong> An idle server process is blocked on <code>accept()</code> — zero CPU, approximately 3–5 MB RSS for a bash process. For 10 languages × 4 threads = 40 processes ≈ 150–200 MB. Acceptable.</p>\n        <p><strong>Integration with the SoraMech thread pool:</strong></p>\n        <p>Each worker thread owns its set of language server sockets. When <code>run_task</code> calls a cross-language box, it sends to the socket and blocks on the read — the thread blocks, not the whole program. Other workers continue processing other boxes on other cores. The server processes run concurrently on whatever cores the OS schedules them to. This gives real parallelism: a bash box and a C box assigned to different workers can run simultaneously.</p>\n        <p><strong>Cross-platform:</strong> Linux full; macOS full; Windows 10 1803+ (2018) supported.</p>\n\n        <h2 id=\"summary\">Summary comparison</h2>\n        <table>\n          <thead><tr><th>Property</th><th>FFI (.so)</th><th>Shared memory</th><th>Unix domain socket</th></tr></thead>\n          <tbody>\n            <tr><td>Speed (per call)</td>      <td>nanoseconds</td>    <td>nanoseconds*</td>      <td>microseconds</td></tr>\n            <tr><td>Languages supported</td>   <td>C-ABI only</td>     <td>any (with caveats)</td><td>any</td></tr>\n            <tr><td>Parallel connections</td>  <td>N/A (in-process)</td><td>yes (with sync)</td>  <td>yes (natural)</td></tr>\n            <tr><td>Linux</td>                 <td>yes</td>            <td>yes</td>               <td>yes</td></tr>\n            <tr><td>macOS</td>                 <td>yes</td>            <td>partial†</td>          <td>yes</td></tr>\n            <tr><td>Windows</td>               <td>yes (.dll)</td>     <td>no (different API)</td><td>yes (Win10+)</td></tr>\n            <tr><td>Complexity</td>            <td>low</td>            <td>medium</td>            <td>low-medium</td></tr>\n          </tbody>\n        </table>\n        <p class=\"tiny dim\">*After initial mmap setup. †shm_open works; /dev/shm filesystem path does not.</p>\n\n        <p>The compiler (issue 219, folded into issue 309) uses FFI for Lua ↔ C wires where the C source is compiled to a <code>.so</code>, and Unix domain sockets for all other cross-language wires. Same-language Lua wires are direct function calls — no IPC at all.</p>\n\n        <h2 id=\"related\">Relevant files</h2>\n        <ul>\n          <li><code>src/004-executor.lua</code> — <code>run_task</code> boundary, ready-queue</li>\n          <li><code>src/007-runner-main.lua</code> — entry point for the interpreter path</li>\n          <li>issue <code>219</code> — compiler that generates the IPC calls (folded into 309)</li>\n          <li>issue <code>104</code> — task boundary design</li>\n          <li>issue <code>213</code> — queue-per-port, thread pool notes</li>\n          <li><a href=\"002-roadmap.html\">§ 02 · Roadmap</a> — phase plan for threading stages</li>\n        </ul>\n\n        <div class=\"page-nav\">\n          <a href=\"003-driver-system.html\"><span class=\"dir\">◂ back</span><span class=\"title\">Driver System</span></a>\n          <a href=\"005-language-specs.html\" class=\"next\"><span class=\"dir\">next ▸</span><span class=\"title\">Language Specs</span></a>\n        </div>\n      </div>\n    </main>\n  </div>\n</body>\n</html>\n",

How to catch them without losing context.</li>\n        </ul>\n\n        <h2 id=\"lexer\">Editor lexer (langs/&lt;name&gt;/lexer.js)</h2>\n        <p>Independent of the runtime spec, each language carries an editor lexer that the source viewer (issue 215) uses to syntax-highlight file content. The lexer ships in the same <code>langs/&lt;name&gt;/</code> directory as the runtime spec — co-located by language, not by concern.</p>\n\n        <h3 id=\"lexer-contract\">Contract</h3>\n        <p>A lexer is an ES module that exports a single function:</p>\n<pre data-lang=\"js\">export function tokenize(text) {\n  return [\n    { type: 'keyword', start: 0,  end: 5 },\n    { type: 'plain',   start: 5,  end: 6 },\n    { type: 'string',  start: 6,  end: 17 },\n    // ...\n  ];\n}</pre>\n        <p>The returned tokens must be ordered, gap-free, and cover the entire input. Each token's <code>type</code> is a free-form string; the viewer applies a CSS class <code>syntax-&lt;type&gt;</code>. The standard set:</p>\n\n        <table>\n          <thead><tr><th>type</th><th>typical use</th></tr></thead>\n          <tbody>\n            <tr><td><code>keyword</code></td>   <td>language keywords</td></tr>\n            <tr><td><code>comment</code></td>   <td>line and block comments</td></tr>\n            <tr><td><code>string</code></td>    <td>quoted strings, char literals, here-docs</td></tr>\n            <tr><td><code>number</code></td>    <td>numeric literals</td></tr>\n            <tr><td><code>operator</code></td>  <td><code>+ - == = : .</code></td></tr>\n            <tr><td><code>identifier</code></td><td>variable / function names</td></tr>\n            <tr><td><code>plain</code></td>     <td>whitespace and unclassified runs</td></tr>\n          </tbody>\n        </table>\n\n        <p>Unknown types fall back to <code>syntax-default</code>. Lexers are free to introduce custom types (<code>regex</code>, <code>annotation</code>, <code>decorator</code>); the viewer just renders them with the default style unless someone adds matching CSS.</p>\n\n        <div data-demo=\"lexerDemo\"></div>\n\n        <h3 id=\"lexer-loading\">Loading</h3>\n        <p>The viewer maps a file's extension to a language name (e.g. <code>.lua</code> → <code>lua</code>, <code>.sh</code> → <code>bash</code>, <code>.c</code> / <code>.h</code> → <code>c</code>) and dynamically imports <code>/langs/&lt;name&gt;/lexer.js</code> on first use. Result is cached for the rest of the session. Files with an unknown extension or a missing lexer fall back to plain rendering.</p>\n\n        <h3 id=\"lexer-references\">Reference implementations</h3>\n        <ul>\n          <li><code>langs/lua/lexer.js</code> — hand-rolled state machine, ~150 lines. Lexers are free to introduce custom types (<code>regex</code>, <code>annotation</code>, <code>decorator</code>); the viewer just renders them with the default style unless someone adds matching CSS.</p>\n\n        <div data-demo=\"lexerDemo\"></div>\n\n        <h3 id=\"lexer-loading\">Loading</h3>\n        <p>The viewer maps a file's extension to a language name (e.g. <code>.lua</code> → <code>lua</code>, <code>.sh</code> → <code>bash</code>, <code>.c</code> / <code>.h</code> → <code>c</code>) and dynamically imports <code>/langs/&lt;name&gt;/lexer.js</code> on first use. The HTML notebook lives at `docs/HTML/` and the markdown TOC now points to it.\n\n**What's there:**\n\n```\ndocs/HTML/\n  index.html                  ← TOC landing with animated dataflow\n  001-architecture.html       ← 5 interactive demos\n  002-roadmap.html            ← timeline cards\n  003-driver-system.html      ← driver-vs-spec animation\n  004-ipc-and-threading.html  ← thread-pool & IPC comparison\n  005-language-specs.html     ← lang_spec_t explorer, live lexer\n  assets/style.css            ← design system\n  assets/nav.js               ← sidebar + scroll-spy\n  assets/demos.js             ← all 13 interactive demos\n```\n\n**Aesthetic.** Engineering notebook lit by an amber desk lamp. Warm near-black background with a soft radial glow, sepia cream text, lamp-amber and oxidized-copper accents, very subtle paper-grain overlay. Type: **Fraunces** (variable serif with optical sizes — including italic display + light-weight headlines), **JetBrains Mono** for code, **Caveat** for handwritten marginalia (\"strings flow like ink ↗\" etc.). Demo frames have a tick-mark top edge like surveyor's tape.\n\n**Sidebar.** Persistent on every page. Brand mark, doc list with section numbers (§00–§05), and a scroll-spy sub-nav that auto-builds from the current page's `<h2>` elements and highlights as you scroll. Built once in `nav.js` so every page is consistent.\n\n**13 interactive demos.**\n- **Architecture page**: three-program diagram with hover-highlight wires; routing-kinds explorer (pick plain/comparator/iterator/weighted/distributor, fire the box, watch the right branch light up with an animated pulse); weighted-slider inspector with live histogram of 1000 simulated runs; slot-store push/pop visualizer with mode toggle (1-cell peek vs N-cell ring); cell-tagging side-by-side (FIFO vs tag-order pop after out-of-order pushes); iterator counter with spawn/run/reset and rotating branch firing.\n- **Roadmap**: timeline cards with status pills, progress bars, hover-glow.\n- **Driver system**: animated comparison of phase-2 shell-out (with a slow dot moving 2s, \"process spawn\" ghosts) vs phase-3 spec direct call (0.15s, `dlsym → call` annotation), with toggle.\n- **IPC & Threading**: log-scaled bar chart comparing FFI / shm / Unix socket / driver latency; click-to-cycle worker pool (idle → working → blocked) with live capacity readout.\n- **Language specs**: clickable `lang_spec_t` callbacks showing when each runs; live Lua tokenizer (edit text in the textarea, watch tokens recolour with a tally).\n\nOpen it locally with:\n\n```\ncd /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech && python3 -m http.server 8765 --bind 127.0.0.1\n```\n\nthen visit `http://127.0.0.1:8765/docs/HTML/`. (Or just `xdg-open docs/HTML/index.html` — only the Google Fonts import needs network, everything else works offline.)"
      }],

Release by default;\n# DEBUG=1 keeps symbols and disables optimization, STRICT=1 promotes\n# warnings to errors. `make clean` removes everything that was built.\n#\n# Invokable from any directory: `make -C /path/to/soramech` works,\n# and the DIR variable can be overridden if needed (e.g. for an\n# out-of-tree checkout). All paths in this Makefile are relative to\n# $(DIR) per the project convention.\n#\n# Designed in issue 309. Implementation of the runner's runtime is\n# split across issues 301–308; this Makefile builds whatever sources\n# exist under src/, libs/task-pool/, and libs/json/, so it scales as\n# those issues land.\n\n# {{{ Resolve project root\nDIR ?= $(abspath $(dir $(lastword $(MAKEFILE_LIST))))\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Toolchain & flags\nCC      ?= gcc\n\n# Shared header search path: every C source can find langs/lang-spec.h\n# and any future libs/<name>/ headers via -I flags below.\nCPPFLAGS = -I$(DIR)/langs -I$(DIR)/libs/task-pool -I$(DIR)/libs/json -I$(DIR)/src\n\n# Default to release; DEBUG and STRICT toggle alternates.\nifeq ($(DEBUG),1)\n  CFLAGS = -O0 -g -DDEBUG -Wall -pthread -fPIC\nelse ifeq ($(STRICT),1)\n  CFLAGS = -O2 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -pthread -fPIC\nelse\n  CFLAGS = -O2 -Wall -pthread -fPIC\nendif\n\nLDFLAGS = -ldl -pthread\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Paths and source discovery\nBUILD_DIR = $(DIR)/build\nPOOL_BIN  = $(DIR)/soramech-pool\n\n# Wildcards: empty subdirs return empty lists, which is fine. As\n# issues 301/302/303/304/305 land their C sources here, they get\n# compiled automatically — no Makefile edit required.\nPOOL_SOURCES = \\\n  $(wildcard $(DIR)/src/*.c) \\\n  $(wildcard $(DIR)/libs/task-pool/*.c) \\\n  $(wildcard $(DIR)/libs/json/*.c)\n\nPOOL_OBJECTS = $(POOL_SOURCES:$(DIR)/%.c=$(BUILD_DIR)/%.o)\n\nLANGS = lua c bash\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Public targets\n.PHONY: all runner specs clean test help\n\nall: runner specs\n\nrunner: $(POOL_BIN)\n\nspecs:\n\t@for lang in $(LANGS); do \\\n\t  echo \"  → langs/$$lang\"; \\\n\t  $(MAKE) -s -C $(DIR)/langs/$$lang DIR=$(DIR) || exit 1; \\\n\tdone\n\nclean:\n\trm -f $(POOL_BIN)\n\trm -rf $(BUILD_DIR)\n\t@for lang in $(LANGS); do \\\n\t  $(MAKE) -s -C $(DIR)/langs/$$lang DIR=$(DIR) clean || true; \\\n\tdone\n\ntest: all\n\t@echo \"Integration tests land with issue 311.\"\n\t@if [ -x $(DIR)/scripts/run-tests.sh ]; then $(DIR)/scripts/run-tests.sh; fi\n\nhelp:\n\t@echo \"SoraMech build:\"\n\t@echo \"  make          — build runner + specs (release)\"\n\t@echo \"  make DEBUG=1  — debug info, no optimization\"\n\t@echo \"  make STRICT=1 — promote warnings to errors\"\n\t@echo \"  make clean    — remove every built artifact\"\n\t@echo \"  make test     — run integration tests (when 311 lands)\"\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ Build rules\n$(POOL_BIN): $(POOL_OBJECTS)\n\t@echo \"  → $(notdir $@)\"\n\t@$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $(CPPFLAGS) -o $@ $^ $(LDFLAGS)\n\n$(BUILD_DIR)/%.o: $(DIR)/%.c\n\t@mkdir -p $(dir $@)\n\t@echo \"  → $(patsubst $(DIR)/%,%,$<)\"\n\t@$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $(CPPFLAGS) -c -o $@ $<\n# }}}\n",

The dispatch\n * layer prints the error context and aborts. There is no recovery,\n * no retry, no per-task failed state. This is intentional.\n *\n * The fast-path callbacks (invoke_native, native_to_json,\n * json_to_native) from issue 312 are not in this initial header —\n * they land when 312 is implemented.\n */\n\n#ifndef SORAMECH_LANG_SPEC_H\n#define SORAMECH_LANG_SPEC_H\n\n#include <stddef.h>\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\nextern \"C\" {\n#endif\n\n/* {{{ lang_spec_t */\ntypedef struct lang_spec {\n    const char *name;       /* \"lua\", \"bash\", \"c\", \"python\", ... */\n    const char *file_ext;   /* \".lua\", \".sh\", \".c\", \".py\"        */\n\n    /* init: once per worker thread at pool startup. Returns an\n     * opaque handle stored in the worker context; the dispatch\n     * layer passes this handle back to invoke() for every call. */\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n\n    /* teardown: once per worker at pool shutdown. Called once per source file at map-load\n     * (or at editor compile-button time). For languages that don't\n     * compile (Lua, Bash), leave this NULL. For C, it runs\n     * gcc -shared -fPIC -o out_path src_path. Returns 0 on\n     * success, nonzero on failure. */\n    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path);\n\n    /* invoke: per box call. Inputs are arrays of (bytes, size) pairs,\n     * already read from slots by the dispatch layer. Returns the\n     * function's output by writing to out_buf and setting *out_size.\n     * Returns 0 on success, nonzero (fatal) on error. */\n    int   (*invoke)(void *handle,\n                    const char *file_path,\n                    const char *fn_name,\n                    const void **input_data,\n                    const int   *input_sizes,\n                    int          n_inputs,\n                    void        *out_buf,\n                    int          out_buf_capacity,\n                    int         *out_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\n}\n#endif\n\n#endif /* SORAMECH_LANG_SPEC_H */\n",

        "input":{
          "content":"/* src/008-pool-runner.c — phase 3 runner entry point.\n *\n * What it is, in a sentence: the C binary that loads a map directory,\n * stands up the thread pool, lets the dispatch layer run every box\n * to quiescence, and writes the JSONL run log on the way out.\n *\n * Designed in issue 301. Source discovery is wildcard-based across\n  `src/*.c`, `libs/task-pool/*.c`, `libs/json/*.c` — additional C\n  sources land as future issues compile them in automatically.\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — minimal `main()` that parses argv,\n  prints usage on `--help`, prints a \"scaffold build\" banner and\n  exits 0 on a map-dir argument. Plus `src/008-pool-runner.info.md`.\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — the public `lang_spec_t` C contract from\n  issue 303 (the four basic callbacks; the fast-path callbacks\n  from issue 312 land later).\n- `langs/{lua,c,bash}/spec.c` + `Makefile` + `spec.info.md` — each\n  builds a `spec.so` that exports `soramech_lang_spec` with all\n  callbacks `NULL`. Verified with `nm -D langs/*/spec.so` — the\n  symbol is exported at `0x4020 D` in every spec.\n- `.clangd` config so the editor LSP resolves the include path the\n  same way the Makefile does.\n- `.file-index-counter` set to `008`.\n\nVerified `make` clean → build → run cycle works in default,\n`DEBUG=1`, and `STRICT=1` modes.\n\nWhat's still ahead inside 309:\n- Vendoring `libs/task-pool/` (lands with 301).\n- Vendoring `libs/json/` (lands with 305 — choice of cJSON / jsmn\n  decided at implementation time).\n- Spec discovery via `/proc/self/exe` (lands with 303's spec\n  registry).\n- Compile / package step for standalone `compiled/pool-runner`\n  (lands with 305 + 307).\n- Real `make test` (lands with 311).\n\nThese follow-ons depend on their respective issues; this issue\nstays open until they're all wired in.",

    "newString":"- `issues/completed/219-map-compiler.md` — original issue, folded\n  into this one\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### Scaffolding milestone — 2026-05-12\n\nWhat's in place:\n- `Makefile` at the project root with `all` / `runner` / `specs` /\n  `clean` / `test` / `help` targets, and `DEBUG=1` / `STRICT=1`\n  build modes. Source discovery is wildcard-based across\n  `src/*.c`, `libs/task-pool/*.c`, `libs/json/*.c` — additional C\n  sources land as future issues compile them in automatically.\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — minimal `main()` that parses argv,\n  prints usage on `--help`, prints a \"scaffold build\" banner and\n  exits 0 on a map-dir argument. Plus `src/008-pool-runner.info.md`.\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — the public `lang_spec_t` C contract from\n  issue 303 (the four basic callbacks; the fast-path callbacks\n  from issue 312 land later).\n- `langs/{lua,c,bash}/spec.c` + `Makefile` + `spec.info.md` — each\n  builds a `spec.so` that exports `soramech_lang_spec` with all\n  callbacks `NULL`. Verified with `nm -D langs/*/spec.so` — the\n  symbol is exported at `0x4020 D` in every spec.\n- `.clangd` config so the editor LSP resolves the include path the\n  same way the Makefile does.\n- `.file-index-counter` set to `008`.\n\nVerified `make` clean → build → run cycle works in default,\n`DEBUG=1`, and `STRICT=1` modes.\n\nWhat's still ahead inside 309:\n- Vendoring `libs/task-pool/` (lands with 301).\n- Vendoring `libs/json/` (lands with 305 — choice of cJSON / jsmn\n  decided at implementation time).\n- Spec discovery via `/proc/self/exe` (lands with 303's spec\n  registry).\n- Compile / package step for standalone `compiled/pool-runner`\n  (lands with 305 + 307).\n- Real `make test` (lands with 311).\n\nThese follow-ons depend on their respective issues; this issue\nstays open until they're all wired in."

    "originalFile":"# Phase 3 Progress\n\nGoal: replace the Lua synchronous runner with a C thread pool runner\nthat executes box graphs in parallel.\n\nThe phase is fully designed; implementation has not yet started.\nIssues 301–311 are the architectural specification. When\nimplementation begins, mark each issue as in progress, then complete,\nand update this file.\n\n## Issues\n\n| ID  | Title                                                       | Status   |\n|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|----------|\n| 301 | thread pool lifecycle and per-worker initialization         | designed |\n| 302 | per-task slot store with wire-held references               | designed |\n| 303 | language runtime spec (pluggable per-language invocation)   | designed |\n| 304 | task dispatch layer (C, replaces synchronous executor)      | designed |\n| 305 | C graph loader (replaces `003-loader.lua`)                  | designed |\n| 306 | Lua language spec implementation                            | designed |\n| 307 | C language spec implementation                              | designed |\n| 308 | Bash language spec implementation                           | designed |\n| 309 | build system & Makefile orchestration                       | designed |\n| 310 | priority queue: wired in, no-op behaviorally                | designed |\n| 311 | integration tests & run output (`last-run.jsonl`)           | designed |\n| 312 | same-language wire fast path (skip JSON for Lua→Lua etc.)   | designed |\n| 313 | research: whole-program same-language merge                 | research / blocked |\n\n## Phase goal checklist\n\n- [ ] SoraMech-owned task pool builds clean (3d-rts as design reference)\n- [ ] Slot store unit-tested (single-value + ring buffer + refcounting)\n- [ ] C graph loader passes phase 2's existing maps\n- [ ] Lua spec runs `maps/hello` end-to-end\n- [ ] C spec compiles and runs a typed-signature box\n- [ ] Bash spec runs an out-of-process box via the socket protocol\n- [ ] Pool runner runs a multi-language map with concurrent workers\n- [ ] Iterator box routes via dispatch layer (no spec invoked)\n- [ ] Comparator box routes via dispatch layer (no spec invoked)\n- [ ] Variable-size outputs work via the large-value heap\n- [ ] `last-run.jsonl` written for every run\n- [ ] All 11 integration test maps pass\n- [ ] Phase 3 demo map runs and produces expected output\n- [ ] Phase 2 synchronous runner retired (`src/004-executor.lua`,\n      `src/007-runner-main.lua`, `src/003-loader.lua`, `drivers/*.sh`)\n\n## Implementation order suggestion\n\nDesigned to surface concrete artifacts early so subsequent issues can\nbuild on them.\n\n1. **309 (build system)** — top-level Makefile, vendored deps, empty\n   stubs for runner and specs. Verify everything compiles.\n2. **302 (slot store)** — pure C, unit-testable, no pool dependency.\n3. **305 (graph loader)** — pure C, parses existing phase 2 maps.\n4. **301 (pool lifecycle)** — wire pool startup, per-worker context,\n   active-task counter, quiescence.\n5. **303 (lang spec interface)** — header file + stub spec to validate\n   the loading mechanism.\n6. **306 (Lua spec)** — easiest reference. Smoke test: `maps/hello`\n   end-to-end.\n7. **304 (dispatch layer)** — connects everything. First fully-running\n   box.\n8. **310 (priority queue)** — small change, can land any time.\n9. **307 (C spec)** — adds compile callback and wrapper generation.\n10. **308 (Bash spec)** — adds out-of-process execution.\n11. **311 (tests + run output)** — formalizes what \"phase 3 works\"\n    means; runs continuously from this point.\n\nIssue 222 (compile button placeholder) lands in phase 2 but its\nbackend is wired in here once 307 and the per-spec compile orchestration\nexist.\n",

    "content":"/* src/009-slot-store.h — per-input-port slot store, public API.\n *\n * What it is, in a sentence: a thread-safe pool of ring-buffer\n * slots, allocated at graph load time, used by the phase 3\n * dispatch layer to route values between boxes.\n *\n * Slots belong to input ports, not tasks. Each box has one slot\n * per input port; the slot persists for the whole run. A wire is\n * a routing declaration — when a producer's task finishes, the\n * dispatch layer pushes copies of the output into every\n * downstream input slot. Fan-out is N pushes; fan-in is N\n * producers pushing into one slot. Designed in issue 302.\n *\n * Three slot modes, chosen via flags at slot_alloc:\n *\n *   1-cell peek (n_cells == 1, no flags)\n *     — for literals and wires from producers that run exactly\n *       once. Push once at startup. Every consumer task peeks\n *       without draining; the cell stays filled.\n *\n *   N-cell pop (n_cells > 1, no flags)\n *     — for wires whose producer runs many times (iterators,\n *       queued inputs). Push appends to tail; pop drains head\n *       FIFO. Consumer task pops one cell per spawn.\n *\n *   N-cell pop, tagged (SLOT_TAGGED)\n *     — same shape as N-cell pop, but pop returns the cell with\n *       the lowest tag, not the head. Used downstream of parallel\n *       iterators where push order is non-deterministic but\n *       consumption order must follow the iterator counter.\n *\n *   atomic counter (SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER, n_cells and cell_capacity\n *     ignored)\n *     — single atomic uint32. Read-and-increment via\n *       slot_read_inc(). Used for iterator / randomizer /\n *       weighted-routing counters. Concurrent reads each get a\n *       distinct value mod the caller-supplied bound.\n *\n * Synchronization is per-slot. There is no allocator-wide lock on\n * the hot read/write path. The atomic-counter slot uses\n * atomic_fetch_add; the ring-buffer slots use a per-slot spinlock\n * around header mutation (one byte, atomic_flag).\n *\n * Lifetime is the run. Slots are freed when the store is\n * destroyed at the end of the run — there is no per-slot refcount\n * and no end-of-stream propagation. Run termination is governed\n * by the pool's active-task counter (issue 301).\n *\n * Errors: a return of -1 from a read/write op means the operation\n * could not be performed (empty pop, buffer too small, type\n * mismatch). The store does not assert or abort; the dispatch\n * layer is expected to check return codes. The hard-crash policy\n * applies at the language-spec layer, not here.\n *\n * What's NOT in this version:\n *  - Size-class free lists and coalescing. The design in issue 302\n *    describes a segregated allocator with eager-coalesce; this\n *    initial implementation uses plain malloc per slot. The pattern\n *    is \"allocate once at graph load, free at run end\", so free-list\n *    optimization buys nothing for the current usage. Lands as a\n *    follow-on if profiling justifies it.\n *  - Large-value heap for variable-size payloads. Slots store\n *    fixed-size cells; very large outputs (LLM responses) will\n *    use a separate two-tier scheme. Follow-on within 302.\n */\n\n#ifndef SORAMECH_SLOT_STORE_H\n#define SORAMECH_SLOT_STORE_H\n\n#include <stdint.h>\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\nextern \"C\" {\n#endif\n\n/* {{{ Types & flags */\ntypedef struct slot_store slot_store_t;\ntypedef int32_t           slot_id_t;\n\n#define SLOT_INVALID  ((slot_id_t)-1)\n\n/* slot_alloc flags */\nenum {\n    SLOT_FLAG_NONE           = 0,\n    SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED         = 1 << 0,\n    SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER = 1 << 1,\n};\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Store lifecycle */\n/* Construct an empty store. Returns NULL on allocation failure. */\nslot_store_t *slot_store_create(void);\n\n/* Free every slot and the store itself. Safe to call on NULL. */\nvoid          slot_store_destroy(slot_store_t *s);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Slot lifecycle */\n/* Allocate a slot.\n *\n *   cell_capacity — bytes per cell. Ignored for SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER.\n *   n_cells       — ring size (1 for peek slots, >1 for pop). Ignored for\n *                   SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER.\n *   flags         — zero, SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED, or SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER.\n *\n * Returns the new slot's id, or SLOT_INVALID on allocation failure or\n * invalid arguments. Ids are stable for the lifetime of the store. */\nslot_id_t     slot_alloc(slot_store_t *s,\n                         int32_t cell_capacity,\n                         int32_t n_cells,\n                         int32_t flags);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Ring-buffer ops */\n/* Push a value into the slot's next free cell.\n *\n *   data, size — value bytes. size must be <= cell_capacity.\n *   tag        — ordering tag. Carried only on SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED slots;\n *                ignored otherwise.\n *\n * Returns 0 on success, -1 if the slot is full or arguments invalid.\n * Not valid on SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER slots (returns -1). */\nint           slot_push(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id,\n                        const void *data, int32_t size, uint32_t tag);\n\n/* Peek at the head cell without draining it.\n *\n *   buf, buf_size — destination. The number of bytes copied is min of\n *                   the cell's filled_size and buf_size.\n *\n * Returns the cell's filled_size on success, -1 if the slot is empty,\n * the buffer is too small, or the slot is the wrong type. The cell\n * remains filled and may be re-peeked by subsequent tasks (1-cell peek\n * mode). */\nint32_t       slot_peek(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id,\n                        void *buf, int32_t buf_size);\n\n/* Drain one cell from the slot.\n *\n *   buf, buf_size — destination.\n *\n * For untagged slots, returns the head cell and advances head FIFO.\n * For SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED slots, returns the cell with the lowest tag\n * among the filled cells and marks that cell empty (head advances as\n * front-of-ring cells empty).\n *\n * Returns the cell's filled_size on success, -1 on empty / wrong type\n * / buffer too small. */\nint32_t       slot_pop(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id,\n                       void *buf, int32_t buf_size);\n\n/* Atomic read-and-increment on SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER slots.\n *\n *   mod — modulus for the returned value. Pass UINT32_MAX for \"no\n *         modulus\".\n *\n * Returns the pre-increment counter value mod the supplied bound.\n * Concurrent readers each get a distinct value (the underlying\n * counter is incremented atomically). Returns UINT32_MAX on type\n * mismatch — the dispatch layer is expected to call this op only\n * on slots it allocated with SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER. */\nuint32_t      slot_read_inc(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod);\n\n/* Check whether the slot has any filled cell available for read.\n * Used by the dispatch layer's spawn-on-input-ready rule (issue 304).\n *\n * Returns 1 if a value is available, 0 otherwise. For ATOMIC_COUNTER\n * slots, always returns 1 (the counter is always readable). */\nint           slot_has_value(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Inspection (test / debug) */\n/* Number of filled cells. For ATOMIC_COUNTER slots, returns 0. */\nint32_t       slot_fill_count(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);\n\n/* Slot count in the store. */\nint32_t       slot_store_size(slot_store_t *s);\n/* }}} */\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\n}\n#endif\n\n#endif /* SORAMECH_SLOT_STORE_H */\n",

        "input":{
          "content":"/* src/009-slot-store.c — per-input-port slot store, implementation.\n *\n * Three slot shapes coexist behind one set of APIs:\n *\n *   - Ring-buffer slots (peek and pop modes) — a header followed by\n *     n_cells cells laid out contiguously. Each cell is a 4-byte\n *     filled_size, optionally a 4-byte tag (for SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED),\n *     then cell_capacity bytes of payload. Untagged slots use the\n *     standard head/tail ring discipline; tagged slots use head/tail\n *     for the bookkeeping of \"where to put the next push\" but pop\n *     scans for the lowest-tag filled cell.\n *\n *   - Atomic-counter slots — no header bookkeeping, no payload cells;\n *     just one atomic_uint that slot_read_inc fetches-and-adds. No\n *     lock needed.\n *\n * Per-slot concurrency is a single atomic_flag spinlock for the\n * ring-buffer slots. Inside the lock the header and cells are mutated\n * without atomics; outside the lock no header bytes are touched.\n *\n * The store itself owns a flat array of slot pointers indexed by\n * slot_id_t. The array grows on demand. Ids are never reused — there\n * is no slot_free; slots live for the run.\n *\n * Designed in issue 302. This file implements the API declared in\n * 009-slot-store.h. Free-list optimization and the large-value heap\n * are deferred per the header's \"what's not in this version\" note.\n */\n\n#include \"009-slot-store.h\"\n\n#include <stdatomic.h>\n#include <stdint.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n\n/* {{{ Internal slot record */\ntypedef struct slot_rec {\n    uint32_t    cell_capacity;   /* bytes per cell payload (ring slots) */\n    uint32_t    n_cells;         /* ring size (ring slots)              */\n    _Atomic uint32_t head;       /* read index, mod n_cells             */\n    _Atomic uint32_t tail;       /* write index, mod n_cells            */\n    atomic_flag lock;            /* per-slot spinlock for header+cells  */\n    uint32_t    flags;           /* SLOT_FLAG_*                         */\n    uint32_t    cell_record;     /* derived: 4 (+4 if tagged) + cap     */\n\n    /* For atomic-counter slots: a single atomic uint, used by\n     * slot_read_inc. Lives separately from `cells` so the two slot\n     * shapes don't share storage interpretation. */\n    _Atomic uint32_t counter;\n\n    /* For ring slots: n_cells * cell_record bytes. Flexible array. */\n    uint8_t     cells[];\n} slot_rec_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Internal store */\nstruct slot_store {\n    slot_rec_t **slots;        /* dynamic array, indexed by slot_id_t */\n    int32_t      count;\n    int32_t      capacity;\n};\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Local helpers — locking */\nstatic inline void lock_slot(slot_rec_t *r)\n{\n    while (atomic_flag_test_and_set_explicit(&r->lock, memory_order_acquire)) {\n        /* spin — contention is expected to be brief because the\n         * locked section is just a header update plus a memcpy. */\n    }\n}\n\nstatic inline void unlock_slot(slot_rec_t *r)\n{\n    atomic_flag_clear_explicit(&r->lock, memory_order_release);\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Local helpers — cell layout */\n/* Pointer to the i-th cell within the slot's flexible array. The cell\n * record layout for ring slots is:\n *\n *   bytes 0..3   : filled_size (uint32_t; 0 means empty)\n *   bytes 4..7   : tag         (uint32_t; only if SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED)\n *   bytes (4|8)..: payload     (cell_capacity bytes)\n */\nstatic inline uint8_t *cell_ptr(slot_rec_t *r, uint32_t i)\n{\n    return r->cells + (size_t)i * r->cell_record;\n}\n\nstatic inline uint32_t cell_filled(slot_rec_t *r, uint32_t i)\n{\n    uint32_t v;\n    memcpy(&v, cell_ptr(r, i), sizeof v);\n    return v;\n}\n\nstatic inline uint32_t cell_tag(slot_rec_t *r, uint32_t i)\n{\n    uint32_t v;\n    memcpy(&v, cell_ptr(r, i) + 4, sizeof v);\n    return v;\n}\n\nstatic inline uint8_t *cell_data(slot_rec_t *r, uint32_t i)\n{\n    return cell_ptr(r, i) + ((r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED) ? 8 : 4);\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ slot_store_create() */\nslot_store_t *slot_store_create(void)\n{\n    slot_store_t *s = calloc(1, sizeof *s);\n    if (!s) return NULL;\n    s->capacity = 16;\n    s->slots    = calloc((size_t)s->capacity, sizeof *s->slots);\n    if (!s->slots) { free(s); return NULL; }\n    return s;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ slot_store_destroy() */\nvoid slot_store_destroy(slot_store_t *s)\n{\n    if (!s) return;\n    for (int32_t i = 0; i < s->count; i++) {\n        free(s->slots[i]);\n    }\n    free(s->slots);\n    free(s);\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ slot_store_size() */\nint32_t slot_store_size(slot_store_t *s)\n{\n    return s ? s->count : 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Local helper — grow_store_if_needed() */\nstatic int grow_store_if_needed(slot_store_t *s)\n{\n    if (s->count < s->capacity) return 0;\n    int32_t new_cap = s->capacity * 2;\n    slot_rec_t **grown = realloc(s->slots, (size_t)new_cap * sizeof *grown);\n    if (!grown) return -1;\n    memset(grown + s->capacity, 0,\n           (size_t)(new_cap - s->capacity) * sizeof *grown);\n    s->slots    = grown;\n    s->capacity = new_cap;\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ slot_alloc() */\nslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *s,\n                     int32_t cell_capacity,\n                     int32_t n_cells,\n                     int32_t flags)\n{\n    if (!s) return SLOT_INVALID;\n\n    size_t bytes_cells = 0;\n    uint32_t cell_record = 0;\n\n    if (flags & SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER) {\n        /* Atomic-counter slot: no ring cells. cell_capacity and\n         * n_cells are ignored. */\n        bytes_cells = 0;\n    } else {\n        if (cell_capacity <= 0 || n_cells <= 0) return SLOT_INVALID;\n        cell_record = (uint32_t)(4\n                                  + ((flags & SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED) ? 4 : 0)\n                                  + cell_capacity);\n        bytes_cells = (size_t)n_cells * cell_record;\n    }\n\n    slot_rec_t *r = calloc(1, sizeof(slot_rec_t) + bytes_cells);\n    if (!r) return SLOT_INVALID;\n\n    r->cell_capacity = (flags & SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER) ? 0 : (uint32_t)cell_capacity;\n    r->n_cells       = (flags & SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER) ? 0 : (uint32_t)n_cells;\n    r->cell_record   = cell_record;\n    r->flags         = (uint32_t)flags;\n    atomic_init(&r->head,    0u);\n    atomic_init(&r->tail,    0u);\n    atomic_init(&r->counter, 0u);\n    /* atomic_flag has no atomic_flag_init in C11; ATOMIC_FLAG_INIT is\n     * for initializers. Clearing it leaves it in the \"not set\" state. */\n    atomic_flag_clear(&r->lock);\n\n    if (grow_store_if_needed(s) != 0) { free(r); return SLOT_INVALID; }\n    slot_id_t id = s->count++;\n    s->slots[id] = r;\n    return id;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Local helper — get_slot() */\nstatic slot_rec_t *get_slot(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id)\n{\n    if (!s || id < 0 || id >= s->count) return NULL;\n    return s->slots[id];\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ slot_push() */\nint slot_push(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id,\n              const void *data, int32_t size, uint32_t tag)\n{\n    slot_rec_t *r = get_slot(s, id);\n    if (!r)                                      return -1;\n    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER)     return -1;\n    if (size < 0 || (uint32_t)size > r->cell_capacity) return -1;\n    if (!data && size > 0)                       return -1;\n\n    lock_slot(r);\n\n    uint32_t head = atomic_load_explicit(&r->head, memory_order_relaxed);\n    uint32_t tail = atomic_load_explicit(&r->tail, memory_order_relaxed);\n    if (tail - head >= r->n_cells) {\n        /* Ring full. */\n        unlock_slot(r);\n        return -1;\n    }\n\n    uint32_t i = tail % r->n_cells;\n    uint8_t *cp = cell_ptr(r, i);\n\n    /* filled_size */\n    uint32_t fs = (uint32_t)size;\n    memcpy(cp, &fs, sizeof fs);\n    /* tag (only if tagged) */\n    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED) {\n        memcpy(cp + 4, &tag, sizeof tag);\n    }\n    /* payload */\n    if (size > 0) {\n        memcpy(cell_data(r, i), data, (size_t)size);\n    }\n\n    atomic_store_explicit(&r->tail, tail + 1u, memory_order_release);\n    unlock_slot(r);\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ slot_peek() */\nint32_t slot_peek(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id,\n                  void *buf, int32_t buf_size)\n{\n    slot_rec_t *r = get_slot(s, id);\n    if (!r)                                  return -1;\n    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER) return -1;\n    if (buf_size < 0 || (!buf && buf_size > 0)) return -1;\n\n    lock_slot(r);\n\n    uint32_t head = atomic_load_explicit(&r->head, memory_order_acquire);\n    uint32_t tail = atomic_load_explicit(&r->tail, memory_order_acquire);\n    if (head == tail) {\n        unlock_slot(r);\n        return -1;\n    }\n\n    uint32_t i = head % r->n_cells;\n    uint32_t fs = cell_filled(r, i);\n    if (fs == 0) {\n        unlock_slot(r);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    if ((uint32_t)buf_size < fs) {\n        unlock_slot(r);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    if (fs > 0) memcpy(buf, cell_data(r, i), fs);\n    /* head not advanced — peek leaves the cell in place. */\n    unlock_slot(r);\n    return (int32_t)fs;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Local helper — find_lowest_tag_index() */\n/* Return the in-ring cell index with the lowest tag among filled\n * cells. The caller holds the slot lock. Returns UINT32_MAX if no\n * filled cells exist. */\nstatic uint32_t find_lowest_tag_index(slot_rec_t *r)\n{\n    uint32_t best     = UINT32_MAX;\n    uint32_t best_tag = UINT32_MAX;\n    for (uint32_t i = 0; i < r->n_cells; i++) {\n        if (cell_filled(r, i) == 0) continue;\n        uint32_t t = cell_tag(r, i);\n        if (best == UINT32_MAX || t < best_tag) {\n            best     = i;\n            best_tag = t;\n        }\n    }\n    return best;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ slot_pop() */\nint32_t slot_pop(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id,\n                 void *buf, int32_t buf_size)\n{\n    slot_rec_t *r = get_slot(s, id);\n    if (!r)                                  return -1;\n    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER) return -1;\n    if (buf_size < 0 || (!buf && buf_size > 0)) return -1;\n\n    lock_slot(r);\n\n    uint32_t pick;\n    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED) {\n        pick = find_lowest_tag_index(r);\n        if (pick == UINT32_MAX) { unlock_slot(r); return -1; }\n    } else {\n        uint32_t head = atomic_load_explicit(&r->head, memory_order_acquire);\n        uint32_t tail = atomic_load_explicit(&r->tail, memory_order_acquire);\n        if (head == tail) { unlock_slot(r); return -1; }\n        pick = head % r->n_cells;\n    }\n\n    uint32_t fs = cell_filled(r, pick);\n    if (fs == 0)                  { unlock_slot(r); return -1; }\n    if ((uint32_t)buf_size < fs)  { unlock_slot(r); return -1; }\n\n    if (fs > 0) memcpy(buf, cell_data(r, pick), fs);\n\n    /* Mark cell empty. */\n    uint32_t zero = 0;\n    memcpy(cell_ptr(r, pick), &zero, sizeof zero);\n\n    /* For untagged: advance head by one. For tagged: walk head\n     * forward over any contiguous empty cells (the head/tail\n     * relationship is preserved so further pushes still land at the\n     * right spot, but stale empties at the front of the ring don't\n     * block future pushes that wrap). */\n    if (!(r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED)) {\n        uint32_t head = atomic_load_explicit(&r->head, memory_order_relaxed);\n        atomic_store_explicit(&r->head, head + 1u, memory_order_release);\n    } else {\n        uint32_t head = atomic_load_explicit(&r->head, memory_order_relaxed);\n        uint32_t tail = atomic_load_explicit(&r->tail, memory_order_relaxed);\n        while (head < tail && cell_filled(r, head % r->n_cells) == 0) {\n            head++;\n        }\n        atomic_store_explicit(&r->head, head, memory_order_release);\n    }\n\n    unlock_slot(r);\n    return (int32_t)fs;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ slot_read_inc() */\nuint32_t slot_read_inc(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod)\n{\n    slot_rec_t *r = get_slot(s, id);\n    if (!r)                                     return UINT32_MAX;\n    if (!(r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER)) return UINT32_MAX;\n    if (mod == 0)                               return UINT32_MAX;\n\n    uint32_t prev = atomic_fetch_add_explicit(&r->counter, 1u,\n                                              memory_order_relaxed);\n    return prev % mod;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ slot_has_value() */\nint slot_has_value(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id)\n{\n    slot_rec_t *r = get_slot(s, id);\n    if (!r) return 0;\n    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER) return 1;\n\n    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED) {\n        /* Tagged: any filled cell counts. Cheap scan; tagged slots\n         * are usually small. */\n        lock_slot(r);\n        int found = 0;\n        for (uint32_t i = 0; i < r->n_cells; i++) {\n            if (cell_filled(r, i) != 0) { found = 1; break; }\n        }\n        unlock_slot(r);\n        return found;\n    }\n\n    uint32_t head = atomic_load_explicit(&r->head, memory_order_acquire);\n    uint32_t tail = atomic_load_explicit(&r->tail, memory_order_acquire);\n    return head != tail;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ slot_fill_count() */\nint32_t slot_fill_count(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id)\n{\n    slot_rec_t *r = get_slot(s, id);\n    if (!r)                                  return 0;\n    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER) return 0;\n\n    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED) {\n        lock_slot(r);\n        int32_t n = 0;\n        for (uint32_t i = 0; i < r->n_cells; i++) {\n            if (cell_filled(r, i) != 0) n++;\n        }\n        unlock_slot(r);\n        return n;\n    }\n\n    uint32_t head = atomic_load_explicit(&r->head, memory_order_acquire);\n    uint32_t tail = atomic_load_explicit(&r->tail, memory_order_acquire);\n    return (int32_t)(tail - head);\n}\n/* }}} */\n",
