    "originalFile":"/* langs/bash/spec.c — Bash language spec for SoraMech.\n *\n * Persistent-subprocess model: each worker thread spawns one bash\n * process at init() and keeps it alive for the run, communicating\n * over a Unix-domain socketpair. Every invoke writes a\n * line-oriented request to the bash side and reads a framed\n * response — orders of magnitude faster than fork+exec per call.\n *\n * Designed in issue 308. The previous iteration's fork+exec path\n * lives only in git history now; this file replaces it wholesale.\n *\n * Protocol details, including the bash-side loop, are in\n * `langs/bash/bash-server.sh`. The C side here is just enough\n * machinery to spawn the subprocess and read/write the framing.\n *\n * Limitations:\n *  - Arguments containing literal newlines are not supported in\n *    this iteration (line-oriented protocol). Most bash boxes\n *    don't need them; binary data should be base64-encoded\n *    upstream.\n *  - The protocol is single-request/single-response; a slow box\n *    serializes calls behind it on the same worker. Multi-worker\n *    pools dispatch in parallel anyway, so this is rarely\n *    the bottleneck.\n */\n\n#include \"lang-spec.h\"\n\n#include <errno.h>\n#include <fcntl.h>\n#include <signal.h>\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n#include <sys/socket.h>\n#include <sys/types.h>\n#include <sys/wait.h>\n#include <time.h>\n#include <unistd.h>\n\n#define DEFAULT_SERVER_PATH \"langs/bash/bash-server.sh\"\n\n/* {{{ Per-worker handle */\ntypedef struct {\n    int     fd;      /* parent-side socketpair fd */\n    pid_t   pid;     /* bash subprocess */\n} bash_handle_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ server_path() — locate bash-server.sh */\n/* For now, allow override via the SORAMECH_BASH_SERVER env var; the\n * default is relative to the cwd (the project root). A more\n * polished version locates the script next to the spec.so via\n * /proc/self/exe, landing with issue 309's spec discovery work. */\nstatic const char *server_path(void)\n{\n    const char *p = getenv(\"SORAMECH_BASH_SERVER\");\n    return (p && *p) ? p : DEFAULT_SERVER_PATH;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ write_all() — write n bytes, retrying on partial writes */\nstatic int write_all(int fd, const void *buf, size_t n)\n{\n    const char *p = buf;\n    size_t left = n;\n    while (left > 0) {\n        ssize_t w = write(fd, p, left);\n        if (w < 0) {\n            if (errno == EINTR) continue;\n            return -1;\n        }\n        if (w == 0) return -1;\n        p    += w;\n        left -= (size_t)w;\n    }\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ read_exact() — read exactly n bytes from fd */\nstatic int read_exact(int fd, void *buf, size_t n)\n{\n    char *p = buf;\n    size_t left = n;\n    while (left > 0) {\n        ssize_t r = read(fd, p, left);\n        if (r < 0) {\n            if (errno == EINTR) continue;\n            return -1;\n        }\n        if (r == 0) return -1;\n        p    += r;\n        left -= (size_t)r;\n    }\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ read_line() — read up to cap bytes including a trailing \\n */\n/* Returns the number of bytes read (including the newline), or -1\n * on error / EOF. The newline is overwritten with '\\0' so the\n * line is a NUL-terminated C string of length (return-1). */\nstatic int read_line(int fd, char *buf, int cap)\n{\n    int n = 0;\n    while (n < cap - 1) {\n        char c;\n        ssize_t r = read(fd, &c, 1);\n        if (r < 0) {\n            if (errno == EINTR) continue;\n            return -1;\n        }\n        if (r == 0) return -1;\n        if (c == '\\n') {\n            buf[n] = '\\0';\n            return n + 1;\n        }\n        buf[n++] = c;\n    }\n    buf[n] = '\\0';\n    return -1;     /* line longer than buffer */\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ bash_init() — spawn the subprocess */\nstatic void *bash_init(int worker_idx)\n{\n    (void)worker_idx;\n\n    /* SOCK_CLOEXEC atomically marks both fds close-on-exec at\n     * creation. This matters because multiple worker threads\n     * concurrently fork their own bash subprocesses; without\n     * CLOEXEC, child A inherits child B's parent-side fd, the\n     * bash on the other end never sees EOF when its real parent\n     * exits, and we leak orphaned bash processes that hang on\n     * read forever. */\n    int sv[2];\n    if (socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM | SOCK_CLOEXEC, 0, sv) != 0) return NULL;\n\n    pid_t pid = fork();\n    if (pid < 0) {\n        close(sv[0]); close(sv[1]);\n        return NULL;\n    }\n    if (pid == 0) {\n        /* Child: route the child-side socket fd to stdin+stdout.\n         * dup2'd fds clear CLOEXEC, so bash's stdin/stdout survive\n         * across exec. The original sv[1] (still CLOEXEC) closes\n         * automatically. */\n        close(sv[0]);\n        if (dup2(sv[1], STDIN_FILENO)  < 0) _exit(126);\n        if (dup2(sv[1], STDOUT_FILENO) < 0) _exit(126);\n        close(sv[1]);\n\n        /* Ignore SIGPIPE so the parent dying doesn't immediately\n         * kill us — let the read on stdin return EOF and exit cleanly. */\n        signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN);\n\n        execlp(\"bash\", \"bash\", server_path(), (char *)NULL);\n        _exit(127);\n    }\n    /* Parent. */\n    close(sv[1]);\n    bash_handle_t *h = malloc(sizeof *h);\n    if (!h) { close(sv[0]); return NULL; }\n    h->fd  = sv[0];\n    h->pid = pid;\n    return h;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ bash_teardown() — graceful shutdown */\nstatic void bash_teardown(void *handle)\n{\n    if (!handle) return;\n    bash_handle_t *h = (bash_handle_t *)handle;\n    /* Send \"QUIT\" so the bash loop exits cleanly; then close the\n     * socket and wait for the child. */\n    if (h->fd >= 0) {\n        (void)write_all(h->fd, \"QUIT\\n\", 5);\n        close(h->fd);\n    }\n    if (h->pid > 0) {\n        int status = 0;\n        /* Give the child a chance to exit on its own; if it doesn't,\n         * SIGTERM it. The waitpid loop handles EINTR. */\n        for (int tries = 0; tries < 200; tries++) {\n            pid_t r = waitpid(h->pid, &status, WNOHANG);\n            if (r == h->pid) goto done;\n            if (r < 0 && errno != EINTR) break;\n            struct timespec ts = { 0, 5 * 1000 * 1000 };  /* 5 ms */\n            nanosleep(&ts, NULL);\n        }\n        kill(h->pid, SIGTERM);\n        waitpid(h->pid, &status, 0);\n    }\ndone:\n    free(h);\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ send_request() — write the request frame */\nstatic int send_request(int fd, const char *file_path, const char *fn_name,\n                        const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes,\n                        int n_inputs)\n{\n    char header[64];\n    int n = snprintf(header, sizeof header, \"%d\\n\", n_inputs);\n    if (n < 0 || n >= (int)sizeof header) return -1;\n    if (write_all(fd, header, (size_t)n)              < 0) return -1;\n    if (write_all(fd, file_path, strlen(file_path))   < 0) return -1;\n    if (write_all(fd, \"\\n\", 1)                        < 0) return -1;\n    if (write_all(fd, fn_name, strlen(fn_name))       < 0) return -1;\n    if (write_all(fd, \"\\n\", 1)                        < 0) return -1;\n    for (int i = 0; i < n_inputs; i++) {\n        if (write_all(fd, input_data[i], (size_t)input_sizes[i]) < 0) return -1;\n        if (write_all(fd, \"\\n\", 1) < 0) return -1;\n    }\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ bash_invoke() */\nstatic int bash_invoke(void *handle,\n                       const char  *file_path,\n                       const char  *fn_name,\n                       const void **input_data,\n                       const int   *input_sizes,\n                       int          n_inputs,\n                       void        *out_buf,\n                       int          out_capacity,\n                       int         *out_size)\n{\n    if (!handle || !file_path || !fn_name) return -1;\n    bash_handle_t *h = (bash_handle_t *)handle;\n\n    if (send_request(h->fd, file_path, fn_name,\n                     input_data, input_sizes, n_inputs) != 0) {\n        return -1;\n    }\n\n    /* Response: status\\n out_len\\n out_bytes. */\n    char line[64];\n    if (read_line(h->fd, line, sizeof line) < 0) return -1;\n    int status = atoi(line);\n\n    if (read_line(h->fd, line, sizeof line) < 0) return -1;\n    int n = atoi(line);\n\n    if (n > out_capacity) {\n        /* Drain the output to keep the protocol synced, then fail. */\n        char drop[1024];\n        int left = n;\n        while (left > 0) {\n            int chunk = left < (int)sizeof drop ? left : (int)sizeof drop;\n            if (read_exact(h->fd, drop, (size_t)chunk) < 0) return -1;\n            left -= chunk;\n        }\n        fprintf(stderr, \"bash spec: %s:%s returned %d bytes; buffer is %d\\n\",\n                file_path, fn_name, n, out_capacity);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    if (n > 0) {\n        if (read_exact(h->fd, out_buf, (size_t)n) < 0) return -1;\n    }\n    if (out_size) *out_size = n;\n\n    if (status != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"bash spec: %s:%s exited with status %d\\n\",\n                file_path, fn_name, status);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ soramech_lang_spec */\nlang_spec_t soramech_lang_spec = {\n    .name     = \"bash\",\n    .file_ext = \".sh\",\n    .init     = bash_init,\n    .teardown = bash_teardown,\n    .compile  = 0,\n    .invoke   = bash_invoke,\n};\n/* }}} */\n",

    "originalFile":"/* langs/bash/spec.c — Bash language spec for SoraMech.\n *\n * Persistent-subprocess model: each worker thread spawns one bash\n * process at init() and keeps it alive for the run, communicating\n * over a Unix-domain socketpair. Every invoke writes a\n * line-oriented request to the bash side and reads a framed\n * response — orders of magnitude faster than fork+exec per call.\n *\n * Designed in issue 308. The previous iteration's fork+exec path\n * lives only in git history now; this file replaces it wholesale.\n *\n * Protocol details, including the bash-side loop, are in\n * `langs/bash/bash-server.sh`. The C side here is just enough\n * machinery to spawn the subprocess and read/write the framing.\n *\n * Limitations:\n *  - Arguments containing literal newlines are not supported in\n *    this iteration (line-oriented protocol). Most bash boxes\n *    don't need them; binary data should be base64-encoded\n *    upstream.\n *  - The protocol is single-request/single-response; a slow box\n *    serializes calls behind it on the same worker. Multi-worker\n *    pools dispatch in parallel anyway, so this is rarely\n *    the bottleneck.\n */\n\n#define _GNU_SOURCE\n#include \"lang-spec.h\"\n\n#include <dlfcn.h>\n#include <errno.h>\n#include <fcntl.h>\n#include <libgen.h>\n#include <signal.h>\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n#include <sys/socket.h>\n#include <sys/stat.h>\n#include <sys/types.h>\n#include <sys/wait.h>\n#include <time.h>\n#include <unistd.h>\n\n#define DEFAULT_SERVER_PATH \"langs/bash/bash-server.sh\"\n\n/* {{{ Per-worker handle */\ntypedef struct {\n    int     fd;      /* parent-side socketpair fd */\n    pid_t   pid;     /* bash subprocess */\n} bash_handle_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ server_path() — locate bash-server.sh */\n/* For now, allow override via the SORAMECH_BASH_SERVER env var; the\n * default is relative to the cwd (the project root). A more\n * polished version locates the script next to the spec.so via\n * /proc/self/exe, landing with issue 309's spec discovery work. */\nstatic const char *server_path(void)\n{\n    const char *p = getenv(\"SORAMECH_BASH_SERVER\");\n    return (p && *p) ? p : DEFAULT_SERVER_PATH;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ write_all() — write n bytes, retrying on partial writes */\nstatic int write_all(int fd, const void *buf, size_t n)\n{\n    const char *p = buf;\n    size_t left = n;\n    while (left > 0) {\n        ssize_t w = write(fd, p, left);\n        if (w < 0) {\n            if (errno == EINTR) continue;\n            return -1;\n        }\n        if (w == 0) return -1;\n        p    += w;\n        left -= (size_t)w;\n    }\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ read_exact() — read exactly n bytes from fd */\nstatic int read_exact(int fd, void *buf, size_t n)\n{\n    char *p = buf;\n    size_t left = n;\n    while (left > 0) {\n        ssize_t r = read(fd, p, left);\n        if (r < 0) {\n            if (errno == EINTR) continue;\n            return -1;\n        }\n        if (r == 0) return -1;\n        p    += r;\n        left -= (size_t)r;\n    }\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ read_line() — read up to cap bytes including a trailing \\n */\n/* Returns the number of bytes read (including the newline), or -1\n * on error / EOF. The newline is overwritten with '\\0' so the\n * line is a NUL-terminated C string of length (return-1). */\nstatic int read_line(int fd, char *buf, int cap)\n{\n    int n = 0;\n    while (n < cap - 1) {\n        char c;\n        ssize_t r = read(fd, &c, 1);\n        if (r < 0) {\n            if (errno == EINTR) continue;\n            return -1;\n        }\n        if (r == 0) return -1;\n        if (c == '\\n') {\n            buf[n] = '\\0';\n            return n + 1;\n        }\n        buf[n++] = c;\n    }\n    buf[n] = '\\0';\n    return -1;     /* line longer than buffer */\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ bash_init() — spawn the subprocess */\nstatic void *bash_init(int worker_idx)\n{\n    (void)worker_idx;\n\n    /* SOCK_CLOEXEC atomically marks both fds close-on-exec at\n     * creation. This matters because multiple worker threads\n     * concurrently fork their own bash subprocesses; without\n     * CLOEXEC, child A inherits child B's parent-side fd, the\n     * bash on the other end never sees EOF when its real parent\n     * exits, and we leak orphaned bash processes that hang on\n     * read forever. */\n    int sv[2];\n    if (socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM | SOCK_CLOEXEC, 0, sv) != 0) return NULL;\n\n    pid_t pid = fork();\n    if (pid < 0) {\n        close(sv[0]); close(sv[1]);\n        return NULL;\n    }\n    if (pid == 0) {\n        /* Child: route the child-side socket fd to stdin+stdout.\n         * dup2'd fds clear CLOEXEC, so bash's stdin/stdout survive\n         * across exec. The original sv[1] (still CLOEXEC) closes\n         * automatically. */\n        close(sv[0]);\n        if (dup2(sv[1], STDIN_FILENO)  < 0) _exit(126);\n        if (dup2(sv[1], STDOUT_FILENO) < 0) _exit(126);\n        close(sv[1]);\n\n        /* Ignore SIGPIPE so the parent dying doesn't immediately\n         * kill us — let the read on stdin return EOF and exit cleanly. */\n        signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN);\n\n        execlp(\"bash\", \"bash\", server_path(), (char *)NULL);\n        _exit(127);\n    }\n    /* Parent. */\n    close(sv[1]);\n    bash_handle_t *h = malloc(sizeof *h);\n    if (!h) { close(sv[0]); return NULL; }\n    h->fd  = sv[0];\n    h->pid = pid;\n    return h;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ bash_teardown() — graceful shutdown */\nstatic void bash_teardown(void *handle)\n{\n    if (!handle) return;\n    bash_handle_t *h = (bash_handle_t *)handle;\n    /* Send \"QUIT\" so the bash loop exits cleanly; then close the\n     * socket and wait for the child. */\n    if (h->fd >= 0) {\n        (void)write_all(h->fd, \"QUIT\\n\", 5);\n        close(h->fd);\n    }\n    if (h->pid > 0) {\n        int status = 0;\n        /* Give the child a chance to exit on its own; if it doesn't,\n         * SIGTERM it. The waitpid loop handles EINTR. */\n        for (int tries = 0; tries < 200; tries++) {\n            pid_t r = waitpid(h->pid, &status, WNOHANG);\n            if (r == h->pid) goto done;\n            if (r < 0 && errno != EINTR) break;\n            struct timespec ts = { 0, 5 * 1000 * 1000 };  /* 5 ms */\n            nanosleep(&ts, NULL);\n        }\n        kill(h->pid, SIGTERM);\n        waitpid(h->pid, &status, 0);\n    }\ndone:\n    free(h);\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ send_request() — write the request frame */\nstatic int send_request(int fd, const char *file_path, const char *fn_name,\n                        const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes,\n                        int n_inputs)\n{\n    char header[64];\n    int n = snprintf(header, sizeof header, \"%d\\n\", n_inputs);\n    if (n < 0 || n >= (int)sizeof header) return -1;\n    if (write_all(fd, header, (size_t)n)              < 0) return -1;\n    if (write_all(fd, file_path, strlen(file_path))   < 0) return -1;\n    if (write_all(fd, \"\\n\", 1)                        < 0) return -1;\n    if (write_all(fd, fn_name, strlen(fn_name))       < 0) return -1;\n    if (write_all(fd, \"\\n\", 1)                        < 0) return -1;\n    for (int i = 0; i < n_inputs; i++) {\n        if (write_all(fd, input_data[i], (size_t)input_sizes[i]) < 0) return -1;\n        if (write_all(fd, \"\\n\", 1) < 0) return -1;\n    }\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ bash_invoke() */\nstatic int bash_invoke(void *handle,\n                       const char  *file_path,\n                       const char  *fn_name,\n                       const void **input_data,\n                       const int   *input_sizes,\n                       int          n_inputs,\n                       void        *out_buf,\n                       int          out_capacity,\n                       int         *out_size)\n{\n    if (!handle || !file_path || !fn_name) return -1;\n    bash_handle_t *h = (bash_handle_t *)handle;\n\n    if (send_request(h->fd, file_path, fn_name,\n                     input_data, input_sizes, n_inputs) != 0) {\n        return -1;\n    }\n\n    /* Response: status\\n out_len\\n out_bytes. */\n    char line[64];\n    if (read_line(h->fd, line, sizeof line) < 0) return -1;\n    int status = atoi(line);\n\n    if (read_line(h->fd, line, sizeof line) < 0) return -1;\n    int n = atoi(line);\n\n    if (n > out_capacity) {\n        /* Drain the output to keep the protocol synced, then fail. */\n        char drop[1024];\n        int left = n;\n        while (left > 0) {\n            int chunk = left < (int)sizeof drop ? left : (int)sizeof drop;\n            if (read_exact(h->fd, drop, (size_t)chunk) < 0) return -1;\n            left -= chunk;\n        }\n        fprintf(stderr, \"bash spec: %s:%s returned %d bytes; buffer is %d\\n\",\n                file_path, fn_name, n, out_capacity);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    if (n > 0) {\n        if (read_exact(h->fd, out_buf, (size_t)n) < 0) return -1;\n    }\n    if (out_size) *out_size = n;\n\n    if (status != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"bash spec: %s:%s exited with status %d\\n\",\n                file_path, fn_name, status);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ soramech_lang_spec */\nlang_spec_t soramech_lang_spec = {\n    .name     = \"bash\",\n    .file_ext = \".sh\",\n    .init     = bash_init,\n    .teardown = bash_teardown,\n    .compile  = 0,\n    .invoke   = bash_invoke,\n};\n/* }}} */\n",

    "originalFile":"#!/bin/bash\n# scripts/run-tests.sh — phase 3 integration tests.\n#\n# Runs every fixture map under tests/maps/ through `soramech-pool`\n# and asserts that the captured outputs match a hardcoded\n# expectation per map. The point is to catch regressions\n# end-to-end — past the spec interface, past the dispatch action,\n# past JSONL writing — rather than via the in-process unit tests.\n#\n# Per the project convention: scripts run from any directory via a\n# hard-coded ${DIR} path with an override argument; all paths are\n# relative to ${DIR}.\n\nset -u\n\nDIR=\"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nif [[ $# -ge 1 ]]; then\n    DIR=\"$1\"\nfi\n\ncd \"$DIR\"\n\npass=0\nfail=0\nfailures=()\n\n# {{{ check_map() — run one fixture, verify expected substrings\ncheck_map() {\n    local map=\"$1\"\n    shift\n    local expected=(\"$@\")\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"$map\"\n\n    local output\n    output=$(\"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map\" 2>&1)\n    local rc=$?\n\n    local missing=\"\"\n    if [[ $rc -ne 0 ]]; then\n        missing=\"exit=$rc\"\n    fi\n    for e in \"${expected[@]}\"; do\n        if [[ \"$output\" != *\"$e\"* ]]; then\n            missing+=\"${missing:+; }missing '$e'\"\n        fi\n    done\n\n    if [[ -z \"$missing\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — %s\\n\" \"$missing\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"$map: $missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ pipeline_output_check() — additional: the pipeline writes to disk\npipeline_output_check() {\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\" > /dev/null 2>&1\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"pipeline file_write output\"\n    if [[ -f \"$file\" ]]; then\n        local content\n        content=$(cat \"$file\")\n        if [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL — expected '11!', got '%s'\\n\" \"$content\"\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"pipeline file: $content\")\n        fi\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output file missing\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"pipeline: $file missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ run all fixtures\necho \"integration tests (fixture maps):\"\n\ncheck_map \"calc\" \\\n    \"add → 42\"\n\ncheck_map \"hello\" \\\n    \"who → World\" \\\n    \"greet → Hello, World!\"\n\ncheck_map \"comparator\" \\\n    \"classify → 8\" \\\n    \"high → HIGH:8\" \\\n    \"low → (no output)\" \\\n    \"mid → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"iter-route\" \\\n    \"iter → hi\" \\\n    \"a → A:hi\" \\\n    \"b → (no output)\" \\\n    \"c → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"pipeline\" \\\n    \"input → 5\" \\\n    \"double → 10\" \\\n    \"addone → 11\" \\\n    \"shout → 11!\"\n\npipeline_output_check\n# }}}\n\necho\necho \"  $pass passed, $fail failed\"\n\nif [[ $fail -gt 0 ]]; then\n    echo\n    echo \"  failures:\"\n    for f in \"${failures[@]}\"; do\n        echo \"    - $f\"\n    done\nfi\n\nexit $fail\n",

    "originalFile":"#!/bin/bash\n# scripts/run-tests.sh — phase 3 integration tests.\n#\n# Runs every fixture map under tests/maps/ through `soramech-pool`\n# and asserts that the captured outputs match a hardcoded\n# expectation per map. The point is to catch regressions\n# end-to-end — past the spec interface, past the dispatch action,\n# past JSONL writing — rather than via the in-process unit tests.\n#\n# Per the project convention: scripts run from any directory via a\n# hard-coded ${DIR} path with an override argument; all paths are\n# relative to ${DIR}.\n\nset -u\n\nDIR=\"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech\"\nif [[ $# -ge 1 ]]; then\n    DIR=\"$1\"\nfi\n\ncd \"$DIR\"\n\npass=0\nfail=0\nfailures=()\n\n# {{{ check_map() — run one fixture, verify expected substrings\ncheck_map() {\n    local map=\"$1\"\n    shift\n    local expected=(\"$@\")\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"$map\"\n\n    local output\n    output=$(\"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/$map\" 2>&1)\n    local rc=$?\n\n    local missing=\"\"\n    if [[ $rc -ne 0 ]]; then\n        missing=\"exit=$rc\"\n    fi\n    for e in \"${expected[@]}\"; do\n        if [[ \"$output\" != *\"$e\"* ]]; then\n            missing+=\"${missing:+; }missing '$e'\"\n        fi\n    done\n\n    if [[ -z \"$missing\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — %s\\n\" \"$missing\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"$map: $missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ pipeline_output_check() — additional: the pipeline writes to disk\npipeline_output_check() {\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    \"$DIR/soramech-pool\" \"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\" > /dev/null 2>&1\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"pipeline file_write output\"\n    if [[ -f \"$file\" ]]; then\n        local content\n        content=$(cat \"$file\")\n        if [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n            printf \"ok\\n\"\n            pass=$((pass + 1))\n        else\n            printf \"FAIL — expected '11!', got '%s'\\n\" \"$content\"\n            fail=$((fail + 1))\n            failures+=(\"pipeline file: $content\")\n        fi\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output file missing\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"pipeline: $file missing\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ compile_pipeline_check() — soramech-compile produces a portable artifact\n# Verifies issue 309's compile pipeline: bundles all spec.so + sources\n# into compiled/, then runs the artifact from /tmp (i.e. with no\n# dependency on the project's cwd) and verifies it produces the same\n# output as the source map.\ncompile_pipeline_check() {\n    local map=\"$DIR/tests/maps/pipeline\"\n    local compiled=\"$map/compiled\"\n    local file=\"/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt\"\n\n    printf \"  %-44s \" \"compile pipeline (portable run)\"\n\n    rm -rf \"$compiled\"\n    if ! \"$DIR/scripts/soramech-compile.sh\" \"$map\" --dir \"$DIR\" >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n        printf \"FAIL — soramech-compile failed\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: script returned non-zero\")\n        return\n    fi\n    if [[ ! -x \"$compiled/pool-runner\" ]]; then\n        printf \"FAIL — compiled/pool-runner missing or not executable\\n\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: pool-runner missing\")\n        return\n    fi\n\n    rm -f \"$file\"\n    local output\n    output=$(cd /tmp && \"$compiled/pool-runner\" \"$compiled\" 2>&1)\n\n    local content=\"\"\n    [[ -f \"$file\" ]] && content=$(cat \"$file\")\n\n    if [[ \"$output\" == *\"addone → 11\"* ]] && [[ \"$content\" == \"11!\" ]]; then\n        printf \"ok\\n\"\n        pass=$((pass + 1))\n    else\n        printf \"FAIL — output='%s' file='%s'\\n\" \"$output\" \"$content\"\n        fail=$((fail + 1))\n        failures+=(\"compile: bad output\")\n    fi\n}\n# }}}\n\n# {{{ run all fixtures\necho \"integration tests (fixture maps):\"\n\ncheck_map \"calc\" \\\n    \"add → 42\"\n\ncheck_map \"hello\" \\\n    \"who → World\" \\\n    \"greet → Hello, World!\"\n\ncheck_map \"comparator\" \\\n    \"classify → 8\" \\\n    \"high → HIGH:8\" \\\n    \"low → (no output)\" \\\n    \"mid → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"iter-route\" \\\n    \"iter → hi\" \\\n    \"a → A:hi\" \\\n    \"b → (no output)\" \\\n    \"c → (no output)\"\n\ncheck_map \"pipeline\" \\\n    \"input → 5\" \\\n    \"double → 10\" \\\n    \"addone → 11\" \\\n    \"shout → 11!\"\n\npipeline_output_check\n# }}}\n\necho\necho \"  $pass passed, $fail failed\"\n\nif [[ $fail -gt 0 ]]; then\n    echo\n    echo \"  failures:\"\n    for f in \"${failures[@]}\"; do\n        echo \"    - $f\"\n    done\nfi\n\nexit $fail\n",
    "userModified":false,

    "stdout":"`dispatch_task_t` gained a `task_id` field assigned at\n`dispatch_spawn` time (atomic fetch-add on\n`ctx->next_task_id`). The same id correlates the\n`task_submit` / `task_start` / `task_end` events emitted\nthrough the event queue. `task_submit` lands on the spawning\nthread (worker_idx = -1 since the task hasn't been picked up\nyet); start/end land on the dispatching worker with its real\n`thread_idx`.\n\n### Iterator multi-spawn + N-cell pop reads — 2026-05-12\n\nThree pieces together unlock real iteration:\n\n1. **Per-input slot mode.** `box->input_slot_modes[i]` is set by\n   `graph_attach_runtime` to either `SLOT_MODE_PEEK` (single\n   cell, the legacy path) or `SLOT_MODE_POP` (multi-cell ring;\n   each read drains one cell). `read_inputs` picks `slot_pop`\n   or `slot_peek` based on the mode.\n2. **multi_spawn propagation.** Iterators are marked\n   `multi_spawn = 1`; a forward BFS propagates the flag through\n   the connection graph so every box reachable from an iterator\n   is also `multi_spawn`. Multi-spawn boxes get N-cell pop slots\n   (currently 16 cells); single-spawn boxes keep their 1-cell\n   peek slots.\n3. **Auto-re-spawn.** After a multi-spawn box's action completes\n   successfully, it calls `dispatch_spawn` on itself if any POP\n   input still has queued values. A single push wakes the entire\n   chain — an iterator with three queued inputs walks the counter\n   through all three branches without external intervention.\n\nThe single-spawn guard now applies only to single-spawn boxes.\nMulti-spawn ones spawn on every push; the per-slot atomic-flag\nspinlock serializes pops so two concurrent tasks each get a\ndistinct cell.\n\n`test_iterator_multi_fire` in `tests/012-dispatch-test.c` is the\nheadline test: push three values to the iterator's input slot,\nspawn once, all three branches a/b/c fire with the right tagged\noutput. The atomic counter walks 0 → 1 → 2 across the\nauto-re-spawned tasks."

The atomic counter walks 0 → 1 → 2 across the\nauto-re-spawned tasks.\n\n### Cell-tagged ordering across parallel iterator workers — 2026-05-19\n\nEarlier multi-spawn slot pushes carried `tag = 0`; pop order was\nfill order (which is FIFO under the per-slot spinlock but\nnon-deterministic across producer interleaving).\n\nTag propagation is now wired through:\n\n- `push_one_connection` / `push_branch` take an explicit `tag`\n  argument forwarded to `slot_push`.\n- Iterator routing passes the freshly-incremented counter as\n  the tag; randomizer and weighted routing pass their counter\n  snapshot so any downstream tagged slot still serves in stable\n  order; plain/comparator pushes pass `0`.\n- `graph_attach_runtime` sets `SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED` on every\n  multi-spawn box's input slots. The slot store's tagged-pop\n  rule (lowest tag first; FIFO among ties via filled-index\n  scan) means that even when two iterator tasks run on\n  different workers in opposite order, the downstream consumer\n  reads them in invocation order.\n\nVerified by re-running all 6 fixture maps and the dedicated\n`test_iterator_multi_fire` test (which now exercises tagged\ninput slots).",

The slot store's tagged-pop","+  rule (lowest tag first; FIFO among ties via filled-index","+  scan) means that even when two iterator tasks run on","+  different workers in opposite order, the downstream consumer","+  reads them in invocation order.","+","+Verified by re-running all 6 fixture maps and the dedicated","+`test_iterator_multi_fire` test (which now exercises tagged","+input slots)."],
        "oldStart":476
      }],
    "newString":"`test_iterator_multi_fire` in `tests/012-dispatch-test.c` is the\nheadline test: push three values to the iterator's input slot,\nspawn once, all three branches a/b/c fire with the right tagged\noutput. The atomic counter walks 0 → 1 → 2 across the\nauto-re-spawned tasks.\n\n### Cell-tagged ordering across parallel iterator workers — 2026-05-19\n\nEarlier multi-spawn slot pushes carried `tag = 0`; pop order was\nfill order (which is FIFO under the per-slot spinlock but\nnon-deterministic across producer interleaving).\n\nTag propagation is now wired through:\n\n- `push_one_connection` / `push_branch` take an explicit `tag`\n  argument forwarded to `slot_push`.\n- Iterator routing passes the freshly-incremented counter as\n  the tag; randomizer and weighted routing pass their counter\n  snapshot so any downstream tagged slot still serves in stable\n  order; plain/comparator pushes pass `0`.\n- `graph_attach_runtime` sets `SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED` on every\n  multi-spawn box's input slots. The slot store's tagged-pop\n  rule (lowest tag first; FIFO among ties via filled-index\n  scan) means that even when two iterator tasks run on\n  different workers in opposite order, the downstream consumer\n  reads them in invocation order.\n\nVerified by re-running all 6 fixture maps and the dedicated\n`test_iterator_multi_fire` test (which now exercises tagged\ninput slots)."
  },

It now\n   uses `dladdr()` on its own symbol to find the loaded `.so`\n   path, takes `dirname()`, and looks for `bash-server.sh` next\n   to itself. SORAMECH_BASH_SERVER still overrides; the\n   cwd-relative path remains as a fallback (with a stderr\n   warning so the fallback isn't silent). This took adding\n   `-ldl` to `langs/bash/Makefile`.\n\nVerified end-to-end: `scripts/run-tests.sh` now includes a\n`compile pipeline (portable run)` check that calls\nsoramech-compile on the pipeline fixture, then invokes the\ncompiled artifact from `/tmp` (so cwd cannot accidentally\nsatisfy any relative path), and asserts both the captured\noutput and the `file_write` destination match the expected\nvalues.\n\nPer-map `compiled/` directories under `tests/maps/*/` are\ngitignored.\n\n### Status as of 2026-05-19\n\nThe follow-ons enumerated above are now all in place. Issue 309\nis effectively done; closeout pending a verification pass once\nthe remaining open phase-3 issues land.",

    "noOutputExpected":false,
    "stdout":"  <arg2>\\n\n  ...\n```\n\n`bash-server.sh` keeps an associative array of sourced files so a\nbox source is sourced exactly once per worker — analogous to the\nLua spec's per-worker module cache (issue 306).\n\nPer-worker teardown plumbed through the pool (issue 301's new\n`pool_set_worker_teardown` callback) sends `QUIT\\n`, closes the\nparent fd, and `waitpid`s the subprocess with a 1-second\nshort-poll fallback to `SIGTERM`. Verified: zero orphan bash\nprocesses after a `soramech-pool` run.\n\nLimitations of the current protocol:\n- Arguments containing literal newlines are not supported\n  (line-oriented framing). Box authors who need them base64-encode.\n- Single-request/single-response; long-running bash boxes\n  serialize behind themselves on the same worker.         "text":"All green under STRICT: 100 unit tests across 14 suites + 7 integration tests pass.\n\n### Round summary\n\n**304 cell-tagged ordering**\n- `push_one_connection` / `push_branch` now take a `tag` argument; iterator routing passes the counter snapshot, randomizer/weighted pass the pre-mix counter, plain/comparator pass 0.\n- `graph_attach_runtime` sets `SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED` on every multi-spawn box's input slots, so parallel iterator workers' pushes are served by the consumer in invocation order regardless of who finishes first.\n\n**309 compile / package pipeline**\n- New `scripts/soramech-compile.sh <map>` produces a self-contained `<map>/compiled/` with copies of `meta.json` / `boxes/` / `src/` / `data/`, language plugins under `langs/<lang>/spec.so` (+ `bash-server.sh`), pre-compiled C boxes in `bin/`, a real copy of `soramech-pool` as `pool-runner`, and a `manifest.json`. Working tree uncommitted.\n\nWant another round, or close out the items that are now at \"as-far-as-makes-sense\" and move them to `issues/completed/`?"

  "message":{
    "content":"can we add an issue file to set up a \"reference counter\" that is built into the map itself? if another program or process uses that specific version of the map, it'll increment a .dot file in the map's compiled directory. then, when it doesn't need it anymore, it's supposed to decrement it - but this doesn't always happen alas. so it's expected to be a bit unreliable and finnicky. each reference has a date, and a backward pointing reference as well so you can check and validate. anyway, if there's a reference counter when building / compiling, we'll compile to a separately named directory that's right next-door. that way we don't break anyone else's functionality until they're ready to be clear. these builds are gitignored, by the way...\n\nthen, let's re-center and prepare for another round.",
    "role":"user"
  }
}

    "file":{
      "content":"# 314 — A small C JSON parser, written for SoraMech\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nThe phase 3 design assumes a vendored JSON parser sits under\n`libs/json/` — issues 305 (graph loader), 311 (JSONL run output),\nand 309 (build system) all reference it. The original plan was to\ndrop in cJSON / jsmn / similar.\n\nAfter thinking about it: a vendored generic parser is one more\nexternal surface to learn and to debug, with idioms that don't\nmatch the rest of the runtime, and complications around large\ninputs / streaming / arena allocation that we'd want to special-case\nanyway. SoraMech needs JSON in two specific places:\n\n1. **Reading** map files (`meta.json`, `boxes/*.json`,\n   `data/*.json`) at graph load. Inputs are kilobyte-scale, parsed\n   once, validated immediately. The output is a tree that the\n   graph loader walks once.\n2. **Writing** run-log events into `tmp/last-run.jsonl` (issue\n   311). Output is per-event, line-oriented, ASCII-safe; the writer\n   thread serialises one event struct per call.\n\nBoth are narrow enough that a small, opinionated parser tailored to\nthe project beats a general-purpose library on every dimension that\nmatters to us.\n",

      "totalLines":253,

        "input":{
          "content":"# 315 — Reference-counted compiled-map artifacts\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`scripts/soramech-compile.sh` from issue 309 is destructive at the\ntop:\n\n```bash\nrm -rf \"$COMPILED\"\nmkdir -p \"$COMPILED\" \"$COMPILED/boxes\" \"$COMPILED/src\" ...\n```\n\nWhatever lived in `<map>/compiled/` before the rebuild is gone. If\nanother process — a long-running runner, a different shell, a\nsibling tool that opened the artifact yesterday — had pinned to\nthat exact compiled layout (a particular `pool-runner` binary, a\nparticular `spec.so` ABI, a particular set of pre-compiled C\nboxes), the rebuild yanks the rug. The holder either crashes,\nsilently retains stale `dlopen` handles, or starts reading new\nfiles mid-flight.\n\nThis is fine in single-user development. It stops being fine the\nmoment a SoraMech artifact is the kind of thing other programs\nhold onto across time.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA compiled artifact carries its own reference count. Other\nprograms that depend on a particular build of a map are expected\nto *acquire* a reference on startup and *release* it on shutdown.\nWhen `soramech-compile` is asked to rebuild a map that has any\nlive references, it does NOT clobber the existing directory.\nInstead it builds a sibling directory next door, leaving the\nreferenced one untouched until its holders are done with it.\n\nThe reference count is **expected to be unreliable**. A crashing\nholder doesn't get the chance to release; an SSH session that\ndrops doesn't either. The design accepts that staleness is the\ncommon case, not the exception — every reference entry carries\nenough metadata to be independently validated and (eventually)\nreaped. The reference count is a hint and a courtesy, not a\nguarantee.\n\nThis is conceptually a copy-on-write filesystem for compiled\nartifacts: writes (rebuilds) fork the universe when readers\nexist; readers can keep reading the version they pinned to;\ngenerations get garbage-collected when nothing observable still\npoints at them.\n\n## Concept\n\nA compiled directory contains a `.refs` file (hidden, dot-prefixed\nso it doesn't clutter directory listings). It's append-only by\ndesign — concurrent acquires never need to take a lock; concurrent\nreleases write a separate marker without rewriting the file.\n\nEach reference has three parts:\n\n1. **A date.** When the reference was acquired. Lets a janitor\n   prune references older than some threshold even if their back\n   pointer can't be validated.\n2. **A back-pointer.** The identity of the holder — enough\n   information that an outside observer can ask \"is this holder\n   still alive, and does it still want this reference?\" without\n   trusting the count alone. Concrete candidates:\n   - process PID + start time (PID alone is not enough; PIDs\n     recycle)\n   - a path to a marker file the holder maintains (presence of\n     the marker = the holder is still live and aware of the\n     ref)\n   - some combination (PID + a marker path)\n3. **An opaque ref id.** A short string the holder can use later\n   to identify *its* reference when it wants to release, so it\n   doesn't accidentally release someone else's.\n\nA release writes an entry referencing the original acquire id.\nNet live refs = acquires whose id isn't in the release set.\n\n## Reference file format\n\nA line-oriented log. Each line is one of two record types:\n\n```\nacquire <id> <iso8601-date> <pid> <pid-start-time-ticks> <marker-path>\nrelease <id> <iso8601-date>\n```\n\nAppend-only. Holders open with `O_APPEND` and write a single line\nper operation. Atomic on POSIX as long as the line fits in\n`PIPE_BUF` (4 KB on Linux) — well within budget for these short\nrecords.\n\nReading: tail through the file, build a set of acquire ids,\nsubtract release ids; remaining ids are nominally live. Then\nvalidate each survivor's back pointer.\n\nA `.refs.lock` file is used only for compaction (rewriting the\nlog to drop matched acquire/release pairs) and for the\nfork-to-sibling decision during compile. Steady-state reads /\nwrites don't lock.\n\n## Acquire / release API\n\nA small helper utility, probably a shell script for portability\nsince holders are written in many languages:\n\n```\nscripts/soramech-ref.sh acquire <compiled-dir> [--id <id>] [--marker <path>]\nscripts/soramech-ref.sh release <compiled-dir> --id <id>\nscripts/soramech-ref.sh list    <compiled-dir>          # JSON, including staleness verdicts\nscripts/soramech-ref.sh reap    <compiled-dir>          # compact + drop dead refs\n```\n\n`acquire` prints the assigned id to stdout; the holder is\nresponsible for plumbing it to wherever it'll need to call\nrelease. If no `--id` was supplied, the script generates one\n(timestamp + random suffix).\n\n`list` walks the log and prints a JSON array of `{id, date,\nholder, valid}` entries. Validation reads the back pointer's\nliveness signal (PID exists & start-time matches, or marker file\nexists).\n\n`reap` is destructive — it rewrites the log to remove entries\nwhose holders failed validation. Run periodically; never\nautomatically as part of compile (compile must not destroy state\nits caller might care about).\n\n## Compile-time fork logic\n\n`soramech-compile.sh` consults `<map>/compiled/.refs` (and any\nsibling generation directories' `.refs` files) before deciding\nwhere to write:\n\n1. If `<map>/compiled/` doesn't exist → build there, fresh.\n2. If it exists but has zero live references → build there, after\n   `rm -rf`. Same destructive behavior as today.\n3. If it exists with one or more live references → pick a sibling\n   directory name (see below) and build there. The original\n   `compiled/` stays intact.\n\nAfter a fork-build, the caller has a new directory; `manifest.json`\nin the new directory records the fork relationship (`forked_from`\nfield pointing at the previous generation's path).\n\n### Sibling directory naming\n\nTwo reasonable schemes; pick whichever the implementer prefers:\n\n- **Generation index:** `compiled.0`, `compiled.1`, `compiled.2`...\n  Always pick `compiled.N` where N is one more than the highest\n  existing generation. Easy to grep for; index order = build\n  order.\n- **Timestamp suffix:** `compiled.2026-05-19T2347` (ISO 8601\n  compact). Order-preserving lexicographically; the name itself\n  tells the operator when it was built.\n\nWhichever wins, the script should also leave a `compiled` symlink\npointing at the newest generation, so callers who want \"the\nlatest\" don't have to enumerate.\n\n## Stale reference handling\n\nA reference is stale if any of the following hold:\n\n- The PID no longer exists on the system.\n- The PID exists but its start time (`/proc/<pid>/stat` field 22)\n  doesn't match the recorded value — different process, recycled\n  PID.\n- The marker file path was supplied at acquire and is now\n  missing.\n\nStale refs are *tolerated*: compile-time fork still triggers if\nANY ref exists, stale or otherwise — the caller can run\n`soramech-ref.sh reap` first if they want to consolidate. ```json
{
  "slug":"mossy-hopping-turtle",
  "userType":"external",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-19T07:33:44.729Z",
  "entrypoint":"cli",
  "gitBranch":"master",
  "sourceToolAssistantUUID":"2cb3dbb2-b22a-4ac5-8f32-03177b7889e2",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "sessionId":"585b6e65-7287-44e7-b133-8bdf3479a266",
  "parentUuid":"2cb3dbb2-b22a-4ac5-8f32-03177b7889e2",
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",
  "promptId":"35ccd4b3-c994-4ef2-a766-40df65694a84",
  "isSidechain":false,
  "toolUseResult":{
    "type":"text",
    "file":{
      "content":"# 302 — Per-task slot store with wire-held references\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nWire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values\nhave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\naccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n\n## Concept\n\n### Slots belong to input ports, not tasks\n\nEach box has **one slot per input port**, allocated when the graph\nloads and persisting for the life of the run. A wire is a routing\ndeclaration: \"the producer's output port pushes a copy of its value\ninto this consumer's named input slot.\" The producer never owns a\nslot — its output is a routing event, not a stored value.\n\nWhen a producer fires, the dispatch layer copies the value into\nevery downstream input slot wired to that output. Fan-out is N\npushes (one per consumer); fan-in is N producers all pushing into\nthe same consumer's slot. Both behaviors fall out of the same\npush-into-input-slot mechanic.\n\nSlots live in process heap memory, accessible to every worker\nthread. Cross-process visibility is not required: language specs\n(issue 303) only ever receive byte pointers — never raw slot\naddresses — so out-of-process specs (Bash) work via sockets, not\nshared memory.\n\n### Tasks are ephemeral; box state is durable\n\nA **task** is one invocation: pop one value from each of the box's\ninput slots, run the box's logic, push the output to every\ndownstream input slot. Tasks have no persistent identity — they're\njust stack frames on workers. Tasks are spawned dynamically by the\ndispatch layer when a box's input set is ready (every input slot\nholds at least one value).\n\nThe **box** is the durable thing: it owns its input port slots, any\ncounter state (for iterators), its language spec handle, and so\non. The box exists from graph load until run end. Tasks come and\ngo.\n\nThis is uniform across iterator and non-iterator boxes. Both run N\ntimes where N depends on how many invocations their inputs supply\n(possibly 1, possibly thousands). The difference is just what the\ntask does:\n- **Plain call task**: invoke spec on the popped values, push the\n  return to outputs.\n- **Iterator task**: read box's counter, route the popped value to\n  output port `iterator_outputs[counter]`, increment counter mod N.\n  No spec invocation.\n- **Comparator task**: invoke spec on the popped values, compare\n  the return against `comparand`, route to the matching `lt` /\n  `eq` / `gt` branch.\n\n### All slots are ring buffers; read mode varies\n\nThere is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells,\neach of `cell_capacity` bytes. The number of cells (`n_cells`) and\nthe read mode are both compile-time properties of the input port:\n\n- **1-cell + peek mode**: the value the producer wrote stays in the\n  cell. Tasks read via `slot_peek` — read without draining — and\n  every subsequent task on this consumer reads the same value\n  unless the producer overwrites it. Used for **single-push wires**\n  (a literal, or a wire from a producer box whose invocation count\n  is exactly 1). Multiple consumer tasks read the value as many\n  times as needed; the cell is never empty.\n- **N-cell + pop mode**: a queue. Producers push; consumers\n  `slot_pop` — drain one cell per task. Used for **multi-push wires**:\n  any wire whose producer has more than one task invocation\n  during the run. The producer's pushes accumulate, the consumer\n  drains in pop order.\n\nCompile-time analysis classifies each wire. A producer is\n\"runs-once\" if no transitive ancestor is an iterator; otherwise\nit's \"runs-N-times.\" Wires from runs-once producers get 1-cell\npeek slots; wires from runs-N-times producers get N-cell pop slots.\n\n`n_cells` for pop slots is sized for worst-case backlog (or a\ndefault like 64 with growth on demand). Lists grow if the producer\noutruns the consumer past the pre-allocation.\n\nFan-in: multiple producers pushing into the same N-cell pop slot\nland in arrival order. The consumer pops FIFO unless the cell\ncarries an ordering tag (see \"Cell tagging\" below).\n\n### Atomic-counter slot mode\n\nA slot allocated with `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` carries a single\n4-byte unsigned integer cell, read via a special op:\n\n```c\nuint32_t slot_read_inc(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod);\n// Returns the current value mod `mod`, then atomically increments\n// the underlying counter. Concurrent readers each get a distinct\n// value. Counter wraps at 2^32; mod handles N-branch routing.\n```\n\nUsed for iterator counters (issue 304): the iterator box has an\nauto-allocated `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot at load time; the\ndispatch action calls `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_branches)`\nto pick its output branch. Multiple iterator tasks can read\nconcurrently from the same counter slot in parallel — each gets a\nunique routing index — without any per-box mutable state and\nwithout the serial dependency of a self-push counter.\n\nThe slot's \"cell\" is just an `atomic_uint32_t`. No push is ever\nperformed; reads do the work. From the dispatch action's\nperspective it's just another slot; from the slot store's\nperspective the read op is special-cased.\n\n### Cell tagging (for parallel-iterator ordering)\n\nA cell can optionally carry a 4-byte ordering tag alongside its\nsize and data:\n\n```\nCell layout (N-cell pop slot)\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     filled_size\n4       4     tag      (0 if untagged; iterator counter snapshot otherwise)\n8       …     data\n```\n\nSlots created for wires from parallel iterators (issue 304) are\ntagged. Pop on a tagged slot returns the cell with the lowest tag,\nnot the head cell — preserving iterator-counter order across pushes\nthat arrived out of order from parallel iterator workers.\n\nUntagged slots default tag to 0 and pop FIFO at no extra cost. The\ntag-aware pop is a per-slot mode flag set at allocation time.\n\n### Asynchrony\nThe store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\nfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\nis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n\n## Slot layout\n\nEach slot is a header followed by `n_cells` cells, each `cell_capacity`\nbytes. The header tracks ring-buffer state and lifetime:\n\n```\nSlot header\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     cell_capacity   (bytes per cell, set at allocation)\n4       4     n_cells         (ring size, set at allocation)\n8       4     head            (read index, mod n_cells)\n12      4     tail            (write index, mod n_cells; cells_filled = tail - head)\n16      1     touched         (per-slot lock: 0=free, 1=another thread mutating)\n17      3     _pad\n20      …     cells           (n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes))\n```\n\nEach cell stores a 4-byte filled-size followed by `cell_capacity`\nbytes of value data. Cells have wildly different capacities across\nslots — capacity is per-slot, not global. The C convention of passing\nsizes alongside arrays applies: the task that allocates a slot knows\nhow big it needs the cells.\n\n`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any header mutation\n(push, pop, refcount changes). A reader that finds `touched == 1`\nspins until it clears. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock —\nif contention proves to matter, replace with a proper mutex without\nchanging the API.\n\nWrites to a cell complete with a memory barrier before `tail` is\nadvanced, so a reader that observes `head < tail` is guaranteed to\nsee the complete value at the head cell.\n\n## Lifetime\n\nSlots are owned by the box that holds the input port. They live\nfrom graph load until run end. There is no per-slot reference\ncounting and no end-of-stream propagation — the slot is freed\nwhen the run ends, alongside its owning box.\n\nRun termination is governed entirely by the pool's active-task\ncounter (issue 301): when no task is running and no further spawns\nare pending, the run is over. There's nothing the slot store needs\nto track to make this work.\n\n### No wait lists\n\nTasks never park on slots. Tasks are spawned by the dispatch\nlayer's spawn-on-input-arrival rule and run to completion; they\nnever block. A slot that has no value yet simply means the\nspawn rule hasn't fired for that consumer yet. No wait list,\nno per-slot wake-up traversal — just a check after each push.\n\n## Backing store\n\nSlots are allocated from process heap memory. The slot store owns a\nper-run allocator (described under \"Allocation strategy\" below) that\nhands out memory chunks to slots. Plain `malloc`-class memory is\nsufficient — every worker thread in the process can read and write\nit, and no spec ever needs to access it from a child process.\n\nSynchronization within a slot uses the per-slot `touched` flag for\nheader mutations. There is no allocator-wide mutex on the\nread/write path; only the per-size-class free lists in the\nallocator have their own locks.\n\n## Slot creation\n\nSlot creation happens at **graph load**, not per task. The graph\nloader walks every box, allocates one ring buffer per input port,\nand parks the slot on the box's per-port slot table. The dispatch\nlayer never allocates new slots at runtime in the steady state —\nall slots that will ever exist are created up front.\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);\n```\n\n`cell_capacity` and `n_cells` come from compile-time analysis of\nthe graph. Boxes downstream of iterators get larger `n_cells` to\nabsorb the iterator's worst-case backlog.\n\nIf a slot's pre-allocated `n_cells` proves too small at runtime\n(producer outpaces consumer beyond the pre-allocation), the slot's\nring grows — see \"Allocation strategy\" below.\n\n## C API surface\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc       (slot_store_t *s, int cell_capacity, int n_cells, int flags);\nvoid      slot_push        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size, uint32_t tag);\nint       slot_peek        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // 1-cell: read without draining\nint       slot_pop         (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // N-cell: drain head (or lowest-tag)\nuint32_t  slot_read_inc    (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod);            // SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER only\nint       slot_has_value   (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);                          // for spawn-rule check\n```\n\nFlags include:\n- `SLOT_TAGGED`: cells carry ordering tags; `slot_pop` returns the\n  lowest-tag cell.\n- `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER`: slot holds a single atomic uint32; reads\n  via `slot_read_inc` only. `slot_push` / `slot_peek` / `slot_pop`\n  are not valid on atomic-counter slots.\n\nPush always takes a `tag` argument; untagged slots ignore it (or\ntreat 0 as \"no order\").\n\n1-cell peek slot use: producer `push` once at startup (literal) or\nwhen its single invocation completes (single-push wire). All\nconsumer tasks `peek` to read the value as many times as their box\nruns. The cell is never empty after the initial push.\n\nN-cell pop slot use: producers `push` repeatedly. Consumer tasks\n`pop` one cell each. For tagged slots, `pop` returns the\nlowest-tag cell; for untagged, FIFO. Pop on an empty slot is a\nbug — the spawn rule guarantees the slot is non-empty before a\ntask spawns.\n\nThere is no `slot_ref` / `slot_unref` — slot lifetime is the run.\n\n## Submission timing\n\nTasks are spawned dynamically in response to slot pushes. Each box\nhas small per-box state used by the dispatch layer:\n\n```\nbox_runtime_state {\n    slot_id_t  *input_slots;     // one per input port (set at load)\n    int        *port_modes;      // PEEK or POP, per input port\n    int         n_inputs;\n    slot_id_t   counter_slot;    // iterator only: SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER slot;\n                                 // 0 / unused otherwise\n};\n```\n\nThe spawning rule:\n- When a producer pushes to one of a box's input slots, the\n  dispatch layer checks **does every input slot have a value\n  available?** \"Available\" means:\n  - For peek-mode (1-cell) slots: cell has been written at least\n    once. Once a peek slot is filled, it stays available — every\n    subsequent spawn-check on this box passes the peek-port check.\n  - For pop-mode (N-cell) slots: queue is non-empty.\n- If yes, spawn a `dispatch_task_t` and submit to the pool. The\n  task pops (or peeks) one value from each input slot when it\n  runs.\n- Each push that completes the input set triggers exactly one\n  spawn. Multiple pushes accumulate in pop slots; each pop\n  consumes one, and if more remain, the next push (or check)\n  re-fires the spawn rule.\n\nThis makes the pool's queue the rate buffer: pushes accumulate\nin pop slots (possibly multiple per slot), and one task per\naccumulated value gets spawned.\n\nTasks never block on slots. They're spawned after inputs are\nready, run to completion, and disappear. Blocking-and-waking\nmachinery is unnecessary — the spawn-on-arrival rule is the\nsynchronization primitive.\n\nThe pool's queue is the only queue. There is no separate \"blocked\ntasks\" structure.\n\n## Allocation strategy: size-class free lists with coalescing fallback\n\nThe slot store uses a segregated free-list allocator. The map is\nanalyzed at compile time to enumerate every distinct slot size the\ngraph will need (each call box declares its output slot size; each\nqueued-input ring declares its total size from cell capacity × queue\ndepth). The allocator builds one free list per distinct size class.\n\nVariable-size and unknown-size payloads (a long LLM response, an\narray whose length is not known until runtime) are handled by a\nseparate **large-value heap** described below — not by allocating\nhuge slots up front.\n\n### The lists\nEach size class is an array (or linked list) of free slots of exactly\nthat size. At startup, each list is pre-populated with enough slots\nto cover the static box count for that size. Lists grow during the\nrun if demand exceeds the pre-allocation.\n\nEach list has its own mutex — allocation and deallocation in different\nsize classes never contend with each other.\n\n### Allocation\nGiven a request for size N bytes:\n1. Find the smallest size class with `class_size ≥ N`.\n2. If that class has a free slot, pop it. Done.\n3. Otherwise, try the next larger size class. Repeat.\n4. If a larger class hits, the slot is oversized for the request.\n   Try to slice the unused tail into a residual slot. If the residual\n   is at least as large as the smallest size class, push it onto that\n   class's list. Otherwise skip the slice — oversize the allocation\n   and live with the waste until the slot is freed.\n5. If no size class has a free slot, attempt to coalesce: walk the\n   address-ordered chunk list looking for adjacent free chunks that\n   together meet the requested size. If found, merge them and return\n   the combined chunk.\n6. If coalescing fails, grow the region (see \"Growth\" below) and\n   append the new slots to the appropriate lists. Then try again.\n7. After steps 5 or 6 complete, queue a deferred cleanup task on the\n   pool. Cleanup runs on a worker thread later and walks the\n   chunk list to opportunistically coalesce contiguous free chunks\n   into the largest possible chunks. Cleanup is best-effort — it\n   does not block any other thread. If memory fragments faster than\n   cleanup can keep up, the next allocation grows the heap; that's\n   fine.\n\n### Deallocation\nWhen refcount drops to zero, the slot is pushed onto its size class's\nfree list. The deallocator also performs a cheap eager-coalesce step:\ncheck the slot's two physical neighbors; if either is free, merge\nthem and push the combined chunk onto the appropriate size class.\nThis is O(1) given the doubly-linked chunk list (see below) and keeps\nsmall-scale fragmentation in check without needing the deferred\ncleanup task to run.\n\n### Physical-order chunk list (for coalescing)\nCoalescing needs to know which chunks are physically adjacent in\nmemory. The size-class free lists don't carry that information.\n\nTwo viable representations:\n\n- **Doubly-linked list** of all chunks (free and allocated) in\n  address order. Splits and merges are O(1) given the chunk pointer.\n  Neighbor lookup is O(1). Pointer chasing is the cost.\n- **Two parallel arrays** (`start[i]`, `end[i]`) sorted by start\n  address. Lookup by binary search is O(log N), but inserts and\n  deletes are O(N) without an additional index. Cache-friendly to\n  scan.\n\nThe linked list is simpler and has the right asymptotic behavior for\nsplits/merges, which dominate. Start there. If profiling later shows\nlist traversal is hot, switch to the array form with an auxiliary\nindex — the API doesn't change.\n\n### Large-value heap (variable-size payloads)\n\nFor values whose size is not known at compile time — long LLM\nresponses, dynamically-sized arrays, anything where the upper bound\nis not a useful number to allocate — the slot does not hold the value\ndirectly. Instead, the slot holds a small fixed-size handle:\n\n```\n{ uint32_t size; uint32_t lvh_offset; }\n```\n\n`lvh_offset` points into a separate **large-value heap**, a\nplain `malloc`-backed region used only for variable-size payloads.\nWhen a box produces a 4 MB LLM response, the dispatch layer:\n1. Allocates 4 MB in the large-value heap.\n2. Writes the bytes there.\n3. Stores the handle (size = 4 MB, offset = …) in the slot.\n\nThe consumer reads the handle from the slot, follows the offset,\ncopies the bytes (or works with them in place). When the slot's\nrefcount hits zero, the slot's deallocator also frees the\nlarge-value-heap region.\n\nThe slot allocator is unchanged — it always sees fixed-size slots.\nThe two-tier approach keeps the hot path simple while still\nsupporting unbounded outputs.\n\nA box opts into large-value output by declaring its output as\n\"variable-size\" in the graph. Compile-time-known outputs use the\nfixed-size path with no indirection.\n\n### Growth\nWhen all size-class lists are exhausted and coalescing cannot satisfy\na request, the allocator grows by calling `malloc` for a new region,\ndividing it into slots, and appending them to the relevant size-class\nlists. Plain heap memory is fine — no spec needs cross-process access\nto slot memory.\n\n### Why this design\n- Compile-time enumeration makes every common allocation a single\n  pop from a list. No size-comparison loops, no walks of free space.\n- Slicing residuals cannot fragment beyond the granularity of the\n  smallest declared size class, since smaller residuals are simply\n  not split.\n- Coalescing is the safety valve for unusual allocation patterns,\n  and it costs nothing on the common path.\n- Growth is rare — if pre-allocation matches static demand, it never\n  fires.\n\n## No type tags\n\nSlots store opaque bytes. The producer wrote N bytes; the consumer\nreads N bytes. What those bytes mean is the language spec's business\non each side, and the wire's metadata in the graph (issue 219's\ncompiler can check producer-output type vs consumer-input type at\nbuild time). The slot store does not interpret values — it does not\nneed to know if they are strings, numbers, JSON, images, or anything\nelse. Removed the type-tag field from the header for that reason.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.\n2. Unit test single-value slots: thread A writes, thread B reads,\n   refcount decrements, slot freed when last ref dropped.\n3. Unit test ring-buffer slots: multiple producers push, single consumer\n   drains in order, no values lost or duplicated.\n4. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: shared memory created at\n   startup, store handle passed to the dispatch layer.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point, owns the shared memory region\n- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task dispatch reads/writes slots\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued input model that\n  ring-buffer slots implement\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### Core milestone — 2026-05-12\n\nWhat shipped:\n- `src/009-slot-store.h` — the public API exactly as the design\n  describes: `slot_alloc` / `slot_push` / `slot_peek` / `slot_pop` /\n  `slot_read_inc` / `slot_has_value` / `slot_fill_count`. Plus the\n  store lifecycle pair and a small inspection helper for tests.\n- `src/009-slot-store.c` — implementation. Plain-malloc per slot\n  (size-class free lists deferred); ring slots and atomic-counter\n  slots both supported; the SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED variant of pop scans\n  for the lowest-tag filled cell. Per-slot spinlock via\n  `atomic_flag`. Atomic counter via `atomic_fetch_add_explicit`,\n  no lock.\n- `tests/009-slot-store-test.c` — 12 unit tests covering peek\n  semantics, FIFO pop, tagged pop ordering (in-order and\n  interleaved), atomic counter (sequential + 8-thread concurrent),\n  bad-argument paths, ring-full / empty edge cases, and a\n  multi-thread producer/consumer race over 5000 values.\n- Makefile additions: `test` target builds test binaries via a\n  pattern rule and runs them. Per-test prerequisites listed\n  explicitly so each binary links the minimal set of source `.o`s.\n- File index counter advanced to `009`.\n\nVerified clean build and 12/12 tests pass in `make STRICT=1`\n(`-Werror -Wextra -Wpedantic`).\n\nWhat's deferred to a follow-on within 302:\n- **Size-class free lists with coalescing.** The current\n  implementation `malloc`s each slot independently. That's correct\n  but unoptimized. Slots are allocated once at graph load and never\n  freed until run end, so under the current usage pattern free-list\n  reuse buys nothing. Lands once profiling justifies it (or once\n  long-running maps surface allocation pressure).\n- **Large-value heap for variable-size payloads.** Slots currently\n  store fixed-size cells; very large outputs (multi-MB LLM\n  responses, dynamically-sized arrays) will need the two-tier\n  scheme described under \"Large-value heap\" above. Blocks no\n  in-flight phase 3 work until a graph wants variable-size outputs.\n\nNeither deferred item blocks 301 / 304 / 305 / 306 / 307 / 308.\n",
