    "content":"/* tests/015-large-value-heap-test.c — unit tests for the\n * variable-size payload allocator (issue 302 follow-on, lvh).\n *\n * The tests cover the three properties that the slot store relies\n * on at the layer above:\n *   1. Pointers returned by lvh_alloc are stable across further\n *      allocations (chunks don't move).\n *   2. Concurrent allocations from many threads never produce\n *      overlapping regions.\n *   3. Allocations larger than the default chunk size succeed.\n *\n * The miscellaneous tests cover the stats accessors and the\n * zero-size convention.\n */\n\n#include \"../src/015-large-value-heap.h\"\n\n#include <pthread.h>\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n\n/* {{{ Local mini test harness */\nstatic int g_pass = 0;\nstatic int g_fail = 0;\n\n#define ASSERT(cond) do { \\\n    if (!(cond)) { \\\n        fprintf(stderr, \"  ASSERT failed at %s:%d: %s\\n\", \\\n                __FILE__, __LINE__, #cond); \\\n        return 0; \\\n    } \\\n} while (0)\n\n#define RUN(test) do { \\\n    int ok = test(); \\\n    printf(\"  %-44s %s\\n\", #test, ok ? \"ok\" : \"FAIL\"); \\\n    if (ok) g_pass++; else g_fail++; \\\n} while (0)\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_create_destroy() */\nstatic int test_create_destroy(void)\n{\n    lvh_t *h = lvh_create(0);\n    ASSERT(h != NULL);\n    ASSERT(lvh_chunk_count(h) == 0);\n    ASSERT(lvh_total_allocated(h) == 0);\n    ASSERT(lvh_total_used(h) == 0);\n    lvh_destroy(h);\n\n    /* destroy on NULL is safe */\n    lvh_destroy(NULL);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_single_alloc_within_chunk() */\nstatic int test_single_alloc_within_chunk(void)\n{\n    lvh_t *h = lvh_create(4096);\n    ASSERT(h != NULL);\n\n    void *p = lvh_alloc(h, 100);\n    ASSERT(p != NULL);\n\n    /* Write through the pointer; read it back. */\n    memset(p, 0xAB, 100);\n    unsigned char *q = (unsigned char *)p;\n    for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) ASSERT(q[i] == 0xAB);\n\n    ASSERT(lvh_chunk_count(h) == 1);\n    ASSERT(lvh_total_allocated(h) >= 4096);\n    ASSERT(lvh_total_used(h) >= 100);\n\n    lvh_destroy(h);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_multiple_allocs_within_chunk() */\nstatic int test_multiple_allocs_within_chunk(void)\n{\n    lvh_t *h = lvh_create(4096);\n    ASSERT(h != NULL);\n\n    void *a = lvh_alloc(h, 100);\n    void *b = lvh_alloc(h, 100);\n    void *c = lvh_alloc(h, 100);\n    ASSERT(a && b && c);\n    ASSERT(a != b && b != c && a != c);\n\n    /* Write different bytes to each; verify no overlap. */\n    memset(a, 0x11, 100);\n    memset(b, 0x22, 100);\n    memset(c, 0x33, 100);\n    ASSERT(((unsigned char *)a)[0] == 0x11);\n    ASSERT(((unsigned char *)b)[0] == 0x22);\n    ASSERT(((unsigned char *)c)[0] == 0x33);\n    ASSERT(((unsigned char *)a)[99] == 0x11);\n    ASSERT(((unsigned char *)b)[99] == 0x22);\n    ASSERT(((unsigned char *)c)[99] == 0x33);\n\n    /* Still one chunk. */\n    ASSERT(lvh_chunk_count(h) == 1);\n\n    lvh_destroy(h);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_oversized_alloc() */\nstatic int test_oversized_alloc(void)\n{\n    lvh_t *h = lvh_create(1024);  /* small chunks on purpose */\n    ASSERT(h != NULL);\n\n    /* Request more than a chunk holds. */\n    void *p = lvh_alloc(h, 100 * 1024);  /* 100 KB */\n    ASSERT(p != NULL);\n\n    /* Writable end-to-end. */\n    memset(p, 0xCD, 100 * 1024);\n    ASSERT(((unsigned char *)p)[0]            == 0xCD);\n    ASSERT(((unsigned char *)p)[100*1024 - 1] == 0xCD);\n\n    /* One chunk, sized for the oversized request (>= 100KB). */\n    ASSERT(lvh_chunk_count(h) == 1);\n    ASSERT(lvh_total_allocated(h) >= 100u * 1024u);\n\n    lvh_destroy(h);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_pointer_stability_across_growth() */\n/* This is the property the slot store relies on: an earlier\n * consumer's pointer must not be invalidated when a later\n * producer's allocation forces a chunk grow. */\nstatic int test_pointer_stability_across_growth(void)\n{\n    lvh_t *h = lvh_create(1024);\n    ASSERT(h != NULL);\n\n    void *first = lvh_alloc(h, 64);\n    ASSERT(first != NULL);\n    memset(first, 0xEE, 64);\n    uintptr_t first_addr = (uintptr_t)first;\n\n    /* Push another ~20 KB through the heap, forcing several\n     * chunks. */\n    for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) {\n        void *p = lvh_alloc(h, 128);\n        ASSERT(p != NULL);\n    }\n    ASSERT(lvh_chunk_count(h) > 1);\n\n    /* Original pointer still has its bytes. */\n    ASSERT((uintptr_t)first == first_addr);\n    for (int i = 0; i < 64; i++) {\n        ASSERT(((unsigned char *)first)[i] == 0xEE);\n    }\n\n    lvh_destroy(h);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_zero_size_alloc() */\nstatic int test_zero_size_alloc(void)\n{\n    lvh_t *h = lvh_create(0);\n    void *p = lvh_alloc(h, 0);\n    ASSERT(p != NULL);  /* non-NULL is the convention */\n    lvh_destroy(h);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_stats_match_reality() */\nstatic int test_stats_match_reality(void)\n{\n    lvh_t *h = lvh_create(4096);\n    ASSERT(lvh_total_used(h) == 0);\n    ASSERT(lvh_total_allocated(h) == 0);\n    ASSERT(lvh_chunk_count(h) == 0);\n\n    lvh_alloc(h, 100);\n    /* Used is 16-aligned; lower bound 112, upper bound 128 (the\n     * exact value depends on LVH_ALIGN). */\n    uint64_t used = lvh_total_used(h);\n    ASSERT(used >= 100 && used <= 128);\n\n    lvh_alloc(h, 200);\n    used = lvh_total_used(h);\n    ASSERT(used >= 300 && used <= 400);\n\n    ASSERT(lvh_chunk_count(h) == 1);\n\n    lvh_destroy(h);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Concurrent alloc test scaffolding */\n#define N_THREADS    8\n#define N_PER_THREAD 1000\n#define ALLOC_SIZE   64\n\ntypedef struct {\n    lvh_t *h;\n    void  *ptrs[N_PER_THREAD];\n    int    thread_idx;\n} worker_arg_t;\n\nstatic void *concurrent_worker(void *vp)\n{\n    worker_arg_t *w = vp;\n    for (int i = 0; i < N_PER_THREAD; i++) {\n        void *p = lvh_alloc(w->h, ALLOC_SIZE);\n        if (!p) { w->ptrs[i] = NULL; continue; }\n        /* Write something thread-specific so unique-pointer checks\n         * later are paired with non-overlap evidence. */\n        memset(p, (unsigned char)(w->thread_idx + 1), ALLOC_SIZE);\n        w->ptrs[i] = p;\n    }\n    return NULL;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_concurrent_alloc() */\n/* Eight threads, 1000 allocs each. Every returned pointer must be\n * unique, every memset must survive (no overlap), and the chunk\n * count + total_used must reflect reality. */\nstatic int test_concurrent_alloc(void)\n{\n    lvh_t *h = lvh_create(4096);\n    ASSERT(h != NULL);\n\n    pthread_t   threads[N_THREADS];\n    worker_arg_t args[N_THREADS];\n\n    for (int t = 0; t < N_THREADS; t++) {\n        args[t].h          = h;\n        args[t].thread_idx = t;\n        pthread_create(&threads[t], NULL, concurrent_worker, &args[t]);\n    }\n    for (int t = 0; t < N_THREADS; t++) {\n        pthread_join(threads[t], NULL);\n    }\n\n    /* Verify each pointer still contains the byte its thread wrote.\n     * If two threads' regions had overlapped, at least some bytes\n     * would be the other thread's marker. */\n    int n_alloced = 0;\n    for (int t = 0; t < N_THREADS; t++) {\n        for (int i = 0; i < N_PER_THREAD; i++) {\n            void *p = args[t].ptrs[i];\n            if (!p) continue;\n            n_alloced++;\n            unsigned char expect = (unsigned char)(t + 1);\n            for (int k = 0; k < ALLOC_SIZE; k++) {\n                ASSERT(((unsigned char *)p)[k] == expect);\n            }\n        }\n    }\n    ASSERT(n_alloced == N_THREADS * N_PER_THREAD);\n\n    /* Pairwise uniqueness — a quadratic check, but for 8000\n     * pointers it's still well under a second and it gives us the\n     * strongest evidence. */\n    void **all = malloc((size_t)n_alloced * sizeof(void *));\n    int n = 0;\n    for (int t = 0; t < N_THREADS; t++) {\n        for (int i = 0; i < N_PER_THREAD; i++) {\n            if (args[t].ptrs[i]) all[n++] = args[t].ptrs[i];\n        }\n    }\n    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {\n        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {\n            ASSERT(all[i] != all[j]);\n        }\n    }\n    free(all);\n\n    lvh_destroy(h);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ main() */\nint main(void)\n{\n    printf(\"015-large-value-heap-test:\\n\");\n    RUN(test_create_destroy);\n    RUN(test_single_alloc_within_chunk);\n    RUN(test_multiple_allocs_within_chunk);\n    RUN(test_oversized_alloc);\n    RUN(test_pointer_stability_across_growth);\n    RUN(test_zero_size_alloc);\n    RUN(test_stats_match_reality);\n    RUN(test_concurrent_alloc);\n    printf(\"\\n  %d passed, %d failed\\n\", g_pass, g_fail);\n    return g_fail == 0 ? 0 : 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n",

    "originalFile":"/* src/009-slot-store.h — per-input-port slot store, public API.\n *\n * What it is, in a sentence: a thread-safe pool of ring-buffer\n * slots, allocated at graph load time, used by the phase 3\n * dispatch layer to route values between boxes.\n *\n * Slots belong to input ports, not tasks. Each box has one slot\n * per input port; the slot persists for the whole run. A wire is\n * a routing declaration — when a producer's task finishes, the\n * dispatch layer pushes copies of the output into every\n * downstream input slot. Fan-out is N pushes; fan-in is N\n * producers pushing into one slot. Designed in issue 302.\n *\n * Three slot modes, chosen via flags at slot_alloc:\n *\n *   1-cell peek (n_cells == 1, no flags)\n *     — for literals and wires from producers that run exactly\n *       once. Push once at startup. Every consumer task peeks\n *       without draining; the cell stays filled.\n *\n *   N-cell pop (n_cells > 1, no flags)\n *     — for wires whose producer runs many times (iterators,\n *       queued inputs). Push appends to tail; pop drains head\n *       FIFO. Consumer task pops one cell per spawn.\n *\n *   N-cell pop, tagged (SLOT_TAGGED)\n *     — same shape as N-cell pop, but pop returns the cell with\n *       the lowest tag, not the head. Used downstream of parallel\n *       iterators where push order is non-deterministic but\n *       consumption order must follow the iterator counter.\n *\n *   atomic counter (SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER, n_cells and cell_capacity\n *     ignored)\n *     — single atomic uint32. Read-and-increment via\n *       slot_read_inc(). Used for iterator / randomizer /\n *       weighted-routing counters. Concurrent reads each get a\n *       distinct value mod the caller-supplied bound.\n *\n * Synchronization is per-slot. There is no allocator-wide lock on\n * the hot read/write path. The atomic-counter slot uses\n * atomic_fetch_add; the ring-buffer slots use a per-slot spinlock\n * around header mutation (one byte, atomic_flag).\n *\n * Lifetime is the run. Slots are freed when the store is\n * destroyed at the end of the run — there is no per-slot refcount\n * and no end-of-stream propagation. Run termination is governed\n * by the pool's active-task counter (issue 301).\n *\n * Errors: a return of -1 from a read/write op means the operation\n * could not be performed (empty pop, buffer too small, type\n * mismatch). The store does not assert or abort; the dispatch\n * layer is expected to check return codes. The hard-crash policy\n * applies at the language-spec layer, not here.\n *\n * What's NOT in this version:\n *  - Size-class free lists and coalescing. The design in issue 302\n *    describes a segregated allocator with eager-coalesce; this\n *    initial implementation uses plain malloc per slot. The pattern\n *    is \"allocate once at graph load, free at run end\", so free-list\n *    optimization buys nothing for the current usage. Lands as a\n *    follow-on if profiling justifies it.\n *  - Large-value heap for variable-size payloads. Slots store\n *    fixed-size cells; very large outputs (LLM responses) will\n *    use a separate two-tier scheme. Follow-on within 302.\n */\n\n#ifndef SORAMECH_SLOT_STORE_H\n#define SORAMECH_SLOT_STORE_H\n\n#include <stdint.h>\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\nextern \"C\" {\n#endif\n\n/* {{{ Types & flags */\ntypedef struct slot_store slot_store_t;\ntypedef int32_t           slot_id_t;\n\n#define SLOT_INVALID  ((slot_id_t)-1)\n\n/* slot_alloc flags */\nenum {\n    SLOT_FLAG_NONE           = 0,\n    SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED         = 1 << 0,\n    SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER = 1 << 1,\n};\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Store lifecycle */\n/* Construct an empty store. Returns NULL on allocation failure. */\nslot_store_t *slot_store_create(void);\n\n/* Free every slot and the store itself. Safe to call on NULL. */\nvoid          slot_store_destroy(slot_store_t *s);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Slot lifecycle */\n/* Allocate a slot.\n *\n *   cell_capacity — bytes per cell. Ignored for SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER.\n *   n_cells       — ring size (1 for peek slots, >1 for pop). Ignored for\n *                   SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER.\n *   flags         — zero, SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED, or SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER.\n *\n * Returns the new slot's id, or SLOT_INVALID on allocation failure or\n * invalid arguments.     "originalFile":"/* src/009-slot-store.h — per-input-port slot store, public API.\n *\n * What it is, in a sentence: a thread-safe pool of ring-buffer\n * slots, allocated at graph load time, used by the phase 3\n * dispatch layer to route values between boxes.\n *\n * Slots belong to input ports, not tasks. Each box has one slot\n * per input port; the slot persists for the whole run. A wire is\n * a routing declaration — when a producer's task finishes, the\n * dispatch layer pushes copies of the output into every\n * downstream input slot. Push once at startup. Every consumer task peeks\n *       without draining; the cell stays filled.\n *\n *   N-cell pop (n_cells > 1, no flags)\n *     — for wires whose producer runs many times (iterators,\n *       queued inputs). Push appends to tail; pop drains head\n *       FIFO. Consumer task pops one cell per spawn.\n *\n *   N-cell pop, tagged (SLOT_TAGGED)\n *     — same shape as N-cell pop, but pop returns the cell with\n *       the lowest tag, not the head. Used downstream of parallel\n *       iterators where push order is non-deterministic but\n *       consumption order must follow the iterator counter.\n *\n *   atomic counter (SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER, n_cells and cell_capacity\n *     ignored)\n *     — single atomic uint32. Read-and-increment via\n *       slot_read_inc(). Used for iterator / randomizer /\n *       weighted-routing counters. Concurrent reads each get a\n *       distinct value mod the caller-supplied bound.\n *\n *   large-value (SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE)\n *     — for outputs whose size is not known at compile time\n *       (multi-MB LLM responses, dynamically-sized arrays). The\n *       cell holds only a pointer; the payload bytes live in a\n *       large-value heap owned by the slot store. cell_capacity\n *       is ignored — push/pop accept any size. May be combined\n *       with SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED to get lowest-tag pop semantics\n *       over variable-size values.\n *\n * Synchronization is per-slot. There is no allocator-wide lock on\n * the hot read/write path. The atomic-counter slot uses\n * atomic_fetch_add; the ring-buffer slots use a per-slot spinlock\n * around header mutation (one byte, atomic_flag).\n *\n * Lifetime is the run. Slots are freed when the store is\n * destroyed at the end of the run — there is no per-slot refcount\n * and no end-of-stream propagation. Run termination is governed\n * by the pool's active-task counter (issue 301).\n *\n * Errors: a return of -1 from a read/write op means the operation\n * could not be performed (empty pop, buffer too small, type\n * mismatch). The store does not assert or abort; the dispatch\n * layer is expected to check return codes. The hard-crash policy\n * applies at the language-spec layer, not here.\n *\n * What's NOT in this version:\n *  - Size-class free lists and coalescing. The pattern\n *    is \"allocate once at graph load, free at run end\", so free-list\n *    optimization buys nothing for the current usage. Lands as a\n *    follow-on if profiling justifies it.\n *  - Large-value heap for variable-size payloads. Slots store\n *    fixed-size cells; very large outputs (LLM responses) will\n *    use a separate two-tier scheme. Follow-on within 302.\n */\n\n#ifndef SORAMECH_SLOT_STORE_H\n#define SORAMECH_SLOT_STORE_H\n\n#include <stdint.h>\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\nextern \"C\" {\n#endif\n\n/* {{{ Types & flags */\ntypedef struct slot_store slot_store_t;\ntypedef int32_t           slot_id_t;\n\n#define SLOT_INVALID  ((slot_id_t)-1)\n\n/* slot_alloc flags */\nenum {\n    SLOT_FLAG_NONE           = 0,\n    SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED         = 1 << 0,\n    SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER = 1 << 1,\n};\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Store lifecycle */\n/* Construct an empty store. Ids are stable for the lifetime of the store. */\nslot_id_t     slot_alloc(slot_store_t *s,\n                         int32_t cell_capacity,\n                         int32_t n_cells,\n                         int32_t flags);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Ring-buffer ops */\n/* Push a value into the slot's next free cell.\n *\n *   data, size — value bytes. size must be <= cell_capacity.\n *   tag        — ordering tag.     "originalFile":"/* src/009-slot-store.h — per-input-port slot store, public API.\n *\n * What it is, in a sentence: a thread-safe pool of ring-buffer\n * slots, allocated at graph load time, used by the phase 3\n * dispatch layer to route values between boxes.\n *\n * Slots belong to input ports, not tasks. Each box has one slot\n * per input port; the slot persists for the whole run. A wire is\n * a routing declaration — when a producer's task finishes, the\n * dispatch layer pushes copies of the output into every\n * downstream input slot. Fan-out is N pushes; fan-in is N\n * producers pushing into one slot. Designed in issue 302.\n *\n * Three slot modes, chosen via flags at slot_alloc:\n *\n *   1-cell peek (n_cells == 1, no flags)\n *     — for literals and wires from producers that run exactly\n *       once. Push once at startup. Every consumer task peeks\n *       without draining; the cell stays filled.\n *\n *   N-cell pop (n_cells > 1, no flags)\n *     — for wires whose producer runs many times (iterators,\n *       queued inputs). Push appends to tail; pop drains head\n *       FIFO. Consumer task pops one cell per spawn.\n *\n *   N-cell pop, tagged (SLOT_TAGGED)\n *     — same shape as N-cell pop, but pop returns the cell with\n *       the lowest tag, not the head. Used downstream of parallel\n *       iterators where push order is non-deterministic but\n *       consumption order must follow the iterator counter.\n *\n *   atomic counter (SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER, n_cells and cell_capacity\n *     ignored)\n *     — single atomic uint32. Read-and-increment via\n *       slot_read_inc(). Used for iterator / randomizer /\n *       weighted-routing counters. Concurrent reads each get a\n *       distinct value mod the caller-supplied bound.\n *\n *   large-value (SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE)\n *     — for outputs whose size is not known at compile time\n *       (multi-MB LLM responses, dynamically-sized arrays). The\n *       cell holds only a pointer; the payload bytes live in a\n *       large-value heap owned by the slot store. cell_capacity\n *       is ignored — push/pop accept any size. May be combined\n *       with SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED to get lowest-tag pop semantics\n *       over variable-size values.\n *\n * Synchronization is per-slot. There is no allocator-wide lock on\n * the hot read/write path. The atomic-counter slot uses\n * atomic_fetch_add; the ring-buffer slots use a per-slot spinlock\n * around header mutation (one byte, atomic_flag).\n *\n * Lifetime is the run. Slots are freed when the store is\n * destroyed at the end of the run — there is no per-slot refcount\n * and no end-of-stream propagation. Run termination is governed\n * by the pool's active-task counter (issue 301).\n *\n * Errors: a return of -1 from a read/write op means the operation\n * could not be performed (empty pop, buffer too small, type\n * mismatch). The store does not assert or abort; the dispatch\n * layer is expected to check return codes. The hard-crash policy\n * applies at the language-spec layer, not here.\n *\n * What's NOT in this version:\n *  - Size-class free lists and coalescing. The design in issue 302\n *    describes a segregated allocator with eager-coalesce; this\n *    initial implementation uses plain malloc per slot. The pattern\n *    is \"allocate once at graph load, free at run end\", so free-list\n *    optimization buys nothing for the current usage. Lands as a\n *    follow-on if profiling justifies it.\n *  - Large-value heap for variable-size payloads. Slots store\n *    fixed-size cells; very large outputs (LLM responses) will\n *    use a separate two-tier scheme. Follow-on within 302.\n */\n\n#ifndef SORAMECH_SLOT_STORE_H\n#define SORAMECH_SLOT_STORE_H\n\n#include <stdint.h>\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\nextern \"C\" {\n#endif\n\n/* {{{ Types & flags */\ntypedef struct slot_store slot_store_t;\ntypedef int32_t           slot_id_t;\n\n#define SLOT_INVALID  ((slot_id_t)-1)\n\n/* slot_alloc flags */\nenum {\n    SLOT_FLAG_NONE           = 0,\n    SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED         = 1 << 0,\n    SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER = 1 << 1,\n    SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE    = 1 << 2,\n};\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Store lifecycle */\n/* Construct an empty store. Returns NULL on allocation failure. */\nslot_store_t *slot_store_create(void);\n\n/* Free every slot and the store itself. Safe to call on NULL. */\nvoid          slot_store_destroy(slot_store_t *s);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Slot lifecycle */\n/* Allocate a slot.\n *\n *   cell_capacity — bytes per cell. Ignored for SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER.\n *   n_cells       — ring size (1 for peek slots, >1 for pop). Ignored for\n *                   SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER.\n *   flags         — zero, SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED, or SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER.\n *\n * Returns the new slot's id, or SLOT_INVALID on allocation failure or\n * invalid arguments. Ids are stable for the lifetime of the store. */\nslot_id_t     slot_alloc(slot_store_t *s,\n                         int32_t cell_capacity,\n                         int32_t n_cells,\n                         int32_t flags);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Ring-buffer ops */\n/* Push a value into the slot's next free cell.\n *\n *   data, size — value bytes. size must be <= cell_capacity.\n *   tag        — ordering tag. Carried only on SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED slots;\n *                ignored otherwise.\n *\n * Returns 0 on success, -1 if the slot is full or arguments invalid.\n * Not valid on SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER slots (returns -1). */\nint           slot_push(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id,\n                        const void *data, int32_t size, uint32_t tag);\n\n/* Peek at the head cell without draining it.\n *\n *   buf, buf_size — destination. The number of bytes copied is min of\n *                   the cell's filled_size and buf_size.\n *\n * Returns the cell's filled_size on success, -1 if the slot is empty,\n * the buffer is too small, or the slot is the wrong type. The cell\n * remains filled and may be re-peeked by subsequent tasks (1-cell peek\n * mode). */\nint32_t       slot_peek(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id,\n                        void *buf, int32_t buf_size);\n\n/* Drain one cell from the slot.\n *\n *   buf, buf_size — destination.\n *\n * For untagged slots, returns the head cell and advances head FIFO.\n * For SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED slots, returns the cell with the lowest tag\n * among the filled cells and marks that cell empty (head advances as\n * front-of-ring cells empty).\n *\n * Returns the cell's filled_size on success, -1 on empty / wrong type\n * / buffer too small. */\nint32_t       slot_pop(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id,\n                       void *buf, int32_t buf_size);\n\n/* Atomic read-and-increment on SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER slots.\n *\n *   mod — modulus for the returned value. Pass UINT32_MAX for \"no\n *         modulus\".\n *\n * Returns the pre-increment counter value mod the supplied bound.\n * Concurrent readers each get a distinct value (the underlying\n * counter is incremented atomically). Returns UINT32_MAX on type\n * mismatch — the dispatch layer is expected to call this op only\n * on slots it allocated with SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER. */\nuint32_t      slot_read_inc(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod);\n\n/* Check whether the slot has any filled cell available for read.\n * Used by the dispatch layer's spawn-on-input-ready rule (issue 304).\n *\n * Returns 1 if a value is available, 0 otherwise. For ATOMIC_COUNTER\n * slots, always returns 1 (the counter is always readable). */\nint           slot_has_value(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Inspection (test / debug) */\n/* Number of filled cells. For ATOMIC_COUNTER slots, returns 0. */\nint32_t       slot_fill_count(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);\n\n/* Slot count in the store. */\nint32_t       slot_store_size(slot_store_t *s);\n/* }}} */\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\n}\n#endif\n\n#endif /* SORAMECH_SLOT_STORE_H */\n",

The pattern\n *    is \"allocate once at graph load, free at run end\", so free-list\n *    optimization buys nothing for the current usage. Lands as a\n *    follow-on if profiling justifies it.\n *  - Large-value heap for variable-size payloads. Slots store\n *    fixed-size cells; very large outputs (LLM responses) will\n *    use a separate two-tier scheme. Follow-on within 302.\n */",

    "newString":"/* {{{ slot_push() */\nint slot_push(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id,\n              const void *data, int32_t size, uint32_t tag)\n{\n    slot_rec_t *r = get_slot(s, id);\n    if (!r)                                      return -1;\n    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER)     return -1;\n    if (size < 0)                                return -1;\n    if (!data && size > 0)                       return -1;\n\n    int large = (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE) != 0;\n    /* For LARGE_VALUE slots size has no per-cell upper bound; the\n     * heap absorbs whatever the caller wants to store. For\n     * fixed-size slots, enforce the cell capacity as before. */\n    if (!large && (uint32_t)size > r->cell_capacity) return -1;\n\n    /* For LARGE_VALUE, allocate the heap region BEFORE taking the\n     * slot's spinlock. The heap has its own mutex; nesting the two\n     * is fine but reducing time-under-spinlock keeps the lock\n     * holder fast for everyone else. */\n    void *heap_ptr = NULL;\n    if (large && size > 0) {\n        heap_ptr = lvh_alloc(s->heap, (size_t)size);\n        if (!heap_ptr) return -1;\n        memcpy(heap_ptr, data, (size_t)size);\n    }\n\n    lock_slot(r);\n\n    uint32_t head = atomic_load_explicit(&r->head, memory_order_relaxed);\n    uint32_t tail = atomic_load_explicit(&r->tail, memory_order_relaxed);\n    if (tail - head >= r->n_cells) {\n        /* Ring full. The heap allocation we just made stays alive\n         * — there's no per-allocation free — but it's bytes the\n         * caller will retry to use, so the cost is bounded by\n         * how often pushes actually fail. */\n        unlock_slot(r);\n        return -1;\n    }\n\n    uint32_t i = tail % r->n_cells;\n    uint8_t *cp = cell_ptr(r, i);\n\n    /* filled_size */\n    uint32_t fs = (uint32_t)size;\n    memcpy(cp, &fs, sizeof fs);\n    /* tag (only if tagged); LARGE_VALUE without TAGGED still has 4\n     * pad bytes in the same position so the payload pointer stays\n     * 8-byte aligned, but we leave them zero. */\n    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED) {\n        memcpy(cp + 4, &tag, sizeof tag);\n    }\n    /* payload */\n    if (large) {\n        /* Store the heap pointer (may be NULL for zero-size). */\n        memcpy(cell_data(r, i), &heap_ptr, sizeof heap_ptr);\n    } else if (size > 0) {\n        memcpy(cell_data(r, i), data, (size_t)size);\n    }\n\n    atomic_store_explicit(&r->tail, tail + 1u, memory_order_release);\n    unlock_slot(r);\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */"

    "oldString":"/* {{{ slot_peek() */\nint32_t slot_peek(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id,\n                  void *buf, int32_t buf_size)\n{\n    slot_rec_t *r = get_slot(s, id);\n    if (!r)                                  return -1;\n    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER) return -1;\n    if (buf_size < 0 || (!buf && buf_size > 0)) return -1;\n\n    lock_slot(r);\n\n    uint32_t head = atomic_load_explicit(&r->head, memory_order_acquire);\n    uint32_t tail = atomic_load_explicit(&r->tail, memory_order_acquire);\n    if (head == tail) {\n        unlock_slot(r);\n        return -1;\n    }\n\n    uint32_t i = head % r->n_cells;\n    uint32_t fs = cell_filled(r, i);\n    if (fs == 0) {\n        unlock_slot(r);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    if ((uint32_t)buf_size < fs) {\n        unlock_slot(r);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    if (fs > 0) memcpy(buf, cell_data(r, i), fs);\n    /* head not advanced — peek leaves the cell in place. */\n    unlock_slot(r);\n    return (int32_t)fs;\n}\n/* }}} */",

        "oldStart":349

    "newString":"/* {{{ slot_peek() */\nint32_t slot_peek(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id,\n                  void *buf, int32_t buf_size)\n{\n    slot_rec_t *r = get_slot(s, id);\n    if (!r)                                  return -1;\n    if (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER) return -1;\n    if (buf_size < 0 || (!buf && buf_size > 0)) return -1;\n\n    int large = (r->flags & SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE) != 0;\n\n    lock_slot(r);\n\n    uint32_t head = atomic_load_explicit(&r->head, memory_order_acquire);\n    uint32_t tail = atomic_load_explicit(&r->tail, memory_order_acquire);\n    if (head == tail) {\n        unlock_slot(r);\n        return -1;\n    }\n\n    uint32_t i = head % r->n_cells;\n    uint32_t fs = cell_filled(r, i);\n    if (fs == 0) {\n        unlock_slot(r);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    if ((uint32_t)buf_size < fs) {\n        unlock_slot(r);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    if (fs > 0) {\n        if (large) {\n            void *p;\n            memcpy(&p, cell_data(r, i), sizeof p);\n            if (p) memcpy(buf, p, fs);\n        } else {\n            memcpy(buf, cell_data(r, i), fs);\n        }\n    }\n    /* head not advanced — peek leaves the cell in place. */\n    unlock_slot(r);\n    return (int32_t)fs;\n}\n/* }}} */"

          "new_string":"/* {{{ test_large_value_push_pop() */\n/* SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE accepts any size on push, regardless of\n * cell_capacity (which is ignored). Bytes live in the slot store's\n * lazy-created lvh heap; the cell holds a stable pointer. Peek\n * and pop both copy from the heap back into the caller buffer. */\nstatic int test_large_value_push_pop(void)\n{\n    slot_store_t *s = slot_store_create();\n    slot_id_t id = slot_alloc(s, 0, 4, SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE);\n    ASSERT(id != SLOT_INVALID);\n\n    /* 100 KB push — well beyond any sane fixed cell size. */\n    int payload_size = 100 * 1024;\n    unsigned char *src = malloc((size_t)payload_size);\n    for (int i = 0; i < payload_size; i++) src[i] = (unsigned char)(i & 0xFF);\n    ASSERT(slot_push(s, id, src, payload_size, 0) == 0);\n\n    /* Peek twice — value stays in the cell. */\n    unsigned char *dst = malloc((size_t)payload_size);\n    int32_t got = slot_peek(s, id, dst, payload_size);\n    ASSERT(got == payload_size);\n    for (int i = 0; i < payload_size; i++) ASSERT(dst[i] == src[i]);\n\n    memset(dst, 0, (size_t)payload_size);\n    got = slot_peek(s, id, dst, payload_size);\n    ASSERT(got == payload_size);\n    ASSERT(dst[0] == 0 && dst[payload_size - 1] == (unsigned char)((payload_size - 1) & 0xFF));\n\n    /* Pop drains. */\n    memset(dst, 0, (size_t)payload_size);\n    got = slot_pop(s, id, dst, payload_size);\n    ASSERT(got == payload_size);\n    for (int i = 0; i < payload_size; i++) ASSERT(dst[i] == src[i]);\n\n    /* Empty now. */\n    ASSERT(slot_pop(s, id, dst, payload_size) == -1);\n\n    free(src); free(dst);\n    slot_store_destroy(s);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_large_value_buf_too_small() */\n/* Pop / peek into an undersized buffer returns -1 and leaves the\n * cell in place (same semantics as fixed-size slots). */\nstatic int test_large_value_buf_too_small(void)\n{\n    slot_store_t *s = slot_store_create();\n    slot_id_t id = slot_alloc(s, 0, 1, SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE);\n    ASSERT(id != SLOT_INVALID);\n\n    char src[200];\n    memset(src, 'A', sizeof src);\n    ASSERT(slot_push(s, id, src, sizeof src, 0) == 0);\n\n    char small_buf[50];\n    ASSERT(slot_peek(s, id, small_buf, sizeof small_buf) == -1);\n    /* Cell still present — full peek succeeds. */\n    char ok_buf[200];\n    ASSERT(slot_peek(s, id, ok_buf, sizeof ok_buf) == (int32_t)sizeof src);\n\n    slot_store_destroy(s);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_large_value_multi_push_fifo() */\n/* N-cell pop semantics still work for LARGE_VALUE slots. Push\n * three values of wildly different sizes; pop returns them in\n * order with their original bytes. */\nstatic int test_large_value_multi_push_fifo(void)\n{\n    slot_store_t *s = slot_store_create();\n    slot_id_t id = slot_alloc(s, 0, 8, SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE);\n    ASSERT(id != SLOT_INVALID);\n\n    char a[]   = \"alpha\";\n    char b[]   = \"bravo-bravo-bravo\";\n    int big_sz = 70 * 1024;\n    char *big  = malloc((size_t)big_sz);\n    memset(big, 'X', (size_t)big_sz);\n\n    ASSERT(slot_push(s, id, a,   (int)strlen(a),   0) == 0);\n    ASSERT(slot_push(s, id, b,   (int)strlen(b),   0) == 0);\n    ASSERT(slot_push(s, id, big, big_sz,           0) == 0);\n    ASSERT(slot_fill_count(s, id) == 3);\n\n    char buf[100 * 1024];\n    int32_t got;\n\n    got = slot_pop(s, id, buf, sizeof buf);\n    ASSERT(got == (int32_t)strlen(a));\n    ASSERT(memcmp(buf, a, (size_t)got) == 0);\n\n    got = slot_pop(s, id, buf, sizeof buf);\n    ASSERT(got == (int32_t)strlen(b));\n    ASSERT(memcmp(buf, b, (size_t)got) == 0);\n\n    got = slot_pop(s, id, buf, sizeof buf);\n    ASSERT(got == big_sz);\n    for (int i = 0; i < big_sz; i++) ASSERT(buf[i] == 'X');\n\n    free(big);\n    slot_store_destroy(s);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_large_value_tagged_ordering() */\n/* SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE combined with SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED: pops are\n * served lowest-tag-first, with bytes intact from the heap. */\nstatic int test_large_value_tagged_ordering(void)\n{\n    slot_store_t *s = slot_store_create();\n    slot_id_t id = slot_alloc(s, 0, 4,\n                              SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE | SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED);\n    ASSERT(id != SLOT_INVALID);\n\n    /* Push in mixed-tag order. */\n    ASSERT(slot_push(s, id, \"third\",  5, 30) == 0);\n    ASSERT(slot_push(s, id, \"first\",  5, 10) == 0);\n    ASSERT(slot_push(s, id, \"second\", 6, 20) == 0);\n\n    char buf[64];\n    int32_t got;\n\n    got = slot_pop(s, id, buf, sizeof buf);\n    ASSERT(got == 5 && memcmp(buf, \"first\", 5) == 0);\n\n    got = slot_pop(s, id, buf, sizeof buf);\n    ASSERT(got == 6 && memcmp(buf, \"second\", 6) == 0);\n\n    got = slot_pop(s, id, buf, sizeof buf);\n    ASSERT(got == 5 && memcmp(buf, \"third\", 5) == 0);\n\n    slot_store_destroy(s);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ main() */\nint main(void)\n{\n    printf(\"009-slot-store-test:\\n\");\n    RUN(peek_1cell);\n    RUN(pop_fifo_ncell);\n    RUN(buf_too_small);\n    RUN(size_too_big_push);\n    RUN(tagged_pop_lowest_first);\n    RUN(tagged_interleaved);\n    RUN(atomic_counter);\n    RUN(atomic_counter_mod_zero);\n    RUN(bad_slot_id);\n    RUN(concurrent_counter);\n    RUN(concurrent_push_pop);\n    RUN(store_size_growth);\n    RUN(large_value_push_pop);\n    RUN(large_value_buf_too_small);\n    RUN(large_value_multi_push_fifo);\n    RUN(large_value_tagged_ordering);\n    printf(\"\\n  %d passed, %d failed\\n\", g_pass, g_fail);\n    return g_fail == 0 ? 0 : 1;\n}\n/* }}} */",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/tests/009-slot-store-test.c"
        }

i < payload_size; i++) src[i] = (unsigned char)(i & 0xFF);\n    ASSERT(slot_push(s, id, src, payload_size, 0) == 0);\n\n    /* Peek twice — value stays in the cell. */\n    unsigned char *dst = malloc((size_t)payload_size);\n    int32_t got = slot_peek(s, id, dst, payload_size);\n    ASSERT(got == payload_size);\n    for (int i = 0; i < payload_size; i++) ASSERT(dst[i] == src[i]);\n\n    memset(dst, 0, (size_t)payload_size);\n    got = slot_peek(s, id, dst, payload_size);\n    ASSERT(got == payload_size);\n    ASSERT(dst[0] == 0 && dst[payload_size - 1] == (unsigned char)((payload_size - 1) & 0xFF));\n\n    /* Pop drains. */\n    memset(dst, 0, (size_t)payload_size);\n    got = slot_pop(s, id, dst, payload_size);\n    ASSERT(got == payload_size);\n    for (int i = 0; i < payload_size; i++) ASSERT(dst[i] == src[i]);\n\n    /* Empty now. */\n    ASSERT(slot_pop(s, id, dst, payload_size) == -1);\n\n    free(src); free(dst);\n    slot_store_destroy(s);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_large_value_buf_too_small() */\n/* Pop / peek into an undersized buffer returns -1 and leaves the\n * cell in place (same semantics as fixed-size slots). */\nstatic int test_large_value_buf_too_small(void)\n{\n    slot_store_t *s = slot_store_create();\n    slot_id_t id = slot_alloc(s, 0, 1, SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE);\n    ASSERT(id != SLOT_INVALID);\n\n    char src[200];\n    memset(src, 'A', sizeof src);\n    ASSERT(slot_push(s, id, src, sizeof src, 0) == 0);\n\n    char small_buf[50];\n    ASSERT(slot_peek(s, id, small_buf, sizeof small_buf) == -1);\n    /* Cell still present — full peek succeeds. */\n    char ok_buf[200];\n    ASSERT(slot_peek(s, id, ok_buf, sizeof ok_buf) == (int32_t)sizeof src);\n\n    slot_store_destroy(s);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_large_value_multi_push_fifo() */\n/* N-cell pop semantics still work for LARGE_VALUE slots. Push\n * three values of wildly different sizes; pop returns them in\n * order with their original bytes. */\nstatic int test_large_value_multi_push_fifo(void)\n{\n    slot_store_t *s = slot_store_create();\n    slot_id_t id = slot_alloc(s, 0, 8, SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE);\n    ASSERT(id != SLOT_INVALID);\n\n    char a[]   = \"alpha\";\n    char b[]   = \"bravo-bravo-bravo\";\n    int big_sz = 70 * 1024;\n    char *big  = malloc((size_t)big_sz);\n    memset(big, 'X', (size_t)big_sz);\n\n    ASSERT(slot_push(s, id, a,   (int)strlen(a),   0) == 0);\n    ASSERT(slot_push(s, id, b,   (int)strlen(b),   0) == 0);\n    ASSERT(slot_push(s, id, big, big_sz,           0) == 0);\n    ASSERT(slot_fill_count(s, id) == 3);\n\n    char buf[100 * 1024];\n    int32_t got;\n\n    got = slot_pop(s, id, buf, sizeof buf);\n    ASSERT(got == (int32_t)strlen(a));\n    ASSERT(memcmp(buf, a, (size_t)got) == 0);\n\n    got = slot_pop(s, id, buf, sizeof buf);\n    ASSERT(got == (int32_t)strlen(b));\n    ASSERT(memcmp(buf, b, (size_t)got) == 0);\n\n    got = slot_pop(s, id, buf, sizeof buf);\n    ASSERT(got == big_sz);\n    for (int i = 0; i < big_sz; i++) ASSERT(buf[i] == 'X');\n\n    free(big);\n    slot_store_destroy(s);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_large_value_tagged_ordering() */\n/* SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE combined with SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED: pops are\n * served lowest-tag-first, with bytes intact from the heap. */\nstatic int test_large_value_tagged_ordering(void)\n{\n    slot_store_t *s = slot_store_create();\n    slot_id_t id = slot_alloc(s, 0, 4,\n                              SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE | SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED);\n    ASSERT(id != SLOT_INVALID);\n\n    /* Push in mixed-tag order. */\n    ASSERT(slot_push(s, id, \"third\",  5, 30) == 0);\n    ASSERT(slot_push(s, id, \"first\",  5, 10) == 0);\n    ASSERT(slot_push(s, id, \"second\", 6, 20) == 0);\n\n    char buf[64];\n    int32_t got;\n\n    got = slot_pop(s, id, buf, sizeof buf);\n    ASSERT(got == 5 && memcmp(buf, \"first\", 5) == 0);\n\n    got = slot_pop(s, id, buf, sizeof buf);\n    ASSERT(got == 6 && memcmp(buf, \"second\", 6) == 0);\n\n    got = slot_pop(s, id, buf, sizeof buf);\n    ASSERT(got == 5 && memcmp(buf, \"third\", 5) == 0);\n\n    slot_store_destroy(s);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ main() */\nint main(void)\n{\n    printf(\"009-slot-store-test:\\n\");\n    RUN(peek_1cell);\n    RUN(pop_fifo_ncell);\n    RUN(buf_too_small);\n    RUN(size_too_big_push);\n    RUN(tagged_pop_lowest_first);\n    RUN(tagged_interleaved);\n    RUN(atomic_counter);\n    RUN(atomic_counter_mod_zero);\n    RUN(bad_slot_id);\n    RUN(concurrent_counter);\n    RUN(concurrent_push_pop);\n    RUN(store_size_growth);\n    RUN(large_value_push_pop);\n    RUN(large_value_buf_too_small);\n    RUN(large_value_multi_push_fifo);\n    RUN(large_value_tagged_ordering);\n    printf(\"\\n  %d passed, %d failed\\n\", g_pass, g_fail);\n    return g_fail == 0 ? 0 : 1;\n}\n/* }}} */"
  },

          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"What's deferred to a follow-on within 302:\n- **Size-class free lists with coalescing.** The current\n  implementation `malloc`s each slot independently. That's correct\n  but unoptimized. Slots are allocated once at graph load and never\n  freed until run end, so under the current usage pattern free-list\n  reuse buys nothing. Lands once profiling justifies it (or once\n  long-running maps surface allocation pressure).\n- **Large-value heap for variable-size payloads.** Slots currently\n  store fixed-size cells; very large outputs (multi-MB LLM\n  responses, dynamically-sized arrays) will need the two-tier\n  scheme described under \"Large-value heap\" above. Blocks no\n  in-flight phase 3 work until a graph wants variable-size outputs.\n\nNeither deferred item blocks 301 / 304 / 305 / 306 / 307 / 308.",
          "new_string":"What's deferred to a follow-on within 302:\n- **Size-class free lists with coalescing.** The current\n  implementation `malloc`s each slot independently. That's correct\n  but unoptimized. Slots are allocated once at graph load and never\n  freed until run end, so under the current usage pattern free-list\n  reuse buys nothing. Lands once profiling justifies it (or once\n  long-running maps surface allocation pressure).\n- **Large-value heap for variable-size payloads.** Slots currently\n  store fixed-size cells; very large outputs (multi-MB LLM\n  responses, dynamically-sized arrays) will need the two-tier\n  scheme described under \"Large-value heap\" above. Blocks no\n  in-flight phase 3 work until a graph wants variable-size outputs.\n\nNeither deferred item blocks 301 / 304 / 305 / 306 / 307 / 308.\n\n### Large-value heap milestone — 2026-05-19\n\nThe variable-size payload follow-on landed in two layers:\n\n1. **`src/015-large-value-heap.{c,h}`** — chunked arena allocator.\n   Default 64 KB chunks; oversized allocations (larger than the\n   default chunk) get their own exact-fit chunk so one large value\n   doesn't bloat the regular bump chunks. Pointer stability is the\n   load-bearing property: chunks never move once allocated, so a\n   consumer's pointer survives any number of subsequent producer\n   allocations. Eight unit tests in\n   `tests/015-large-value-heap-test.c` cover the create/destroy\n   round-trip, single + multi alloc within a chunk, oversized\n   allocations getting their own chunks, pointer stability across\n   forced growth, zero-size allocations returning non-NULL, the\n   stats accessors, and an eight-thread / eight-thousand-alloc\n   concurrency stress test that asserts every returned pointer is\n   unique and writable.\n\n2. **Slot-store integration.** Added `SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE` to\n   `slot_alloc`. Cell layout for LARGE_VALUE slots is\n   `filled_size (4 bytes) + pad/tag (4 bytes) + stable pointer\n   (8 bytes)` — the 8-byte payload offset keeps the pointer\n   naturally aligned regardless of whether SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED is\n   also set. The slot store lazy-creates one shared lvh heap on\n   the first LARGE_VALUE allocation; the heap is destroyed\n   alongside the store. Push allocates from the heap *outside*\n   the slot spinlock (the heap has its own mutex; nesting is\n   fine, but reducing time-under-spinlock keeps the lock fast for\n   other producers). Peek and pop follow the cell's pointer and\n   memcpy the requested bytes back into the caller's buffer.\n\nFour new slot-store tests cover the new path:\n`large_value_push_pop` (100 KB payload, double-peek, then pop);\n`large_value_buf_too_small` (oversized payload + small dest →\n-1, cell preserved); `large_value_multi_push_fifo` (three\ndifferent-size values pushed and popped in order); and\n`large_value_tagged_ordering` (LARGE_VALUE + TAGGED → pops\nreturn lowest-tag-first with bytes intact).\n\nWhat this unblocks: any box that wants to emit a variable-size\noutput can now declare its downstream consumer slots with\nSLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE and produce payloads whose size isn't\nknown at graph-load time. The wiring from declared box output\ntype to the LARGE_VALUE flag in `graph_attach_runtime` lands as\na follow-on once a fixture or real graph requires it; the\nfoundation is in place.\n\nWhat's still deferred within 302:\n- **Size-class free lists with coalescing.** Still no need.\n- **Per-allocation free in the large-value heap.** The heap\n  grows monotonically for the life of a run. Long-running\n  iterator loops that emit large values will pin memory until\n  run end. Acceptable for current fixtures; a size-class\n  allocator with eager-coalesce is the upgrade path if profiling\n  flags it.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md"
        }
      }],
    "role":"assistant",

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"113 tests green under STRICT. The large-value heap is live and integrated into the slot store.\n\n### Round summary\n\n**302 large-value heap** — landed as a follow-on inside the existing 302 ticket.\n\n- **`src/015-large-value-heap.{c,h}`** — chunked arena allocator. Default 64 KB chunks; oversized requests get exact-fit dedicated chunks; pointers are stable across growth (chunks don't move once allocated). Single-mutex concurrency model — fine because the user's memcpy happens outside the lock. Stats: `total_allocated`, `total_used`, `chunk_count`. No per-allocation free in this iteration; the heap is monotonic-growth for a run.\n- **Slot-store integration** — new `SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE` flag. Cell layout is 4-byte filled_size + 4-byte tag/pad + 8-byte stable pointer; the slot store lazy-creates one shared `lvh_t` on the first LARGE_VALUE allocation and destroys it with the store. Push allocates outside the spinlock; peek/pop follow the pointer and copy into the caller buffer. Cleanly composes with `SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED` so iterator-ordered variable-size streams work.\n- **Tests** — 8 new lvh tests (incl. 8-thread × 1000-alloc stress with pairwise uniqueness check) + 4 new slot-store tests covering push/pop with 100 KB payloads, oversize-dest rejection, multi-push FIFO, and TAGGED+LARGE_VALUE ordering.\n- **Issue files** — 302 implementation log updated, phase-3 progress reflects the milestone, file-index-counter advanced to 015.\n\nWhat this unblocks: any box declaring variable-size output (multi-MB LLM responses, dynamic arrays, binary blobs) can now have its downstream slots allocated `SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE` and stream through. Wiring the graph loader to set the flag from a box's declared output type is the next small step once a fixture wants it.\n\n**Test counts**: 16 slot-store + 8 lvh + the rest = **106 unit + 7 integration = 113 green under STRICT**.\n\n---\n\n### What 307 typed C wrapper generation would do\n\nToday, a C-box author has to write a function that takes SoraMech's bytes-in / bytes-out ABI — they receive a packed byte buffer of inputs and have to deserialize, do the work, and serialize the return. The author writes the marshalling boilerplate for every box.\n\n307's typed wrapper proposes that the author write a **natural C function with normal typed arguments and a normal return value**:\n\n```c\n// user writes this — no SoraMech-specific anything:\nint classify(const char *text, int weight) {\n    if (text[0] >= '0' && text[0] <= '9') return weight * 1;\n    return weight * 2;\n}\n```\n\n…and declares the signature in the box's JSON:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"classify\", \"lang\": \"c\", \"ref\": \"classify.c\", \"fn\": \"classify\",\n  \"inputs\":  [{\"name\": \"text\", \"type\": \"string\"}, {\"name\": \"weight\", \"type\": \"int\"}],\n  \"returns\": \"int\"\n}\n```\n\nThe C spec then **generates a wrapper `.c` file** at compile time that bridges SoraMech's ABI to the user's natural function:\n\n```c\n// auto-generated:\nextern int classify(const char *, int);\nint sm_box_entry(const uint8_t *in_buf, uint32_t in_size,\n                 uint8_t *out_buf, uint32_t out_cap, uint32_t *out_size) {\n    // unpack `text` as null-terminated string and `weight` as int from in_buf\n    // call: int r = classify(text, weight);\n    // serialize r into out_buf, set *out_size\n    return 0;\n}\n```\n\nThe wrapper plus the user's `.c` get compiled together; the spec always `dlsym`s `sm_box_entry`. The huge wins:\n\n1. **Library functions become boxes with no glue code.** A box can declare `\"fn\": \"compress2\"`, `\"headers\": [\"<zlib.h>\"]`, `\"link_libs\": [\"z\"]` and call into zlib directly with no user-written `.c` file at all. Same for OpenCV, libcurl, JSON-C, etc — any C library with a header.\n2. **Type safety at compile time.** Mismatch between declared `inputs` and the actual function signature surfaces as a gcc error in the generated wrapper, not a runtime crash.\n3. **Idiomatic user code.** The user's `.c` looks like ordinary C — no `int box(SM_BOX_ARGS)` macro, no extracting from a buffer, no laying-out a return.\n\nThe remaining piece is essentially a small code-generator that knows the type system: `string` → `const char *`, `int` → `int32_t`, `double` → `double`, `bytes` → `const uint8_t *, size_t`, and so on. Compile cost is one extra gcc invocation per C box per build.\n\n---\n\n### Re-center\n\n| ID  | Standing                                                            |\n|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------------|\n| 301 | done                                                                 |\n| 302 | **done** (core + large-value heap; size-class allocator out of scope)|\n| 303 | done                                                                 |\n| 304 | done (all routing + cell-tagged ordering)                            |\n| 305 | done                                                                 |\n| 306 | done                                                                 |\n| 307 | done; typed wrapper deferred (summarized above)                      |\n| 308 | done                                                                 |\n| 309 | done                                                                 |\n| 310 | done                                                                 |\n| 311 | done                                                                 |\n| 312 | infra done; specialized native serializations deferred               |\n| 313 | research / parked                                                    |\n| 314 | done                                                                 |\n| 315 | open — design only (refcounted compiled artifacts)                   |\n\nPlausible next-round picks, most-valuable first:\n\n1. **315 implementation** — recently designed; build the `soramech-ref.sh` helper, teach the compile script to fork-on-live-refs, add an integration check. Discrete and small.\n2. **307 typed wrapper generation** — the summary above. Real product-feel improvement for C-box authors. Code-generator + tests.\n3. **Move done items to `issues/completed/` + first phase-3 commit** — bookkeeping; nothing untracked beyond what we just produced.\n4. **312 specialized native serializations** — pick e.g. Lua-to-Lua and skip JSON over the bridge for that case.\n\nWhich direction?"

        "input":{
          "content":"# 316 — Simple test runner script\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`make test` builds and runs every unit-test binary plus the\nintegration runner. The output is helpful when you want to verify\nthat everything still passes at the end of a working session, but\nit's noisy when you're iterating on one specific change:\n\n- The build phase prints `→ src/foo.c`, `→ src/bar.c`, ... for\n  every file that compiles or relinks. On a clean tree that's\n  dozens of lines before the first test runs.\n- Tests are run from inside a Make recipe (a `for` loop). If one\n  binary fails, the recipe aborts and you don't see the results\n  for binaries that would have run after it.\n- The integration runner (`scripts/run-tests.sh`) is interleaved\n  with unit tests, mixing two scales of test output in one stream.\n\nThe current behavior is fine for \"ship it\" verification. It's\nsuboptimal as a development loop.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA separate script (`scripts/run-unit-tests.sh`) that runs the\nalready-built unit-test binaries one by one and reports their\nresults in a uniform format. No build step. No make. Just:\nlocate the binaries, run them in turn, capture stdout/stderr,\nprint a one-line per-binary summary, and at the end print a\ntotals line and a list of any failures.\n\nGoals:\n\n1. **Cheap to invoke.** No make recursion, no spec rebuilds,\n   no integration tests. If the build is current, the script\n   runs in well under a second.\n2. **Continues past failures.** Every test binary runs, even if\n   an earlier one fails. The summary at the bottom names what\n   went wrong.\n3. **Pretty output by default; mineable output on request.** A\n   `--quiet` mode that prints just the totals line is enough for\n   CI pre-merge gates. A `--verbose` mode dumps each binary's\n   full output. The default is per-binary one-line status.\n4. **Filterable.** A positional argument like\n   `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh 009` runs only the binaries whose\n   names start with `009`, so iterating on one slot-store change\n   doesn't require re-running every test.\n\nOut of scope: building the binaries, running integration tests\n(that's `scripts/run-tests.sh`), running specs (those are\nimplicitly tested via the binaries that depend on them).\n\n## Concept\n\nThe build system already produces `build/tests/<name>-test`\nbinaries; one per test source file under `tests/`. The script\ndiscovers them via a glob, sorts them by filename (which sorts\nby leading numeric index, which is the project's natural\nread-order), and runs each one.\n\nEach binary already prints its own header (`009-slot-store-test:`)\nand per-test status lines. The script captures the output, parses\nthe last line (`N passed, M failed`) for the per-binary verdict,\nand prints a per-binary summary like:\n\n```\n  009-slot-store-test                          16 / 16  ok\n  010-graph-loader-test                        13 / 13  ok\n  015-large-value-heap-test                     8 /  8  ok\n  ...\n```\n\nA failing binary prints its captured output below the summary\nline so the failure is visible without re-running.\n\nThe very last line is:\n\n```\n  113 / 113 tests passed (14 binaries)\n```\n\n…or, on failure:\n\n```\n  111 / 113 tests passed (14 binaries; 1 binary with failures: 009-slot-store-test)\n```\n\nExit code: zero if every binary passes; non-zero with the count\nof failing binaries otherwise.\n\n## Convention compliance\n\nPer the project's script rules (CLAUDE.md):\n\n- Hard-coded `${DIR}` at the top; first argument optionally\n  overrides it.\n- All paths under `${DIR}`.\n- Each shell command on its own line (no chained `||` /\n  `&&` pipelines for control flow; assign command output to\n  variables and branch on the variable).\n- Lives at `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh`, runnable from any cwd.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. Write `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh` with the layout described\n   above.\n2. Verify it picks up every existing `build/tests/*-test`\n   binary and produces the expected totals.\n3. Verify the filter argument works: `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh\n   015` runs just the lvh test binary.\n4. Verify `--quiet` and `--verbose` modes both produce useful\n   output.\n5. Provoke a failure (modify one test temporarily) and confirm\n   the failure is reported, exit code is non-zero, and the\n   captured output is visible.\n6. Document the script in `Makefile`'s `help` target, or add a\n   `make quicktest` alias that calls it.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh` — new\n- `Makefile` — optional `quicktest` target\n- `scripts/run-tests.sh` — sibling script for integration tests;\n  this issue covers the unit-test counterpart\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Should the script also verify the binaries are up to date with\n  their sources? Cheap: `stat` the binary and its `.c` and\n  complain if the source is newer. The user might prefer \"just\n  run what's built\" so they can deliberately test old binaries.\n  Default to no warning; offer a `--check-stale` flag.\n- Filter syntax: prefix-match on the test name is simple; should\n  it accept glob patterns too? Start simple. Extend if needed.\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/316-simple-test-runner.md"
        }
      }],

    "content":"# 316 — Simple test runner script\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`make test` builds and runs every unit-test binary plus the\nintegration runner. The output is helpful when you want to verify\nthat everything still passes at the end of a working session, but\nit's noisy when you're iterating on one specific change:\n\n- The build phase prints `→ src/foo.c`, `→ src/bar.c`, ... for\n  every file that compiles or relinks. On a clean tree that's\n  dozens of lines before the first test runs.\n- Tests are run from inside a Make recipe (a `for` loop). If one\n  binary fails, the recipe aborts and you don't see the results\n  for binaries that would have run after it.\n- The integration runner (`scripts/run-tests.sh`) is interleaved\n  with unit tests, mixing two scales of test output in one stream.\n\nThe current behavior is fine for \"ship it\" verification. It's\nsuboptimal as a development loop.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA separate script (`scripts/run-unit-tests.sh`) that runs the\nalready-built unit-test binaries one by one and reports their\nresults in a uniform format. No build step. No make. Just:\nlocate the binaries, run them in turn, capture stdout/stderr,\nprint a one-line per-binary summary, and at the end print a\ntotals line and a list of any failures.\n\nGoals:\n\n1. **Cheap to invoke.** No make recursion, no spec rebuilds,\n   no integration tests. If the build is current, the script\n   runs in well under a second.\n2. **Continues past failures.** Every test binary runs, even if\n   an earlier one fails. The summary at the bottom names what\n   went wrong.\n3. **Pretty output by default; mineable output on request.** A\n   `--quiet` mode that prints just the totals line is enough for\n   CI pre-merge gates. A `--verbose` mode dumps each binary's\n   full output. The default is per-binary one-line status.\n4. **Filterable.** A positional argument like\n   `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh 009` runs only the binaries whose\n   names start with `009`, so iterating on one slot-store change\n   doesn't require re-running every test.\n\nOut of scope: building the binaries, running integration tests\n(that's `scripts/run-tests.sh`), running specs (those are\nimplicitly tested via the binaries that depend on them).\n\n## Concept\n\nThe build system already produces `build/tests/<name>-test`\nbinaries; one per test source file under `tests/`. The script\ndiscovers them via a glob, sorts them by filename (which sorts\nby leading numeric index, which is the project's natural\nread-order), and runs each one.\n\nEach binary already prints its own header (`009-slot-store-test:`)\nand per-test status lines. The script captures the output, parses\nthe last line (`N passed, M failed`) for the per-binary verdict,\nand prints a per-binary summary like:\n\n```\n  009-slot-store-test                          16 / 16  ok\n  010-graph-loader-test                        13 / 13  ok\n  015-large-value-heap-test                     8 /  8  ok\n  ...\n```\n\nA failing binary prints its captured output below the summary\nline so the failure is visible without re-running.\n\nThe very last line is:\n\n```\n  113 / 113 tests passed (14 binaries)\n```\n\n…or, on failure:\n\n```\n  111 / 113 tests passed (14 binaries; 1 binary with failures: 009-slot-store-test)\n```\n\nExit code: zero if every binary passes; non-zero with the count\nof failing binaries otherwise.\n\n## Convention compliance\n\nPer the project's script rules (CLAUDE.md):\n\n- Hard-coded `${DIR}` at the top; first argument optionally\n  overrides it.\n- All paths under `${DIR}`.\n- Each shell command on its own line (no chained `||` /\n  `&&` pipelines for control flow; assign command output to\n  variables and branch on the variable).\n- Lives at `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh`, runnable from any cwd.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. Write `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh` with the layout described\n   above.\n2. Verify it picks up every existing `build/tests/*-test`\n   binary and produces the expected totals.\n3. Verify the filter argument works: `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh\n   015` runs just the lvh test binary.\n4. Verify `--quiet` and `--verbose` modes both produce useful\n   output.\n5. Provoke a failure (modify one test temporarily) and confirm\n   the failure is reported, exit code is non-zero, and the\n   captured output is visible.\n6. Document the script in `Makefile`'s `help` target, or add a\n   `make quicktest` alias that calls it.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh` — new\n- `Makefile` — optional `quicktest` target\n- `scripts/run-tests.sh` — sibling script for integration tests;\n  this issue covers the unit-test counterpart\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Should the script also verify the binaries are up to date with\n  their sources? Cheap: `stat` the binary and its `.c` and\n  complain if the source is newer. The user might prefer \"just\n  run what's built\" so they can deliberately test old binaries.\n  Default to no warning; offer a `--check-stale` flag.\n- Filter syntax: prefix-match on the test name is simple; should\n  it accept glob patterns too? Start simple. Extend if needed.\n",

        "input":{
          "content":"# 317 — Language spec JSON bridge for data boxes\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA data box (`kind: data` in box JSON) emits a value the rest of\nthe graph routes downstream. Today the runner reads the box's\n`ref` file as raw bytes and emits them — there's no concept of\n\"authoring this datum in a particular language using that\nlanguage's natural structures.\" If you want to declare a Lua\ntable as a data box's value, you either:\n\n- Hand-translate the table to JSON, save it as a `.json` file,\n  and lose the Lua syntax niceties; or\n- Make it a call box that returns the table, paying for a full\n  spec invocation just to read a constant; or\n- Hard-code the bytes inline in the box's `data` field, with no\n  syntactic help from any host language.\n\nThis is the wrong shape. **A box author writes idiomatic code in\nthe language of their choice.** That's the rule 307 establishes\nfor call boxes: a C-box author writes a plain C function, no\nSoraMech-specific glue. The data-box equivalent should hold —\na Lua-data-box author should write a Lua file that returns\nwhatever they want returned (a table, a string, a number), and\nSoraMech should know how to lift that into the graph as a JSON\nwire value without the author writing a single SoraMech-specific\ncharacter.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEvery language spec gains two callbacks, declared in\n`lang_spec_t` (issue 303):\n\n```c\n/* Serialize a native-language value into JSON text.\n *\n *   ctx       — per-worker handle from spec.init.\n *   src       — caller-meaningful pointer to the native value.\n *               Format is spec-specific (see \"Native handle\n *               representation\" below).\n *   src_size  — size hint, or 0 if the spec interprets `src`\n *               without a length.\n *   out_buf   — destination buffer for JSON text (caller-owned).\n *   out_cap   — capacity of out_buf.\n *   out_size  — set to the bytes written.\n *\n * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error. Writes an error message\n * via the spec's existing error-reporting plumbing. */\nint (*native_to_json)(void *ctx,\n                      const void *src, uint32_t src_size,\n                      char *out_buf, uint32_t out_cap, uint32_t *out_size);\n\n/* Inverse: parse JSON text into a native-language value. The\n * native value is stored wherever the spec considers natural\n * (Lua: pushed to the worker's lua_State stack; C: written into\n * a typed struct supplied by `dst`; Bash: written as a textual\n * representation back into dst).\n *\n *   ctx       — per-worker handle.\n *   src       — JSON text.\n *   src_size  — JSON text length in bytes.\n *   dst       — caller-supplied target; semantics per spec.\n *   dst_cap   — capacity, where meaningful.\n *   dst_size  — set to the bytes / native units consumed.\n *\n * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error. */\nint (*json_to_native)(void *ctx,\n                      const char *src, uint32_t src_size,\n                      void *dst, uint32_t dst_cap, uint32_t *dst_size);\n```\n\nThese are the same fields 312's same-language fast path\nreserves; this issue is the one that requires every spec to\n**actually implement them**, driven by the data-box use case.\n(312 needs them too, but its driver is performance; 317 needs\nthem for correctness — a data box can't function without them.)\n\n### The rule, restated\n\nThe author of a data box writes a `.lua` / `.c` / `.sh` /\n`.<whatever>` file that returns or produces a value using\n*their language's native idioms*. No SoraMech macros. No\nSoraMech includes. No SoraMech-specific JSON shape constraints\nbeyond \"what your spec's native_to_json can convert.\"\n\nIf the author returns a Lua table, the Lua spec's\n`native_to_json` converts it. If they return a C struct, the C\nspec's `native_to_json` walks it according to the type declared\nin the box. If they print JSON-ish text from a bash script, the\nbash spec's `native_to_json` is a no-op identity (the script\nalready produced JSON).\n\nThe contract belongs to the spec author, not the box author.\nThat's the inversion: **SoraMech bends to the language, not the\nother way around.**\n\n## Native handle representation\n\nThe shape of `src` / `dst` in the callbacks is per-spec. Each\nspec documents what it accepts:\n\n- **Lua spec**: `src` is the index of a value already pushed\n  onto the worker's `lua_State`. `src_size` is unused. The\n  spec's `native_to_json` reads the value at that stack index\n  and writes JSON. `json_to_native` pushes the parsed JSON value\n  onto the stack, and `dst_size` reports the number of stack\n  slots used (always 1 for SoraMech's flat-value model).\n- **C spec**: `src` is a typed pointer + the box's declared\n  output type drives the walk. `src_size` is the type's\n  storage footprint. Mirror image for `json_to_native`. (This\n  ties into 307's typed-wrapper-generation work — the same\n  type system describes both the wrapper signature and the\n  JSON shape.)\n- **Bash spec**: `src` is text the script produced.\n  `native_to_json` validates and reshapes to JSON if needed (a\n  bash script that prints `42` becomes JSON `42`; a script that\n  prints `{\"a\":1}` passes through unchanged). `json_to_native`\n  is similarly a near-identity. The spec author is encouraged\n  to require scripts produce well-formed JSON in the first\n  place rather than write a bash-syntax parser.\n\nThe dispatch layer doesn't know or care which representation a\nspec uses. It only ever passes `src` and `src_size` to the\nspec's callback. The spec is opaque to the runtime; that's the\nwhole point.\n\n## Data box semantics\n\nA data box's `data` field becomes optional. The box gains\noptional `lang` and `ref` fields:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"config\",\n  \"kind\": \"data\",\n  \"lang\": \"lua\",\n  \"ref\": \"config.lua\"\n}\n```\n\nAt graph load, the runner:\n\n1. Resolves the spec for `lang`.\n2. Calls the spec's `init` (already done at worker startup).\n3. At box-fire time, asks the spec to execute the `ref` file\n   and produce a native value (this is essentially the same\n   \"load this file, run it, get its return value\" path the\n   spec already implements for call boxes — call boxes call a\n   named function; data boxes take the file's return value).\n4. Calls the spec's `native_to_json` to convert the native\n   value to JSON text.\n5. Pushes that JSON text down the wire as the box's output —\n   same as today's data path, just with the value sourced\n   from a language-native file.\n\nIf the box has no `lang` and a literal `data` field, the legacy\ninline-data path applies unchanged.\n\n## Why every spec must implement these\n\nThe same JSON the data box emits is consumed by some downstream\nbox (call, comparator, file_write, whatever). That downstream\nbox, if it's in a different language, will eventually need\n*its* spec's `json_to_native` to convert the JSON back. So the\ntwo callbacks are paired — every spec that participates in the\ngraph needs both. A spec that implements `native_to_json` but\nnot `json_to_native` can only be data-box sources; a spec with\nonly `json_to_native` can only be call-box sinks. We require\nboth so any language can play any role.\n\nSpecs that haven't been updated yet should set both callbacks\nto a stub that returns -1 with a clear error message (\"spec\n`<name>`: native_to_json not implemented; this box's value\ncan't be routed cross-language\"). The hard-fail makes the gap\nloud rather than producing wrong output.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. Extend the `lang_spec_t` declaration in\n   `langs/lang-spec.h` if not already done by 312's\n   infrastructure work. (Per the round summary, the slot is\n   reserved.)\n2. Implement `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` in each\n   spec:\n   - **Lua spec**: walk the value at the stack index. Use the\n     existing C JSON writer (`libs/json/json.c`). Handle Lua\n     tables both as arrays (1-indexed contiguous integer keys)\n     and as objects. Refuse functions, userdata, threads.\n   - **C spec**: depends on 307's typed-wrapper machinery. For\n     now, a stub that only supports scalar types (int, double,\n     string) is enough to get data boxes working in C.\n   - **Bash spec**: validate-and-pass-through. The script is\n     expected to produce JSON. `native_to_json` runs the JSON\n     parser to validate; `json_to_native` is identity.\n3. Extend the data box runtime path in `src/012-dispatch.c`\n   (or wherever data boxes dispatch from) to consult `lang` /\n   `ref` when set and route through the spec callback chain.\n4. Add a fixture: `tests/maps/cross-lang-data/` with a Lua\n   data box, a C consumer, and a Bash consumer all reading the\n   same value. The integration check asserts each consumer\n   sees the right data.\n5. Update each spec's `*.info.md` to document the native handle\n   shape its callbacks expect.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — extend the contract\n- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` —\n  implement the callbacks\n- `langs/{lua,c,bash}/spec.info.md` — document native handle\n  semantics per spec\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — data-box dispatch path\n- `tests/maps/cross-lang-data/` — new fixture (see step 4)\n- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — same author-writes-natural-\n  code principle; this issue extends it from call boxes to data\n  boxes\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — reuses the same\n  spec callbacks for a different (performance) reason\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Bash's `json_to_native` is a near-identity because the\n  scripts already deal in text. Is there value in having it\n  validate and reformat for consistency? Probably yes; cheap\n  insurance against malformed downstream input.\n- Should the Lua spec auto-detect array-vs-object tables, or\n  require the box author to annotate? Auto-detect (contiguous\n  1-indexed integer keys → array; otherwise object) is what\n  every other lua-to-json library does and is intuitive enough.\n- C spec's `native_to_json` for arbitrary structs is a real\n  rabbit hole. Tie scope to 307 — the same type declarations\n  drive both the wrapper and the JSON walk. Until 307 lands,\n  only scalar types are supported for C data boxes.\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/317-spec-json-bridge-for-data-boxes.md"
        }
      }],
