    "content":"# 317 — Language spec JSON bridge for data boxes\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA data box (`kind: data` in box JSON) emits a value the rest of\nthe graph routes downstream. Today the runner reads the box's\n`ref` file as raw bytes and emits them — there's no concept of\n\"authoring this datum in a particular language using that\nlanguage's natural structures.\" If you want to declare a Lua\ntable as a data box's value, you either:\n\n- Hand-translate the table to JSON, save it as a `.json` file,\n  and lose the Lua syntax niceties; or\n- Make it a call box that returns the table, paying for a full\n  spec invocation just to read a constant; or\n- Hard-code the bytes inline in the box's `data` field, with no\n  syntactic help from any host language.\n\nThis is the wrong shape. **A box author writes idiomatic code in\nthe language of their choice.** That's the rule 307 establishes\nfor call boxes: a C-box author writes a plain C function, no\nSoraMech-specific glue. The data-box equivalent should hold —\na Lua-data-box author should write a Lua file that returns\nwhatever they want returned (a table, a string, a number), and\nSoraMech should know how to lift that into the graph as a JSON\nwire value without the author writing a single SoraMech-specific\ncharacter.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEvery language spec gains two callbacks, declared in\n`lang_spec_t` (issue 303):\n\n```c\n/* Serialize a native-language value into JSON text.\n *\n *   ctx       — per-worker handle from spec.init.\n *   src       — caller-meaningful pointer to the native value.\n *               Format is spec-specific (see \"Native handle\n *               representation\" below).\n *   src_size  — size hint, or 0 if the spec interprets `src`\n *               without a length.\n *   out_buf   — destination buffer for JSON text (caller-owned).\n *   out_cap   — capacity of out_buf.\n *   out_size  — set to the bytes written.\n *\n * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error. Writes an error message\n * via the spec's existing error-reporting plumbing. */\nint (*native_to_json)(void *ctx,\n                      const void *src, uint32_t src_size,\n                      char *out_buf, uint32_t out_cap, uint32_t *out_size);\n\n/* Inverse: parse JSON text into a native-language value. The\n * native value is stored wherever the spec considers natural\n * (Lua: pushed to the worker's lua_State stack; C: written into\n * a typed struct supplied by `dst`; Bash: written as a textual\n * representation back into dst).\n *\n *   ctx       — per-worker handle.\n *   src       — JSON text.\n *   src_size  — JSON text length in bytes.\n *   dst       — caller-supplied target; semantics per spec.\n *   dst_cap   — capacity, where meaningful.\n *   dst_size  — set to the bytes / native units consumed.\n *\n * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error. */\nint (*json_to_native)(void *ctx,\n                      const char *src, uint32_t src_size,\n                      void *dst, uint32_t dst_cap, uint32_t *dst_size);\n```\n\nThese are the same fields 312's same-language fast path\nreserves; this issue is the one that requires every spec to\n**actually implement them**, driven by the data-box use case.\n(312 needs them too, but its driver is performance; 317 needs\nthem for correctness — a data box can't function without them.)\n\n### The rule, restated\n\nThe author of a data box writes a `.lua` / `.c` / `.sh` /\n`.<whatever>` file that returns or produces a value using\n*their language's native idioms*. No SoraMech macros. No\nSoraMech includes. No SoraMech-specific JSON shape constraints\nbeyond \"what your spec's native_to_json can convert.\"\n\nIf the author returns a Lua table, the Lua spec's\n`native_to_json` converts it. If they return a C struct, the C\nspec's `native_to_json` walks it according to the type declared\nin the box. If they print JSON-ish text from a bash script, the\nbash spec's `native_to_json` is a no-op identity (the script\nalready produced JSON).\n\nThe contract belongs to the spec author, not the box author.\nThat's the inversion: **SoraMech bends to the language, not the\nother way around.**\n\n## Native handle representation\n\nThe shape of `src` / `dst` in the callbacks is per-spec. Each\nspec documents what it accepts:\n\n- **Lua spec**: `src` is the index of a value already pushed\n  onto the worker's `lua_State`. `src_size` is unused. The\n  spec's `native_to_json` reads the value at that stack index\n  and writes JSON. `json_to_native` pushes the parsed JSON value\n  onto the stack, and `dst_size` reports the number of stack\n  slots used (always 1 for SoraMech's flat-value model).\n- **C spec**: `src` is a typed pointer + the box's declared\n  output type drives the walk. `src_size` is the type's\n  storage footprint. Mirror image for `json_to_native`. (This\n  ties into 307's typed-wrapper-generation work — the same\n  type system describes both the wrapper signature and the\n  JSON shape.)\n- **Bash spec**: `src` is text the script produced.\n  `native_to_json` validates and reshapes to JSON if needed (a\n  bash script that prints `42` becomes JSON `42`; a script that\n  prints `{\"a\":1}` passes through unchanged). `json_to_native`\n  is similarly a near-identity. The spec author is encouraged\n  to require scripts produce well-formed JSON in the first\n  place rather than write a bash-syntax parser.\n\nThe dispatch layer doesn't know or care which representation a\nspec uses. It only ever passes `src` and `src_size` to the\nspec's callback. The spec is opaque to the runtime; that's the\nwhole point.\n\n## Data box semantics\n\nA data box's `data` field becomes optional. The box gains\noptional `lang` and `ref` fields:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"config\",\n  \"kind\": \"data\",\n  \"lang\": \"lua\",\n  \"ref\": \"config.lua\"\n}\n```\n\nAt graph load, the runner:\n\n1. Resolves the spec for `lang`.\n2. Calls the spec's `init` (already done at worker startup).\n3. At box-fire time, asks the spec to execute the `ref` file\n   and produce a native value (this is essentially the same\n   \"load this file, run it, get its return value\" path the\n   spec already implements for call boxes — call boxes call a\n   named function; data boxes take the file's return value).\n4. Calls the spec's `native_to_json` to convert the native\n   value to JSON text.\n5. Pushes that JSON text down the wire as the box's output —\n   same as today's data path, just with the value sourced\n   from a language-native file.\n\nIf the box has no `lang` and a literal `data` field, the legacy\ninline-data path applies unchanged.\n\n## Why every spec must implement these\n\nThe same JSON the data box emits is consumed by some downstream\nbox (call, comparator, file_write, whatever). That downstream\nbox, if it's in a different language, will eventually need\n*its* spec's `json_to_native` to convert the JSON back. So the\ntwo callbacks are paired — every spec that participates in the\ngraph needs both. A spec that implements `native_to_json` but\nnot `json_to_native` can only be data-box sources; a spec with\nonly `json_to_native` can only be call-box sinks. We require\nboth so any language can play any role.\n\nSpecs that haven't been updated yet should set both callbacks\nto a stub that returns -1 with a clear error message (\"spec\n`<name>`: native_to_json not implemented; this box's value\ncan't be routed cross-language\"). The hard-fail makes the gap\nloud rather than producing wrong output.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. Extend the `lang_spec_t` declaration in\n   `langs/lang-spec.h` if not already done by 312's\n   infrastructure work. (Per the round summary, the slot is\n   reserved.)\n2. Implement `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` in each\n   spec:\n   - **Lua spec**: walk the value at the stack index. Use the\n     existing C JSON writer (`libs/json/json.c`). Handle Lua\n     tables both as arrays (1-indexed contiguous integer keys)\n     and as objects. Refuse functions, userdata, threads.\n   - **C spec**: depends on 307's typed-wrapper machinery. For\n     now, a stub that only supports scalar types (int, double,\n     string) is enough to get data boxes working in C.\n   - **Bash spec**: validate-and-pass-through. The script is\n     expected to produce JSON. `native_to_json` runs the JSON\n     parser to validate; `json_to_native` is identity.\n3. Extend the data box runtime path in `src/012-dispatch.c`\n   (or wherever data boxes dispatch from) to consult `lang` /\n   `ref` when set and route through the spec callback chain.\n4. Add a fixture: `tests/maps/cross-lang-data/` with a Lua\n   data box, a C consumer, and a Bash consumer all reading the\n   same value. The integration check asserts each consumer\n   sees the right data.\n5. Update each spec's `*.info.md` to document the native handle\n   shape its callbacks expect.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — extend the contract\n- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` —\n  implement the callbacks\n- `langs/{lua,c,bash}/spec.info.md` — document native handle\n  semantics per spec\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — data-box dispatch path\n- `tests/maps/cross-lang-data/` — new fixture (see step 4)\n- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — same author-writes-natural-\n  code principle; this issue extends it from call boxes to data\n  boxes\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — reuses the same\n  spec callbacks for a different (performance) reason\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Bash's `json_to_native` is a near-identity because the\n  scripts already deal in text. Is there value in having it\n  validate and reformat for consistency? Probably yes; cheap\n  insurance against malformed downstream input.\n- Should the Lua spec auto-detect array-vs-object tables, or\n  require the box author to annotate? Auto-detect (contiguous\n  1-indexed integer keys → array; otherwise object) is what\n  every other lua-to-json library does and is intuitive enough.\n- C spec's `native_to_json` for arbitrary structs is a real\n  rabbit hole. Tie scope to 307 — the same type declarations\n  drive both the wrapper and the JSON walk. Until 307 lands,\n  only scalar types are supported for C data boxes.\n",

        "type":"text",
        "text":"Files created: `316-simple-test-runner.md`, `317-spec-json-bridge-for-data-boxes.md`. 307's \"language never bends to SoraMech\" rule is now stated as a rule at the top of its box-convention section.\n\n### 312 — how the dynamic dispatch actually works\n\nYou asked: *how are we planning to dynamically do this? are we requiring the spec to explain how?*\n\nYes — **the spec explains how, completely.** The dispatch layer is generic; it only knows which callback to call based on a single bit on each box. Here's the shape:\n\n**The spec contract has three layers of invocation:**\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    /* The universal fallback. JSON-in, JSON-out. Every spec must\n     * implement this — it's the cross-language lingua franca. */\n    int (*invoke)(handle, fn, in_json,  in_size,  out_json,  out_cap, out_size);\n\n    /* The fast path. The spec defines what \"native\" means for\n     * itself — a Lua spec might pass values via the worker's\n     * lua_State, a C spec might pass typed structs, a future\n     * msgpack-aware spec might pass packed binary. Optional;\n     * NULL means \"no fast path available, always go through invoke\". */\n    int (*invoke_native)(handle, fn, native_in, in_size, native_out, out_cap, out_size);\n\n    /* The bridge. Used at language boundaries: a Lua producer\n     * feeding a C consumer goes Lua-native → JSON → C-native. */\n    int (*native_to_json)(...);\n    int (*json_to_native)(...);\n} lang_spec_t;\n```\n\n**The dispatch's role is purely routing**, not optimization. At graph load (already implemented per the 312 fast-path classification work), each call box is tagged with a single bit: `use_native_invoke`. The bit is true iff every input slot feeding this box is produced by a same-language box AND every output of this box feeds only same-language consumers — i.e., this box sits inside a same-language island.\n\nAt dispatch time, the resolution is one if-else:\n\n```c\nlang_invoke_fn fn = b->use_native_invoke && spec->invoke_native\n                    ? spec->invoke_native     /* binary native format */\n                    : spec->invoke;           /* JSON */\n```\n\nThat's it. The dispatch doesn't know what \"native\" means for Lua vs C vs Bash — it just trusts that if two boxes have the same spec and the box's bit says native, the producer-side native output and consumer-side native input speak the same private dialect.\n\n**What each spec must declare:**\n\n- A stable binary serialization of its native values that producer-side `invoke_native` writes and consumer-side `invoke_native` reads. This is the bit the spec authors design themselves. Examples of what a spec could pick:\n  - **Lua**: a length-prefixed binary table dump (table → repeated `{key_size, key_bytes, value_kind, value_bytes}`). Faster than JSON because no string parsing, no escape decoding, types are tagged inline.\n  - **C**: raw memcpy of the declared struct layout (the wrapper from 307 knows the type). Zero serialization — just bytes on the wire.\n  - **Bash**: arguably no fast path makes sense; bash always deals in text. The spec leaves `invoke_native` as NULL and the dispatch falls through to `invoke` (which is JSON, which is fine — bash boxes are slow regardless).\n\nThe dispatch doesn't pick the format. The spec author picks the format. The dispatch just routes through whichever callback the spec advertises.\n\nThis is the same pattern issue 317 uses for data boxes: the spec is the only thing that knows how to convert between native and JSON; the runtime is the conductor that calls the right baton-handoff at the right moment.\n\n---\n\n### Commits — proceeding one issue at a time\n\nSince each completed issue gets its own commit, let me line up what's commitable right now from this round. The genuinely-done items, ordered by smallest-blast-radius first so each commit is reviewable:\n\n1. **314** — strict leading-zero rule in JSON parser\n2. **310** — priority queue (no new changes in this round; already complete)\n3. **308** — `dladdr`-based `bash-server.sh` lookup\n4. **304** — cell-tagged iterator ordering\n5. **309** — compile pipeline (depends on 308 for portability)\n6. **302** — large-value heap\n7. **311** — JSONL writer + LOG_VALUES + LOG_SLOTS + compile-pipeline integration check\n8. **301**, **303**, **305**, **306**, **307** (core only) — older issues that finished earlier but haven't been moved\n9. **315**, **316**, **317** — three new design-only issues\n\nWant me to start working through these one-by-one (move issue file to `issues/completed/`, commit just that issue's changes), or would you rather:\n- batch the design-only ones (315/316/317) into one initial commit since they're just doc adds, then do the substantive ones individually\n- start from a specific issue you care about most\n- skip the closeout dance entirely for now and pick a next implementation target (316 test runner would be quick; 317 data-box bridge would be high-leverage)\n\nI'd vote: commit the three new issue files individually first (each is just one file, easy review), then commit the in-tree changes by issue (304 cell-tagged, 308 dladdr, 309 compile script, 302 lvh, 311 compile-pipeline check) moving each from open to `issues/completed/`. Older fully-done issues (301/303/305/306/310) can be moved to completed with empty content-changes-since-this-commit. That's around 8 commits to get to a clean tree.\n\nSound right?"

  "promptId":"f136d985-b67e-4a12-b6a1-28132a23d5ec",
  "message":{
    "content":"  The dispatch's role is purely routing, not optimization. At graph load\n  (already implemented per the 312 fast-path classification work), each call\n  box is tagged with a single bit: use_native_invoke. The bit is true iff\n  every input slot feeding this box is produced by a same-language box AND\n  every output of this box feeds only same-language consumers — i.e., this\n  box sits inside a same-language island.\n\n  At dispatch time, the resolution is one if-else:\n\n  lang_invoke_fn fn = b->use_native_invoke && spec->invoke_native\n                      ? spec->invoke_native     /* binary native format */\n                      : spec->invoke;           /* JSON */\n\n  That's it. The dispatch doesn't know what \"native\" means for Lua vs C vs\n  Bash — it just trusts that if two boxes have the same spec and the box's\n  bit says native, the producer-side native output and consumer-side native\n  input speak the same private dialect.\n\n\nwe should make it so that if the inputs are lua, and the box is lua, then it can do native, even if the output is going to a C box. Same for the other way - if the input is C and the box is lua, then it can't do native on that path, but if the output is lua then we can do native there.\n\nthe rest of the issue commits can be made. Just make sure it's one commit per issue file.",
    "role":"user"
  }
}

      "content":"## Compile-time wire classification\n\nEvery wire gets a `fast_path: true | false` flag set at build time\n(issue 309 build step):\n\n```python\nfor wire in graph.wires:\n    src_lang = box_at(wire.from).lang\n    dst_lang = box_at(wire.to).lang\n    wire.fast_path = (src_lang == dst_lang)\n```\n\nThe flag becomes part of the compiled manifest. Runtime never\nre-evaluates language pairing.\n\n## Producer-side decision\n\nA producer's output goes into one slot, but multiple consumers may\nread from it. If they're all the same language, the producer can\nwrite native bytes. If any consumer is in a different language, the\nproducer must write JSON (and same-language consumers convert via\n`json_to_native` to recover native form).\n\nTwo ways to decide:\n1. **Per-output decision** — analyze all consumers of the output\n   slot at compile time. All same lang → native; mixed → JSON.\n2. **Always JSON producer / convert at consumer** — simpler, but\n   pays the encode cost even when no cross-language consumer is\n   present.\n\nOption 1 is the right call. The compile step records the producer's\noutput format on the box record (`output_format: \"native\" | \"json\"`),\nand same-language consumers know to read native bytes directly,\ncross-language consumers call `json_to_native` first.\n\n## Runtime dispatch\n\nThe dispatch action's input-read path branches on the wire flag:\n\n```c\nfor (int i = 0; i < n_inputs; i++) {\n    slot_peek(input_slots[i], buf, buf_capacity);\n    if (input_wires[i].fast_path && producer_format == NATIVE) {\n        // bytes are already this language's native form\n        ...\n    } else if (producer_format == JSON) {\n        // bytes are JSON, decode into native form\n        json_to_native(buf, buf_size, native_buf, native_capacity, &native_size);\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\nThen `invoke_native` is called with native-form bytes regardless of\nhow they were obtained. Same on the output side: if the box's output\nformat is `native`, write native bytes; if `json`, encode then\nwrite.\n\n## Edge cases\n\n- **All-same-language graph**: every wire is fast-path; `invoke_json`\n  never runs. Spec writers can stub it out.\n- **All-different-language graph**: every wire is JSON;\n  `invoke_native` handles bytes that came back from `json_to_native`.\n- **One same-language wire, several cross-language wires from the same\n  producer**: the producer writes JSON. Same-language consumer\n  decodes via `json_to_native` (still cheaper than full encode +\n  decode round-trip — only one direction of conversion is paid,\n  not two).\n- **Type changes mid-development**: a wire that was Lua→Lua becomes\n  Lua→C as the user changes a downstream box's language. Compile\n  flips the flag; the producer now writes JSON. No runtime\n  surprises, no migration.\n\n## Implementation cost\n\nThe two-invoke spec interface adds maybe 30 lines per language\nspec. The compile-time wire classification is one pass over the\ngraph. The dispatch action's input-read branch is one `if` on the\nwire flag. None of this is hot-path complex; the gain is one less\nJSON encode/decode per same-language hop, which is the whole point.\n\n## Future: whole-program same-language compilation\n\nA bigger optimization beyond this issue: at compile time, merge\nall same-language boxes into one translation unit. The C spec\nbecomes whole-program; the Lua spec produces one bytecode chunk\ncovering every Lua function. Box-boundary crossings become regular\nfunction calls — no slot store, no dispatch layer, no spec\ninvocation. Only cross-language wires retain the slot machinery.\n\nThis is a phase-3.5+ optimization and a much bigger lift —\nrequires the spec's `compile` callback to coordinate across all\nboxes of its language, plus a runtime mode that bypasses the\ndispatch layer for fully-merged regions of the graph. The\nwire-level fast path in this issue is the immediate, smaller win.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Spec interface** (issue 303): add `invoke_native`,\n   `invoke_json`, `native_to_json`, `json_to_native` callbacks.\n   Update the contract doc.\n2. **Compile step** (issue 309): walk wires, set `fast_path` flag,\n   set `output_format` per box.\n3. **Dispatch action** (issue 304): branch on `fast_path` /\n   `output_format` when reading inputs and when writing the\n   output.\n4. **Per-language specs** (306, 307, 308): implement both invoke\n   paths. Bash's fast path is a thin alias around the JSON path.\n   C's fast path is `memcpy`. Lua's fast path picks a native\n   encoding (cjson for tables; raw bytes for primitives).\n5. **Tests**: smoke tests confirming a 100k-iteration Lua→Lua\n   pipeline with the fast path runs measurably faster than the\n   same pipeline with the JSON path, and that mixed-language\n   pipelines still work.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — adds the new callbacks\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — branch on fast_path\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — wire-flag enrichment\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md`, `307-c-language-spec.md`,\n  `308-bash-language-spec.md` — per-spec native implementations\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot still stores opaque\n  bytes; the format negotiation is at the spec layer, not the\n  store\n\n## Implementation note: ask the user about type-annotated cross-language encodings\n\nBefore implementing this issue, the implementer must ask the user",

The compile step records the producer's\noutput format on the box record (`output_format: \"native\" | \"json\"`),\nand same-language consumers know to read native bytes directly,\ncross-language consumers call `json_to_native` first.",
          "new_string":"## Per-edge format negotiation\n\nClassification is **per edge**, not per box. A box always\nexecutes its user function in native form. The format on the\nwire is decided independently for each input edge and each\noutput edge based on the language pair across that edge:\n\n```\ninput edge native?   = (producer.lang == this_box.lang)\noutput edge native?  = (this_box.lang == consumer.lang)\n```\n\nSo a Lua box sitting in the middle of `[C → Lua → C]` works\nlike this:\n\n- Input edge from the C producer: cross-lang, so the slot\n  carries JSON. On read, the Lua spec calls `json_to_native`\n  to lift it into a Lua value.\n- The box's user function runs natively in Lua. It returns a\n  Lua value.\n- Output edges to the two C consumers: cross-lang, so the spec\n  calls `native_to_json` once and pushes JSON bytes to each\n  consumer's slot.\n\nA Lua box in `[Lua → Lua → C]` works differently *along its\nown edges*:\n\n- Input edge from the Lua producer: same-lang, slot carries\n  native binary. No conversion on read.\n- User function runs.\n- Output edges: one is same-lang (push native), the other is\n  cross-lang (call `native_to_json`, push JSON). The producer\n  pushes once to each consumer's slot in the right format.\n\nThis means **same-lang neighbors get the fast path even when\nsome other neighbor is cross-lang**. The classification doesn't\ncollapse on the first cross-language edge it finds; it stays\nper-edge.\n\n### Why per-edge, not per-box\n\nThe earlier design considered an \"all same-lang or fall back\nto JSON for all\" rule (the simpler classification). It's\nstrictly dominated by the per-edge rule:\n\n- The dominant case is \"a Lua sub-graph occasionally talks to\n  C.\" Per-box would force the Lua-to-Lua interior to round-trip\n  through JSON for every box that has *any* C neighbor.\n- Per-edge keeps the cost local to the actual cross-lang\n  boundary. The interior of any same-lang island skips JSON;\n  only the boundary edges pay.\n- The implementation cost is identical: same number of bits per\n  box, just stored per-port/per-edge instead of per-box.\n\n### What each box records at graph load\n\nFor each box:\n\n- `input_edge_native[i]` — one bit per input port. True iff the\n  producer feeding that port has the same language as this box.\n- `output_edge_native[j]` — one bit per outgoing connection\n  (not per output port — a single output port can fan to\n  multiple consumers, each of which is classified independently\n  because the language pair may differ across consumers).\n\nBoth arrays are computed during `graph_attach_runtime` and live\non the box record. No runtime re-evaluation.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md"
        }

    "originalFile":"# 312 — Same-language wire fast path: skip JSON for adjacent same-language boxes\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nThe wire format between boxes is JSON (`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`,\nissue 302's \"no type tags\" — slot store stores opaque bytes; the\nlanguage spec encodes/decodes). Every wire pays the JSON encode +\ndecode cost on every value pass, even when the producer and the\nconsumer are the same language and could use a faster\nlanguage-native serialization.\n\nFor a Lua → Lua wire passing a 10-element table:\n1. Producer's spec: `cjson.encode(table)` → string of N bytes\n2. `slot_push(slot, string, N)`\n3. `slot_peek(slot, buf, N)`\n4. Consumer's spec: `cjson.decode(buf)` → Lua table\n\nSteps 1 and 4 are the cost. They're language-agnostic and unnecessary\nwhen both endpoints share a language.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEach language spec exposes **two invoke paths**:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;\n    const char *file_ext;\n\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n    int   (*compile)(...);\n\n    // Universal path — JSON bytes in, JSON bytes out\n    int   (*invoke_json)  (void *handle, /* common args */);\n\n    // Fast path — language-native bytes in, language-native bytes out\n    int   (*invoke_native)(void *handle, /* common args */);\n\n    // Bridges used when a value crosses a language boundary\n    int   (*native_to_json)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n    int   (*json_to_native)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n```\n\n`invoke_native` is required (every spec implements one). Per-language\n\"native\" format:\n- **Lua**: `lua_dump` for closures, `cjson` or msgpack for tables, raw\n  bytes for strings/numbers. Spec's choice as long as it's\n  symmetric with its own decoder.\n- **C**: raw struct memcpy. The compile-time wrapper (issue 307)\n  knows the types; serialization is `memcpy(slot_buf, &val, sizeof\n  val)`.\n- **Bash**: strings only — Bash has no other native form, so the\n  fast path is identical to the JSON path. Implement as a thin\n  alias.\n\n`invoke_json` is the universal interop format. Required for any\nlanguage that participates in cross-language wires. A spec that\nonly ever talks to itself can skip `invoke_json` (compile error if\na wire crosses to it from another language).\n\n## Compile-time wire classification\n\nEvery wire gets a `fast_path: true | false` flag set at build time\n(issue 309 build step):\n\n```python\nfor wire in graph.wires:\n    src_lang = box_at(wire.from).lang\n    dst_lang = box_at(wire.to).lang\n    wire.fast_path = (src_lang == dst_lang)\n```\n\nThe flag becomes part of the compiled manifest. Runtime never\nre-evaluates language pairing.\n\n## Producer-side decision\n\nA producer's output goes into one slot, but multiple consumers may\nread from it. If they're all the same language, the producer can\nwrite native bytes. If any consumer is in a different language, the\nproducer must write JSON (and same-language consumers convert via\n`json_to_native` to recover native form).\n\nTwo ways to decide:\n1. **Per-output decision** — analyze all consumers of the output\n   slot at compile time. All same lang → native; mixed → JSON.\n2. **Always JSON producer / convert at consumer** — simpler, but\n   pays the encode cost even when no cross-language consumer is\n   present.\n\nOption 1 is the right call. The compile step records the producer's\noutput format on the box record (`output_format: \"native\" | \"json\"`),\nand same-language consumers know to read native bytes directly,\ncross-language consumers call `json_to_native` first.\n\n## Runtime dispatch\n\nThe dispatch action's input-read path branches on the wire flag:\n\n```c\nfor (int i = 0; i < n_inputs; i++) {\n    slot_peek(input_slots[i], buf, buf_capacity);\n    if (input_wires[i].fast_path && producer_format == NATIVE) {\n        // bytes are already this language's native form\n        ...\n    } else if (producer_format == JSON) {\n        // bytes are JSON, decode into native form\n        json_to_native(buf, buf_size, native_buf, native_capacity, &native_size);\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\nThen `invoke_native` is called with native-form bytes regardless of\nhow they were obtained. Same on the output side: if the box's output\nformat is `native`, write native bytes; if `json`, encode then\nwrite.\n\n## Edge cases\n\n- **All-same-language graph**: every wire is fast-path; `invoke_json`\n  never runs. Spec writers can stub it out.\n- **All-different-language graph**: every wire is JSON;\n  `invoke_native` handles bytes that came back from `json_to_native`.\n- **One same-language wire, several cross-language wires from the same\n  producer**: the producer writes JSON. Same-language consumer\n  decodes via `json_to_native` (still cheaper than full encode +\n  decode round-trip — only one direction of conversion is paid,\n  not two).\n- **Type changes mid-development**: a wire that was Lua→Lua becomes\n  Lua→C as the user changes a downstream box's language. Compile\n  flips the flag; the producer now writes JSON. No runtime\n  surprises, no migration.\n\n## Implementation cost\n\nThe two-invoke spec interface adds maybe 30 lines per language\nspec. The compile-time wire classification is one pass over the\ngraph. The dispatch action's input-read branch is one `if` on the\nwire flag. None of this is hot-path complex; the gain is one less\nJSON encode/decode per same-language hop, which is the whole point.\n\n## Future: whole-program same-language compilation\n\nA bigger optimization beyond this issue: at compile time, merge\nall same-language boxes into one translation unit. The C spec\nbecomes whole-program; the Lua spec produces one bytecode chunk\ncovering every Lua function. Box-boundary crossings become regular\nfunction calls — no slot store, no dispatch layer, no spec\ninvocation. Only cross-language wires retain the slot machinery.\n\nThis is a phase-3.5+ optimization and a much bigger lift —\nrequires the spec's `compile` callback to coordinate across all\nboxes of its language, plus a runtime mode that bypasses the\ndispatch layer for fully-merged regions of the graph. The\nwire-level fast path in this issue is the immediate, smaller win.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Spec interface** (issue 303): add `invoke_native`,\n   `invoke_json`, `native_to_json`, `json_to_native` callbacks.\n   Update the contract doc.\n2. **Compile step** (issue 309): walk wires, set `fast_path` flag,\n   set `output_format` per box.\n3. **Dispatch action** (issue 304): branch on `fast_path` /\n   `output_format` when reading inputs and when writing the\n   output.\n4. **Per-language specs** (306, 307, 308): implement both invoke\n   paths. Bash's fast path is a thin alias around the JSON path.\n   C's fast path is `memcpy`. Lua's fast path picks a native\n   encoding (cjson for tables; raw bytes for primitives).\n5. **Tests**: smoke tests confirming a 100k-iteration Lua→Lua\n   pipeline with the fast path runs measurably faster than the\n   same pipeline with the JSON path, and that mixed-language\n   pipelines still work.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — adds the new callbacks\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — branch on fast_path\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — wire-flag enrichment\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md`, `307-c-language-spec.md`,\n  `308-bash-language-spec.md` — per-spec native implementations\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot still stores opaque\n  bytes; the format negotiation is at the spec layer, not the\n  store\n\n## Implementation note: ask the user about type-annotated cross-language encodings\n\nBefore implementing this issue, the implementer must ask the user\nto decide on **type-annotated wire encodings** for cross-language\nhops — primitives go raw bytes (4-byte int as 4 bytes, not as the\nJSON string `\"42\"`), strings go length-prefixed UTF-8, structured\ntypes go JSON. That decision affects the spec interface (whether\n`json_to_native` is enough or whether we need a `decode_wire(type,\nbytes)` shape) and the wire-format byte layout. Don't proceed with\nthe implementation without explicit user direction on this; the\ntwo designs aren't trivially interchangeable later.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Whether a spec must implement `invoke_json`**: leaning yes, so\n  any spec can talk to any other spec. A spec that wants to\n  shortcut can declare cross-language wires unsupported via\n  compile-time error, but that's an opt-out, not the default.\n- **How to share the bridge functions across consumers**: native_to_json\n  on the producer side runs once per output (not per consumer), and\n  the JSON bytes go in the slot. Each cross-language consumer pays\n  json_to_native independently. Same-language consumers pay nothing.\n  Symmetrically: if the producer chose native and there's one\n  cross-language consumer, that consumer pays native_to_json then\n  json_to_native_their_lang. Two conversions for one cross-language\n  hop in this case. Probably fine; it's a corner case.\n",

    "newString":"## Runtime dispatch\n\nThe dispatch action calls `invoke_native` always (when the spec\nprovides one). The boundary work is per-edge in two places:\ninput-read and output-push.\n\n### Input-read: per-input-port\n\n```c\nfor (int i = 0; i < n_inputs; i++) {\n    slot_pop(input_slots[i], wire_buf, wire_buf_cap);\n    if (b->input_edge_native[i]) {\n        // wire bytes are native form already; hand to invoke_native as-is\n        native_inputs[i] = wire_buf;\n    } else {\n        // wire bytes are JSON; lift into native form\n        spec->json_to_native(ctx, wire_buf, wire_size,\n                             native_buf, native_cap, &native_size);\n        native_inputs[i] = native_buf;\n    }\n}\nspec->invoke_native(ctx, fn, native_inputs, n_inputs,\n                    native_out, native_out_cap, &native_out_size);\n```\n\n### Output-push: per-outgoing-connection\n\n```c\nfor (int j = 0; j < b->n_connections; j++) {\n    if (b->output_edge_native[j]) {\n        // consumer is same-lang; push native bytes directly\n        slot_push(consumer_slot, native_out, native_out_size, tag);\n    } else {\n        // consumer is cross-lang; serialize to JSON once per such edge\n        spec->native_to_json(ctx, native_out, native_out_size,\n                             json_buf, json_buf_cap, &json_size);\n        slot_push(consumer_slot, json_buf, json_size, tag);\n    }\n}\n```\n\nIf multiple cross-lang consumers share the producer's language,\nthe dispatch can cache the JSON encoding from the first such\nedge and reuse it for the rest (optimization, not required for\ncorrectness).\n\nIf the spec's `invoke_native` is NULL (e.g., bash), the dispatch\nfalls back to the universal `invoke` (JSON-in, JSON-out) and\ntreats every edge as JSON. This is the slow path; it's always\ncorrect."

    "stdout":"- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot still stores opaque\n  bytes; the format negotiation is at the spec layer, not the\n  store\n\n## Implementation note: ask the user about type-annotated cross-language encodings\n\nBefore implementing this issue, the implementer must ask the user\nto decide on **type-annotated wire encodings** for cross-language\nhops — primitives go raw bytes (4-byte int as 4 bytes, not as the\nJSON string `\"42\"`), strings go length-prefixed UTF-8, structured\ntypes go JSON.     "newString":"- **How to share the bridge functions across consumers**: native_to_json\n  on the producer side runs once per output (not per consumer), and\n  the JSON bytes go in the slot. Each cross-language consumer pays\n  json_to_native independently. Same-language consumers pay nothing.\n  Symmetrically: if the producer chose native and there's one\n  cross-language consumer, that consumer pays native_to_json then\n  json_to_native_their_lang. Two conversions for one cross-language\n  hop in this case. Probably fine; it's a corner case.\n\n## Implementation status\n\nWhat's in place (per the round summaries on 2026-05-12 to\n2026-05-19):\n\n- `lang_spec_t` extended with `invoke_native`, `invoke_json`,\n  `native_to_json`, `json_to_native` callback slots (issue 303\n  spec interface).\n- Each of the three specs declares all four callbacks. Today\n  they all alias to the single existing `invoke` implementation;\n  the actual specialization (real native_to_json / json_to_native\n  bodies, real per-language binary native form) is not yet\n  implemented.\n- `graph_attach_runtime` computes a per-box `use_native_invoke`\n  bit (true iff all input producers and all output consumers\n  share this box's language). The dispatch picks\n  `invoke_native > invoke_json > invoke` based on that single\n  bit.\n\nWhat's still ahead:\n\n- **Replace per-box `use_native_invoke` with per-edge\n  classification.** The current bit is the simpler approximation\n  of the per-edge design above. It needs to be split into\n  `b->input_edge_native[i]` and `b->output_edge_native[j]` arrays\n  computed at graph load, with the dispatch's input-read and\n  output-push paths each consulting the relevant array.\n- **Per-language native binary serializations.** Each spec\n  needs a real `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` (also\n  required by issue 317 for data boxes), plus a real\n  `invoke_native` that operates on whatever the spec considers\n  its native handoff format.\n- The type-annotated cross-language encoding decision flagged\n  above is still pending user direction."
  },

A Lua box sitting between a C producer and\na C consumer can still read native from a Lua sibling on a\ndifferent input port, and can still write native to a Lua\nsibling on a different output edge. The cost of cross-language\nshould be local to the cross-language edge, not to the box.\n\nReframed as per-edge: each input port carries a 'is the producer\nmy language' bit, each outgoing connection carries 'is the\nconsumer my language', the dispatch consults the relevant bit\nwhen reading inputs and pushing outputs. The same number of bits\nper box; just stored per-port/per-edge rather than collapsed.\n\nAlso adds a status section recording what's actually in place\n(callback slots reserved, classification at a per-box\napproximation, every spec aliasing its callbacks to the JSON\npath) versus what's still ahead (real per-edge bits, real\nper-language native serialisations).\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>\nEOF\n)\"",

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Six commits landed, one per issue file:\n\n```\nc9bd357 Reflect recent rounds in phase-3 progress\nf4559fe 312 — per-edge fast-path classification, plus an honest status\nbb180fd 307 — sharpen the language-agnostic rule, record compile + invoke log\nbec8061 Open 317 — language spec JSON bridge for data boxes\n1b0dd37 Open 316 — simple test-runner script\n72c572b Open 315 — reference-counted compiled-map artifacts\n```\n\n### Per-edge classification — captured in 312's design\n\nThe refinement is now written into 312. The key shift: the box doesn't carry a single \"fast path or not\" bit. Each input port carries `input_edge_native[i]` (does the producer share my language?) and each outgoing connection carries `output_edge_native[j]` (does the consumer share my language?). Read-time and push-time consult the relevant bit; a Lua box sitting between a C producer and a C consumer still gets the native fast path with any Lua siblings on its other ports.\n\nThe \"Implementation status\" section in 312 now distinguishes what's actually in code (the per-box approximation) from the per-edge design that still needs to land.\n\n### What's still uncommitted\n\n75 files: the implementation code (`src/011-spec-registry.*`, `src/012-dispatch.*`, `src/013-jsonl-events.*`, `src/014-event-queue.*`, `src/015-large-value-heap.*`, slot-store and graph-loader edits, all the test files, lang-spec changes, scripts, fixtures) plus the implementation-log additions on issues 301–311 + 314.\n\nThe honest difficulty: many of these source files span multiple issues. `src/012-dispatch.c` carries work for 304 (routing kinds + cell-tagged ordering), 311 (event emission), and 312 (native invoke resolution). `src/010-graph-loader.c` carries work for 305 (loader), 304 (cell-tagged slot flags), and 312 (fast-path classification). `src/009-slot-store.c` carries 302 (LVH).\n\nTo keep \"one commit per issue\" while landing real implementation, I'd need to split these files by hunk. Three options:\n\n1. **Strict per-issue, per-hunk slicing** — go through each multi-issue file with `git add -p`-style hunk picking and produce one commit per issue. Slow and error-prone but maximally faithful to the rule.\n2. **Per-feature commits with named issue scope** — each commit takes a coherent slice (e.g., \"Cell-tagged ordering for parallel iterators — 304\") and names the primary issue in the title. If a commit incidentally drags in a line that also serves another issue, mention it in the body. Less strict but more reviewable.\n3. **Defer all implementation commits, keep the working tree dirty** — make the next round of *new* design work as its own commits and let the existing implementation accumulate until we decide on a slicing strategy.\n\nI lean **2** for the next step — it's faithful to the spirit (each commit is one issue's story) without the brittleness of hunk-by-hunk surgery. Also: the core dump `core.18888` (147 MB) sitting at the project root should get gitignored as a tiny tidy commit, separate from issue work.\n\nWhich direction?"

    "originalFile":"/* src/010-graph-loader.h — C graph loader (phase 3), public API.\n *\n * What it is, in a sentence: reads a map directory off disk, parses\n * every JSON file in it, and produces an in-memory graph_t that the\n * dispatch layer (issue 304) and the pool runner (issue 301) walk\n * to drive a run.\n *\n * Designed in issue 305. Aligned to the unified routing schema\n * from issue 233 — every call box carries a routing.kind, and the\n * legacy `comparand` / `iterator_outputs` fields are gone. The data\n * and file_write box kinds from issue 229 are dispatch-layer\n * primitives — they have no function to invoke.\n *\n * Memory model: every string the graph_t holds (box ids, refs,\n * function names, branch tags, paths, input port names) lives in a\n * single json_arena_t owned by the graph_t. graph_destroy frees the\n * arena, the box / connection / input arrays, and the graph_t in\n * one call.\n *\n * Errors: graph_load returns NULL on failure and sets *err to a\n * malloc'd diagnostic of the form \"<file>:<line>: <message>\". The\n * caller frees *err. Connections currently store\n *    string refs (to_box / to_input); resolving those to integer\n *    indices, verifying both endpoints exist, and detecting\n *    non-iterator cycles all land in the next iteration.\n *  - Phase 5: slot size class enumeration.\n *  - Phase 6: entry-box detection.\n *  - Phase 7: language enumeration.\n *\n * None of those block 301 / 303 / 306 from starting.\n */\n\n#ifndef SORAMECH_GRAPH_LOADER_H\n#define SORAMECH_GRAPH_LOADER_H\n\n#include <stddef.h>\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\nextern \"C\" {\n#endif\n\n/* {{{ Box kinds */\ntypedef enum {\n    BOX_CALL,         /* runs a function via a language spec        */\n    BOX_DATA,         /* file source — dispatch reads `path` at run */\n    BOX_FILE_WRITE,   /* file sink  — dispatch writes inputs at run */\n} box_kind_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Routing kinds (issue 233 unified schema) */\ntypedef enum {\n    ROUTING_PLAIN,\n    ROUTING_COMPARATOR,\n    ROUTING_ITERATOR,\n    ROUTING_RANDOMIZER,    /* not yet parsed; reserved */\n    ROUTING_WEIGHTED,      /* not yet parsed; reserved */\n    ROUTING_DISTRIBUTOR,   /* not yet parsed; reserved */\n} routing_kind_t;\n\ntypedef struct {\n    routing_kind_t kind;\n    int            n_outputs;   /* iterator / randomizer / weighted / distributor */\n    double         comparand;   /* comparator */\n    /* Weighted routing: arena-owned double array of n_outputs\n     * entries.       /* \"string\" by convention     */\n    const char *literal;    /* NULL or arena-owned value  */\n    int         optional;   /* issue 230 optional flag    */\n} input_decl_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Outgoing connection */\n/* String refs are preserved for diagnostics; resolved integer\n * indices are filled in by the topology pass and let the dispatch\n * layer (issue 304) avoid string lookups at runtime. */\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *to_box;       /* destination box id (arena-owned)        */\n    const char *to_input;     /* destination port name                   */\n    const char *from_branch;  /* NULL for plain output; else branch name */\n    int         to_box_idx;   /* resolved index into graph->boxes        */\n    int         to_input_idx; /* resolved index into target's inputs[]   */\n} connection_t;\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Box */\ntypedef struct {\n    const char    *id;\n    box_kind_t     kind;\n\n    /* Call boxes */\n    const char    *lang;           "new_string":"    for (int i = 0; i < g->n_boxes; i++) {\n        box_t *b = &g->boxes[i];\n        b->input_edge_native  = NULL;\n        b->output_edge_native = NULL;\n        b->use_native_invoke  = 0;\n        if (b->kind != BOX_CALL || !b->lang) continue;\n\n        /* Allocate per-port input bits and per-connection output\n         * bits. malloc rather than calloc — we fill every entry\n         * explicitly below. */\n        if (b->n_inputs > 0) {\n            b->input_edge_native = malloc((size_t)b->n_inputs * sizeof(int));\n            if (!b->input_edge_native) { if (err) *err = err_fmt(\"oom\"); return NULL; }\n            for (int j = 0; j < b->n_inputs; j++) b->input_edge_native[j] = 0;\n        }\n        if (b->n_connections > 0) {\n            b->output_edge_native = malloc((size_t)b->n_connections * sizeof(int));\n            if (!b->output_edge_native) { if (err) *err = err_fmt(\"oom\"); return NULL; }\n            for (int j = 0; j < b->n_connections; j++) b->output_edge_native[j] = 0;\n        }\n\n        /* Outgoing edges: for each connection, the consumer's lang\n         * is native iff it's also a call box in this box's\n         * language. Data / file_write consumers are not native\n         * (they don't carry a language). */\n        int all_outs_native = 1;\n        for (int j = 0; j < b->n_connections; j++) {\n            int dst = b->connections[j].to_box_idx;\n            if (dst < 0) { all_outs_native = 0; continue; }\n            const box_t *c = &g->boxes[dst];\n            int native = (c->kind == BOX_CALL && c->lang\n                          && strcmp(c->lang, b->lang) == 0);\n            b->output_edge_native[j] = native;\n            if (!native) all_outs_native = 0;\n        }\n\n        /* Incoming edges: walk every producer in the graph; if a\n         * producer has a connection pointing at this box's input\n         * port `to_input_idx`, classify that input by the\n         * producer's language. */\n        int all_ins_native = 1;\n        for (int p = 0; p < g->n_boxes; p++) {\n            const box_t *prod = &g->boxes[p];\n            for (int k = 0; k < prod->n_connections; k++) {\n                if (prod->connections[k].to_box_idx != i) continue;\n                int port = prod->connections[k].to_input_idx;\n                if (port < 0 || port >= b->n_inputs) continue;\n                int native = (prod->kind == BOX_CALL && prod->lang\n                              && strcmp(prod->lang, b->lang) == 0);\n                /* If multiple producers feed the same input port\n                 * with different languages, the slot carries mixed\n                 * content. Take the conservative AND: any non-\n                 * native producer downgrades the port to JSON. */\n                if (!native) b->input_edge_native[port] = 0;\n                else if (b->input_edge_native[port] == 0\n                         && k == 0 /* first producer for this port */) {\n                    /* Without per-port-first-producer tracking,\n                     * default-deny is safer: rely on the explicit\n                     * AND-with-native logic above and the initial\n                     * zero from malloc. */\n                }\n            }\n        }\n        /* Re-walk to set the native bits for ports where every\n         * feeding producer is same-lang. (The earlier loop only\n         * clears bits.) */\n        for (int port = 0; port < b->n_inputs; port++) {\n            int any_producer    = 0;\n            int all_native      = 1;\n            for (int p = 0; p < g->n_boxes; p++) {\n                const box_t *prod = &g->boxes[p];\n                for (int k = 0; k < prod->n_connections; k++) {\n                    if (prod->connections[k].to_box_idx != i) continue;\n                    if (prod->connections[k].to_input_idx != port) continue;\n                    any_producer = 1;\n                    int native = (prod->kind == BOX_CALL && prod->lang\n                                  && strcmp(prod->lang, b->lang) == 0);\n                    if (!native) all_native = 0;\n                }\n            }\n            b->input_edge_native[port] = (any_producer && all_native) ? 1 : 0;\n            if (!b->input_edge_native[port]) all_ins_native = 0;\n        }\n        if (b->n_inputs == 0) {\n            /* Sourceless boxes (literals only) have no input edges;\n             * they neither contribute to nor break native status. */\n        }\n\n        /* Retain the per-box bit for dispatch sites that haven't\n         * been migrated to per-edge consultation yet. Only true\n         * when EVERY edge in both directions is native. */\n        b->use_native_invoke = (all_ins_native && all_outs_native) ? 1 : 0;\n    }\n    return g;\n}",

Data / file_write consumers are not native\n         * (they don't carry a language). */\n        int all_outs_native = 1;\n        for (int j = 0; j < b->n_connections; j++) {\n            int dst = b->connections[j].to_box_idx;\n            if (dst < 0) { all_outs_native = 0; continue; }\n            const box_t *c = &g->boxes[dst];\n            int native = (c->kind == BOX_CALL && c->lang\n                          && strcmp(c->lang, b->lang) == 0);\n            b->output_edge_native[j] = native;\n            if (!native) all_outs_native = 0;\n        }\n\n        /* Incoming edges: walk every producer in the graph; if a\n         * producer has a connection pointing at this box's input\n         * port `to_input_idx`, classify that input by the\n         * producer's language. */\n        int all_ins_native = 1;\n        for (int p = 0; p < g->n_boxes; p++) {\n            const box_t *prod = &g->boxes[p];\n            for (int k = 0; k < prod->n_connections; k++) {\n                if (prod->connections[k].to_box_idx != i) continue;\n                int port = prod->connections[k].to_input_idx;\n                if (port < 0 || port >= b->n_inputs) continue;\n                int native = (prod->kind == BOX_CALL && prod->lang\n                              && strcmp(prod->lang, b->lang) == 0);\n                /* If multiple producers feed the same input port\n                 * with different languages, the slot carries mixed\n                 * content. Take the conservative AND: any non-\n                 * native producer downgrades the port to JSON. */\n                if (!native) b->input_edge_native[port] = 0;\n                else if (b->input_edge_native[port] == 0\n                         && k == 0 /* first producer for this port */) {\n                    /* Without per-port-first-producer tracking,\n                     * default-deny is safer: rely on the explicit\n                     * AND-with-native logic above and the initial\n                     * zero from malloc. */\n                }\n            }\n        }\n        /* Re-walk to set the native bits for ports where every\n         * feeding producer is same-lang. (The earlier loop only\n         * clears bits.) */\n        for (int port = 0; port < b->n_inputs; port++) {\n            int any_producer    = 0;\n            int all_native      = 1;\n            for (int p = 0; p < g->n_boxes; p++) {\n                const box_t *prod = &g->boxes[p];\n                for (int k = 0; k < prod->n_connections; k++) {\n                    if (prod->connections[k].to_box_idx != i) continue;\n                    if (prod->connections[k].to_input_idx != port) continue;\n                    any_producer = 1;\n                    int native = (prod->kind == BOX_CALL && prod->lang\n                                  && strcmp(prod->lang, b->lang) == 0);\n                    if (!native) all_native = 0;\n                }\n            }\n            b->input_edge_native[port] = (any_producer && all_native) ? 1 : 0;\n            if (!b->input_edge_native[port]) all_ins_native = 0;\n        }\n        if (b->n_inputs == 0) {\n            /* Sourceless boxes (literals only) have no input edges;\n             * they neither contribute to nor break native status. */\n        }\n\n        /* Retain the per-box bit for dispatch sites that haven't\n         * been migrated to per-edge consultation yet. Only true\n         * when EVERY edge in both directions is native. */\n        b->use_native_invoke = (all_ins_native && all_outs_native) ? 1 : 0;\n    }\n    return g;\n}"
  },

otherwise not. */\nstatic int test_native_invoke_classification(void)\n{\n    char *err = NULL;\n\n    /* hello: data box feeds greet (lua). greet's only producer is\n     * a data box (no lang), no consumers — eligible. */\n    {\n        graph_t *g = graph_load(\"tests/maps/hello\", &err);\n        ASSERT(g);\n        const box_t *greet = graph_box_by_id(g, \"greet\");\n        const box_t *who   = graph_box_by_id(g, \"who\");\n        ASSERT(greet->use_native_invoke == 1);\n        ASSERT(who->use_native_invoke   == 0);   /* who is BOX_DATA */\n        graph_destroy(g);\n    }\n\n    /* comparator: all four boxes are lua, no cross-language wires\n     * → every call box is native-eligible. */\n    {\n        graph_t *g = graph_load(\"tests/maps/comparator\", &err);\n        ASSERT(g);\n        ASSERT(graph_box_by_id(g, \"classify\")->use_native_invoke == 1);\n        ASSERT(graph_box_by_id(g, \"low\")     ->use_native_invoke == 1);\n        ASSERT(graph_box_by_id(g, \"mid\")     ->use_native_invoke == 1);\n        ASSERT(graph_box_by_id(g, \"high\")    ->use_native_invoke == 1);\n        graph_destroy(g);\n    }\n\n    /* pipeline: lua → c → bash chain → no call box stays inside\n     * one language → none should be native-eligible. */\n    {\n        graph_t *g = graph_load(\"tests/maps/pipeline\", &err);\n        ASSERT(g);\n        ASSERT(graph_box_by_id(g, \"double\")->use_native_invoke == 0);\n        ASSERT(graph_box_by_id(g, \"addone\")->use_native_invoke == 0);\n        ASSERT(graph_box_by_id(g, \"shout\") ->use_native_invoke == 0);\n        graph_destroy(g);\n    }\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_randomizer_weighted_parsing() */\n/* Verifies issue 304's randomizer and weighted routing schemas\n * load cleanly with the right per-kind fields. */\nstatic int test_randomizer_weighted_parsing(void)",

      "content":"/* {{{ dispatch_push_literals() */\nint dispatch_push_literals(dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, char **err)\n{\n    if (!ctx) {\n        if (err) *err = err_fmt(\"dispatch_push_literals: NULL ctx\");\n        return -1;\n    }\n    for (int i = 0; i < ctx->n_boxes; i++) {\n        const box_t *b = graph_box(ctx->graph, i);\n        if (!b || !b->input_slot_ids) continue;\n        for (int j = 0; j < b->n_inputs; j++) {\n            const input_decl_t *p = &b->inputs[j];\n            if (!p->literal) continue;\n            int sz = (int)strlen(p->literal);\n            if (slot_push(ctx->slots, b->input_slot_ids[j],\n                          p->literal, sz, 0) != 0) {\n                if (err) *err = err_fmt(\"box '%s' input '%s': \"\n                                        \"literal push failed\",\n                                        b->id, p->name);\n                return -1;\n            }\n        }\n    }\n    return 0;\n}",

        "input":{
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"/* {{{ test_native_invoke_classification() */\n/* Verifies issue 312's same-language fast-path classification:\n * a call box whose every adjacent call box shares its language\n * is marked use_native_invoke; otherwise not. */\nstatic int test_native_invoke_classification(void)\n{\n    char *err = NULL;\n\n    /* hello: data box feeds greet (lua). greet's only producer is\n     * a data box (no lang), no consumers — eligible. */\n    {\n        graph_t *g = graph_load(\"tests/maps/hello\", &err);\n        ASSERT(g);\n        const box_t *greet = graph_box_by_id(g, \"greet\");\n        const box_t *who   = graph_box_by_id(g, \"who\");\n        ASSERT(greet->use_native_invoke == 1);\n        ASSERT(who->use_native_invoke   == 0);   /* who is BOX_DATA */\n        graph_destroy(g);\n    }\n\n    /* comparator: all four boxes are lua, no cross-language wires\n     * → every call box is native-eligible. */\n    {\n        graph_t *g = graph_load(\"tests/maps/comparator\", &err);\n        ASSERT(g);\n        ASSERT(graph_box_by_id(g, \"classify\")->use_native_invoke == 1);\n        ASSERT(graph_box_by_id(g, \"low\")     ->use_native_invoke == 1);\n        ASSERT(graph_box_by_id(g, \"mid\")     ->use_native_invoke == 1);\n        ASSERT(graph_box_by_id(g, \"high\")    ->use_native_invoke == 1);\n        graph_destroy(g);\n    }\n\n    /* pipeline: lua → c → bash chain → no call box stays inside\n     * one language → none should be native-eligible. */\n    {\n        graph_t *g = graph_load(\"tests/maps/pipeline\", &err);\n        ASSERT(g);\n        ASSERT(graph_box_by_id(g, \"double\")->use_native_invoke == 0);\n        ASSERT(graph_box_by_id(g, \"addone\")->use_native_invoke == 0);\n        ASSERT(graph_box_by_id(g, \"shout\") ->use_native_invoke == 0);\n        graph_destroy(g);\n    }\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */",
          "new_string":"/* {{{ test_native_invoke_classification() */\n/* Verifies issue 312's per-edge fast-path classification:\n *\n *  - input_edge_native[port]  is 1 iff every producer feeding\n *    that port is a call box in the consumer's language.\n *    Literals and data-box producers count as NOT native — they\n *    emit JSON text the consumer's spec must parse.\n *  - output_edge_native[edge] is 1 iff the consumer at the other\n *    end of that connection is a call box in this box's language.\n *  - use_native_invoke remains as the per-box AND of every edge,\n *    used by dispatch sites not yet migrated to per-edge. */\nstatic int test_native_invoke_classification(void)\n{\n    char *err = NULL;\n\n    /* hello: greet (lua) has a literal-fed input → input edge is\n     * JSON. greet has no outgoing connections in this fixture.\n     * Per-edge: input 0 not native; vacuous all-outs. Per-box AND\n     * = 0 because the input is a JSON edge. */\n    {\n        graph_t *g = graph_load(\"tests/maps/hello\", &err);\n        ASSERT(g);\n        const box_t *greet = graph_box_by_id(g, \"greet\");\n        const box_t *who   = graph_box_by_id(g, \"who\");\n        ASSERT(greet->n_inputs == 2);\n        ASSERT(greet->input_edge_native != NULL);\n        ASSERT(greet->input_edge_native[0] == 0);  /* fed by data box `who` */\n        ASSERT(greet->input_edge_native[1] == 0);  /* literal */\n        ASSERT(greet->use_native_invoke == 0);\n        ASSERT(who->use_native_invoke   == 0);     /* who is BOX_DATA */\n        graph_destroy(g);\n    }\n\n    /* comparator: classify (lua) has a literal input but its\n     * three outgoing edges all feed lua call boxes → outputs are\n     * native, input is JSON. low/mid/high have no outgoing\n     * connections and their input comes from classify (a Lua call\n     * box) → input native, vacuous outs, all-native = use_native. */\n    {\n        graph_t *g = graph_load(\"tests/maps/comparator\", &err);\n        ASSERT(g);\n        const box_t *classify = graph_box_by_id(g, \"classify\");\n        const box_t *low      = graph_box_by_id(g, \"low\");\n\n        ASSERT(classify->input_edge_native[0]  == 0);  /* literal */\n        ASSERT(classify->n_connections         == 3);\n        ASSERT(classify->output_edge_native[0] == 1);  /* lt → low (lua) */\n        ASSERT(classify->output_edge_native[1] == 1);  /* eq → mid (lua) */\n        ASSERT(classify->output_edge_native[2] == 1);  /* gt → high (lua) */\n        ASSERT(classify->use_native_invoke     == 0);  /* per-box AND fails on input */\n\n        ASSERT(low->input_edge_native[0]   == 1);      /* fed by lua classify */\n        ASSERT(low->use_native_invoke      == 1);\n        ASSERT(graph_box_by_id(g, \"mid\") ->use_native_invoke == 1);\n        ASSERT(graph_box_by_id(g, \"high\")->use_native_invoke == 1);\n        graph_destroy(g);\n    }\n\n    /* pipeline: lua → c → bash chain. Every adjacent edge crosses\n     * a language boundary; per-edge bits are 0 across the board. */\n    {\n        graph_t *g = graph_load(\"tests/maps/pipeline\", &err);\n        ASSERT(g);\n        const box_t *dbl = graph_box_by_id(g, \"double\");  /* lua */\n        ASSERT(dbl->n_connections >= 1);\n        ASSERT(dbl->output_edge_native[0] == 0);          /* → addone (c) */\n        ASSERT(dbl->use_native_invoke == 0);\n        ASSERT(graph_box_by_id(g, \"addone\")->use_native_invoke == 0);\n        ASSERT(graph_box_by_id(g, \"shout\") ->use_native_invoke == 0);\n        graph_destroy(g);\n    }\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/tests/010-graph-loader-test.c"
        }
      }],

'012' or '00' don't pass\nthe parse — they parse as the integer zero and a trailing token,\nwhich is what the C standard would call a syntax error and which\nRFC 8259 explicitly forbids. Length-clamped writes\ninto a caller buffer, indentation control, primitive helpers,\nexplicit object/array bracket scopes, string escapes that handle\ncontrol bytes and surrogate pairs, an overflow-aware return path\nthat reports the bytes needed when the buffer is too small.\nTwelve writer-side tests cover the primitives, escapes,\nnesting, empty containers, overflow, and a round-trip that\nparses the writer's output.\n\nCo-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>\nEOF\n)\"",

    "originalFile":"/* libs/task-pool/pool.h — SoraMech-owned thread pool, public API.\n *\n * What it is, in a sentence: N worker threads pulling tasks off a\n * single mutex-protected queue, with a one-shot init barrier and a\n * condition-variable-based quiescence wait.\n *\n * Designed in issue 301. Reference: the 3d-rts pool at\n * /home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h\n * (design only, not vendored).\n *\n * Lifecycle:\n *\n *   1. pool_create(n_workers)\n *        - spawns the worker threads\n *        - each worker sets its TLS context and parks at the init\n *          barrier (no init work to do yet; 303 plugs spec init in\n *          here later)\n *   2. pool_init_barrier(pool)\n *        - blocks until every worker has reached the barrier\n *        - releases them all simultaneously\n *        - one-shot; returns; barrier never engages again\n *   3. pool_spawn / pool_wait_quiescent — main loop of work\n *   4. pool_destroy(pool)\n *        - flips the shutdown flag, broadcasts the queue cv,\n *          joins every worker, frees the pool\n *\n * Per-worker context is reachable from inside any task action via\n * the `pool_current_worker` TLS pointer. The handle slots are\n * reserved for the spec registry (issue 303); ignore them for now.\n *\n * Thread safety: every public function is safe to call from any\n * thread. pool_spawn from inside an action is fine and is how\n * iterators and graph traversal will work.\n */\n\n#ifndef SORAMECH_POOL_H\n#define SORAMECH_POOL_H\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\nextern \"C\" {\n#endif\n\n/* {{{ Types */\ntypedef struct pool pool_t;\n\n/* A pool action takes one void* argument and returns nothing.\n * Errors are the action's business — the pool just dispatches. */\ntypedef void (*pool_action_t)(void *arg);\n\n/* Per-worker context. Reserved for issue 303's per-language runtime\n * handles; the pool itself only uses thread_idx and pool. */\n#define POOL_LANG_SLOTS 16\n\ntypedef struct worker_ctx {\n    int     thread_idx;\n    pool_t *pool;\n    void   *handles[POOL_LANG_SLOTS];\n} worker_ctx_t;\n\n/* Set on every worker thread before the init barrier; readable from\n * any pool action. */\nextern __thread worker_ctx_t *pool_current_worker;\n\n#define POOL_MAX_WORKERS 16\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Lifecycle */\n/* Create a pool with n_workers threads. If n_workers <= 0, defaults\n * to sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN) capped at POOL_MAX_WORKERS. The\n * SORAMECH_WORKERS environment variable, if set and >0, overrides\n * the default. Returns NULL on allocation or pthread_create failure. */\npool_t *pool_create(int n_workers);\n\n/* Per-worker init callback (optional). Runs on every worker thread\n * after TLS is set up and before the worker parks at the init\n * barrier. Returns 0 on success; nonzero is reported by\n * pool_init_barrier as a fatal error. The callback is the canonical\n * place to populate ctx->handles[] with per-language spec state\n * (issue 303 plumbs spec_registry_init_worker into here). */\ntypedef int (*pool_init_cb_t)(int worker_idx, worker_ctx_t *ctx, void *user);\n\n/* Register the per-worker init callback. Must be called before\n * pool_init_barrier. Calling it after pool_init_barrier or more\n * than once is a programming error. */\nvoid    pool_set_worker_init(pool_t *p, pool_init_cb_t cb, void *user);\n\n/* Optional per-worker teardown callback. Runs on each worker\n * thread inside `pool_destroy`, after the worker exits the task\n * loop and before it returns. The canonical use is the spec\n * registry's `spec_registry_teardown_worker` so each language's\n * per-worker handle (e.g. a Lua state, a bash subprocess) can\n * shut down cleanly instead of leaking through process exit. */\ntypedef void (*pool_teardown_cb_t)(int worker_idx, worker_ctx_t *ctx, void *user);\nvoid    pool_set_worker_teardown(pool_t *p, pool_teardown_cb_t cb, void *user);\n\n/* Block until every worker has finished its init sequence and is\n * parked at the barrier; then release them all. Returns 0 on\n * success; -1 if any worker's init callback returned nonzero (in\n * which case the barrier never released the workers and the pool\n * should be torn down). */\nint     pool_init_barrier(pool_t *p);\n\n/* Stop accepting tasks, drain whatever's queued, join every worker,\n * free the pool. Safe on NULL. */\nvoid    pool_destroy(pool_t *p);\n\nint     pool_n_workers(const pool_t *p);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Submission and wait */\n/* Submit a task. Safe from any thread (including from inside another\n * action).       "content":"/* {{{ test_priority_order() */\n/* Spawn several tasks before the init barrier releases the worker,\n * then verify the dequeue order respects priority (higher first)\n * with FIFO tiebreaking at equal priority. Single-worker pool is\n * used so dequeue order maps directly to execution order. */\nstatic pthread_mutex_t g_seq_mtx = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;\nstatic int g_seq[16];\nstatic int g_seq_len;\n\nstatic void seq_action(void *arg)\n{\n    int id = (int)(intptr_t)arg;\n    pthread_mutex_lock(&g_seq_mtx);\n    g_seq[g_seq_len++] = id;\n    pthread_mutex_unlock(&g_seq_mtx);\n}\n\nstatic int test_priority_order(void)\n{\n    g_seq_len = 0;\n    pool_t *p = pool_create(1);\n    ASSERT(p);\n\n    /* Queue 6 tasks BEFORE the worker is released. ids encode order\n     * of spawn; the test asserts on order of execution. */\n    pool_spawn(p, seq_action, (void *)(intptr_t)1, 0);\n    pool_spawn(p, seq_action, (void *)(intptr_t)2, 5);\n    pool_spawn(p, seq_action, (void *)(intptr_t)3, 0);\n    pool_spawn(p, seq_action, (void *)(intptr_t)4, 9);\n    pool_spawn(p, seq_action, (void *)(intptr_t)5, 5);\n    pool_spawn(p, seq_action, (void *)(intptr_t)6, -1);\n\n    pool_init_barrier(p);\n    pool_wait_quiescent(p);\n\n    /* Expected order:\n     *   4 (prio 9)\n     *   2, 5 (prio 5, FIFO)\n     *   1, 3 (prio 0, FIFO)\n     *   6 (prio -1)\n     */\n    static const int expected[] = { 4, 2, 5, 1, 3, 6 };\n    ASSERT(g_seq_len == 6);\n    for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) ASSERT(g_seq[i] == expected[i]);\n\n    pool_destroy(p);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ main() */\nint main(void)\n{\n    printf(\"301-pool-test:\\n\");\n    RUN(create_destroy_no_tasks);",

  "parentUuid":"8a9936de-7168-4e06-8d60-955599990599",
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",
  "promptId":"c357e360-e57c-4973-8e89-413d8872104a",
  "isSidechain":false,
  "toolUseResult":{
    "replaceAll":false,
    "structuredPatch":[{
        "oldLines":7,
        "newStart":83,
        "newLines":7,
        "lines":["     atomic_store(&g_count, 0);","     pool_t *p = pool_create(2);","     pool_init_barrier(p);","-    pool_spawn(p, inc_action, NULL, 0);","+    pool_spawn(p, inc_action, NULL);","     pool_wait_quiescent(p);","     ASSERT(atomic_load(&g_count) == 1);","     pool_destroy(p);"],
        "oldStart":83
      }],
    "originalFile":"/* tests/301-pool-test.c — unit tests for the thread pool.\n *\n * Covers the lifecycle (create / init barrier / destroy), single-\n * and many-task spawn, quiescence, the TLS worker context, recursive\n * spawn from inside an action, and a stress race that hammers the\n * queue mutex from multiple producers.\n *\n * Designed in issue 301.\n */\n\n#include \"pool.h\"\n\n#include <pthread.h>\n#include <stdatomic.h>\n#include <stdint.h>\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n\n/* {{{ Test harness */\nstatic int g_pass = 0;\nstatic int g_fail = 0;\n\n#define ASSERT(cond) \\\n    do { if (!(cond)) { \\\n        fprintf(stderr, \"      %s:%d: %s\\n\", __FILE__, __LINE__, #cond); \\\n        return 0; \\\n    } } while (0)\n\n#define RUN(name) \\\n    do { \\\n        fprintf(stdout, \"  %-44s \", #name); fflush(stdout); \\\n        if (test_##name()) { fprintf(stdout, \"ok\\n\"); g_pass++; } \\\n        else                { fprintf(stdout, \"FAIL\\n\"); g_fail++; } \\\n    } while (0)\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_create_destroy_no_tasks() */\nstatic int test_create_destroy_no_tasks(void)\n{\n    pool_t *p = pool_create(4);\n    ASSERT(p);\n    ASSERT(pool_n_workers(p) == 4);\n    pool_init_barrier(p);\n    pool_wait_quiescent(p);   /* immediate — no tasks */\n    pool_destroy(p);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_default_n_workers() */\nstatic int test_default_n_workers(void)\n{\n    pool_t *p = pool_create(0);\n    ASSERT(p);\n    /* 1..POOL_MAX_WORKERS depending on machine. */\n    ASSERT(pool_n_workers(p) >= 1);\n    ASSERT(pool_n_workers(p) <= POOL_MAX_WORKERS);\n    pool_init_barrier(p);\n    pool_destroy(p);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_cap_at_max_workers() */\nstatic int test_cap_at_max_workers(void)\n{\n    pool_t *p = pool_create(POOL_MAX_WORKERS + 50);\n    ASSERT(p);\n    ASSERT(pool_n_workers(p) == POOL_MAX_WORKERS);\n    pool_init_barrier(p);\n    pool_destroy(p);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_spawn_one() */\nstatic atomic_int g_count;\nstatic void inc_action(void *arg) { (void)arg; atomic_fetch_add(&g_count, 1); }\n\nstatic int test_spawn_one(void)\n{\n    atomic_store(&g_count, 0);\n    pool_t *p = pool_create(2);\n    pool_init_barrier(p);\n    pool_spawn(p, inc_action, NULL, 0);\n    pool_wait_quiescent(p);\n    ASSERT(atomic_load(&g_count) == 1);\n    pool_destroy(p);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_spawn_many() */\nstatic int test_spawn_many(void)\n{\n    enum { N = 1000 };\n    atomic_store(&g_count, 0);\n    pool_t *p = pool_create(4);\n    pool_init_barrier(p);\n    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) pool_spawn(p, inc_action, NULL, 0);\n    pool_wait_quiescent(p);\n    ASSERT(atomic_load(&g_count) == N);\n    pool_destroy(p);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_current_worker_tls() */\nstatic atomic_int g_max_idx;\nstatic void check_worker_action(void *arg)\n{\n    (void)arg;\n    worker_ctx_t *ctx = pool_current_worker;\n    if (!ctx) return;\n    int idx = ctx->thread_idx;\n    int prev = atomic_load(&g_max_idx);\n    while (idx > prev && !atomic_compare_exchange_weak(&g_max_idx, &prev, idx)) {\n        /* retry */\n    }\n}\n\nstatic int test_current_worker_tls(void)\n{\n    atomic_store(&g_max_idx, -1);\n    pool_t *p = pool_create(4);\n    pool_init_barrier(p);\n    /* Spawn enough tasks that every worker likely picks one up. */\n    for (int i = 0; i < 256; i++) pool_spawn(p, check_worker_action, NULL, 0);\n    pool_wait_quiescent(p);\n    /* At least one worker observed a non-negative thread_idx. With\n     * 256 tasks across 4 workers we should see most/all of them. */\n    ASSERT(atomic_load(&g_max_idx) >= 0);\n    ASSERT(atomic_load(&g_max_idx) < pool_n_workers(p));\n    pool_destroy(p);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_recursive_spawn() */\nstatic atomic_int g_recursive;\n\nstatic void recursive_action(void *arg)\n{\n    int depth = (int)(intptr_t)arg;\n    atomic_fetch_add(&g_recursive, 1);\n    if (depth > 0) {\n        /* Spawn a child from inside the worker. */\n        pool_spawn(pool_current_worker->pool, recursive_action,\n                   (void *)(intptr_t)(depth - 1), 0);\n    }\n}\n\nstatic int test_recursive_spawn(void)\n{\n    atomic_store(&g_recursive, 0);\n    pool_t *p = pool_create(4);\n    pool_init_barrier(p);\n    /* depth 10 → 11 invocations (10..0). */\n    pool_spawn(p, recursive_action, (void *)(intptr_t)10, 0);\n    pool_wait_quiescent(p);\n    ASSERT(atomic_load(&g_recursive) == 11);\n    pool_destroy(p);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_concurrent_producers() */\nstruct producer_args { pool_t *p; int n; };\n\nstatic void *producer_thread(void *arg)\n{\n    struct producer_args *a = arg;\n    for (int i = 0; i < a->n; i++) pool_spawn(a->p, inc_action, NULL, 0);\n    return NULL;\n}\n\nstatic int test_concurrent_producers(void)\n{\n    enum { N_PROD = 8, PER = 500 };\n    atomic_store(&g_count, 0);\n    pool_t *p = pool_create(4);\n    pool_init_barrier(p);\n\n    pthread_t producers[N_PROD];\n    struct producer_args args = { p, PER };\n    for (int i = 0;
