  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Good thought. Let me unpack the auto-parsing question, then propose a 307 split that reflects it.\n\n### Where the declaration gets parsed\n\nTwo cases to handle, and they want different rules:\n\n**Case A — user-written `.c` file (`ref` set):** the user's source already declares the function with proper C types. Forcing them to re-state the same types in JSON is duplication, drift-prone, and contradicts 307's rule that the source should look like normal C. Better: **parse the signature directly out of the `.c` file.**\n\n**Case B — library function with no user `.c` (`ref` omitted):** there's no source to parse — `compress2` lives behind `<zlib.h>`. Here the user *has* to declare the signature in the box JSON (`inputs`, `returns`, `headers`, `link_libs`), because that's the only place the declaration exists in this map's tree.\n\nSame wrapper generator consumes both — they produce the same internal \"typed signature\" representation that drives code-gen.\n\n### Parsing the C signature\n\nC is hard in general; function signatures within our type vocabulary are easy. Options for where the parser lives:\n\n1. **Regex**: brittle on multiline, attributes, comments. Skip.\n2. **libclang**: heavyweight dependency just to read one function header.\n3. **A small hand-written recursive-descent parser specialized to our type set** (`int`, `double`, `const char *`, `bytes` ↔ `const uint8_t *, size_t`, `struct foo`). A few hundred lines of C, lives next to the wrapper generator. Errors loudly when it doesn't understand a type. This is the right move.\n\nThe parser opens the `.c` file, scans for the function with the name `box.fn`, parses its declaration line(s), and produces:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    enum sm_type return_type;\n    int           n_params;\n    struct { enum sm_type type; const char *name; } params[16];\n} sm_signature_t;\n```\n\nThe wrapper generator takes a `sm_signature_t` (from either path) and emits the `.c`.\n\n**Location:** `langs/c/sig-parser.{c,h}` for the parser, `langs/c/wrapper-gen.{c,h}` for the code generator. Both live next to `langs/c/spec.c` so the build only touches one directory.\n\n### The JSON declaration shrinks\n\nWith auto-parsing, the user-written case becomes:\n\n```json\n{ \"id\": \"classify\", \"kind\": \"call\", \"lang\": \"c\", \"ref\": \"classify.c\", \"fn\": \"classify\" }\n```\n\nThat's it. No `inputs`, no `returns` — the parser reads them from `classify.c`. The graph loader's existing `inputs[]` array stays as the *declared port list* for routing/literal-value purposes; the C spec just doesn't require types in that list.\n\nThe library-function case keeps the full JSON declaration since there's no source file to parse:\n\n```json\n{ \"id\": \"compress\", \"kind\": \"call\", \"lang\": \"c\", \"fn\": \"compress2\",\n  \"headers\": [\"<zlib.h>\"], \"link_libs\": [\"z\"],\n  \"inputs\":  [{\"name\": \"src\", \"type\": \"bytes\"}, {\"name\": \"level\", \"type\": \"int\"}],\n  \"returns\": \"bytes\" }\n```\n\n### Proposed 307 split (revised for auto-parsing)\n\n- **307a — type system + serialization runtime.** The `enum sm_type`, the per-type pack/unpack functions, the `sm_signature_t` representation. Pure header + tiny `.c`. Foundation for everything else.\n\n- **307b — C signature parser** (`langs/c/sig-parser.{c,h}`). Reads a `.c` file, finds the named function, parses its signature into `sm_signature_t`. Unit tests against fixture `.c` files.\n\n- **307c — wrapper code generator** (`langs/c/wrapper-gen.{c,h}`). Takes `sm_signature_t`, emits `wrapper.c` defining `sm_box_entry`. Compiled with the user's `.c` (or alone, for library mode) into one `.so`. This is where the spec's `compile` callback hooks in.\n\n- **307d — library-function-as-box (no `ref`)**. The case where the JSON carries the declaration and `headers`/`link_libs` drive `-l` flags. Reuses 307c's generator with the JSON-supplied signature.\n\nFour sub-issues. Foundation → parser → generator → library-mode. Each commits independently in dependency order.\n\nWant me to write all four sub-issue files now (substantive design, no code yet), or just **307a** first so we lock in the type system before designing the rest?\n\nThe other parallel work (231, 217 — those are phase-2 editor issues I think? not in my view) shouldn't conflict; 307 lives entirely under `langs/c/` plus a small extension to the box-JSON schema in the graph loader."
      }],

        "type":"text",
        "text":"You're right on all three. Let me think these through.\n\n### Point 1: a header file *is* a declaration we can parse\n\nYou're correct — I conflated \"no source\" with \"no declaration.\" A header file declares the signature in real C. The parser doesn't care whether the file is `.c` or `.h`; it cares whether it can find the function's prototype. For `compress2`, the prototype lives in `<zlib.h>` as:\n\n```c\nZEXTERN int ZEXPORT compress2 OF((Bytef *dest, uLongf *destLen,\n                                  const Bytef *source, uLong sourceLen,\n                                  int level));\n```\n\n…which is a perfectly parseable C declaration once the macros (`ZEXTERN`, `ZEXPORT`, `OF`) are preprocessed away. So the right model is: **every C box has a `ref` that points at a file (`.c` or `.h`)**, and the parser reads the declaration from there. No separate library mode.\n\nFor system headers, the `ref` resolves through standard include paths — the user writes `\"ref\": \"<zlib.h>\"` and SoraMech does what gcc does (`-I /usr/include`, etc). If `link_libs` is needed (the linker won't find `compress2` without `-lz`), that's still a JSON field, but it's a build concern, not a signature concern.\n\n### Point 2: \"understand every type\" — agreed, no second-class types\n\nRight. A hand-rolled parser that errors loudly on `size_t` because we didn't list it is hostile. The user's function is whatever the user wrote, and SoraMech has to keep up.\n\nThe right tool here is **the C preprocessor itself**, which already understands the entire C type system *as far as the user's compiler is concerned*. Pipeline:\n\n1. Run `cpp` on the `ref` file with the right include paths. This expands macros, resolves `#include`s, leaves a flat declaration we can parse.\n2. Walk the preprocessed output looking for `fn`'s declaration. Parse the return type and parameter list as C declarators.\n3. Resolve typedef chains until we hit fundamental types (`int`, `double`, pointer-to-T, struct-with-fields, etc).\n4. For each fundamental type, look up the matching serialization rule in our type system.\n\n`cpp` is a free dependency — gcc ships with it, and we're already requiring gcc for 307's compile step. We get full type support, real typedef resolution, real macro expansion, for the cost of one subprocess invocation per parse.\n\nFor genuinely-not-serializable types (function pointers across the wire, unions without a discriminator, opaque void-pointers to caller-owned heap memory), the parser produces a precise error: *\"box `X` parameter `Y`: cannot serialize type `Z` — function pointers can't cross the dispatch layer; restructure the API or write a wrapper.\"* The user gets to fix it in their code; we don't bend the type system.\n\nFor supported types: every C primitive plus pointer-to-primitive plus struct-of-supported-fields plus array-of-supported-element plus length-prefixed bytes. That covers the vast majority of C library APIs.\n\n### Point 3: the user doesn't write JSON\n\nRight — JSON is the persistence layer the editor reads and writes. The user clicks slots in the editor UI. So 307's job isn't to design a JSON schema for users; it's to provide a **signature inference API** the editor calls to populate slots.\n\nThe flow from the editor's perspective:\n\n1. User adds a C box. Slot 1: \"Source file.\" User browses to `classify.c` (or `<zlib.h>`).\n2. Editor calls `sig_parser_list_functions(\"classify.c\")` — returns `[\"classify\"]`. Slot 2: \"Function\" — dropdown populates.\n3. User picks `classify`. Editor calls `sig_parser_get_signature(\"classify.c\", \"classify\")` — returns the typed signature.\n4. Editor renders the inferred ports: input slot named `text` (string), input slot named `weight` (int), output slot of type `int`. User confirms or hooks up wires.\n5. If linking is needed (the header is `<zlib.h>` for `compress2`), the editor offers a \"Library\" slot with autocompletion (`pkg-config --list-all` or `ldconfig -p | grep`).\n\nThe JSON the editor writes is therefore minimal — `id`, `kind: \"call\"`, `lang: \"c\"`, `ref`, `fn`, plus `link_libs` if it asked. Everything else is *derived* from the source by the parser at runtime. The graph loader caches the parse result alongside the box so the editor doesn't have to re-parse on every render.\n\n**This means 307 ships a small library API**: `langs/c/sig-parser.{c,h}` exposes `sig_parser_list_functions(path)` and `sig_parser_get_signature(path, fn)` plus a representation for the editor to render. The editor wires that in (phase-2 work, separate ticket).\n\n### Revised sub-issue split\n\n- **307a — Type system and serialization runtime.** Enum of supported C types (primitives, pointer-to-T, struct-with-fields, length-prefixed bytes, array-of-T). Pack/unpack helpers per type. The internal `sm_signature_t` data structure. Header + small `.c`, fully unit-tested in isolation.\n\n- **307b — C signature parser via cpp + recursive descent.** Driver invokes `cpp` on the `ref` file with declared include paths, parses the resulting declarator stream, returns `sm_signature_t`. Handles typedef resolution, qualifiers (`const`, `volatile`), pointer/array nesting, struct field walks. Errors precisely on un-serializable shapes. Test fixtures cover hand-written `.c` files and several real system headers.\n\n- **307c — Wrapper code generator.** Takes `sm_signature_t`, emits `sm_box_entry` in a generated `wrapper.c`. The C spec's `compile` callback orchestrates: parse → generate → compile `wrapper.c + ref.c` (or just `wrapper.c` if `ref` is a header) into one `.so`.\n\n- **307d — Editor inference API.** `sig_parser_list_functions(path)` + `sig_parser_get_signature(path, fn)` exposed for the editor to call. Cached results live in a per-map sidecar JSON so the editor doesn't reparse on every render.\n\nFour sub-issues. The first three are dependency-ordered (a → b → c). 307d is the editor-facing surface that lands once a → c exist.\n\nNote that 307a + 307b form a *real* foundation — once the parser exists, **issue 317 (the data-box JSON bridge)** gets its C implementation almost for free, because the same `sm_signature_t` description is exactly what `native_to_json` needs to walk a struct field by field. So 307 unblocks 317c (the C side of the bridge).\n\nWant me to write all four sub-issue files now? Or just **307a** as the foundation and we revise as we go?"

    "content":" cpp is a free dependency\n\nwe shouldn't use c++ in the thread pool system. Just C.\n\n  For genuinely-not-serializable types (function pointers across the wire, unions without a discriminator, opaque void-pointers to\n  caller-owned heap memory), the parser produces a precise error: \"box X parameter Y: cannot serialize type Z — function pointers can't cross\n   the dispatch layer; restructure the API or write a wrapper.\" The user gets to fix it in their code; we don't bend the type system.\n\n\nCan you clarify this a bit? Where in the code, are you saying in the spec or the library functions? The libraries should be usable as-is - some nerd wrote really complicated stuff back in the 90s and now we have to handle it. In the spec, we should make sure that we're very careful about how we ask the users to define their responses to certain edge-case actions.\n\n  For supported types: every C primitive plus pointer-to-primitive plus struct-of-supported-fields plus array-of-supported-element plus\n  length-prefixed bytes. That covers the vast majority of C library APIs.\n\nwe need to cover all of them. The nice thing is that C is just the built-in types, and also structs. That's it, right? So if we create some sort of datastructure parser that reads all the way down and serializes it to json when transferring between languages, then we should be good, right? Are we positive that the json translation layer between non-native compatible languages will be interpretable? What happens if we have a datastructure in C, and want to read it in Lua? Will the table get built correctly?\n\nwhat happens if we have lua specific stuff that needs to get built into a C struct? A function stored in a table could be a function pointer, and everything else is just C compatible right?\n\n  This means 307 ships a small library API: langs/c/sig-parser.{c,h} exposes sig_parser_list_functions(path) and\n  sig_parser_get_signature(path, fn) plus a representation for the editor to render. The editor wires that in (phase-2 work, separate\n  ticket).\n\n\nis this part of the spec? if so, how?",

  }

        "type":"text",
        "text":"Good corrections. Let me clarify each.\n\n### `cpp` is the C preprocessor, not C++\n\nSloppy naming on my part. I meant the C preprocessor — the standalone tool that handles `#include`, `#define`, macro expansion. It's a C utility, ships with gcc, and we're already shelling out to gcc for the compile step. To remove the ambiguity entirely we just invoke `gcc -E` (preprocess-only mode) which is what compilers actually call. No C++ in the pool runner.\n\n### Library types vs spec rules — yes, separate\n\nImportant distinction you drew, and it changes the design. Two different scopes:\n\n**Library functions are immutable.** Some 1990s C library function takes a `void (*callback)(int)` parameter and returns a `struct rusage*`. We don't get to refuse it. The parser walks the signature, identifies the un-serializable pieces, and the resulting \"signature\" carries flags like *\"param 2 is a callback hole\"* and *\"return value is a pointer to an opaque struct.\"*\n\n**The spec config is where the user resolves the holes.** When the editor renders the box for this library function, the un-serializable parameters become *editor slots that demand a resolution rule*. Concretely, for each hole the user picks one of:\n\n- **Wire from another box** (the default for serializable params)\n- **Pass a constant** (the user types a literal value into a slot)\n- **Pass NULL / a default zero** (for optional params)\n- **Callback into the graph** (the parameter is a function pointer; the user picks a Lua/C/bash box that should run when the C library invokes the callback; SoraMech generates a C trampoline)\n- **Ignore the return value** (for ptr-to-opaque returns the user doesn't care about)\n\nThe schema captures these choices per parameter and the wrapper generator emits the appropriate glue. Box JSON for a library box becomes something like:\n\n```json\n{ \"id\": \"qsort_box\", \"kind\": \"call\", \"lang\": \"c\",\n  \"ref\": \"<stdlib.h>\", \"fn\": \"qsort\", \"link_libs\": [],\n  \"param_rules\": {\n    \"base\":    \"wire_in:items\",\n    \"nmemb\":   \"wire_in:count\",\n    \"size\":    \"constant:4\",\n    \"compar\":  \"callback:Lua:compare_box\"\n  } }\n```\n\n(Editor writes this; user doesn't type it.)\n\nThis isolates the rule \"errors loudly on un-serializable types\" to **only the user-written code case** (where the user does control the API and can fix it). For library functions the parser produces a signature with holes, and the holes get filled in the spec config.\n\n### \"C is just built-ins and structs, right?\"\n\nAlmost. The full set of type *forms* in C is:\n\n- **Primitives** — `int` / `long` / `char` / `double` / etc, plus the signed/unsigned and width variants\n- **Pointers** — `T*` for any T\n- **Arrays** — `T[N]` (or `T[]` decayed at function-call sites)\n- **Structs** — collection of named fields\n- **Unions** — alternative interpretations of the same memory\n- **Enums** — named integer constants, but always backed by an `int`\n- **Function pointers** — a special-case pointer\n- **`typedef`s** — aliases for any of the above\n\nFor JSON round-tripping:\n\n- Primitives → JSON number/boolean/string. Always works.\n- Pointer-to-primitive + length → \"bytes\" or \"array of T.\" Works.\n- Pointer-to-struct + length → JSON array of objects. Works.\n- Structs → JSON objects. Works.\n- Arrays → JSON arrays. Works.\n- Enums → JSON number (or JSON string by name, our choice). Works.\n- Unions → ambiguous without a discriminator; user resolves in the spec config (which variant is active).\n- Function pointers → callback holes per above.\n- Pointers without a length → ambiguous (how many elements?); user resolves in the spec config (either \"one element\" / \"null-terminated\" / \"size from param N\").\n\nSo the parser walks any C type tree down to primitives and produces a serialization plan. The plan can have unresolved nodes (callback holes, union discriminator unknowns, length-unknown pointers) that the spec config fills in.\n\n### C struct → Lua table round-trip\n\nYes, this works cleanly. C → JSON → Lua:\n\n```\nstruct point { int x; int y; }  →  { \"x\": 1, \"y\": 2 }  →  { x=1, y=2 }  (Lua table)\n```\n\nLua → JSON → C requires the destination C type to be known (which it always is, because the receiving C box declared its input). The Lua spec's `native_to_json` walks the table and emits JSON; the receiving C box's wrapper parses the JSON into the typed struct it expects. Mismatches (Lua table missing a field, wrong type, extra fields) get rejected at unpack time with a precise error.\n\n### Lua-specific values landing in C\n\nThe hard cases you pointed at:\n\n- **Lua function in a Lua table that crosses to C.** Only meaningful if the receiving C field is a function pointer. SoraMech handles this via the callback rule: the user declares in the spec that this C field is a callback to a Lua function; the wrapper generator emits a C trampoline that captures a reference to the Lua function (registered in `LUA_REGISTRYINDEX`) and invokes it when called.\n- **Lua-only types (coroutine, userdata, metatables):** can't cross to C. The Lua spec's `native_to_json` refuses them with a clear error. The user moves them or restructures.\n\nSo the rule is: Lua → C only succeeds if every Lua value has a C type that can receive it. Most do (numbers, strings, tables-as-structs, functions-as-callbacks). The exotic ones (coroutines, raw userdata) don't.\n\n### Is `infer_signature` part of the spec?\n\nYes — and you've pushed me to make it part of the spec contract uniformly. Every spec exposes:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    /* ... */\n} sm_signature_t;\n\n/* List the function names declared in `path` that this spec can\n * recognise. Editor uses this to populate the function-name\n * dropdown after the user picks a source file. */\nchar **(*list_functions)(void *handle, const char *path, int *out_count);\n\n/* Return the inferred signature for `path::fn` plus any holes\n * the user needs to resolve. The editor uses this to render\n * input/output slots and to render the \"param rules\" form when\n * holes are present. */\nsm_signature_t *(*infer_signature)(void *handle,\n                                   const char *path, const char *fn);\n```\n\nTwo more `lang_spec_t` callbacks. The C spec's implementation does the gcc-`-E`-then-parse dance. The Lua spec inspects the file via the per-worker `lua_State` (find a returned function, check its `debug.getinfo` for parameter names, infer types from the user-declared annotations or sentinel-default heuristics). The Bash spec probably returns a trivial signature (every input is a string, return is a string) because bash functions don't carry types.\n\nThis means the **editor speaks one API to every language**, and 307's parser becomes the C-side implementation of a contract that 317 already shares. Both issues converge on the same spec extension.\n\n### Updated sub-issue split\n\nThree changes drop out of this conversation:\n\n- **307a** stays as \"type system + serialization runtime.\" Now explicit about handling every C type form (primitives, pointer-to-T, arrays, structs, unions, enums, function pointers, typedefs).\n- **307b** is \"C signature parser via `gcc -E` + recursive-descent declarator parser.\" Returns `sm_signature_t` with explicit hole-markers for un-serializable params.\n- **307c** is \"wrapper code generator.\" Consumes `sm_signature_t` plus the user's spec config (`param_rules`) and emits the bridge `.c`.\n- **307d** is now \"the `list_functions` / `infer_signature` extension to `lang_spec_t`, and the C spec's implementation of them.\" This is the editor-facing API.\n\nPlus a meta-note: **307d's spec extension is also what 317 needs.** The two issues converge — 317 adds `native_to_json` / `json_to_native` for cross-language data flow, and 307d adds `list_functions` / `infer_signature` for editor introspection. They're four callbacks landing in the same spec interface, on parallel tracks.\n\nWant me to start writing **307a** as a sub-issue blueprint now, with the design points from this conversation woven in?"
